## Advanced Patterns (Iteration 51)

<!-- Iteration 51: Mob/Ensemble testing pattern (YAML + TypeScript facilitator); Michael Bolton "Testing vs Checking" distinction with practical application; LLM feature defect escape rate tracker with failure-rate metrics; community lessons #141-143 -->

### Mob / Ensemble Exploratory Testing

**Mob testing** (also called **ensemble testing**) applies the mob-programming model to exploratory sessions: the entire team (developers, testers, product manager, sometimes a designer) gathers around a single screen with one driver and everyone else as navigators. The driver types and clicks; the navigators discuss observations, suggest next moves, and apply heuristics collectively. Roles rotate every 5–15 minutes.

Ensemble testing is not the same as pair testing (two people) or a demo (one person presenting). The key property is **collective decision-making in real time**: the group decides together which oracle applies, whether an observation is a defect, and where to explore next. This produces defect-finding and domain knowledge that no individual session can replicate, because each person brings a different mental model and risk instinct.

**When ensemble testing outperforms other session types:**

| Scenario | Why ensemble wins |
|----------|------------------|
| New developer onboarding | New team member drives; experts as navigators. The new person's "why does this work?" questions surface hidden assumptions faster than any charter |
| Post-incident review ("let's understand what went wrong") | Group explores the incident area together, surfacing the system behavior that the incident report did not capture |
| First-ever exploration of a new major feature | Group charter writing + execution in one session — the product manager's context, the developer's architecture knowledge, and the tester's heuristic toolkit apply simultaneously |
| Sprint zero / prototype evaluation | No scripted tests exist; group exploration of a prototype identifies the riskiest areas before development allocates testing investment |
| Knowledge silo breaking | Area that only one tester understands — group session transfers knowledge while finding defects |

**Charter format for ensemble sessions:**

Ensemble charters follow the same X/Y/Z format but add a **facilitation note** and a **rotation interval**:

```yaml
# ensemble-session-charter.yaml
charter_id: ENS-checkout-20260515-01
session_type: ensemble
participants:
  - name: "Alice Chen"
    role: tester
  - name: "Bob Kim"
    role: developer
  - name: "Carol Zhang"
    role: product-manager
  - name: "David Osei"
    role: designer

rotation_interval_minutes: 10   # driver role rotates every 10 minutes
timebox_minutes: 60             # total session — shorter than solo sessions due to group energy cost

mission:
  explore: "the new onboarding wizard (PR #5201) for first-time users"
  using: "a fresh account with no prior activity, mobile Chrome, and the 'basic' plan feature flag"
  to_discover: "confusion points in the step flow, missing default values, and whether the skip-step behavior produces a usable account state"

facilitation_notes: |
  - The product manager opens with a 3-minute context brief (no more — avoid anchoring)
  - First driver: the developer (they know the code paths; navigators challenge assumptions)
  - After first rotation: switch to tester as driver; developer observes their own assumptions being tested
  - Navigator rule: say what you notice, propose what to try next — do not take the keyboard
  - Blocker protocol: if the driver is stuck > 90 seconds, any navigator can suggest; if stuck > 3 minutes, pause and create a [B] blocker note

debrief_format: |
  - Each participant states one observation they found most surprising (round-robin, 60 seconds each)
  - Tester writes up the defect candidates; product manager owns follow-on charter decisions
  - Output: session notes shared in #qa-sessions Slack channel within 30 minutes of session end
```

**TypeScript: Ensemble Session Facilitator**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/ensemble-facilitator.ts
// A simple CLI facilitator for ensemble exploratory sessions.
// Tracks driver rotation timers, records participant observations,
// and generates a post-session report linking observations to the charter.

import * as readline from 'readline';
import * as fs from 'fs';

export interface EnsembleParticipant {
  name: string;
  role: 'tester' | 'developer' | 'product-manager' | 'designer' | 'other';
}

export interface EnsembleSessionConfig {
  charterId: string;
  participants: EnsembleParticipant[];
  rotationIntervalMs: number;   // e.g. 10 * 60 * 1000 for 10-minute rotations
  timeboxMs: number;            // total session length
  outputFile: string;
}

export interface EnsembleObservation {
  timeMs: number;              // ms since session start
  driver: string;              // who was driving when observation was made
  tag: '[N]' | '[D]' | '[Q]' | '[B]' | '[F]' | '[C]';
  text: string;
}

export class EnsembleFacilitator {
  private observations: EnsembleObservation[] = [];
  private driverIndex = 0;
  private sessionStart = Date.now();
  private rotationTimer: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | null = null;

  constructor(private config: EnsembleSessionConfig) {}

  get currentDriver(): EnsembleParticipant {
    return this.config.participants[this.driverIndex % this.config.participants.length];
  }

  start(): void {
    console.log(`\n=== Ensemble Session: ${this.config.charterId} ===`);
    console.log(`Participants: ${this.config.participants.map((p) => `${p.name} (${p.role})`).join(', ')}`);
    console.log(`First driver: ${this.currentDriver.name}`);
    console.log(`Rotation: every ${this.config.rotationIntervalMs / 1000 / 60} minutes`);
    console.log(`Timebox: ${this.config.timeboxMs / 1000 / 60} minutes total\n`);

    // Start rotation timer
    this.rotationTimer = setInterval(() => {
      this.driverIndex++;
      const next = this.currentDriver;
      console.log(`\n[ROTATION] Driver → ${next.name} (${next.role}). ${this.remainingMinutes()} minutes remaining.\n`);
    }, this.config.rotationIntervalMs);

    // End session after timebox
    setTimeout(() => this.end(), this.config.timeboxMs);
  }

  private remainingMinutes(): number {
    const elapsed = Date.now() - this.sessionStart;
    return Math.max(0, Math.round((this.config.timeboxMs - elapsed) / 1000 / 60));
  }

  observe(tag: EnsembleObservation['tag'], text: string): void {
    const obs: EnsembleObservation = {
      timeMs: Date.now() - this.sessionStart,
      driver: this.currentDriver.name,
      tag,
      text,
    };
    this.observations.push(obs);
    const minElapsed = Math.round(obs.timeMs / 1000 / 60);
    console.log(`[T+${minElapsed}m] ${tag} (driver: ${obs.driver}) ${text}`);
  }

  end(): void {
    if (this.rotationTimer) clearInterval(this.rotationTimer);

    const defects = this.observations.filter((o) => o.tag === '[D]');
    const followOns = this.observations.filter((o) => o.tag === '[F]');
    const blockers = this.observations.filter((o) => o.tag === '[B]');

    const report = {
      charterId: this.config.charterId,
      totalDurationMinutes: Math.round((Date.now() - this.sessionStart) / 1000 / 60),
      participants: this.config.participants.map((p) => p.name),
      defectCandidates: defects.length,
      followOnCharters: followOns.length,
      blockers: blockers.length,
      observations: this.observations,
    };

    fs.writeFileSync(this.config.outputFile, JSON.stringify(report, null, 2), 'utf-8');
    console.log(`\n=== Ensemble session ended ===`);
    console.log(`Defect candidates: ${defects.length}`);
    console.log(`Follow-on charters: ${followOns.length}`);
    console.log(`Blockers: ${blockers.length}`);
    console.log(`Report: ${this.config.outputFile}`);
  }
}

// Usage:
// const facilitator = new EnsembleFacilitator({
//   charterId: 'ENS-checkout-20260515-01',
//   participants: [
//     { name: 'Alice Chen', role: 'tester' },
//     { name: 'Bob Kim', role: 'developer' },
//     { name: 'Carol Zhang', role: 'product-manager' },
//   ],
//   rotationIntervalMs: 10 * 60 * 1000,
//   timeboxMs: 60 * 60 * 1000,
//   outputFile: './sessions/ENS-checkout-20260515-01.json',
// });
// facilitator.start();
// facilitator.observe('[D]', 'Skip button on step 3 leaves account with no payment method set — no warning shown');
// facilitator.observe('[Q]', 'Is step 4 optional? The PM marked it required in the spec but the UI allows skipping.');
```

### Michael Bolton's "Testing vs Checking" Distinction in Exploratory Practice

Michael Bolton drew a foundational distinction between **testing** and **checking** that directly shapes how to design and evaluate exploratory sessions:

- **Checking** is the automated, rule-governed, reproducible comparison of actual outcomes against a known expected outcome. A Playwright assertion — `expect(button).toBeVisible()` — is checking. The rule is fixed; the expected outcome is known; the result is binary.
- **Testing** is the skilled human activity of evaluating a product against undefined or incompletely defined criteria, using judgment, curiosity, and experience to discover what was not anticipated. An exploratory session is testing. The tester discovers things that no prior specification captured.

This distinction is not semantic pedantry — it has direct operational consequences for how teams report and scope their quality work:

| Dimension | Checking | Testing |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| Who performs it | CI infrastructure (automated) | Skilled tester (human) |
| Input | Known expected outputs, fixed assertions | Open questions, oracles, heuristics |
| Failure mode | False positives from stale assertions; never finds unknown issues | Misses issues that scripted checking would catch reliably |
| What it produces | Reproducible regression confidence | Novel defect discovery, risk insight |
| Scales with cost | Near-zero marginal cost per run | Linear cost (tester time) |
| Scope | Whatever was anticipated when the check was written | Whatever is surprising, confusing, or dangerous — often unanticipated |

**Practical application in SBTM:**

When a team's coverage report only lists "tests run" (a checking metric), it conflates the automated regression suite with the exploratory testing programme. The SBTM session count is a **testing** metric — it measures how much skilled investigation happened. Reporting both separately prevents the automation proxy problem: a team can have 2,000 automated checks passing and zero exploratory testing sessions in a sprint. The automation number looks reassuring; the zero sessions is a quality gap.

**Charter language implication:**

A charter that says "Verify that the payment form validates the CVV field" describes a **check** — a single assertion with a known expected outcome. A charter that says "Explore the payment form validation to discover unexpected paths where invalid input is accepted without feedback" describes **testing** — an open inquiry with no preset answer. Teams that write checklist-style charters have inadvertently converted their exploratory sessions into manual scripted test execution. The Bolton distinction provides the diagnostic: if your charter's "Z" statement has a predetermined answer, it is a check, not a test.

**Calibrating the testing/checking split per sprint:**

A healthy sprint typically has:
- Automated checking covering regression paths (run on every CI build)
- 4–8 exploratory testing sessions covering new features, integration paths, and high-risk areas

If the ratio is 100% checking and 0% testing, the team is relying on the completeness of its anticipation at the time the assertions were written — which is always lower than reality. If it is 100% testing and 0% checking, the team finds novel defects but has no regression safety net. Both extremes are failure modes. The Bolton distinction makes the split explicit and auditable.

### LLM Feature Defect Escape Rate Tracker with Failure-Rate Metrics

Defect escape rate for LLM-powered features requires a different measurement model than for deterministic features. Because LLM outputs are probabilistic, a single test run cannot confirm correct behavior — a 1-in-20 failure rate on a safety property is a defect, but a single passing run provides no evidence of the absence of that defect. The correct oracle model is **property-based failure rate over multiple runs**.

The following TypeScript utility tracks LLM feature exploration sessions using a failure-rate model. Each property under test is evaluated across N runs; the escape rate is computed as the ratio of properties where the in-session failure rate exceeded the threshold but the defect was not filed and later reproduced in production.

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/llm-escape-rate-tracker.ts
// Tracks failure rates for LLM feature properties across multiple runs.
// A "property" is a testable quality of an LLM feature: no PII leakage,
// no policy-violating content, no hallucinated citations, correct JSON schema output.
// Each property is evaluated over N runs during a session; the result is
// a failure rate (0.0–1.0) and a verdict (pass/investigate/file).

export interface LLMProperty {
  id: string;
  description: string;
  /** Maximum acceptable failure rate (0.0–1.0). If observed rate exceeds this, the verdict is 'file'. */
  acceptableFailureRate: number;
  /** Minimum number of runs needed for a statistically meaningful sample */
  minRuns: number;
}

export interface LLMRunResult {
  propertyId: string;
  runIndex: number;
  input: string;
  output: string;
  passed: boolean;
  failureReason?: string;
}

export type LLMPropertyVerdict = 'pass' | 'investigate' | 'file' | 'insufficient-data';

export interface LLMPropertySummary {
  property: LLMProperty;
  totalRuns: number;
  failedRuns: number;
  observedFailureRate: number;
  verdict: LLMPropertyVerdict;
  failureExamples: Array<{ input: string; output: string; reason: string }>;
}

export interface LLMSessionReport {
  charterId: string;
  feature: string;
  sessionDate: string;
  propertiesSummary: LLMPropertySummary[];
  overallVerdict: 'pass' | 'defects-filed' | 'investigate';
  defectsToFile: string[];
}

export function summarizePropertyRuns(
  property: LLMProperty,
  runs: LLMRunResult[]
): LLMPropertySummary {
  const propertyRuns = runs.filter((r) => r.propertyId === property.id);
  const totalRuns = propertyRuns.length;
  const failedRuns = propertyRuns.filter((r) => !r.passed).length;
  const observedFailureRate = totalRuns > 0 ? failedRuns / totalRuns : 0;

  let verdict: LLMPropertyVerdict;
  if (totalRuns < property.minRuns) {
    verdict = 'insufficient-data';
  } else if (observedFailureRate > property.acceptableFailureRate) {
    verdict = 'file';
  } else if (observedFailureRate > 0) {
    verdict = 'investigate';
  } else {
    verdict = 'pass';
  }

  const failureExamples = propertyRuns
    .filter((r) => !r.passed && r.failureReason)
    .slice(0, 3)
    .map((r) => ({ input: r.input, output: r.output, reason: r.failureReason! }));

  return { property, totalRuns, failedRuns, observedFailureRate, verdict, failureExamples };
}

export function generateLLMSessionReport(
  charterId: string,
  feature: string,
  sessionDate: string,
  properties: LLMProperty[],
  runs: LLMRunResult[]
): LLMSessionReport {
  const summaries = properties.map((p) => summarizePropertyRuns(p, runs));
  const defectsToFile = summaries
    .filter((s) => s.verdict === 'file')
    .map(
      (s) =>
        `[LLM-DEFECT] ${s.property.description}: ${(s.observedFailureRate * 100).toFixed(0)}% failure rate ` +
        `(${s.failedRuns}/${s.totalRuns} runs) — threshold ${(s.property.acceptableFailureRate * 100).toFixed(0)}%`
    );

  const overallVerdict =
    defectsToFile.length > 0
      ? 'defects-filed'
      : summaries.some((s) => s.verdict === 'investigate')
      ? 'investigate'
      : 'pass';

  return { charterId, feature, sessionDate, propertiesSummary: summaries, overallVerdict, defectsToFile };
}

export function printLLMSessionReport(report: LLMSessionReport): void {
  console.log(`\n=== LLM Feature Session Report: ${report.charterId} ===`);
  console.log(`Feature: ${report.feature} | Date: ${report.sessionDate}`);
  console.log(`Overall verdict: ${report.overallVerdict.toUpperCase()}\n`);

  for (const s of report.propertiesSummary) {
    const icon = s.verdict === 'file' ? '🔴 FILE' : s.verdict === 'investigate' ? '🟡 INVESTIGATE' : s.verdict === 'pass' ? '✅ PASS' : '⬜ INSUFFICIENT';
    console.log(`  ${icon}  ${s.property.description}`);
    console.log(`         Runs: ${s.totalRuns} | Failed: ${s.failedRuns} | Rate: ${(s.observedFailureRate * 100).toFixed(0)}% (threshold: ${(s.property.acceptableFailureRate * 100).toFixed(0)}%)`);
    if (s.failureExamples.length > 0) {
      console.log(`         Example failure: "${s.failureExamples[0].reason}" (input: "${s.failureExamples[0].input.slice(0, 60)}...")`);
    }
  }

  if (report.defectsToFile.length > 0) {
    console.log(`\nDefects to file:`);
    report.defectsToFile.forEach((d) => console.log(`  - ${d}`));
  }
  console.log('');
}

// Example usage — exploring an LLM-powered product description generator:
// const properties: LLMProperty[] = [
//   { id: 'no-pii', description: 'Output contains no PII from the product database', acceptableFailureRate: 0, minRuns: 20 },
//   { id: 'json-schema', description: 'Output matches the expected JSON schema', acceptableFailureRate: 0.05, minRuns: 10 },
//   { id: 'no-hallucination', description: 'All product specs cited are present in the input', acceptableFailureRate: 0.1, minRuns: 15 },
// ];
//
// const runs: LLMRunResult[] = [
//   { propertyId: 'json-schema', runIndex: 0, input: 'Widget X', output: '{"name":"Widget X","price":29.99}', passed: true },
//   { propertyId: 'json-schema', runIndex: 1, input: 'Widget Y', output: 'Here is the product: Widget Y costs $19', passed: false, failureReason: 'Output is prose, not JSON' },
//   // ... more runs

// printLLMSessionReport(report);
```

**Charter template for LLM feature exploration:**

```yaml
# charter: LLM feature exploratory session
charter_id: CHR-llm-<feature>-<YYYYMMDD>-01
session_type: llm-feature-exploration
timebox_minutes: 90

mission:
  explore: "the <LLM feature name> in <context — e.g. the product description generator>"
  using: |
    a representative set of 20–30 input variants covering:
    - happy-path inputs (valid, well-formed)
    - boundary inputs (very short, very long, empty)
    - adversarial inputs (prompt injection attempts, policy-edge content)
    - multilingual / locale-specific inputs (if the feature is used globally)
  to_discover: |
    the failure rate for each property under test (PII leakage, schema conformance,
    hallucination rate, policy-edge outputs) and whether any property's failure rate
    exceeds the team's defined acceptance threshold

properties_under_test:
  - id: pii-leakage
    description: "Output contains no PII not present in the explicit input"
    acceptable_failure_rate: 0.0    # zero tolerance
    min_runs: 20

  - id: json-schema-conformance
    description: "Output matches the expected output schema (all required fields, correct types)"
    acceptable_failure_rate: 0.05   # ≤5% failures acceptable for format errors
    min_runs: 10

  - id: hallucination-citation
    description: "No facts cited that are not present in the input context"
    acceptable_failure_rate: 0.1    # ≤10% before filing — investigate between 0.01–0.1
    min_runs: 15

  - id: no-policy-violation
    description: "No output that violates the product's content policy"
    acceptable_failure_rate: 0.0    # zero tolerance
    min_runs: 20

oracle: HICCUPPS
  # Claims: does it match the feature spec's promised behavior?
  # Standards: does it comply with GDPR/CCPA if PII is at risk?
  # Purpose: does the output serve the stated purpose (helpful product description)?
  # UserExpectation: would a user find the output helpful and trustworthy?

note_taking_additions_for_llm:
  - For each failing run, note: input, output, which property failed, and the failure reason
  - Group failures by pattern (all failures on long inputs → likely context window boundary)
  - Record runs where output "almost" violates a property — these are high-risk patterns
    even if they don't trigger the threshold in this session
```

## Additional Community Lessons (Iteration 51)

141. **[community] Ensemble testing sessions consistently surface requirement ambiguities that solo sessions and pair sessions miss.** When a developer, tester, and product manager explore a feature together, the single most common outcome — reported across multiple teams — is not finding a defect in the code but finding a defect in the shared understanding: the developer built what they thought the spec said; the product manager describes a different behavior as "obviously correct"; the tester observes a behavior that matches neither interpretation. These discovery-of-misalignment events are invisible in solo or pair sessions because only one mental model is active. Ensemble sessions make the shared mental model visible in real time, producing charter updates and spec corrections within the same session that found the ambiguity. Teams that schedule at least one ensemble session per sprint on the highest-uncertainty feature report fewer "that's not what I meant" conversations at sprint review.

142. **[community] The "testing vs checking" distinction from Michael Bolton is the most productive framing for convincing engineering leadership to invest in exploratory sessions.** Engineering leaders who grew up in CI/CD cultures often assume that 85% code coverage and a green build imply adequate testing. The "checking vs testing" reframe resolves this: "we have excellent checking (automated, CI-gated, near-zero marginal cost) and insufficient testing (skilled human investigation of unanticipated behavior)." This framing does not attack automation — it positions exploration as the complement that automated checking structurally cannot provide. Teams that use this framing in OKR planning conversations report that session budgets are approved faster and with less justification overhead than teams that argue "we need more manual testing."

143. **[community] LLM feature defect escape rates are systematically higher than for deterministic features in teams that treat LLM outputs as "black-box pass/fail" rather than as probabilistic properties.** Teams that apply traditional binary pass/fail to LLM feature exploration (one run, does it work?) consistently report production incidents where "the feature worked in testing" but produces policy-violating or incorrect outputs at low frequency in production. The root cause is not a test environment gap — it is a measurement model gap: binary testing of probabilistic features produces confidence from single-run evidence that does not generalize to production distributions. Teams that switch to property-based failure-rate measurement (minimum 15–20 runs per property, with explicit acceptable failure thresholds) report that their LLM feature escape rate drops to levels comparable to their deterministic feature escape rates within two release cycles. The shift requires no additional tooling — only a change in the session protocol.

### Continuous Exploratory Testing in Trunk-Based Development

Teams shipping to trunk multiple times per day face a structural mismatch with sprint-cadence SBTM: there is no "end of sprint" to batch exploration into, and features merge continuously rather than landing in discrete releases. This section covers the adapted patterns practitioners use to run session-based exploration in trunk-based development without creating a quality bottleneck.

**Core insight**: In trunk-based development, the unit of exploration is the **pull request**, not the sprint. Each PR that touches a high-risk area triggers a focused 30–45 minute "nano-session" rather than waiting for a sprint-end block of exploration. The session charter is written by the tester when reviewing the PR description, using the PR diff as the "with Y" context.

**PR-scoped charter template:**

```yaml
# pr-scoped-charter.yaml
# Nano-session charter for trunk-based development.
# Created when a PR touches a high-risk area; runs before merge approval.

charter_id: PR-5301-auth-20260513-01
source_pr: "https://github.com/org/repo/pull/5301"
pr_summary: "Add TOTP-based MFA to the login flow"
session_type: nano          # 30–45 min exploratory session, single tester
timebox_minutes: 40

risk_trigger:
  area: auth
  reason: "MFA changes affect all users; regression risk is high; no existing automation for TOTP flows"

mission:
  explore: "the new TOTP MFA enrollment and verification flow introduced in PR #5301"
  using: |
    a test account with no prior MFA configuration, the TOTP authenticator app simulator,
    and three edge scenarios: valid code, expired code (> 30s after generation), and
    backup-code-based recovery
  to_discover: |
    whether the TOTP enrollment flow handles authenticator app binding errors,
    whether expired codes produce clear user-facing errors (not silent failures),
    and whether backup code exhaustion is communicated before the user is locked out

oracle: HICCUPPS
  # Claims: PR description says expired TOTP codes show "Code expired — please try again"
  # User expectations: users expect immediate, distinct feedback for expired vs wrong codes
  # Standards: NIST 800-63B requires authenticator binding confirmation before activation

debrief_output:
  target_channel: "#pr-reviews"
  format: "1-paragraph summary + defect candidates + merge-block flag (yes/no)"
  sla_minutes: 60   # debrief posted within 60 minutes of session end
```

**Automation gate integration**: PR-scoped nano-sessions run in parallel with CI checks, not after them. The tester starts the session when the PR CI check begins, and the session ends around the same time as CI. If the session finds a merge-blocking defect, the PR is blocked regardless of CI status. If CI fails, the session is paused — blocked time is logged and a new session is scheduled after the CI fix.

**TypeScript: PR-Scoped Session Monitor**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/pr-session-monitor.ts
// Monitors a PR-scoped nano-session and posts a structured debrief
// to the team's Slack channel when the session ends.
// Integrates with GitHub PR API to add a review comment if merge-blocking.

export interface PRScopedSession {
  charterId: string;
  prUrl: string;
  prNumber: number;
  riskArea: string;
  testerName: string;
  startTimeMs: number;
  timeboxMs: number;
}

export interface PRSessionOutcome {
  defectCandidates: Array<{
    severity: 'merge-blocking' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
    description: string;
    oracleDimension: string;
  }>;
  coverageNotes: string;
  testerConfidence: number; // 0–5
  mergeBlockFlag: boolean;
  followOnCharters: string[];
}

export interface PRDebriefPayload {
  charterId: string;
  prUrl: string;
  sessionDurationMs: number;
  outcome: PRSessionOutcome;
  generatedAt: string;
}

export function buildPRDebrief(
  session: PRScopedSession,
  outcome: PRSessionOutcome
): PRDebriefPayload {
  const sessionDurationMs = Date.now() - session.startTimeMs;
  return {
    charterId: session.charterId,
    prUrl: session.prUrl,
    sessionDurationMs,
    outcome,
    generatedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  };
}

export function formatDebriefSlackMessage(payload: PRDebriefPayload): string {
  const durationMin = Math.round(payload.sessionDurationMs / 60000);
  const blockIcon = payload.outcome.mergeBlockFlag ? ':red_circle: *MERGE BLOCKED*' : ':large_green_circle: Merge OK';
  const defectLines = payload.outcome.defectCandidates
    .map((d) => `  • [${d.severity.toUpperCase()}] ${d.description} (oracle: ${d.oracleDimension})`)
    .join('\n');
  const followOnLines = payload.outcome.followOnCharters.length > 0
    ? `\n*Follow-on charters:* ${payload.outcome.followOnCharters.join(', ')}`
    : '';

  return [
    `*Nano-session debrief — ${payload.charterId}* (${durationMin} min)`,
    `PR: ${payload.prUrl}`,
    `${blockIcon} | Confidence: ${payload.outcome.testerConfidence}/5`,
    payload.outcome.defectCandidates.length > 0
      ? `\n*Defect candidates:*\n${defectLines}`
      : '\nNo defect candidates.',
    payload.outcome.coverageNotes ? `\n*Coverage notes:* ${payload.outcome.coverageNotes}` : '',
    followOnLines,
  ].filter(Boolean).join('\n');
}

// Usage example:
// const session: PRScopedSession = {
//   charterId: 'PR-5301-auth-20260513-01',
//   prUrl: 'https://github.com/org/repo/pull/5301',
//   prNumber: 5301,
//   riskArea: 'auth',
//   testerName: 'Alice Chen',
//   startTimeMs: Date.now(),
//   timeboxMs: 40 * 60 * 1000,
// };
// const debrief = buildPRDebrief(session, outcome);
// const message = formatDebriefSlackMessage(debrief);
// await slackClient.chat.postMessage({ channel: '#pr-reviews', text: message });
```

**When PR-scoped nano-sessions replace longer sprint sessions**: Not all PRs need a nano-session. Use a risk filter: only PRs that touch auth, payments, data migration, public APIs, or areas with a defect history in the last 90 days trigger a charter. Lower-risk PRs (documentation, dependency bumps, test-only changes) skip exploration. Teams that apply this risk filter report spending 2–3 hours per week on PR-scoped nano-sessions while maintaining defect escape rates equivalent to a full sprint-end exploration block.

### Keyboard-Only and Screen-Reader Session Protocols

Accessibility exploration is most effective when conducted as a series of structured keyboard-only and screen-reader sessions rather than as a checklist pass. This section provides the protocol details for running these sessions as first-class SBTM charters.

**Why keyboard-only sessions deserve their own charter type**: Automated accessibility tools (axe-core, Deque, Lighthouse) catch approximately 57% of WCAG 2.1 AA defects automatically. The remaining 43% require human judgment: interactive widget focus order, logical reading sequence, context-sensitive ARIA labels, and cognitive usability gaps. Keyboard-only and screen-reader sessions catch these structural accessibility defects that automated tools miss. The key distinction: tools verify *attribute presence*; sessions verify *experience quality*.

**Keyboard-only session charter template:**

```yaml
# keyboard-only-charter.yaml
# Exploratory session using keyboard navigation exclusively (no mouse).
# Tests focus management, skip links, keyboard traps, and logical tab order.

charter_id: A11Y-KB-checkout-20260513-01
session_type: keyboard-only
timebox_minutes: 60
tooling:
  - "Physical keyboard only — mouse and trackpad disabled for session duration"
  - "Browser: Chrome with keyboard shortcuts reference open in adjacent window"
  - "Axe DevTools panel open — for reference, not the primary oracle"

mission:
  explore: "the guest checkout flow (cart → shipping → payment → confirmation)"
  using: |
    keyboard navigation only (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Arrow keys, Escape);
    a populated cart with 2 items and no saved address;
    screen resolution 1280x768 (typical laptop viewport)
  to_discover: |
    whether each interactive element is reachable by keyboard in a logical order,
    whether modal dialogs and dropdowns trap focus correctly,
    whether focus returns to the correct element after modal dismissal,
    and whether any step produces a keyboard trap that requires mouse intervention

exploration_heuristics:
  - "Tab through every focusable element — verify visual focus indicator is always visible"
  - "On every modal/dialog: verify Escape closes it; verify focus returns to trigger element"
  - "On every dropdown/combobox: verify Arrow key navigation works; verify Enter selects"
  - "On every form: verify required field validation is announced (not just color-coded)"
  - "Skip-link test: Tab on page load — does a 'Skip to main content' link appear as first focus target?"
  - "After form submit error: verify focus moves to the error summary, not the page top"

oracle: HICCUPPS
  # Standards: WCAG 2.1 AA SC 2.1.1 (Keyboard), SC 2.4.3 (Focus Order), SC 2.4.7 (Focus Visible)
  # Claims: the product's accessibility statement claims WCAG 2.1 AA conformance
  # User expectations: keyboard-dependent users (motor disabilities, power users) expect full operability
```

**Screen-reader session protocol** — distinct from keyboard-only:

A screen-reader session uses the same keyboard navigation but adds an active screen reader (NVDA + Firefox on Windows, VoiceOver + Safari on macOS, TalkBack on Android). The oracle shifts from visual focus to *announced content*: what does the screen reader say vs what the visual UI shows?

Critical protocol notes:
- **Run NVDA in browse mode first, then interaction mode**: screen readers have two modes; most WCAG defects surface in the transition between them. Always test both.
- **Listen for context gaps**: buttons labeled "Close" are insufficient when three modals are possible on one page. The screen reader cannot see the visual context; only the accessible name is announced.
- **Test dynamic content announcements**: does the screen reader announce a cart total update when quantity changes? Animated counters and live regions need explicit `aria-live` attributes to be announced.
- **ARIA override accuracy**: `aria-label` overrides the visual text. A button labeled visually "Remove" but with `aria-label="Remove item from cart"` is correct. A button with `aria-label="Click here"` is a defect even if the visual label is clear.

**TypeScript: Keyboard Navigation Audit Logger**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/keyboard-audit-logger.ts
// Logs keyboard navigation observations during a keyboard-only exploratory session.
// Captures focus element sequences, trap events, and ARIA label mismatches
// for post-session report generation and follow-on automated test generation.

export interface FocusObservation {
  sequenceIndex: number;
  elementSelector: string;
  elementRole: string;          // e.g. 'button', 'link', 'combobox'
  accessibleName: string;
  focusIndicatorVisible: boolean;
  expectedTab: 'in-sequence' | 'skipped' | 'unexpected-focus';
  notes?: string;
}

export interface KeyboardTrapEvent {
  elementSelector: string;
  description: string;          // e.g. 'Modal dialog: Escape does not close, focus stays inside'
  wcagCriterion: string;        // e.g. 'SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap'
  severity: 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium';
}

export interface KeyboardSessionLog {
  charterId: string;
  sessionDate: string;
  testerName: string;
  feature: string;
  focusSequence: FocusObservation[];
  trapEvents: KeyboardTrapEvent[];
  skipLinkPresent: boolean;
  skipLinkFunctional: boolean;
  totalTabStops: number;
  defectCandidates: string[];
  testerConfidence: number;
}

export function summarizeKeyboardSession(log: KeyboardSessionLog): string {
  const trapCount = log.trapEvents.length;
  const criticalTraps = log.trapEvents.filter((t) => t.severity === 'critical').length;
  const focusInvisible = log.focusSequence.filter((f) => !f.focusIndicatorVisible).length;
  const unexpectedFocus = log.focusSequence.filter((f) => f.expectedTab === 'unexpected-focus').length;

  const lines: string[] = [
    `Keyboard Session Summary — ${log.charterId}`,
    `Feature: ${log.feature} | Date: ${log.sessionDate} | Tester: ${log.testerName}`,
    `Tab stops explored: ${log.totalTabStops}`,
    `Skip link: ${log.skipLinkPresent ? (log.skipLinkFunctional ? 'present + functional' : 'present but non-functional') : 'ABSENT'}`,
    `Focus indicator invisible: ${focusInvisible} element(s)`,
    `Keyboard traps: ${trapCount} (${criticalTraps} critical)`,
    `Unexpected focus events: ${unexpectedFocus}`,
    `Defect candidates: ${log.defectCandidates.length}`,
    `Tester confidence: ${log.testerConfidence}/5`,
  ];

  if (log.trapEvents.length > 0) {
    lines.push('\nKeyboard trap details:');
    log.trapEvents.forEach((t) =>
      lines.push(`  [${t.severity.toUpperCase()}] ${t.wcagCriterion}: ${t.description}`)
    );
  }

  return lines.join('\n');
}
```

### Charter Portfolio Management at Scale

As teams accumulate hundreds of charters over multiple sprints, the charter library itself becomes a knowledge asset that needs management. Without systematic organization, teams recreate charters for areas already explored, lose track of which areas have aged coverage, and cannot identify emerging risk clusters from historical data.

**Charter lifecycle states:**

| State | Meaning | Typical duration before review |
|-------|---------|-------------------------------|
| `draft` | Charter written, not yet executed | Max 2 sprints; draft charters not run in 2 sprints are either promoted or archived |
| `active` | Currently scheduled for execution this sprint | Sprint duration |
| `completed` | Session run, debrief done, findings filed | Permanent; becomes historical record |
| `archived` | Area de-risked (feature stable, full automation coverage added) | Reviewable quarterly |
| `stale` | Completed > 90 days ago, area has changed significantly | Triggers re-charter decision |
| `blocked` | Session could not run (environment issues, feature unavailable) | Max 1 sprint; escalate if persists |

**Charter stale detection heuristic**: A completed charter becomes stale when (a) the feature area has been modified by 5+ PRs since the charter ran, OR (b) 90 days have elapsed since the last session on this area, OR (c) a production defect was found in this area since the last session. Stale charters are not deleted — they are flagged for re-charter, because the original charter's "to discover Z" statement often becomes the starting point for the new charter's "with Y" context.

**TypeScript: Charter Portfolio Manager**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/charter-portfolio-manager.ts
// Manages the lifecycle of a charter portfolio.
// Detects stale charters, generates coverage gap reports,
// and produces a risk-weighted charter priority queue for sprint planning.

export type CharterLifecycleState =
  | 'draft'
  | 'active'
  | 'completed'
  | 'archived'
  | 'stale'
  | 'blocked';

export interface CharterRecord {
  id: string;
  area: string;               // Feature/module area (e.g. 'checkout.payment')
  riskLevel: 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
  state: CharterLifecycleState;
  lastSessionDate?: string;   // ISO date of most recent completed session
  prsTouched: number;         // PRs touching this area since last session
  productionDefectsInArea: number; // Production defects in area since last session
  coverageConfidence?: number; // 0–5 from last debrief
}

export interface StalenessPolicy {
  maxDaysSinceSession: number;     // default 90
  maxPrsTouched: number;           // default 5
  maxProductionDefects: number;    // default 0 (any production defect triggers stale)
}

export function detectStaleCharters(
  charters: CharterRecord[],
  policy: StalenessPolicy,
  today: Date = new Date()
): CharterRecord[] {
  return charters
    .filter((c) => c.state === 'completed')
    .filter((c) => {
      if (!c.lastSessionDate) return true;
      const daysSince = Math.floor(
        (today.getTime() - new Date(c.lastSessionDate).getTime()) / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24)
      );
      return (
        daysSince > policy.maxDaysSinceSession ||
        c.prsTouched > policy.maxPrsTouched ||
        c.productionDefectsInArea > policy.maxProductionDefects
      );
    });
}

export function prioritizeCharters(charters: CharterRecord[]): CharterRecord[] {
  const riskWeight: Record<string, number> = {
    critical: 4, high: 3, medium: 2, low: 1,
  };
  // Draft and stale charters only; sort by risk level descending, then by prsTouched
  return charters
    .filter((c) => c.state === 'draft' || c.state === 'stale')
    .sort((a, b) => {
      const riskDiff = (riskWeight[b.riskLevel] ?? 0) - (riskWeight[a.riskLevel] ?? 0);
      if (riskDiff !== 0) return riskDiff;
      return (b.prsTouched ?? 0) - (a.prsTouched ?? 0);
    });
}

export function generateCoverageGapReport(charters: CharterRecord[]): string {
  const uncovered = charters.filter((c) => c.state === 'draft' || c.state === 'stale');
  const critical = uncovered.filter((c) => c.riskLevel === 'critical' || c.riskLevel === 'high');
  const lines = [
    `Charter Portfolio Coverage Gap Report`,
    `Total charters: ${charters.length} | Uncovered/stale: ${uncovered.length} | High-risk gaps: ${critical.length}`,
    '',
    'Priority queue (draft + stale, by risk):',
  ];
  prioritizeCharters(charters).forEach((c, i) => {
    lines.push(`  ${i + 1}. [${c.riskLevel.toUpperCase()}] ${c.area} (${c.state}) — ${c.prsTouched} PRs since last session`);
  });
  return lines.join('\n');
}
```

### Chaos-Resilience Charter Alignment

Teams that run chaos engineering experiments (Chaos Monkey, Gremlin, LitmusChaos) alongside exploratory testing create a powerful alignment: chaos experiments define the failure conditions, and session charters verify the user-observable behavior under those conditions. Without this alignment, chaos experiments produce infrastructure metrics (availability, latency) but miss user experience quality under partial failure.

**Charter strategy for chaos-aligned exploration:**

For each chaos experiment that runs in a staging environment, create a corresponding exploratory session charter that explores the user-facing behavior while the failure is active. The chaos experiment is the "with Y" context in the charter.

```yaml
# chaos-aligned-charter.yaml
# Exploratory session run while a chaos experiment is active in staging.
# The chaos tool creates the failure condition; the explorer observes user-visible behavior.

charter_id: CHAOS-db-latency-checkout-20260513-01
session_type: chaos-aligned
chaos_experiment:
  tool: "Gremlin"
  experiment_id: "EXP-db-read-latency-500ms"
  failure_type: "latency injection"
  target: "primary database read path"
  duration_minutes: 60

timebox_minutes: 45  # session runs inside the chaos experiment window

mission:
  explore: "the checkout and order history flows"
  using: |
    an active Gremlin latency injection adding 500ms to all database read queries,
    a test account with 10 prior orders, and normal user actions (browsing, adding to cart,
    completing checkout, loading order history)
  to_discover: |
    whether degraded database latency produces clear user-facing feedback (loading
    indicators, graceful timeout messages) or silent failures (blank pages, missing
    data, infinite loaders), and whether any user path produces a data-consistency
    defect (order submitted but not confirmed, cart items lost) under latency

oracle: HICCUPPS
  # User expectations: users expect feedback within 3s or a clear error; silent failure is unacceptable
  # Claims: the product's SLO states 99.9% of checkout completions within 5s; verify at 500ms injected latency
  # Purpose: checkout must complete reliably under degraded conditions; silent data loss is a business defect

note_taking:
  - Flag: any response that takes > 3s without a loading indicator = defect candidate
  - Flag: any operation that produces no feedback (success or error) within 10s = critical defect
  - Flag: any data inconsistency between what was submitted and what appears in order history
```

**Why chaos-aligned charters find a defect class that chaos metrics alone cannot**: Infrastructure chaos experiments report availability and latency percentiles. They cannot report "the checkout confirmation page shows a spinner for 45 seconds and then silently clears the cart without confirming the order." Only a human tester observing the user-facing behavior during the chaos window catches this class of defect — which is a different defect from the database being slow. The database recovered; the UI state machine did not handle the recovery correctly. Chaos-aligned charters specifically target this gap.

### AI-Assisted Defect Deduplication Across Session Archives

Teams that run many sessions per sprint accumulate hundreds of defect candidates across their session archive. Without systematic deduplication, the same underlying root cause is filed multiple times under different surface descriptions. A session in week 2 finds "the search results page shows stale data after a filter change"; a session in week 5 finds "the product listing doesn't update when the category filter is applied." Both are manifestations of the same stale-cache defect, but they are filed as separate defect candidates with separate priorities.

**Deduplication strategy using semantic clustering**: The practical approach (deployable without a dedicated ML model) uses normalized text similarity across defect candidate descriptions from the session archive. Descriptions that cluster above a threshold are surfaced for human review — a tester reviews the cluster and decides whether they are the same root cause or genuinely separate defects.

**TypeScript: Session Archive Defect Deduplicator**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/defect-deduplicator.ts
// Detects likely-duplicate defect candidates across session archives
// using token overlap similarity (no external ML dependency required).
// Surfaces clusters above a configurable threshold for human triage review.

export interface DefectCandidate {
  id: string;
  sessionId: string;
  sessionDate: string;
  description: string;
  area: string;
  severity: 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
  status: 'open' | 'filed' | 'duplicate' | 'closed';
}

export interface DuplicateCluster {
  representativeId: string;
  duplicateCandidateIds: string[];
  similarity: number;             // 0–1; overlap-based
  recommendedAction: 'review' | 'auto-merge';
}

/** Tokenize and normalize a defect description for comparison */
function tokenize(text: string): Set<string> {
  const stopWords = new Set(['a', 'an', 'the', 'is', 'are', 'was', 'were', 'and', 'or', 'not', 'in', 'on', 'at', 'to', 'for', 'of', 'with', 'when', 'after']);
  return new Set(
    text
      .toLowerCase()
      .replace(/[^\w\s]/g, ' ')
      .split(/\s+/)
      .filter((t) => t.length > 2 && !stopWords.has(t))
  );
}

/** Jaccard similarity between two token sets */
function jaccardSimilarity(a: Set<string>, b: Set<string>): number {
  const intersection = new Set([...a].filter((t) => b.has(t)));
  const union = new Set([...a, ...b]);
  return union.size === 0 ? 0 : intersection.size / union.size;
}

export function detectDuplicateClusters(
  candidates: DefectCandidate[],
  similarityThreshold: number = 0.4,
  autoMergeThreshold: number = 0.7
): DuplicateCluster[] {
  const open = candidates.filter((c) => c.status === 'open' || c.status === 'filed');
  const tokenized = open.map((c) => ({ id: c.id, tokens: tokenize(c.description) }));
  const clusters: DuplicateCluster[] = [];
  const clustered = new Set<string>();

  for (let i = 0; i < tokenized.length; i++) {
    if (clustered.has(tokenized[i].id)) continue;
    const duplicates: Array<{ id: string; similarity: number }> = [];

    for (let j = i + 1; j < tokenized.length; j++) {
      if (clustered.has(tokenized[j].id)) continue;
      const sim = jaccardSimilarity(tokenized[i].tokens, tokenized[j].tokens);
      if (sim >= similarityThreshold) {
        duplicates.push({ id: tokenized[j].id, similarity: sim });
        clustered.add(tokenized[j].id);
      }
    }

    if (duplicates.length > 0) {
      const maxSim = Math.max(...duplicates.map((d) => d.similarity));
      clusters.push({
        representativeId: tokenized[i].id,
        duplicateCandidateIds: duplicates.map((d) => d.id),
        similarity: maxSim,
        recommendedAction: maxSim >= autoMergeThreshold ? 'auto-merge' : 'review',
      });
      clustered.add(tokenized[i].id);
    }
  }

  return clusters.sort((a, b) => b.similarity - a.similarity);
}

// Usage example:
// const clusters = detectDuplicateClusters(allDefectCandidates);
// clusters.forEach((cluster) => {
//   console.log(`Cluster: ${cluster.representativeId} + ${cluster.duplicateCandidateIds.join(', ')}`);
//   console.log(`  Similarity: ${(cluster.similarity * 100).toFixed(0)}% — ${cluster.recommendedAction}`);
// });
```

**Practical threshold guidance**: A Jaccard similarity of 0.4 captures descriptions that share 40% of their meaningful tokens — sufficient to surface likely duplicates for human review without false positives from incidentally similar language. At 0.7+, descriptions are likely describing the same behavior and can be auto-tagged as duplicate candidates (still requiring human confirmation before closing). Teams running this deduplication pass weekly on their session archive reduce duplicate defect candidate volume by 25–40% based on practitioner reports.

### Thread-Based SBTM Reporting

Thread-based reporting is an async-first alternative to synchronous debriefs for teams distributed across time zones. Instead of a synchronous debrief meeting, the session output is posted as a structured thread in a shared channel (Slack, Teams, GitHub Discussion), and the thread conversation replaces the debrief dialogue over a 24-hour window.

**Protocol:**

1. Tester completes the session and posts the session sheet as a thread root post within 30 minutes of session end.
2. The root post must contain: charter ID, mission summary, session duration, note summary (counts by type), defect candidates with severity and oracle dimension, tester confidence, and releasable flag.
3. Team members add replies within 24 hours asking the clarifying questions that a synchronous debrief would surface. The tester responds inline.
4. Any follow-on charters identified in replies are created and added to the sprint backlog by the tester before the thread is archived.
5. The thread is marked "debriefed" (via a reaction emoji or a bot command) once all questions have responses.

**Thread root post template (Markdown/Slack format):**

```markdown
**Exploratory Session Debrief — CHR-auth-20260513-01**

**Charter**: Explore SSO login edge cases with expired SAML assertions and clock-skew scenarios to discover whether users receive actionable error messages or silent failures
**Session**: 2026-05-13 | 90 min | Tester: Alice Chen
**Environment**: Staging v2.41.3 | SSO provider: Okta sandbox

**Note summary:**
- [N] Notes: 18 | [D] Defect candidates: 4 | [Q] Questions for dev: 2 | [F] Follow-on charters: 1

**Defect candidates:**
1. [HIGH] Expired SAML assertion (>5 min clock skew) → "Something went wrong" error with no recovery path (oracle: Claims — spec says "login error with retry option") | WCAG: error not programmatically associated with form field
2. [MEDIUM] Clock-skew edge case: 4m58s skew → login succeeds silently despite being within the rejection window on some IdP configs — non-deterministic (oracle: Consistency — behavior varies by IdP config)
3. [MEDIUM] "Remember this device" checkbox state not preserved after SSO redirect on Firefox 124 (oracle: History — worked in 2.40.x)
4. [LOW] SSO logout redirect URI in the error state points to /login rather than /sso/login — causes confusion for SSO-only accounts (oracle: User expectations)

**Follow-on charter:** CHR-auth-sso-multiidp-20260520 — explore multi-IdP SSO configuration variability with Okta + Azure AD + SAML 2.0 + OIDC simultaneously active

**Tester confidence: 4/5** — strong coverage of error paths; did not explore OIDC-only flows (IdP unavailable in staging sandbox)
**Releasable: No** — defect #1 (HIGH, no recovery path on expired assertion) must be resolved before release

_Please reply with questions or add follow-on charter suggestions. Thread will be marked debriefed once all questions are addressed._
```

**When thread-based debrief is preferable to synchronous debrief**: distributed teams, async-first cultures, sessions run outside business hours, and situations where the debrief needs a written record (compliance, audit trail). Thread-based debriefs produce a richer written record than synchronous debriefs but require more written discipline from the tester — the session sheet must stand alone without the tester's verbal context.

## Additional Community Lessons (Cycle 19)

144. **[community] Teams that adopted PR-scoped nano-sessions for high-risk areas reported that the practice changed developer behavior more than tester behavior.** When developers knew that a nano-session would be scheduled for any PR touching auth, payments, or data migration, they began writing more detailed PR descriptions — not to satisfy a checklist, but because the tester's charter "to discover Z" statement directly reflected the quality of the PR description's explanation of intent. A PR that said "add TOTP MFA" produced a weaker charter than a PR that said "add TOTP MFA with the following edge cases handled: expired code (30s window), backup code recovery, re-enrollment after device loss." The tester's charter quality was a direct mirror of the PR description quality. Teams that ran nano-sessions for 3+ months reported that PR description quality improved measurably — a side effect that the teams attributed to the social accountability of "the tester is going to explore exactly what I wrote here."

145. **[community] Keyboard-only exploratory sessions consistently surface a defect class that automated axe-core scans miss: focus order violations that are technically valid HTML but semantically incorrect.** A form with fields in the DOM order `[label: First Name] [input: Last Name] [label: Last Name] [input: First Name]` (swapped inputs and labels) passes axe-core because the labels are correctly associated via `for`/`id` attributes. A keyboard-only tester notices immediately that pressing Tab moves focus to "Last Name" while the visual label says "First Name" — the tab order mirrors the DOM order, not the visual layout order. This class of defect requires a human tester to notice the mismatch between what the screen reads and what the tab order navigates. Automated tools verify attribute-level correctness; session-based exploration verifies perceptual correctness. Teams that added a quarterly keyboard-only session to their a11y charter library found this defect class on first run in 60% of tested features.

146. **[community] Charter portfolio staleness is the most underdiagnosed form of coverage debt in mature QA organizations.** Teams with more than 18 months of charter history consistently discover, on first portfolio audit, that 30–50% of their "completed" charters cover features that have changed significantly since the charter ran. The charter completed successfully; the findings were filed; the session count went up. But the feature's behavior has diverged from what the charter explored, making the coverage signal misleading: the sprint dashboard shows "authentication: 3 sessions completed, confidence 4/5" while the authentication flow has been rewritten twice since those sessions ran. Charter staleness audits (using the stale detection heuristic: > 90 days + > 5 PRs in area + any production defect in area) consistently surface 5–10 re-charter candidates per 50-charter portfolio — candidates that, when re-chartered and re-explored, produce the same defect yield as first-ever exploration of a new feature.

147. **[community] Chaos-aligned exploratory sessions find a specific defect pattern that neither chaos experiments nor standard exploratory sessions find in isolation: the "recovery worse than the failure" class.** A chaos experiment measures whether a service recovers from a latency injection. An exploratory session without chaos measures whether the feature works under normal conditions. A chaos-aligned session — exploration running while the chaos experiment is active — finds that the service recovers correctly (the infrastructure metric is fine) but the UI presents stale data, incorrect loading states, or partial results during the recovery window. The user experience during the recovery is worse than the user experience during the failure itself: during the failure, users see an error; during recovery, users see incorrect data presented as current. This "recovery worse than failure" pattern is reliably found in chaos-aligned sessions and reliably missed by both chaos tooling and standard exploratory sessions.

148. **[community] Defect deduplication using token similarity across session archives reveals that the same area generates duplicate defect candidates at a consistent rate across teams — typically 20–35% of all defect candidates in a high-churn area are duplicates of earlier candidates that were closed without full root cause analysis.** The pattern: a defect is filed, a surface fix is applied (the specific error path is handled), but the root cause (e.g., a caching layer that doesn't invalidate correctly) remains. The next session in the same area finds the same root cause manifesting through a different surface behavior, and files a new candidate. Without deduplication across the session archive (not just the current sprint), the root cause is addressed symptom by symptom rather than structurally. Teams that ran deduplication passes on their session archives before quarterly planning found that 80% of their "new" defect candidates in high-churn areas had a parent candidate in the archive from a previous quarter — evidence of recurring root causes that warranted a deeper investigation charter rather than another surface fix.

149. **[community] Thread-based SBTM debriefs reveal a systematic gap in session documentation: testers who are comfortable debriefing verbally consistently produce inadequate written session sheets when required to post the debrief as a thread root post.** The transition from verbal to written debrief exposes what was being carried in working memory rather than in the session notes. A tester who can answer "what did you mean by weird behavior at step 3?" verbally in 30 seconds cannot answer it from their written notes if those notes say "step 3: weird." Teams that switched to thread-based debriefs discovered this gap within the first sprint and used it productively: the quality of the thread root post became a proxy metric for session note quality. Teams that added a peer review step (one other tester reads the root post before it goes to the channel) saw session note quality improve within two sprints — the social visibility of the written debrief created an incentive to write better notes during the session, not retrospectively.

150. **[community] The "to discover Z" part of a charter is the highest-leverage investment in improving session yield, and it is the part that most teams treat as boilerplate.** Analysis of charter libraries across multiple teams shows that the most common "Z" pattern is a direct restatement of "X": "Explore the payment flow to discover issues with the payment flow." This produces a session with no clear success criterion — the tester explores, finds whatever they find, and the debrief cannot evaluate whether the session answered its own question. Teams that rewrote their charter "Z" statements as explicit questions ("Does the payment flow handle post-redirect failures from the payment gateway without duplicating the charge?") reported three measurable improvements: (1) sessions ran more efficiently because the tester knew what they were looking for, (2) debriefs were shorter because the first question ("did we answer the charter question?") resolved immediately rather than requiring open-ended discussion, and (3) coverage gaps became visible as unanswered charter questions rather than as "no bugs found" — a meaningful distinction when absence of bugs may mean absence of coverage.

151. **[community] Exploratory testing of microservices resilience requires a charter strategy fundamentally different from UI exploration: the "user" is an API consumer, the "behavior" is an HTTP response or message queue event, and the "environment" requires deliberate failure injection rather than normal usage.** Teams that applied standard UI-focused session protocols to microservice resilience exploration produced sessions that tested happy-path API flows — the same coverage provided by existing integration tests — and found no novel defects. Teams that re-chartered with chaos-aligned, API-focused protocols (injecting downstream service failures, network partitions, and schema evolution scenarios as the "with Y" context) consistently found the resilience defect patterns that production incidents eventually surfaced: cascading timeouts where one slow downstream service locked all connection pool threads, circuit breaker configurations that opened on errors but never probed to recover, and retry storms where multiple upstream services simultaneously retried against a recovering downstream service. The re-chartered sessions found these defects in staging; the unchari-aligned sessions found them in production. The structural difference: UI exploration probes user-facing behavior under normal conditions; resilience exploration probes service-facing behavior under deliberate failure conditions.

### Specification-by-Example as Charter Seed  [community]

Specification-by-Example (SbE) produces concrete examples of expected system behavior as part of story refinement (a.k.a. Example Mapping). These examples are the ideal raw material for exploratory charter writing: they define what the team *thought* would happen, which makes them a precise oracle for discovery — "does the system actually behave like these examples claim?"

**Charter seed derivation pattern:**

Each Example Mapping card class maps to a charter component:

| Example Mapping artefact | Maps to charter component | Rationale |
|--------------------------|--------------------------|-----------|
| **Rule** (AC heading) | "Explore X" target | The rule names the behavior boundary to probe |
| **Example** (green card, happy path) | "with Y" context | The example specifies the scenario conditions |
| **Question** (red card, unresolved) | "to discover Z" goal | Unanswered questions become explicit discovery missions |
| **Edge case example** (yellow card) | Separate charter per edge | Edge cases are highest-yield exploration targets |

The workflow: after a story's Example Mapping session, the tester takes every red card (open question) and every yellow card (edge case) and converts them directly into charter "Z" statements. This produces charters that are tightly coupled to the story's known unknowns rather than to the tester's intuition.

**When this matters**: teams that run Example Mapping but then write charters from scratch (ignoring the session output) lose the shared understanding captured in the mapping. The red cards represent genuine uncertainty the team acknowledged. If those red cards don't appear in the charter "Z" statements, the session's insights are not being converted into test coverage.

**TypeScript: Example-Mapping-to-Charter Converter**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/example-map-to-charter.ts
// Converts Example Mapping output (rules, examples, questions, edge cases)
// into structured exploratory charters with pre-populated "to discover Z" goals.

export interface ExampleMappingCard {
  type: 'rule' | 'example' | 'question' | 'edge-case';
  text: string;
  ruleRef?: string; // which rule does this card belong to?
}

export interface ExploratoryCharter {
  id: string;
  explore: string;
  withContext: string;
  toDiscover: string;
  sourceCardType: ExampleMappingCard['type'];
  priority: 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
}

export function deriveChartersFromExampleMap(
  storyId: string,
  cards: ExampleMappingCard[]
): ExploratoryCharter[] {
  const charters: ExploratoryCharter[] = [];
  let seq = 0;

  // Red cards (open questions) → highest-priority charters
  const questions = cards.filter((c) => c.type === 'question');
  for (const q of questions) {
    const rule = cards.find((c) => c.type === 'rule' && c.text === q.ruleRef);
    charters.push({
      id: `CHR-${storyId}-q${++seq}`,
      explore: rule?.text ?? 'the feature area related to this open question',
      withContext: 'the conditions described by the team as uncertain during example mapping',
      toDiscover: q.text, // the question IS the discovery goal
      sourceCardType: 'question',
      priority: 'high',
    });
  }

  // Yellow cards (edge cases) → medium-priority charters
  const edges = cards.filter((c) => c.type === 'edge-case');
  for (const e of edges) {
    const rule = cards.find((c) => c.type === 'rule' && c.text === e.ruleRef);
    charters.push({
      id: `CHR-${storyId}-e${++seq}`,
      explore: rule?.text ?? 'the feature edge behavior',
      withContext: e.text,
      toDiscover: `whether the edge case "${e.text}" is handled correctly and gracefully`,
      sourceCardType: 'edge-case',
      priority: 'medium',
    });
  }

  return charters;
}

// Usage:
// const cards: ExampleMappingCard[] = [
//   { type: 'rule', text: 'Guest checkout must work without account creation' },
//   { type: 'question', text: 'What happens if the guest email already has an account?', ruleRef: 'Guest checkout must work without account creation' },
//   { type: 'edge-case', text: 'Guest email contains + alias (user+tag@domain.com)', ruleRef: 'Guest checkout must work without account creation' },
// ];
// const charters = deriveChartersFromExampleMap('STORY-1234', cards);
// → charters[0]: explore "Guest checkout...", to discover "What happens if the guest email already has an account?"
```

### Charter-to-Automation Graduation Workflow  [community]

The "charter-to-automation" pipeline is the structural link between exploratory testing and the automated test suite. When a session produces a reproducible defect candidate, the fix creates a known-behavior boundary — a specific input/state/output triple that should never regress. Automating this triple is not optional: it is the mechanism by which exploratory testing feeds the regression suite rather than being a parallel, disconnected activity.

**Graduation decision matrix:**

| Defect candidate property | Automate? | Rationale |
|--------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| Reproducible with deterministic inputs | Yes | Automation provides reliable regression signal |
| Fixed by a targeted code change | Yes | The fix defines the expected behavior; automate it |
| Intermittent or timing-dependent | No (quarantine first) | Automating a flaky scenario produces a flaky test — address root cause first |
| Cosmetic / visual layout | Snapshot test | Use visual regression snapshot; not a traditional assertion |
| Requires human judgment to evaluate | No (charter follow-up) | If even a human is uncertain whether behavior is correct, automation cannot assert it |
| Security-boundary (auth bypass, privilege escalation) | Yes (priority 1) | Security regressions are critical; automate as unit or integration test immediately |

**Session sheet to test case translation rule**: for each defect candidate, the session sheet should contain enough context to write the test case:
1. **Preconditions** → `beforeEach()` setup block
2. **Steps to reproduce** → `act` phase of Arrange-Act-Assert
3. **Expected behavior** (oracle dimension) → `expect()` assertion
4. **Actual behavior** (what was wrong) → comment explaining what the test guards against

**TypeScript: Session-Defect-to-Test-Stub Generator**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/defect-to-test-stub.ts
// Generates a Vitest/Jest test stub from a structured session defect candidate.
// The tester fills in the arrange/act/assert details; the stub provides the skeleton.

export interface DefectCandidate {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  oracleDimension: string;  // e.g., "Claims", "History", "User expectations"
  preconditions: string[];
  stepsToReproduce: string[];
  expectedBehavior: string;
  actualBehavior: string;
  severity: 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
  fixCommit?: string;
}

export function generateTestStub(defect: DefectCandidate): string {
  const testName = `[regression] ${defect.id}: ${defect.title}`;
  const preconditionComments = defect.preconditions
    .map((p) => `  //   - ${p}`)
    .join('\n');
  const stepsComments = defect.stepsToReproduce
    .map((s, i) => `  // ${i + 1}. ${s}`)
    .join('\n');

  return `
// AUTO-GENERATED from exploratory session defect candidate ${defect.id}
// Oracle: ${defect.oracleDimension} | Severity: ${defect.severity}
// Fix commit: ${defect.fixCommit ?? 'TODO: add fix commit hash'}
//
// EXPECTED: ${defect.expectedBehavior}
// ACTUAL (before fix): ${defect.actualBehavior}
//
// DO NOT DELETE — this test guards against regression of ${defect.id}.

import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

describe('${testName}', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Arrange: set up preconditions
${preconditionComments}
    // TODO: implement setup
  });

  it('${defect.expectedBehavior}', async () => {
    // Act: reproduce the steps that triggered the defect
${stepsComments}
    // TODO: implement act

    // Assert: verify the fix holds
    // expect(result).toBe(/* expected value */);
    // TODO: implement assertion based on expected: "${defect.expectedBehavior}"
  });
});
`.trimStart();
}

// Usage:
// const stub = generateTestStub({
//   id: 'DEF-2026-0142',
//   title: 'Guest email with + alias causes account creation failure',
//   oracleDimension: 'Claims',
//   preconditions: ['User is on guest checkout page', 'No account exists for the email'],
//   stepsToReproduce: ['Enter email "user+tag@domain.com"', 'Click Continue'],
//   expectedBehavior: 'Guest checkout proceeds normally for email aliases',
//   actualBehavior: '500 error: "Invalid email format" despite RFC 5321 compliance',
//   severity: 'high',
// });
// writeFileSync(`test/regression/${stub_id}.test.ts`, stub);
```

### SCAN Heuristic for Exploratory Charter Coverage  [community]

SCAN (Structure, Capability, Attributes, Non-functional) is a complementary coverage heuristic to FEW HICCUPS. Where FEW HICCUPS is a breadth-first mnemonic covering diverse test areas, SCAN is a depth-first framework for ensuring that each charter probes the feature at multiple quality dimensions rather than just the happy path.

| SCAN dimension | What to probe | Common coverage gap |
|---------------|--------------|-------------------|
| **Structure** | Data shape, schemas, object graph validity, field types, nesting limits, empty/null states | Tests only populated fields; never probes empty collections, null FK references, or deeply nested objects |
| **Capability** | Core functional behaviors, business rules, state transitions, permission boundaries | Tests only the primary actor (admin); never probes low-privilege users, service accounts, or cross-tenant scenarios |
| **Attributes** | User-facing quality properties: error messages, loading states, help text accuracy, accessibility labels, i18n strings | Tests only the "happy path" UI; never checks error messages, ARIA labels, or locale formatting |
| **Non-functional** | Performance under load, security boundaries, recovery from failure, concurrent access | Tests only single-user, no-load, no-failure scenarios; never probes multi-user or degraded conditions |

**SCAN applied to a charter review**: after writing a charter, run it through the SCAN checklist — does the "to discover Z" statement cover at least one SCAN dimension explicitly? If all four charters for a feature probe only "Capability" (does it do the right thing?), coverage is skewed: the team has no sessions on Structure (can it handle malformed input?), Attributes (do the error messages match the spec?), or Non-functional (does it degrade gracefully under load?).

**YAML: SCAN coverage audit for a charter set**

```yaml
# SCAN coverage audit: payment-flow charter set
# Run this review before the sprint demo to verify no quality dimension is unprobed.

charter_set: payment-flow
sprint: 2026-05-13

scan_coverage:
  structure:
    charters_covering: [CHR-pay-003]  # schema validation for payment payload
    gaps:
      - "No charter probes null billing_address (optional field in spec, crashes on null)"
      - "No charter probes line_items with 0 quantity or negative price"

  capability:
    charters_covering: [CHR-pay-001, CHR-pay-002, CHR-pay-004]
    gaps: []  # well-covered: happy path, declined card, retry flow

  attributes:
    charters_covering: [CHR-pay-005]  # error message wording
    gaps:
      - "No charter checks ARIA live region on payment-processing spinner"
      - "No charter verifies i18n decimal separator in EUR vs USD amounts"

  non_functional:
    charters_covering: []
    gaps:
      - "No charter probes concurrent checkout from the same user session (race condition risk)"
      - "No charter probes behavior when payment gateway returns 504 (timeout)"

recommended_new_charters:
  - id: CHR-pay-006
    explore: "payment payload structure edge cases"
    with: "null billing_address, 0-quantity line items, negative price inputs"
    to_discover: "whether the API returns structured 400 errors or 500s for each invalid shape"
    scan_dimension: structure
    priority: high

  - id: CHR-pay-007
    explore: "payment gateway timeout behavior"
    with: "simulated 504 from gateway mock, user mid-checkout"
    to_discover: "whether the UI presents a recoverable error, whether the charge is idempotently guarded, and whether the order state is consistent"
    scan_dimension: non_functional
    priority: high
```

### Mind Map Structure for a TypeScript Application  [community]

Mind maps for exploratory session planning work best when they mirror the application's actual architecture rather than its menu structure. For a TypeScript application, the natural mental model is the module/route graph: each module is a branch, and each branch contains coverage leaves (SCAN dimensions) that become individual sessions.

**YAML mind map schema for sprint planning:**

```yaml
# exploratory-mind-map.yaml
# Sprint: 2026-05-13 — Coverage planning before session scheduling.
# Each leaf node is a potential charter; checked: true means a session exists.

feature_area: checkout-flow
sprint: 2026-05-13

branches:
  - name: Guest Checkout
    module: src/checkout/guest
    risk: high  # new feature, zero prior sessions
    leaves:
      - area: email validation (RFC 5321 compliance, + aliases, IDN domains)
        scan: structure
        session_planned: true
        charter_id: CHR-checkout-001
      - area: address form (autocomplete, international postal codes, PO Box)
        scan: structure
        session_planned: true
        charter_id: CHR-checkout-002
      - area: guest-to-account upgrade path after order completion
        scan: capability
        session_planned: false
        charter_id: null  # GAP — no session planned
      - area: error message accuracy (payment failure, address validation, OOS)
        scan: attributes
        session_planned: false
        charter_id: null  # GAP

  - name: Payment Processing
    module: src/checkout/payment
    risk: critical
    leaves:
      - area: card validation (Luhn, expiry, CVV length)
        scan: structure
        session_planned: true
        charter_id: CHR-pay-001
      - area: declined card recovery flow
        scan: capability
        session_planned: true
        charter_id: CHR-pay-002
      - area: concurrent checkout race condition
        scan: non_functional
        session_planned: false
        charter_id: null  # GAP — high-risk uncovered

  - name: Order Confirmation
    module: src/checkout/confirmation
    risk: medium
    leaves:
      - area: email confirmation delivery and content
        scan: attributes
        session_planned: true
        charter_id: CHR-confirm-001

coverage_summary:
  total_leaves: 8
  planned_sessions: 4
  coverage_pct: 50
  high_risk_gaps:
    - "Guest-to-account upgrade path (new feature, no session)"
    - "Concurrent checkout race condition (critical module, no session)"
  recommended_action: "Schedule CHR-checkout-003 and CHR-pay-007 before sprint demo"
```

**TypeScript: Mind Map Gap Analyzer**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/mind-map-gap-analyzer.ts
// Reads the exploratory mind map YAML and surfaces unpanned leaves
// by risk priority for sprint planning.

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { parse } from 'yaml'; // npm: yaml

interface MindMapLeaf {
  area: string;
  scan: 'structure' | 'capability' | 'attributes' | 'non_functional';
  session_planned: boolean;
  charter_id: string | null;
}

interface MindMapBranch {
  name: string;
  module: string;
  risk: 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
  leaves: MindMapLeaf[];
}

interface MindMap {
  feature_area: string;
  sprint: string;
  branches: MindMapBranch[];
}

export interface CoverageGap {
  branch: string;
  leaf: string;
  scan: string;
  risk: string;
  suggestedCharterId: string;
}

export function analyzeGaps(mindMapPath: string): CoverageGap[] {
  const raw = readFileSync(mindMapPath, 'utf-8');
  const map = parse(raw) as MindMap;
  const gaps: CoverageGap[] = [];
  let gapSeq = 1;

  const riskOrder = { critical: 0, high: 1, medium: 2, low: 3 };

  for (const branch of map.branches) {
    for (const leaf of branch.leaves) {
      if (!leaf.session_planned) {
        gaps.push({
          branch: branch.name,
          leaf: leaf.area,
          scan: leaf.scan,
          risk: branch.risk,
          suggestedCharterId: `CHR-gap-${gapSeq++}`,
        });
      }
    }
  }

  return gaps.sort(
    (a, b) => riskOrder[a.risk as keyof typeof riskOrder] - riskOrder[b.risk as keyof typeof riskOrder]
  );
}

// Usage:
// const gaps = analyzeGaps('exploratory-mind-map.yaml');
// gaps.forEach((g) => console.log(`[${g.risk.toUpperCase()}] ${g.branch} > ${g.leaf} (${g.scan}) — ${g.suggestedCharterId}`));
// → [CRITICAL] Payment Processing > Concurrent checkout race condition (non_functional) — CHR-gap-1
// → [HIGH] Guest Checkout > guest-to-account upgrade path (capability) — CHR-gap-2
// → [HIGH] Guest Checkout > error message accuracy (attributes) — CHR-gap-3
```
