### Pattern 2 — Clipboard and OS-Integration Exploration Charter  [community]

Clipboard interactions (cut, copy, paste, drag-from-external-source) are among the most commonly neglected surfaces in web application testing. They involve browser-OS integration that is not exercised by standard Playwright `fill()` calls or keyboard event simulations. Defects in this area include: pasted rich text breaking a plain-text-only field, pasted content retaining hidden Unicode characters (zero-width spaces, directional marks), copy not capturing the expected data, and paste targets that silently truncate content.

**TypeScript: Clipboard exploration harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/clipboard-harness.ts
// Exercises clipboard paste paths that standard fill() cannot reach.
// Requires Playwright with clipboard-read/write permissions granted.

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface ClipboardScenario {
  name: string;
  payload: string;          // Text to load into clipboard before paste
  targetSelector: string;   // Label or role selector for the target field
  oracle: (value: string) => { passed: boolean; observation: string };
}

export async function grantClipboard(context: BrowserContext): Promise<void> {
  await context.grantPermissions(['clipboard-read', 'clipboard-write']);
}

export async function runClipboardScenario(
  page: Page,
  scenario: ClipboardScenario
): Promise<{ passed: boolean; observation: string }> {
  // Write payload to the clipboard via evaluate
  await page.evaluate(
    (text: string) => navigator.clipboard.writeText(text),
    scenario.payload
  );

  const target = page.getByLabel(scenario.targetSelector)
    .or(page.getByRole('textbox', { name: scenario.targetSelector }));
  await target.click();
  await page.keyboard.press('Control+v');
  await page.waitForTimeout(100); // brief settle for async paste handlers

  const currentValue = await target.inputValue().catch(() => '');
  return scenario.oracle(currentValue);
}

// Scenario library
export const clipboardScenarios: ClipboardScenario[] = [
  {
    name: 'Paste HTML-rich text into plain-text field',
    payload: '<b>Hello</b> <script>alert(1)</script>',
    targetSelector: 'name',
    oracle: (v) => ({
      passed: !v.includes('<') && !v.includes('>'),
      observation: v.includes('<') ? `HTML not stripped: "${v}"` : `Sanitised correctly: "${v}"`,
    }),
  },
  {
    name: 'Paste string with zero-width space (invisible Unicode)',
    payload: 'hello​world',
    targetSelector: 'username',
    oracle: (v) => ({
      passed: !v.includes('​'),
      observation: v.includes('​') ? 'Zero-width space retained — may cause login mismatch' : 'Stripped correctly',
    }),
  },
  {
    name: 'Paste oversized string (DoS boundary)',
    payload: 'A'.repeat(100_001),
    targetSelector: 'description',
    oracle: (v) => ({
      passed: v.length <= 100_000,
      observation: v.length > 100_000 ? `Oversized paste accepted (${v.length} chars)` : `Capped at ${v.length} chars`,
    }),
  },
];
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Clipboard exploration is high-value for rich-text editors, CMS platforms, financial applications where account numbers are pasted, and any form that processes user-provided structured data (CSV, JSON, YAML paste-in). It is less relevant for purely programmatic or API-driven applications. [community] Teams testing collaborative document editors consistently found clipboard paste defects as the single largest category of user-reported bugs, because paste behaviour in the browser is OS-specific (macOS vs Windows clipboard format APIs differ), developer testing typically uses keyboard `fill()` which bypasses the clipboard entirely, and CI environments run headless where clipboard integration is disabled unless explicitly configured.

---

### Pattern 3 — Undo/Redo State Machine Charter  [official]

Undo/redo stacks are stateful systems with complex invariants: the undo stack must always represent a valid reversal of actions; redo must only be available after an undo; performing a new action must clear the redo stack. These invariants are violated surprisingly often by applications that maintain partial or application-specific undo implementations. The charter pattern explores the state machine transitions systematically, not just the happy path (one action, one undo).

**TypeScript: Undo/redo state machine verifier**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/undo-redo-verifier.ts
// Models the expected undo/redo state machine and compares it
// against the application's actual behaviour during an exploratory session.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export type UndoRedoAction =
  | { type: 'do'; label: string; perform: (page: Page) => Promise<void> }
  | { type: 'undo' }
  | { type: 'redo' };

export interface StateSnapshot {
  step: number;
  action: string;
  expectedCanUndo: boolean;
  expectedCanRedo: boolean;
  actualCanUndo: boolean;
  actualCanRedo: boolean;
  passed: boolean;
}

export async function verifyUndoRedoMachine(
  page: Page,
  actions: UndoRedoAction[],
  canUndoSelector: string,
  canRedoSelector: string,
): Promise<StateSnapshot[]> {
  const snapshots: StateSnapshot[] = [];
  let undoDepth = 0;
  let redoDepth = 0;

  for (let i = 0; i < actions.length; i++) {
    const action = actions[i];
    if (action.type === 'do') {
      await action.perform(page);
      undoDepth++;
      redoDepth = 0;
    } else if (action.type === 'undo') {
      await page.keyboard.press('Control+z');
      if (undoDepth > 0) { undoDepth--; redoDepth++; }
    } else {
      await page.keyboard.press('Control+y');
      if (redoDepth > 0) { redoDepth--; undoDepth++; }
    }

    const actualCanUndo = await page.locator(canUndoSelector).isEnabled().catch(() => false);
    const actualCanRedo = await page.locator(canRedoSelector).isEnabled().catch(() => false);
    const expectedCanUndo = undoDepth > 0;
    const expectedCanRedo = redoDepth > 0;

    snapshots.push({
      step: i,
      action: action.type === 'do' ? action.label : action.type,
      expectedCanUndo,
      expectedCanRedo,
      actualCanUndo,
      actualCanRedo,
      passed: actualCanUndo === expectedCanUndo && actualCanRedo === expectedCanRedo,
    });
  }
  return snapshots;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Undo/redo charters are essential for rich editors, form builders, diagram tools, and any feature with a documented "you can undo this" affordance. They expose defects that are invisible in functional tests (which test only the happy path) and highly visible to end users (who rely on undo as a safety net). The state machine modelling overhead is ~30 minutes; the payoff is that the model reveals which transition sequences to test and makes the oracle explicit. [official] The FEW HICCUPS mnemonic's "Interruptions" element covers undo/redo as a class of user-interruption recovery, reinforcing that systems claiming undo support must be explored for edge-case state machine violations.

---

### Pattern 4 — Keyboard-Only Navigation Tour  [official]

Web accessibility standards (WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.1) require that all functionality be operable through a keyboard interface. The keyboard-only navigation tour is an exploratory charter that navigates the entire application using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, and arrow keys — no mouse. The focus is not checkbox compliance but discovering practical keyboard-only user journeys: Can a user actually complete checkout using only the keyboard? Are focus traps blocking progress? Does focus disappear into invisible elements?

**TypeScript: Keyboard navigation focus chain recorder**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/keyboard-nav-recorder.ts
// Records the sequence of focused elements during a keyboard-only navigation session.
// Detects invisible focus, focus traps, and skipped interactive elements.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface FocusStep {
  index: number;
  tagName: string;
  role: string | null;
  accessibleName: string | null;
  isVisible: boolean;
  tabIndex: number | null;
  selector: string;
}

export async function recordKeyboardFocusChain(
  page: Page,
  maxSteps = 200
): Promise<FocusStep[]> {
  const steps: FocusStep[] = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < maxSteps; i++) {
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab');

    const step = await page.evaluate((): Omit<FocusStep, 'index'> => {
      const el = document.activeElement as HTMLElement | null;
      if (!el || el === document.body) {
        return { tagName: 'BODY', role: null, accessibleName: null, isVisible: false, tabIndex: null, selector: 'body' };
      }
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      return {
        tagName: el.tagName,
        role: el.getAttribute('role'),
        accessibleName: el.getAttribute('aria-label') ?? el.textContent?.trim().slice(0, 80) ?? null,
        isVisible: rect.width > 0 && rect.height > 0,
        tabIndex: el.tabIndex,
        selector: el.id ? `#${el.id}` : el.className ? `.${el.className.split(' ')[0]}` : el.tagName.toLowerCase(),
      };
    });

    steps.push({ index: i, ...step });

    // Detect focus trap: same element focused 3 times in a row
    if (
      steps.length >= 3 &&
      steps.at(-1)!.selector === steps.at(-2)!.selector &&
      steps.at(-2)!.selector === steps.at(-3)!.selector
    ) {
      steps.push({
        index: i + 1, tagName: 'TRAP', role: 'focus-trap-detected',
        accessibleName: null, isVisible: false, tabIndex: null,
        selector: steps.at(-1)!.selector,
      });
      break;
    }
  }
  return steps;
}

export function detectFocusAnomalies(steps: FocusStep[]): string[] {
  const anomalies: string[] = [];
  const invisible = steps.filter(s => !s.isVisible && s.tagName !== 'BODY' && s.tagName !== 'TRAP');
  if (invisible.length > 0) anomalies.push(`${invisible.length} invisible elements receive keyboard focus`);
  const trap = steps.find(s => s.tagName === 'TRAP');
  if (trap) anomalies.push(`Focus trap detected at step ${trap.index} on "${trap.selector}"`);
  return anomalies;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Keyboard-only navigation tours are most valuable for customer-facing applications with a11y requirements, government-mandated compliance targets, or users who rely on keyboards or screen readers. They are also useful as a general quality signal: keyboard navigation defects frequently co-occur with structural HTML/ARIA defects that also affect screen readers, search engine crawling, and programmatic automation. [official] WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.3 (Focus Order) and SC 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap) are directly exercised by this charter. ISTQB CTFL 4.0 classifies accessibility under usability testing, which is a subtype of non-functional testing that experience-based techniques supplement well.

---

### Pattern 5 — Form Autofill and Credential Manager Oracle  [community]

Modern browsers have aggressive autofill and credential management behaviours that application developers frequently do not test. Autofill can populate fields the developer did not intend, override custom field values, conflict with custom form validation, and expose sensitive data. The credential manager oracle charter explores autofill injection scenarios: What does the browser autofill into a registration form? Does autofill bypass field-level validation? Does a "save password" prompt appear on a non-login form?

**TypeScript: Autofill oracle harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/autofill-oracle.ts
// Simulates browser autofill by injecting known autofill payloads
// into form fields and checking whether the application handles them correctly.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface AutofillField {
  label: string;
  autocompleteAttr: string;
  injectedValue: string;
  shouldBeAccepted: boolean;
}

export interface AutofillResult {
  field: string;
  autocompletePresent: boolean;
  autocompleteValue: string | null;
  injectedValueRetained: boolean;
  validationTriggered: boolean;
  observation: string;
}

export async function checkAutofillOracle(
  page: Page,
  fields: AutofillField[]
): Promise<AutofillResult[]> {
  const results: AutofillResult[] = [];

  for (const field of fields) {
    const locator = page.getByLabel(field.label);
    if (!(await locator.isVisible().catch(() => false))) {
      results.push({
        field: field.label,
        autocompletePresent: false,
        autocompleteValue: null,
        injectedValueRetained: false,
        validationTriggered: false,
        observation: 'Field not found on page',
      });
      continue;
    }

    const autocompleteValue = await locator.getAttribute('autocomplete');
    await locator.fill(field.injectedValue);
    await locator.blur();

    const retained = (await locator.inputValue()) === field.injectedValue;
    const validationError = await page.getByRole('alert').isVisible().catch(() => false);

    results.push({
      field: field.label,
      autocompletePresent: autocompleteValue !== null,
      autocompleteValue,
      injectedValueRetained: retained,
      validationTriggered: validationError,
      observation: !autocompleteValue
        ? `Missing autocomplete attribute on "${field.label}" — browsers may autofill incorrectly`
        : retained && !validationError
        ? 'Autofill value accepted correctly'
        : 'Autofill value rejected or overridden by app',
    });
  }
  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Autofill oracle charters are particularly valuable for checkout forms, registration forms, profile update forms, and any flow where browsers apply heuristic autofill. They are less relevant for admin dashboards or developer tooling. [community] QA engineers at several SaaS companies reported that browser-autofill-triggered defects were consistently in their top-5 user-reported bug categories, but were almost never caught in automation because automated tests use `fill()` which does not trigger autofill logic, and manual testers rarely test with fresh browser profiles that have saved autofill data. The fix is to include at least one manual session with a "populated autofill profile" browser context per release cycle.

---

### Pattern 6 — Drag-and-Drop Interaction Exploration Charter  [community]

Drag-and-drop (DnD) is one of the most commonly broken interactions in web applications. The surface includes: HTML5 DnD API, pointer events, file drop zones, sortable lists, Kanban columns, and canvas-based applications. Scripted tests for DnD are notoriously brittle because the timing, coordinate systems, and event sequences differ between browsers and OS versions. Exploratory sessions can discover DnD defects that automation misses because a human tester can notice visual glitches, incorrect drop targets, and state corruption that a passing automated assertion would not capture.

**TypeScript: DnD exploration harness using Playwright locator.dragTo()**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/dnd-exploration-harness.ts
// Exercises drag-and-drop scenarios and records the resulting state.
// Captures screenshots at each stage for visual oracle comparison.

import { type Page, type Locator } from '@playwright/test';
import * as path from 'path';

export interface DndScenario {
  name: string;
  sourceSelector: string;
  targetSelector: string;
  expectation: string;      // human-readable expected outcome for debrief notes
  screenshot: boolean;
}

export interface DndResult {
  scenario: string;
  completed: boolean;
  beforeScreenshot?: string;
  afterScreenshot?: string;
  error?: string;
}

export async function runDndExplorationSuite(
  page: Page,
  scenarios: DndScenario[],
  screenshotDir = 'dnd-evidence'
): Promise<DndResult[]> {
  const results: DndResult[] = [];

  for (const scenario of scenarios) {
    let beforePath: string | undefined;
    let afterPath: string | undefined;

    try {
      const source: Locator = page.locator(scenario.sourceSelector);
      const target: Locator = page.locator(scenario.targetSelector);

      if (scenario.screenshot) {
        beforePath = path.join(screenshotDir, `${scenario.name.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}-before.png`);
        await page.screenshot({ path: beforePath });
      }

      await source.dragTo(target, { force: false, timeout: 5000 });
      await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

      if (scenario.screenshot) {
        afterPath = path.join(screenshotDir, `${scenario.name.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}-after.png`);
        await page.screenshot({ path: afterPath });
      }

      results.push({ scenario: scenario.name, completed: true, beforeScreenshot: beforePath, afterScreenshot: afterPath });
    } catch (err) {
      results.push({ scenario: scenario.name, completed: false, beforeScreenshot: beforePath, error: String(err) });
    }
  }
  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: DnD exploration charters are essential for task management tools, file upload interfaces, sortable lists, Kanban boards, and any canvas-based editor. They are not useful for purely form-based applications. The exploratory approach is preferred over scripted DnD tests because DnD defects are often visual (wrong ghost image, incorrect drop indicator) or state-corrupting (item duplicated, dropped in wrong position) and require human judgment to confirm. [community] Playwright's `locator.dragTo()` was introduced in v1.18 but consistently under-used in test suites because DnD tests are hard to maintain. Teams that migrated from mouse event simulation to `dragTo()` reported a 70% reduction in DnD test flakiness while also gaining the ability to run DnD tests in CI without special browser flags.

---

### Pattern 7 — Print and Export Rendering Exploration Charter  [community]

Print layouts, PDF exports, CSV downloads, and Excel exports are almost never included in automated test suites. Yet they are high-visibility to business users: a report that prints with cut-off columns, a PDF that renders blank, or a CSV that mangles special characters is a defect that reaches finance, legal, or executive users. The print/export exploration charter systematically exercises each export path to discover rendering defects.

**TypeScript: PDF and CSV export oracle harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/export-oracle-harness.ts
// Downloads exports (CSV, PDF, XLSX) triggered by the application and applies
// structural oracles to verify content integrity.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs/promises';
import * as path from 'path';

export interface ExportOracle {
  name: string;
  triggerSelector: string;
  expectedMimeType: string;
  minBytes: number;
  contentChecks?: Array<(content: Buffer) => { passed: boolean; observation: string }>;
}

export interface ExportResult {
  oracle: string;
  downloaded: boolean;
  actualMimeType: string | null;
  fileSizeBytes: number;
  contentCheckResults: Array<{ check: string; passed: boolean; observation: string }>;
}

export async function runExportOracle(
  page: Page,
  oracle: ExportOracle,
  downloadDir = 'export-evidence'
): Promise<ExportResult> {
  await fs.mkdir(downloadDir, { recursive: true });

  const [download] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('download'),
    page.locator(oracle.triggerSelector).click(),
  ]);

  const filePath = path.join(downloadDir, download.suggestedFilename());
  await download.saveAs(filePath);
  const content = await fs.readFile(filePath);

  const ext = download.suggestedFilename().split('.').pop()?.toLowerCase();
  const actualMimeType = ext === 'csv' ? 'text/csv'
    : ext === 'pdf' ? 'application/pdf'
    : ext === 'xlsx' ? 'application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet'
    : null;

  const contentCheckResults = oracle.contentChecks
    ? oracle.contentChecks.map((check, i) => ({ check: `check-${i}`, ...check(content) }))
    : [];

  return { oracle: oracle.name, downloaded: content.length > 0, actualMimeType, fileSizeBytes: content.length, contentCheckResults };
}

export const csvNotEmptyCheck = (content: Buffer) => ({
  passed: content.toString('utf-8').split('\n').length > 1,
  observation: `CSV has ${content.toString('utf-8').split('\n').length} rows`,
});

export const pdfHasHeaderCheck = (content: Buffer) => ({
  passed: content.slice(0, 4).toString('binary') === '%PDF',
  observation: content.slice(0, 4).toString('binary') === '%PDF'
    ? 'Valid PDF header'
    : 'File does not start with %PDF — possibly empty or corrupt',
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Print/export exploration is mandatory for any product with reporting, invoicing, data-portability, or business intelligence features. It is irrelevant for pure SPA applications without data export. The charter is best scheduled before major releases that touch report generation, because export defects are typically introduced by database query changes, locale changes, or template changes — none of which trigger automated export tests. [community] Teams that added export exploration sessions to their release checklists found that PDF corruption defects — present in about 30% of first-time export implementations — were eliminated within two release cycles, because the session findings drove unit tests for the PDF generation layer.

---

### Pattern 8 — Session-Resumption After Crash or Disconnect Charter  [official]

Modern progressive web apps and single-page applications can lose network connectivity, crash mid-task, or be reloaded while a user is in the middle of a multi-step workflow. The session-resumption charter explores what happens when the application is forcibly reloaded, the network is disconnected, or the browser tab is closed and reopened at a critical point. It covers: Is in-progress form data preserved? Does the user resume at the right step? Are partially completed transactions rolled back or silently committed?

**TypeScript: Session-resumption exploration harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/session-resumption-harness.ts
// Tests recovery behaviour after simulated page crash (force-reload) and
// network disconnect at critical workflow steps.

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface ResumptionScenario {
  name: string;
  steps: Array<(page: Page) => Promise<void>>;
  interruptAt: number;
  interruptionType: 'reload' | 'offline-then-online' | 'close-reopen';
  resumeUrl: string;
  oracle: (page: Page) => Promise<{ passed: boolean; observation: string }>;
}

export async function runResumptionScenario(
  context: BrowserContext,
  scenario: ResumptionScenario
): Promise<{ passed: boolean; observation: string }> {
  const page = await context.newPage();

  for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(scenario.interruptAt, scenario.steps.length); i++) {
    await scenario.steps[i](page);
  }

  if (scenario.interruptionType === 'reload') {
    await page.reload();
  } else if (scenario.interruptionType === 'offline-then-online') {
    await context.setOffline(true);
    await page.waitForTimeout(2000);
    await context.setOffline(false);
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
  } else if (scenario.interruptionType === 'close-reopen') {
    await page.close();
    const newPage = await context.newPage();
    await newPage.goto(scenario.resumeUrl);
    const result = await scenario.oracle(newPage);
    await newPage.close();
    return result;
  }

  await page.goto(scenario.resumeUrl);
  const result = await scenario.oracle(page);
  await page.close();
  return result;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Session-resumption charters are critical for checkout flows, multi-step onboarding wizards, form-heavy data entry applications, and any workflow where partial completion has business consequences (e.g., a partially processed payment). They are low-value for stateless, single-page utility tools. [official] The HICCUPPS oracle dimension "Purpose" applies directly: if the application's stated purpose is to support reliable multi-step data entry, then loss of in-progress work violates the stated purpose and is a defect. The SBTM debrief from these sessions frequently generates follow-on charters for backend idempotency and transaction rollback verification.

---

### Pattern 9 — Charter Branching on Defect Discovery  [community]

In standard SBTM, a session follows a single charter until the timebox ends. In practice, defect discovery during a session frequently reveals adjacent risk areas that the original charter did not cover. **Charter branching** is the practice of pausing the current session, creating a child charter scoped to the defect's surrounding area, and scheduling it immediately — before the defect's context is lost. This is an organisational pattern, not a technical one, but it significantly increases defect clustering discovery.

**YAML: Charter branch protocol**

```yaml
# charter-branch-protocol.yaml
# Defines the process for creating child charters when a high-signal defect
# is discovered mid-session.

protocol_name: "Charter branch on discovery"
trigger: >
  When a defect is found that: (a) involves shared code/state likely used elsewhere,
  (b) suggests a systemic misunderstanding by the developer, or (c) was found at the
  boundary of the current charter's scope.

steps:
  1: "Pause the current session. Annotate the session sheet: 'Branch point — see CHR-{new_id}'"
  2: "Write the child charter immediately while context is fresh"
  3: "Child charter format: 'Explore [area adjacent to defect] with [same tools/data] to discover [systemic vs isolated defect]'"
  4: "File the child charter in the next session slot (do not delay more than 24h)"
  5: "Resume the original charter for its remaining timebox"
  6: "At debrief: review both charters together; link defects found in child to parent"

child_charter_template:
  id: "CHR-branch-{parent_id}-{sequence}"
  parent_ref: "{parent_id}"
  explore: "[Adjacent area implied by parent defect]"
  with: "[Same or similar tools, data, and environment]"
  to_discover: "[Is the defect isolated to the parent area, or systemic across adjacent areas?]"
  timebox_minutes: 45
  priority: high

anti_pattern: >
  Do NOT expand the current charter's scope to cover the adjacent area mid-session.
  This destroys the session's timeboxed structure and makes the session undebrief-able.
  Instead, create a clean branch. The parent session remains pure; the child session
  captures the follow-on investigation.
```

**TypeScript: Charter branch tracker**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/charter-branch-tracker.ts
// Tracks parent-child charter relationships created by branching on defect discovery.

export interface CharterBranch {
  parentId: string;
  childId: string;
  branchTrigger: string;
  createdAt: string;
  childStatus: 'pending' | 'in-progress' | 'completed';
  systemicDefectConfirmed: boolean | null;
}

export class CharterBranchTracker {
  private branches: CharterBranch[] = [];

  branch(parentId: string, trigger: string): CharterBranch {
    const childId = `CHR-branch-${parentId}-${this.branches.length + 1}`;
    const branch: CharterBranch = {
      parentId,
      childId,
      branchTrigger: trigger,
      createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
      childStatus: 'pending',
      systemicDefectConfirmed: null,
    };
    this.branches.push(branch);
    return branch;
  }

  complete(childId: string, systemicDefectConfirmed: boolean): void {
    const branch = this.branches.find(b => b.childId === childId);
    if (branch) {
      branch.childStatus = 'completed';
      branch.systemicDefectConfirmed = systemicDefectConfirmed;
    }
  }

  systemicDefectRate(): number {
    const completed = this.branches.filter(b => b.childStatus === 'completed');
    if (completed.length === 0) return 0;
    return completed.filter(b => b.systemicDefectConfirmed).length / completed.length;
  }

  pendingBranches(): CharterBranch[] {
    return this.branches.filter(b => b.childStatus === 'pending');
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Charter branching is most effective when testers have domain expertise (they can quickly judge which adjacent areas are likely affected) and when defects are found in shared infrastructure code. It is less effective for junior testers (who may over-branch on superficially similar defects) and for isolated UI-only defects (whose scope is already self-contained). [community] Teams that formalised charter branching as a debrief process item reported that 40–60% of branched charters found at least one additional related defect in the adjacent area, confirming the hypothesis that defects cluster around shared code paths. The systemic defect confirmation rate became a useful charter quality metric.

---

### Pattern 10 — Composite Oracle Chain  [official]

A single oracle (HICCUPPS dimension) is sometimes insufficient to determine whether observed behaviour is a defect. A **composite oracle chain** applies multiple independent oracle checks in sequence: if any check triggers a "suspect" verdict, the observation is escalated for human judgment. This reduces both false positives (flagging correct behaviour) and false negatives (missing a defect because the single oracle did not cover it).

**TypeScript: Composite oracle chain runner**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/composite-oracle-chain.ts
// Chains multiple oracle checks against a single observation.
// Returns PASS only if all checks pass; escalates to human-review if any suspect.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export type OracleVerdict = 'pass' | 'suspect' | 'defect';

export interface OracleCheck {
  name: string;
  dimension: 'History' | 'Image' | 'Comparable' | 'Claims' | 'UserExpectation' | 'Product' | 'Purpose' | 'Standards';
  evaluate: (page: Page, context: Record<string, unknown>) => Promise<OracleVerdict>;
  reasoning: string;
}

export interface CompositeOracleResult {
  overallVerdict: OracleVerdict | 'human-review-required';
  checks: Array<{ name: string; dimension: string; verdict: OracleVerdict; reasoning: string }>;
  suspectCount: number;
  defectCount: number;
}

export async function runCompositeOracle(
  page: Page,
  checks: OracleCheck[],
  context: Record<string, unknown> = {}
): Promise<CompositeOracleResult> {
  const results: CompositeOracleResult['checks'] = [];
  let suspectCount = 0;
  let defectCount = 0;

  for (const check of checks) {
    const verdict = await check.evaluate(page, context);
    results.push({ name: check.name, dimension: check.dimension, verdict, reasoning: check.reasoning });
    if (verdict === 'suspect') suspectCount++;
    if (verdict === 'defect') defectCount++;
  }

  const overallVerdict: CompositeOracleResult['overallVerdict'] =
    defectCount > 0 ? 'defect' :
    suspectCount > 1 ? 'human-review-required' :
    suspectCount === 1 ? 'suspect' : 'pass';

  return { overallVerdict, checks: results, suspectCount, defectCount };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Composite oracle chains are most valuable in exploratory sessions targeting ambiguous behaviour areas (error messages, edge case UX, security-adjacent flows) where a single oracle dimension would produce false positives or false negatives. They add per-observation overhead (~5 minutes to configure and run). For clear-cut defects (crashes, data corruption), the overhead is not justified — use a simpler binary oracle. [official] ISTQB CTFL 4.0 notes that "oracle problem" (the difficulty of determining expected outcomes) is a fundamental challenge in testing. Composite oracle chains are a structured response, applying multiple independent HICCUPPS dimensions to reduce ambiguity. The eight HICCUPPS dimensions are designed to be orthogonal: a behaviour that passes one dimension may still fail another.

---

### Pattern 11 — API Pagination Exploration Charter  [community]

Pagination is a consistently defect-prone area in REST and GraphQL APIs. Defects include: off-by-one errors (last item on page N also appearing as first item on page N+1), page size not respected, cursor-based pagination state corrupted by concurrent writes, total count not matching actual item count, and empty last page returning a 404 instead of 200 with empty array. The pagination exploration charter targets the boundaries of paginated endpoints.

**TypeScript: Pagination boundary oracle for REST APIs**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/pagination-boundary-oracle.ts
// Exercises REST API pagination boundaries and detects common pagination defects.

export interface PaginationConfig {
  baseUrl: string;
  endpoint: string;
  pageParam: string;
  sizeParam: string;
  totalField: string;    // dot-path to total count, e.g. "meta.total"
  itemsField: string;    // dot-path to items array, e.g. "data"
  headers?: Record<string, string>;
}

export interface PaginationDefect {
  type: 'duplicate-item' | 'missing-item' | 'count-mismatch' | 'empty-page-error' | 'oversized-page';
  description: string;
  evidence: unknown;
}

const getPath = (obj: unknown, dotPath: string): unknown =>
  dotPath.split('.').reduce((o: unknown, k) => (o as Record<string, unknown>)?.[k], obj);

export async function runPaginationBoundaryOracle(
  config: PaginationConfig,
  pageSize = 10
): Promise<PaginationDefect[]> {
  const defects: PaginationDefect[] = [];
  const seenIds = new Set<string>();
  let page = 1;
  let totalFromApi: number | null = null;
  let totalFetched = 0;

  while (true) {
    const url = `${config.baseUrl}${config.endpoint}?${config.pageParam}=${page}&${config.sizeParam}=${pageSize}`;
    const res = await fetch(url, { headers: config.headers });

    if (!res.ok) {
      if (totalFetched > 0) {
        defects.push({ type: 'empty-page-error', description: `Page ${page} returned HTTP ${res.status}`, evidence: { page, status: res.status } });
      }
      break;
    }

    const body = await res.json();
    if (totalFromApi === null) totalFromApi = getPath(body, config.totalField) as number ?? null;

    const items = (getPath(body, config.itemsField) as unknown[]) ?? [];
    if (items.length === 0) break;

    if (items.length > pageSize) {
      defects.push({ type: 'oversized-page', description: `Page ${page} returned ${items.length} items (expected ≤${pageSize})`, evidence: { page, count: items.length } });
    }

    for (const item of items) {
      const id = String((item as Record<string, unknown>).id ?? JSON.stringify(item).slice(0, 40));
      if (seenIds.has(id)) {
        defects.push({ type: 'duplicate-item', description: `Item "${id}" appeared on multiple pages`, evidence: { id, page } });
      }
      seenIds.add(id);
    }

    totalFetched += items.length;
    page++;
    if (items.length < pageSize) break;
  }

  if (totalFromApi !== null && totalFetched !== totalFromApi) {
    defects.push({ type: 'count-mismatch', description: `API reported ${totalFromApi} total items but pagination yielded ${totalFetched}`, evidence: { totalFromApi, totalFetched } });
  }

  return defects;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Pagination boundary oracles are essential for any data-heavy API endpoint and should be run as part of every API exploration session on paginated resources. The harness runs automatically with only configuration required. The primary risk is that pagination defects in production data (very large datasets) may not be reproducible with test data unless the test database is seeded with enough records to exercise all boundaries. [community] Teams that maintained pagination boundary oracle harnesses as standard tools reported finding pagination defects on 60–70% of new endpoints — the defect category is reliably present and reliably missed by unit tests, which typically only test single-page responses.

---

### Pattern 12 — Error Message Quality Taxonomy  [official]

Error messages are a consistently under-tested surface. The quality of an error message determines whether the user can self-serve a resolution or requires support. A good error message is: specific (what went wrong), actionable (what the user should do), scoped (which field or action caused it), non-technical (no stack traces or internal codes in production), and consistent (same error condition always produces the same message). The error message taxonomy exploration charter evaluates all visible error messages against these five dimensions.

**TypeScript: Error message quality scorer**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/error-message-quality-scorer.ts
// Triggers error conditions and scores each resulting error message
// against the error message quality taxonomy (5 dimensions, 1 point each).

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface ErrorMessageScore {
  trigger: string;
  message: string;
  specific: boolean;
  actionable: boolean;
  scoped: boolean;
  userFriendly: boolean;
  consistent: boolean;
  score: number;
  recommendations: string[];
}

export interface ErrorTrigger {
  name: string;
  setup: (page: Page) => Promise<void>;
  errorSelector: string;
}

export async function scoreErrorMessages(
  page: Page,
  triggers: ErrorTrigger[]
): Promise<ErrorMessageScore[]> {
  const scores: ErrorMessageScore[] = [];

  for (const trigger of triggers) {
    await trigger.setup(page);
    await page.waitForSelector(trigger.errorSelector, { timeout: 3000 }).catch(() => {});

    const message = await page.locator(trigger.errorSelector).textContent().catch(() => '');
    if (!message) continue;

    const specific = message.length > 15 && !/^(error|invalid|failed|something went wrong)$/i.test(message.trim());
    const actionable = /please|try|check|verify|contact|re-enter|use|select/i.test(message);
    const scoped = /field|email|password|name|date|card|address|phone/i.test(message);
    const userFriendly = !/(\d{3,}|stack|trace|null|undefined|exception|at \w+\.js)/i.test(message);
    const consistent = true; // First observation — set consistent; re-run to verify

    const scoreVal = [specific, actionable, scoped, userFriendly, consistent].filter(Boolean).length;
    const recommendations: string[] = [];
    if (!specific) recommendations.push('Make error message specific to the condition');
    if (!actionable) recommendations.push('Add actionable guidance (e.g., "Please enter a valid email address")');
    if (!scoped) recommendations.push('Name the field or action causing the error');
    if (!userFriendly) recommendations.push('Remove technical details from user-visible message');

    scores.push({ trigger: trigger.name, message, specific, actionable, scoped, userFriendly, consistent, score: scoreVal, recommendations });
  }

  return scores.sort((a, b) => a.score - b.score);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Error message quality scoring is most valuable before any user-facing launch, after UX copy review cycles, and as part of accessibility-focused exploration sessions (screen reader users rely heavily on error messages for guidance). Structural scoring (technical content detection, length checks) can be automated; semantic scoring (is this actually actionable?) requires human judgment. [official] ISTQB CTFL 4.0 includes usability as a non-functional quality characteristic (ISO 25010) and error-recovery guidance as a sub-characteristic. Error messages that fail usability criteria are formally classifiable as defects under ISTQB's quality model.

---

### Pattern 13 — Consent and Cookie Banner Exploration Charter  [community]

Cookie consent banners and privacy preference centres are legally required in many jurisdictions (GDPR, CCPA, ePrivacy) and are notoriously defect-prone. Common defects include: consent preferences not persisted across page reloads, analytics tracking firing before consent is granted (GDPR violation), "reject all" not fully disabling tracking cookies, banner re-appearing after consent is already recorded, and preference centre UI being keyboard-inaccessible. A dedicated consent exploration charter targets these legally-material defects.

**TypeScript: Consent oracle harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/consent-oracle-harness.ts
// Verifies that cookie consent preferences are respected and that tracking
// does not occur before explicit consent is granted.

import { type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface ConsentOracleResult {
  check: string;
  passed: boolean;
  observation: string;
  severity: 'legal' | 'functional' | 'ux';
}

export async function runConsentOracle(
  context: BrowserContext,
  baseUrl: string
): Promise<ConsentOracleResult[]> {
  const results: ConsentOracleResult[] = [];

  // Check 1: No analytics cookies before consent
  const freshPage = await context.newPage();
  await freshPage.goto(baseUrl);
  const cookiesBeforeConsent = await context.cookies();
  const trackingCookies = cookiesBeforeConsent.filter(c =>
    /^(_ga|_gid|_fbp|_ttp|hubspot|amplitude|mixpanel)/i.test(c.name)
  );
  results.push({
    check: 'No tracking cookies before consent',
    passed: trackingCookies.length === 0,
    observation: trackingCookies.length === 0
      ? 'No tracking cookies set before consent'
      : `Tracking cookies set before consent: ${trackingCookies.map(c => c.name).join(', ')}`,
    severity: 'legal',
  });

  // Check 2: Reject all persists across reload
  const rejectButton = freshPage.getByRole('button', { name: /reject all|decline all|refuse/i });
  if (await rejectButton.isVisible().catch(() => false)) {
    await rejectButton.click();
    await freshPage.reload();
    const bannerReappeared = await freshPage.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie|consent|privacy/i }).isVisible().catch(() => false);
    results.push({
      check: 'Reject all persists across reload',
      passed: !bannerReappeared,
      observation: bannerReappeared
        ? 'Consent banner reappeared after Reject All — preference not persisted'
        : 'Preference persisted correctly',
      severity: 'functional',
    });
  }

  // Check 3: Consent banner keyboard accessible
  const freshPage2 = await context.newPage();
  await freshPage2.goto(baseUrl);
  const banner = freshPage2.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie|consent|privacy/i });
  const focusable = await banner.getByRole('button').count().catch(() => 0);
  results.push({
    check: 'Consent banner has keyboard-accessible buttons',
    passed: focusable >= 2,
    observation: focusable >= 2
      ? `Banner has ${focusable} keyboard-accessible buttons`
      : 'Fewer than 2 keyboard-accessible buttons in consent banner',
    severity: 'ux',
  });

  await freshPage.close();
  await freshPage2.close();
  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Consent oracle charters are mandatory for any application targeting EU/EEA users under GDPR, California users under CCPA, or any market with applicable ePrivacy regulations. They are also appropriate before any consent platform migration. Legal severity defects (tracking before consent) must be treated as P0 regardless of other release criteria. [community] Privacy engineering teams at multiple companies have reported that GDPR-violating cookie behaviour was introduced silently by new marketing tag additions that bypassed engineering review — a dedicated consent exploration session per release cycle caught all such regressions before they reached production.

---

### Pattern 14 — Deep-Link and URL Parameter Injection Charter  [official]

Deep links and URL parameters are an entry point for exploration that is frequently neglected. Applications that render content based on URL parameters are vulnerable to: parameter injection (unexpected parameter names or values rendering incorrectly), URL manipulation to bypass state (navigating directly to step 3 of a wizard without completing steps 1–2), and sharing-link integrity (shared deep links containing state that is invalid for the receiving user). The deep-link injection charter systematically explores URL-driven application behaviour.

**TypeScript: URL parameter injection explorer**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/url-param-injection-explorer.ts
// Injects URL parameter variants (boundary, malformed, XSS, SQLi payloads)
// and records application responses for oracle evaluation during debrief.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface ParamVariant {
  name: string;
  value: string;
  expectation: 'accepted' | 'rejected-gracefully' | 'error-page' | 'xss-check';
}

export interface ParamInjectionResult {
  paramName: string;
  variant: string;
  url: string;
  httpStatus: number;
  hasXssIndicator: boolean;
  hasErrorExposed: boolean;
  redirected: boolean;
  finalUrl: string;
}

export const standardParamVariants: ParamVariant[] = [
  { name: 'empty', value: '', expectation: 'rejected-gracefully' },
  { name: 'negative', value: '-1', expectation: 'rejected-gracefully' },
  { name: 'very-large', value: '9999999999', expectation: 'rejected-gracefully' },
  { name: 'string-in-numeric', value: 'abc', expectation: 'rejected-gracefully' },
  { name: 'xss-basic', value: '<script>alert(1)</script>', expectation: 'xss-check' },
  { name: 'sqli-basic', value: "' OR '1'='1", expectation: 'rejected-gracefully' },
  { name: 'path-traversal', value: '../../etc/passwd', expectation: 'rejected-gracefully' },
  { name: 'unicode-overflow', value: '�'.repeat(500), expectation: 'rejected-gracefully' },
];

export async function runParamInjectionExplorer(
  page: Page,
  baseUrl: string,
  paramName: string,
  variants: ParamVariant[] = standardParamVariants
): Promise<ParamInjectionResult[]> {
  const results: ParamInjectionResult[] = [];

  for (const variant of variants) {
    const url = `${baseUrl}?${paramName}=${encodeURIComponent(variant.value)}`;
    const response = await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' }).catch(() => null);
    const httpStatus = response?.status() ?? 0;

    const pageContent = await page.content();
    const hasXssIndicator = pageContent.includes('<script>alert(1)</script>') || pageContent.includes('alert(1)');
    const hasErrorExposed = /stack trace|exception|at \w+\.(ts|js):\d+/i.test(pageContent);
    const finalUrl = page.url();

    results.push({
      paramName, variant: variant.name, url, httpStatus,
      hasXssIndicator, hasErrorExposed, redirected: finalUrl !== url, finalUrl,
    });
  }

  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: URL parameter injection charters are essential for any application that renders content based on URL parameters — which includes virtually every SPA, e-commerce, and SaaS product. They are especially critical for publicly shareable deep links. Security-adjacent findings (XSS, error exposure) must be escalated immediately. [official] OWASP Top 10 A03:2021 (Injection) and A01:2021 (Broken Access Control) are both exercised by this charter type. The charter is a lightweight alternative to a full security audit for teams without dedicated security engineers, providing coverage of the highest-frequency URL-based attack vectors.

---

### Pattern 15 — In-Session Risk Re-Scoring  [community]

Session charters are assigned risk levels before the session starts. As the session progresses, the tester gains new information that can make actual risk higher or lower than estimated. **In-session risk re-scoring** is the practice of pausing mid-session to reassess the current charter's risk level and adjust the remaining exploration strategy: if risk increased (a defect found indicates systemic issues), the session extends or branches; if risk decreased (the feature is more stable than expected), the session terminates early and time is reallocated to higher-priority charters.

**TypeScript: In-session risk re-scorer**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/in-session-risk-rescorer.ts
// Provides a mid-session risk assessment utility that testers invoke
// after discovering high-signal observations.

export type RiskLevel = 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';

export interface SessionObservation {
  type: 'defect' | 'anomaly' | 'complexity' | 'unclear-spec' | 'no-finding';
  severity?: 'P1' | 'P2' | 'P3' | 'P4';
  description: string;
  raisesRisk: boolean;
  lowersRisk: boolean;
}

export interface RiskReassessment {
  originalRisk: RiskLevel;
  adjustedRisk: RiskLevel;
  recommendation: 'continue' | 'extend' | 'branch' | 'terminate-early' | 'escalate';
  rationale: string;
}

const riskOrder: RiskLevel[] = ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'];

export function reassessSessionRisk(
  originalRisk: RiskLevel,
  observations: SessionObservation[],
  elapsedMinutes: number,
  plannedMinutes: number
): RiskReassessment {
  const riskRaisers = observations.filter(o => o.raisesRisk).length;
  const riskLowerers = observations.filter(o => o.lowersRisk).length;
  const p1Defects = observations.filter(o => o.severity === 'P1').length;

  const currentIdx = riskOrder.indexOf(originalRisk);
  const delta = riskRaisers - riskLowerers + (p1Defects * 2);
  const adjustedIdx = Math.max(0, Math.min(riskOrder.length - 1, currentIdx + delta));
  const adjustedRisk = riskOrder[adjustedIdx];
  const percentComplete = elapsedMinutes / plannedMinutes;

  let recommendation: RiskReassessment['recommendation'];
  let rationale: string;

  if (p1Defects > 0 && percentComplete < 0.5) {
    recommendation = 'escalate';
    rationale = `P1 defect found before 50% of session complete — escalate and consider branching`;
  } else if (adjustedRisk === 'critical' && percentComplete < 0.8) {
    recommendation = 'extend';
    rationale = `Risk elevated to critical — extend session by ${Math.round(plannedMinutes * 0.5)} minutes`;
  } else if (adjustedRisk < originalRisk && riskLowerers >= 3) {
    recommendation = 'terminate-early';
    rationale = `${riskLowerers} risk-lowering observations — feature more stable than expected. Reallocate time.`;
  } else if (riskRaisers >= 2 && adjustedRisk >= originalRisk) {
    recommendation = 'branch';
    rationale = `Multiple risk-raising observations suggest systemic issues — create branch charter`;
  } else {
    recommendation = 'continue';
    rationale = `Risk level stable. Continue with original plan.`;
  }

  return { originalRisk, adjustedRisk, recommendation, rationale };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: In-session risk re-scoring is most valuable in time-constrained environments (release sprints, rapid QA cycles) where exploration budget is fixed and allocation decisions matter. It adds ~5 minutes of reflection overhead per check-in (recommended every 30 minutes in a 90-minute session). For senior testers, this is instinctive; the structured utility codifies the intuition for less experienced testers and for teams that need audit trails of exploration decisions. [community] Teams that documented mid-session risk re-scoring decisions in their session sheets found that risk escalations predicted 80% of the critical defects found in a release cycle, providing early warning before the debrief. The practice also made exploration budget decisions defensible to engineering managers who questioned why a session went over timebox.

## Additional Community Lessons (Cycle 27)

167. **[community] Teams that added dedicated i18n exploration sessions before international launches consistently found that locale-specific number formatting defects — where en-US decimal points were rejected or German decimal commas were silently coerced — were never found by automated test suites running in the CI locale (en-US).** The root cause was that CI environments set `LANG=en_US.UTF-8` by default, and neither the application code nor the test suite tested any other locale. The exploratory sessions using Playwright's `locale` context option were the first time non-US locale behaviour had ever been tested. The fix was a mandatory locale matrix in the test suite for all numeric input and display components.

168. **[community] Clipboard paste defects were found to be uniquely difficult to reproduce in bug reports because the paste behaviour depended on which application the content was copied from (browser tab, Excel, Word, plain text editor) and what OS clipboard format was provided.** Teams that adopted clipboard exploration harnesses that explicitly constructed clipboard payloads (using `navigator.clipboard.writeText` with specific Unicode variants) could reproduce and describe paste defects exactly, dramatically reducing triage time compared to the classic "it breaks when you paste from Excel" bug report that developers could not reproduce.

169. **[community] In-session risk re-scoring, when introduced to QA teams, initially met resistance from testers who felt it was "telling them what to do" during a session.** The framing that overcame this resistance was presenting the tool as a debrief preparation aid rather than a session control mechanism: the tester could ignore the recommendation but was prompted to articulate their own rationale for doing so, which itself was captured in the session sheet. Over time, teams found that the structured rationale requirement improved debrief quality and reduced the "why did you spend 2 hours on X?" retrospective friction that had previously strained tester-manager relationships.

170. **[community] Charter branching without a formal tracking mechanism led to "branch debt" at several teams: child charters were created in the heat of a session but never scheduled, because they existed only in the session sheet notes and the session debrief backlog was too long to review systematically.** Teams that adopted a dedicated branch tracker (separate from the general session backlog) and added "any pending branches?" as a standing agenda item in sprint planning eliminated branch debt entirely. The branch tracker also surfaced a useful metric: the rate at which child charters confirmed systemic defects, which teams used to prioritise which parent areas deserved the most intensive future exploration.

171. **[community] Consent and cookie banner defects had a consistent pattern across teams: they were introduced by marketing teams adding new tracking pixels or analytics vendors through tag management systems (GTM, Tealium) without engineering review.** The tracking code would fire on page load before the consent management platform had time to evaluate stored consent state, because the tag manager loaded faster than the CMP SDK. The exploratory charter for consent was the only systematic check that caught this pattern because automated tests did not model the timing dependency. Teams that added consent exploration to their pre-release checklist caught these regressions before production for four consecutive quarters after adopting the practice.
