### Pattern 6 — Intersection Observer Lazy-Load Fidelity Charter  [community]

Modern applications use `IntersectionObserver` for lazy-loading images, infinite scroll, and ad impression tracking. Defects are consistently under-tested: images that never load after the user scrolls past them without triggering the threshold, viewport-edge elements that never receive `isIntersecting = true` due to threshold rounding, and infinite-scroll containers that emit duplicate load events when scrolling rapidly.

**TypeScript: Intersection observer fidelity harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/intersection-observer-oracle.ts
// Scrolls through a lazily-loaded list at varying velocities and verifies
// that all intersecting elements are eventually loaded. Intercepts the
// IntersectionObserver constructor to count callbacks and detect duplicates.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface LazyLoadScenario {
  description: string;
  containerSelector: string;
  lazyItemSelector: string;
  loadedStateAttribute: string;  // e.g. 'src' for images, 'data-loaded' for custom
  scrollVelocityPx: number;
  expectedItemCount: number;
}

export interface LazyLoadOracleResult {
  scenario: string;
  itemsLoaded: number;
  itemsUnloaded: number;
  duplicateEventCount: number;
  allItemsEventuallyLoaded: boolean;
}

export async function runLazyLoadOracle(
  page: Page,
  scenario: LazyLoadScenario
): Promise<LazyLoadOracleResult> {
  await page.evaluate((lazySelector) => {
    (window as any).__ioCallbackCount = 0;
    const OriginalIO = window.IntersectionObserver;
    window.IntersectionObserver = class extends OriginalIO {
      constructor(cb: IntersectionObserverCallback, opts?: IntersectionObserverInit) {
        super((entries, obs) => {
          entries.forEach((e) => {
            if (e.isIntersecting) (window as any).__ioCallbackCount++;
          });
          cb(entries, obs);
        }, opts);
      }
    };
  }, scenario.lazyItemSelector);

  const scrollHeight: number = await page.evaluate(
    (sel) => document.querySelector(sel)?.scrollHeight ?? 0,
    scenario.containerSelector
  );

  let scrollPos = 0;
  while (scrollPos < scrollHeight) {
    await page.evaluate(
      ({ sel, pos }) => document.querySelector(sel)?.scrollTo({ top: pos }),
      { sel: scenario.containerSelector, pos: scrollPos }
    );
    scrollPos += scenario.scrollVelocityPx;
    await page.waitForTimeout(50);
  }

  await page.waitForTimeout(1500);

  const itemsLoaded = await page.locator(
    `${scenario.containerSelector} ${scenario.lazyItemSelector}[${scenario.loadedStateAttribute}]`
  ).count().catch(() => 0);

  const ioCallbackCount: number = await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__ioCallbackCount ?? 0);
  const duplicateEventCount = Math.max(0, ioCallbackCount - scenario.expectedItemCount);

  return {
    scenario: scenario.description,
    itemsLoaded,
    itemsUnloaded: scenario.expectedItemCount - itemsLoaded,
    duplicateEventCount,
    allItemsEventuallyLoaded: itemsLoaded >= scenario.expectedItemCount,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: IntersectionObserver fidelity charters are high-value for applications with lazy-loaded image galleries, infinite scroll, or ad impression tracking. Especially important after changes to container CSS (`overflow`, `position`) or observer threshold values. Do NOT substitute for visual inspection at various scroll velocities — the TypeScript harness catches event-count defects but cannot verify whether loaded images render correctly. Named alternative: Lighthouse "Defer offscreen images" audit flags lazy-load configuration issues at load time but does not simulate scroll-triggered behavioral defects. [community]

---

### Pattern 7 — Web Animation and Reduced Motion Accessibility Charter  [official]

CSS animations, JavaScript Web Animations API sequences, and transition effects can cause vestibular disorders in users with motion sensitivities. The `prefers-reduced-motion` media query is the standard mitigation — but it is frequently implemented incompletely: applied to some components, ignored in third-party widgets, and bypassed by JavaScript animation libraries (GSAP, Framer Motion, Lottie) that check no CSS variable.

**YAML charter template**

```yaml
charter:
  id: CHR-reduced-motion-001
  explore: >
    All animated components and page transitions under
    prefers-reduced-motion: reduce media query condition
  using: >
    Playwright page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' });
    manual scroll through all major page sections;
    keyboard navigation through interactive components;
    SPA route transitions (navigate between 3+ routes);
    modal open/close animations; notification enter/exit;
    loading spinners and skeleton screens;
    carousel and slider components;
    browser DevTools Animation panel to capture keyframes still running
  toDiscover: >
    Whether any animation continues to run under reduced-motion;
    whether SPA route transitions are instant or still animated;
    whether third-party widgets (chat, cookie banner) honour the preference;
    whether JavaScript-driven animations check the media query;
    whether layout breaks when animations are removed (animation-fill-mode
    dependency: forwards, backwards, both)
  risk: medium
  timebox: 60min
  animation_categories:
    - page_transitions: SPA route changes
    - entrance_animations: content that animates in on first render
    - interaction_feedback: hover, focus, active state transitions
    - async_indicators: loading spinners, progress bars, skeleton screens
    - decorative: background particles, parallax, scroll-driven animations
  oracle: >
    Standards (WCAG 2.1 SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions — Level AAA),
    Claims (product accessibility statement),
    Purpose (application must be fully usable without motion)
  debrief_questions:
    - Did any animation continue to run despite reduced-motion being set?
    - Did any layout break when animations were suppressed?
    - Were third-party widget animations exempt from the reduced-motion preference?
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Reduced motion charters are required for any application with an accessibility commitment (WCAG AA or above). Use `page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })` in Playwright — it correctly sets the media query at the browser level. Do NOT assume a CSS-only `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` rule covers all animations — JavaScript animation libraries must be audited separately. Named alternative: Axe accessibility scanner flags missing reduced-motion support as a violation but cannot simulate the actual animation behavior; this charter provides the complementary behavioral verification. [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — Concurrent Form Submission Race Condition Charter  [community]

Race conditions in form submission are a pervasive defect class: double-click on Submit, navigation away mid-submission, submission while background validation is in flight, or two tabs submitting simultaneously. Applications that do not guard against concurrent submission produce duplicate records, orphaned transactions, or inconsistent state. This charter explores the submission lifecycle under concurrency stress.

**TypeScript: Concurrent submission race oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/concurrent-submission-oracle.ts
// Submits the same form twice in rapid succession (simulating double-click or
// double-tap) and verifies that the application produces exactly one side effect.
// Also tests mid-submission navigation (form submit + immediate goto).

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface SubmissionScenario {
  description: string;
  formUrl: string;
  fillForm: (page: Page) => Promise<void>;
  submitSelector: string;
  verifyExactlyOneRecord: (page: Page) => Promise<boolean>;
}

export interface ConcurrentSubmissionResult {
  scenario: string;
  doubleClickProducedDuplicate: boolean;
  buttonDisabledAfterFirstClick: boolean;
  midNavigationSubmissionHandled: boolean;
}

export async function runConcurrentSubmissionOracle(
  context: BrowserContext,
  scenario: SubmissionScenario
): Promise<ConcurrentSubmissionResult> {
  // Test 1: double-click produces single submission
  const page1 = await context.newPage();
  await page1.goto(scenario.formUrl);
  await scenario.fillForm(page1);
  const button = page1.locator(scenario.submitSelector);
  await button.click();
  const disabledAfterFirst = await button.isDisabled().catch(() => false);
  await button.click({ force: true }).catch(() => { /* may be disabled — expected */ });
  await page1.waitForTimeout(2000);
  const doubleClickProducedDuplicate =
    !(await scenario.verifyExactlyOneRecord(page1).catch(() => false));

  // Test 2: navigate away while submission is in-flight
  const page2 = await context.newPage();
  await page2.goto(scenario.formUrl);
  await scenario.fillForm(page2);
  await page2.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 500));
    await route.continue();
  });
  await page2.locator(scenario.submitSelector).click();
  await page2.goto(scenario.formUrl); // navigate away immediately
  const midNavigationSubmissionHandled = await page2
    .getByRole('alert')
    .filter({ hasText: /saved|pending|incomplete/i })
    .count()
    .then((c) => c >= 0)
    .catch(() => false);

  await page1.close();
  await page2.close();

  return {
    scenario: scenario.description,
    doubleClickProducedDuplicate,
    buttonDisabledAfterFirstClick: disabledAfterFirst,
    midNavigationSubmissionHandled,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Concurrent submission charters are mandatory for any form that creates, modifies, or deletes records — especially financial transactions, user registration, and subscription management. Do NOT substitute for idempotency key implementation in the API — the charter discovers the problem; the server-side fix requires idempotency keys or unique constraint enforcement. Named alternative: Stripe, Braintree, and most payment APIs provide idempotency key support; this charter verifies the UI-layer submit guard is also in place as defense-in-depth. [community]

---

### Pattern 9 — File System Access API Exploration Charter  [official]

The File System Access API (`showOpenFilePicker`, `showSaveFilePicker`, `showDirectoryPicker`) gives web applications direct read/write access to the local file system. It introduces a unique exploratory surface: permission revocation mid-session, concurrent writes from another application, and large-file handling without progress indication. These scenarios are entirely absent from typical scripted test suites because they require OS-level coordination.

**YAML charter template**

```yaml
charter:
  id: CHR-file-system-access-001
  explore: >
    File System Access API integration across open, save,
    and directory-picker flows in the document editor feature
  using: >
    Playwright File Chooser intercept for picker dialogs;
    test files: 0-byte, 1-byte, simulated 4 GB (sparse file),
    no extension, MIME type mismatch (image.jpg containing MP4 data),
    read-only (chmod 444), file on a network/SMB share;
    file rename simulation during active session;
    OS-specific path separators (Windows backslash vs Unix forward slash)
  toDiscover: >
    Whether a 0-byte file is handled gracefully (no crash, clear message);
    whether a 4 GB file triggers a progress indicator or freezes the UI;
    whether renaming the underlying file while it is open produces a
    recoverable error rather than an unhandled exception;
    whether MIME type mismatch is detected and communicated;
    whether the save dialog re-opens if the write fails;
    whether read-only file attempts produce a clear permission error;
    whether unsaved work is preserved if the write fails
  risk: high
  timebox: 75min
  test_files:
    - zero_bytes: empty file
    - tiny: 1 byte, valid content type
    - huge: simulated large sparse file
    - no_extension: file without extension
    - mime_mismatch: image.jpg that contains MP4 data
    - read_only: system read-only attribute set
  oracle: >
    Claims (File System Access API spec — FileSystemSyncAccessHandle error types),
    User expectations (write failure must not silently discard unsaved work),
    Purpose (application must remain stable when OS-level file operations fail)
  debrief_questions:
    - Was unsaved work preserved if the write failed?
    - Did any OS path separator cause a defect on Windows?
    - Was the 4 GB file handled with a progress indicator?
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: File System Access API charters are mandatory for any web application offering direct file open/save functionality (code editors, document editors, design tools). This API is not available in Firefox or Safari without a polyfill — cross-browser testing is essential. Do NOT defer this charter post-release — File System Access API defects are difficult to reproduce in production without the exact OS, file system, and file conditions. [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — Mutation Observer and DOM Stability Oracle  [community]

Applications that dynamically modify the DOM (infinite scroll, virtual lists, real-time dashboards) have a class of defects detectable only by watching the mutation stream: elements inserted in wrong order, elements removed while the user is interacting (focus loss), aria-live regions flooded causing screen-reader storms, and MutationObserver callbacks that trigger recursive DOM changes causing stack overflows.

**TypeScript: DOM mutation stability oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/dom-mutation-oracle.ts
// Attaches a MutationObserver to a dynamic container and records mutation
// counts, rates, and aria-live flooding to surface DOM instability:
// runaway mutation loops, excessive aria-live updates, focus-stealing insertions.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface MutationStabilityResult {
  scenario: string;
  totalMutations: number;
  ariaLiveUpdates: number;
  mutationRatePerSecond: number;
  runawayLoopDetected: boolean;
  focusStealingDetected: boolean;
  largestSingleBatchSize: number;
}

export async function runDomMutationOracle(
  page: Page,
  containerSelector: string,
  observationWindowMs: number,
  journeyAction: (page: Page) => Promise<void>,
  description = 'DOM mutation stability check'
): Promise<MutationStabilityResult> {
  await page.evaluate((sel) => {
    (window as any).__mutationLog = { total: 0, ariaLive: 0, batches: [] as number[] };
    const container = document.querySelector(sel);
    if (!container) return;
    const obs = new MutationObserver((records) => {
      const log = (window as any).__mutationLog;
      log.total += records.length;
      log.batches.push(records.length);
      for (const rec of records) {
        if (rec.type === 'childList' && rec.target instanceof Element) {
          const live = rec.target.getAttribute('aria-live');
          if (live === 'polite' || live === 'assertive') log.ariaLive++;
        }
      }
    });
    obs.observe(container, { childList: true, subtree: true, attributes: true });
    (window as any).__mutationObserverRef = obs;
  }, containerSelector);

  const startTime = Date.now();
  await journeyAction(page);
  await page.waitForTimeout(observationWindowMs);
  const elapsedMs = Date.now() - startTime;

  const log: { total: number; ariaLive: number; batches: number[] } =
    await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__mutationLog ?? { total: 0, ariaLive: 0, batches: [] });
  await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__mutationObserverRef?.disconnect());

  const mutationRatePerSecond = (log.total / elapsedMs) * 1000;
  const largestSingleBatchSize = log.batches.length > 0 ? Math.max(...log.batches) : 0;
  const runawayLoopDetected = mutationRatePerSecond > 200;

  const focusStealingDetected = await page.evaluate(
    () => document.activeElement === document.body
  ).catch(() => false);

  return {
    scenario: description,
    totalMutations: log.total,
    ariaLiveUpdates: log.ariaLive,
    mutationRatePerSecond,
    runawayLoopDetected,
    focusStealingDetected,
    largestSingleBatchSize,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: DOM mutation oracle charters are high-value for real-time dashboards, live chat interfaces, live search, and virtual list implementations. Apply after any change to a WebSocket-fed UI component or an aria-live region. Do NOT instrument the entire document body — scope the observer to the smallest container possible to avoid noise from unrelated parts of the page. Named alternative: Chrome DevTools Performance tab records DOM mutations in the flame chart but requires manual analysis; this harness provides automated anomaly detection. [community]

---

### Pattern 11 — Feature Deprecation and Sunset Warning Charter  [official]

Applications deprecate features gradually: API endpoints with deprecation headers, in-app banners, or admin config options hidden before removal. Exploratory charters for deprecation verification ensure that sunset messages appear at the right time, the deprecated path still works during transition, and the replacement path is correctly linked. Teams that skip this charter discover post-sunset that some users were still on the deprecated path and received no warning.

**YAML charter template**

```yaml
charter:
  id: CHR-feature-deprecation-001
  explore: >
    Deprecation and sunset communication for the v1 order API
    and the legacy CSV export flow scheduled for removal in v2.0
  using: >
    API calls to v1 endpoints to verify deprecation headers
    (Deprecation, Sunset, Link headers per RFC 8594);
    authenticated user sessions accessing the legacy CSV export UI;
    user accounts at different ages (new, 6-month, 1-year dormant)
    to verify personalised deprecation messaging; accessibility
    checker on all deprecation banner components
  toDiscover: >
    Whether all v1 endpoints return Deprecation and Sunset headers
    per RFC 8594 with the correct sunset date; whether the in-app
    deprecation banner is dismissible and whether dismiss state persists
    across sessions; whether dormant users still see the deprecation notice;
    whether the banner links to the migration guide correctly;
    whether the legacy flow remains functional during the transition
    period and fails gracefully after the sunset date
  risk: medium
  timebox: 60min
  deprecated_surfaces:
    - surface: v1 order API
      sunset_date: "2026-07-01"
      deprecation_header_path: /api/v1/orders
      replacement_path: /api/v2/orders
    - surface: legacy CSV export
      sunset_date: "2026-06-15"
      ui_path: /admin/exports/legacy
      replacement_path: /admin/exports
  oracle: >
    Claims (deprecation notices sent to users, API documentation),
    Standards (RFC 8594 — Deprecation header; RFC 8607 — Sunset header),
    History (previous deprecation cycles and user complaints)
  debrief_questions:
    - Did all deprecated endpoints return Deprecation and Sunset headers?
    - Was the banner dismiss state session-persistent?
    - Were dormant-account users correctly included in deprecation notifications?
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Feature deprecation charters are mandatory for any planned deprecation cycle and should be run immediately after deprecation notices are deployed — not only at the sunset date. Do NOT skip for API deprecations even when usage metrics show "zero clients" — monitoring gaps frequently undercount actual usage, and removing a "zero-usage" endpoint has caused production incidents at multiple teams. Named alternative: `deprecation-checker` CI tools scan code for deprecated API calls at build time; the charter provides the complementary runtime verification that notices reach users correctly. [official]

---

### Pattern 12 — Scroll Restoration and Navigation History Charter  [community]

SPAs with client-side routing (React Router, Next.js App Router, SvelteKit) frequently have defects in scroll restoration: navigating Back does not restore scroll position, navigating Forward to a dynamically-loaded list shows the top of the page, and manual `window.scrollTo(0,0)` calls fight with the browser's native scroll restoration. These defects are invisible to scripted tests because they require multi-step forward/back navigation sequences.

**TypeScript: Scroll restoration oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/scroll-restoration-oracle.ts
// Navigates through a multi-page flow, scrolling on each page, then navigates
// back and verifies scroll positions are correctly restored. Tests both
// browser-native restoration (history.scrollRestoration = 'auto') and
// SPA-managed restoration (history.scrollRestoration = 'manual').

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface ScrollRestorationScenario {
  description: string;
  steps: Array<{ url: string; scrollToY: number; description: string }>;
  backNavigationCount: number;
}

export interface ScrollRestorationResult {
  scenario: string;
  scrollPositionsByStep: Array<{
    url: string; expectedY: number; actualY: number; correct: boolean;
  }>;
  nativeScrollRestorationMode: string;
  allPositionsRestored: boolean;
}

export async function runScrollRestorationOracle(
  page: Page,
  scenario: ScrollRestorationScenario
): Promise<ScrollRestorationResult> {
  const scrollPositionsByStep: ScrollRestorationResult['scrollPositionsByStep'] = [];

  for (const step of scenario.steps) {
    await page.goto(step.url, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });
    await page.evaluate((y) => window.scrollTo({ top: y }), step.scrollToY);
    await page.waitForTimeout(300);
  }

  const nativeScrollRestorationMode: string =
    await page.evaluate(() => history.scrollRestoration ?? 'unknown');

  for (let i = 0; i < scenario.backNavigationCount; i++) {
    await page.goBack({ waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });
    await page.waitForTimeout(500);

    const currentUrl = page.url();
    const expectedStep = scenario.steps[scenario.steps.length - 1 - i];
    if (expectedStep) {
      const actualY: number = await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollY);
      scrollPositionsByStep.push({
        url: currentUrl,
        expectedY: expectedStep.scrollToY,
        actualY,
        correct: Math.abs(actualY - expectedStep.scrollToY) <= 50,
      });
    }
  }

  return {
    scenario: scenario.description,
    scrollPositionsByStep,
    nativeScrollRestorationMode,
    allPositionsRestored: scrollPositionsByStep.every((s) => s.correct),
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Scroll restoration charters are high-value for SPAs with content-heavy list pages (search results, product catalogs, news feeds) where users navigate away and return. Especially important after React Router version upgrades, Next.js App Router migrations, and when `history.scrollRestoration` is explicitly set to `'manual'` without a corresponding restore implementation. Do NOT overlook virtual list rendering interactions (react-virtual, tanstack-virtual) — virtual lists only render visible items, making scroll state restoration non-trivial. Named alternative: Next.js App Router has built-in scroll restoration; framework-native behavior should be verified before building custom logic. [community]

---

### Pattern 13 — Progressive Enhancement and JavaScript-Disabled Charter  [official]

Progressive enhancement requires that core application functionality is accessible without JavaScript. Modern SPAs rarely test this, and the gap between "works without JS" and "blank page" has widened as SSR hydration patterns become more complex. The JS-disabled charter explores which flows remain usable, what the no-JS fallback experience looks like, and whether security-critical functionality (auth, CSRF token submission) works without JavaScript.

**TypeScript: Progressive enhancement oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/progressive-enhancement-oracle.ts
// Navigates key application routes with JavaScript disabled and records
// what is rendered and what is interactive. Categorises each route as:
// fully functional | degraded-but-usable | broken | blank.

import { type Browser } from '@playwright/test';

export type EnhancementTier = 'fully-functional' | 'degraded-usable' | 'broken' | 'blank';

export interface ProgressiveEnhancementResult {
  route: string;
  tier: EnhancementTier;
  visibleTextLength: number;
  interactiveElementCount: number;
  formCount: number;
  headlineText: string;
  noscriptMessages: string[];
}

export async function runProgressiveEnhancementOracle(
  browser: Browser,
  baseUrl: string,
  routes: string[]
): Promise<ProgressiveEnhancementResult[]> {
  const context = await browser.newContext({ javaScriptEnabled: false });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  const results: ProgressiveEnhancementResult[] = [];

  for (const route of routes) {
    await page.goto(`${baseUrl}${route}`, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });

    const visibleTextLength: number =
      await page.evaluate(() => document.body?.innerText?.length ?? 0).catch(() => 0);

    const interactiveElementCount: number = await page.locator(
      'button:visible, a[href]:visible, input:visible, select:visible, textarea:visible'
    ).count().catch(() => 0);

    const formCount: number = await page.locator('form').count().catch(() => 0);

    const headlineText: string =
      await page.locator('h1').first().textContent().catch(() => '') ?? '';

    const noscriptMessages: string[] = await page.evaluate(() => {
      const el = document.querySelector('noscript');
      return el ? [el.textContent?.trim() ?? ''] : [];
    });

    let tier: EnhancementTier;
    if (visibleTextLength < 50 && interactiveElementCount === 0) tier = 'blank';
    else if (noscriptMessages.length > 0 && interactiveElementCount === 0) tier = 'broken';
    else if (interactiveElementCount > 0 && formCount > 0) tier = 'fully-functional';
    else tier = 'degraded-usable';

    results.push({
      route, tier, visibleTextLength, interactiveElementCount,
      formCount, headlineText, noscriptMessages,
    });
  }

  await context.close();
  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Progressive enhancement charters are mandatory for government and public-sector applications (legally required in many jurisdictions), applications with significant low-power device user bases, and applications serving users in high-latency environments where script loading fails. Do NOT skip after SSR framework migrations — hydration errors and FOUC are commonly introduced during Next.js, Remix, or SvelteKit migrations. Named alternative: WebAIM's Wave tool identifies no-JS rendering issues for static pages; the charter covers the dynamic multi-route application space that static analysis cannot. [official]

---

### Pattern 14 — Long Session Memory Leak Exploration Charter  [community]

Applications used continuously for hours (dashboards, monitoring tools, support interfaces, trading platforms) accumulate memory leaks visible only after sustained use: DOM nodes in detached trees, closure-captured event listener references preventing GC, and WebSocket subscriptions not cleaned up after component unmount. These defects are invisible to short scripted tests and only surface after 30–60 minutes of real use.

**TypeScript: Long session memory leak monitor**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/memory-leak-monitor.ts
// Takes periodic heap measurements during a sustained session and identifies
// leak candidates by growth trend. Uses Playwright's CDP session to capture
// JS heap statistics from the Performance.getMetrics CDP command.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface HeapSnapshot {
  timestampMs: number;
  usedJsHeapSizeMb: number;
  domNodeCount: number;
}

export interface MemoryLeakReport {
  durationMs: number;
  snapshots: HeapSnapshot[];
  heapGrowthMb: number;
  domGrowth: number;
  leakLikelyDetected: boolean;
  leakDescription: string;
}

export async function monitorSessionMemory(
  page: Page,
  sessionAction: (page: Page) => Promise<void>,
  intervalMs = 15_000,
  maxSnapshots = 20
): Promise<MemoryLeakReport> {
  const snapshots: HeapSnapshot[] = [];
  let cdp: import('@playwright/test').CDPSession | null = null;

  try {
    cdp = await page.context().newCDPSession(page);
    await cdp.send('Performance.enable');
  } catch { /* CDP unavailable — degrade gracefully */ }

  const startTime = Date.now();
  let snapshotCount = 0;

  async function takeSnapshot(): Promise<void> {
    if (snapshotCount++ >= maxSnapshots) return;
    let usedMb = 0;
    if (cdp) {
      try {
        const metrics = await cdp.send('Performance.getMetrics');
        const jsHeap = (metrics.metrics as any[]).find((m) => m.name === 'JSHeapUsedSize');
        usedMb = jsHeap ? jsHeap.value / 1_048_576 : 0;
      } catch { /* ignore CDP errors */ }
    }
    const domNodeCount: number =
      await page.evaluate(() => document.querySelectorAll('*').length).catch(() => 0);
    snapshots.push({ timestampMs: Date.now() - startTime, usedJsHeapSizeMb: usedMb, domNodeCount });
  }

  await takeSnapshot();
  const timer = setInterval(() => { takeSnapshot().catch(() => {}); }, intervalMs);
  await sessionAction(page);
  clearInterval(timer);
  await takeSnapshot();

  const durationMs = Date.now() - startTime;
  const first = snapshots[0];
  const last = snapshots[snapshots.length - 1];
  const heapGrowthMb = last.usedJsHeapSizeMb - first.usedJsHeapSizeMb;
  const domGrowth = last.domNodeCount - first.domNodeCount;
  const leakLikelyDetected = heapGrowthMb > 20 || domGrowth / (durationMs / 60_000) > 500;

  return {
    durationMs, snapshots, heapGrowthMb, domGrowth, leakLikelyDetected,
    leakDescription: leakLikelyDetected
      ? `Heap grew ${heapGrowthMb.toFixed(1)} MB; DOM grew ${domGrowth} nodes over ${(durationMs / 60_000).toFixed(1)} min`
      : 'No significant memory growth detected',
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Memory leak charters are essential for applications designed for extended sessions. Especially important after adding real-time WebSocket subscriptions, new React/Vue lifecycle logic, or migrating to a new state management library. Do NOT use heap size alone as the leak signal — GC can defer collection; trend over multiple snapshots is more reliable. Named alternative: Chrome Memory panel and Heap Snapshot viewer provide definitive manual analysis; this harness gives an automated trend signal during CI-level exploratory sessions. [community]

---

### Pattern 15 — API Rate Limiting and Throttle Behaviour Charter  [official]

APIs enforce rate limits to prevent abuse. Exploratory charters for rate limiting verify that: rate-limit headers are returned correctly (`X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `Retry-After`), the application displays a user-intelligible message on 429 rather than crashing, automatic retries honour the `Retry-After` interval, and different consumer tiers have correctly enforced limits. Silent 429 handling — where the UI appears to submit but the request is dropped — is a common defect causing silent data loss.

**TypeScript: API rate limit oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/rate-limit-oracle.ts
// Fires declaredLimitPerWindow + 3 requests to an endpoint and verifies:
// the (limit+1)th request returns 429, the response includes Retry-After,
// and no 2xx responses arrive after the declared limit is exceeded
// (which would indicate silent request dropping rather than 429 enforcement).

import { type APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface RateLimitScenario {
  description: string;
  endpoint: string;
  method: 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  body?: Record<string, unknown>;
  declaredLimitPerWindow: number;
  windowSeconds: number;
}

export interface RateLimitOracleResult {
  scenario: string;
  requestsFired: number;
  firstRateLimitedRequest: number | null;
  responsesWithCorrectLimitHeaders: number;
  retryAfterHeaderPresent: boolean;
  retryAfterValue: number | null;
  anyRequestSilentlyDropped: boolean;
  summaryStatuses: Record<number, number>;
}

export async function runRateLimitOracle(
  request: APIRequestContext,
  scenario: RateLimitScenario
): Promise<RateLimitOracleResult> {
  const totalRequests = scenario.declaredLimitPerWindow + 3;
  const summaryStatuses: Record<number, number> = {};
  let firstRateLimitedRequest: number | null = null;
  let correctHeaderCount = 0;
  let retryAfterHeaderPresent = false;
  let retryAfterValue: number | null = null;

  for (let i = 1; i <= totalRequests; i++) {
    const response = await (request as any)[scenario.method.toLowerCase()](
      scenario.endpoint,
      { headers: scenario.headers, data: scenario.body }
    );
    const status: number = response.status();
    summaryStatuses[status] = (summaryStatuses[status] ?? 0) + 1;

    if (status === 429 && firstRateLimitedRequest === null) {
      firstRateLimitedRequest = i;
      const retryAfter = response.headers()['retry-after'];
      retryAfterHeaderPresent = !!retryAfter;
      retryAfterValue = retryAfter ? parseInt(retryAfter, 10) : null;
    }

    const remaining = response.headers()['x-ratelimit-remaining'];
    const limit = response.headers()['x-ratelimit-limit'];
    if (remaining !== undefined && limit !== undefined) correctHeaderCount++;
  }

  const successCount = Object.entries(summaryStatuses)
    .filter(([s]) => parseInt(s) >= 200 && parseInt(s) < 300)
    .reduce((acc, [, c]) => acc + c, 0);
  const anyRequestSilentlyDropped = successCount > scenario.declaredLimitPerWindow;

  return {
    scenario: scenario.description,
    requestsFired: totalRequests,
    firstRateLimitedRequest,
    responsesWithCorrectLimitHeaders: correctHeaderCount,
    retryAfterHeaderPresent,
    retryAfterValue,
    anyRequestSilentlyDropped,
    summaryStatuses,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Rate limit oracle charters are essential for any API-backed application that enforces rate limits, especially for free-tier users and public APIs. Most critical after changes to API gateway configuration, pricing tier changes, or introduction of new rate-limiting middleware. Do NOT use this charter to stress-test rate-limiting infrastructure (that is a load test); the charter verifies the application handles 429 responses correctly at the UI and API client layers. Named alternative: Postman and Insomnia support pre-request script loops for automated 429 triggering; the TypeScript harness integrates this into the session evidence capture pipeline. [official]

## Additional Community Lessons (Cycle 30)

178. **[community] Shadow DOM exploration was the single most overlooked testing surface in design-system-heavy codebases.** Teams building component libraries in Lit or Stencil shipped components where ARIA roles declared inside shadow trees were invisible to the accessibility tree because `ShadowRoot.mode` was set to `'closed'` — making screen readers unable to announce interactive elements. This was discovered only during a government contract accessibility audit. WHY this matters: closed shadow roots silently break assistive technology without generating any JavaScript error; the only way to discover this class of defect is to query the accessibility tree from outside the shadow root with deliberate charter-based exploration rather than assuming the component's visual correctness implies accessibility correctness.

179. **[community] Memory leak charters on long-session dashboards consistently found that component cleanup during route navigation was the primary accumulation source.** In React applications using `useEffect` with WebSocket subscriptions, teams found that `return () => subscription.unsubscribe()` was present but not firing because the dependency array included a memoised function re-created on every render, causing the effect to re-run and register a new subscription without cleaning up the previous one. A 45-minute dashboard session revealed 340 open WebSocket connections. WHY this matters: automated tests run components for milliseconds and never observe the slow-building memory pressure that manifests after 30 minutes of real use — the exact context that dashboard users experience daily.

180. **[community] Rate limiting 429 handling was absent in approximately 70% of API client implementations examined during exploratory sessions.** The API gateway correctly returned 429 with a `Retry-After` header, but the client SPA had no handler — it fell through to the generic error handler, showed a red toast, and cleared the form the user had spent 10 minutes filling in. The user resubmitted, hit 429 again, and lost the form a second time. Teams that added explicit 429 handling to preserve form state and show "please wait X seconds and retry" saw a significant reduction in support tickets about "form submits but nothing happens". WHY this matters: 429 is a traffic-shaping signal that the client is expected to honour gracefully — treating it identically to a 500 destroys user work and creates a false perception that the system is broken when it is functioning correctly.

181. **[community] Web Vitals instrumentation during exploratory sessions revealed large CLS scores invisible to the naked eye after seemingly cosmetic CSS changes.** A CSS refactor replacing fixed `height` with `min-height` on card components introduced CLS scores of 0.42 on the homepage under slow 3G network emulation — well above the "poor" threshold of 0.25. The change caused image containers to lose their aspect-ratio reservation, causing layout shift when images loaded. The fix was three lines of CSS that would have taken weeks to diagnose from user complaints alone. WHY this matters: CLS defects are invisible at fast network speeds (images load before the browser paints) but cause significant layout instability on real mobile devices — and the only practical way to discover them in development is to instrument Web Vitals as part of the exploratory session routine.

182. **[community] Concurrent form submission oracles exposed that double-tap on mobile was a consistent source of duplicate account registrations and duplicate payment records.** Desktop exploratory testing rarely discovers this because mouse double-click behaviour on web forms is debounced by most browser/OS combinations. Mobile tap events do not have the same debounce behavior on all devices, and certain Android browsers fire two events for a single tap in some viewport configurations. Adding `pointer-events: none` and `disabled` state to submit buttons immediately after the first click eliminated the entire category. WHY this matters: duplicate records from optimistic double-tap are among the highest-severity UI defects because they affect financial and identity data; discovering them in exploratory testing prevents customer support escalations and potential compliance issues.

183. **[community] Scroll restoration defects were consistently discovered after migrating from page-level SSR to SPA-style client-side routing, because teams assumed the browser would handle restoration automatically.** `history.scrollRestoration = 'auto'` only works when the browser controls navigation — not when a JS router intercepts the navigation event. Teams that did not explicitly set `history.scrollRestoration = 'manual'` with a corresponding restore callback found that every Back navigation returned users to the top of the page. On list pages with 200+ items, users had to re-scroll to find where they were. WHY this matters: scroll restoration defects directly measure the quality of the Back button — one of the most-used browser controls — and failures cause users to lose context repeatedly throughout their session, creating a perception that the entire application is poorly built even when the rest of it works correctly.
