## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 1 — Timeout and Deadline Propagation Charter  [official]

Distributed systems propagate request deadlines through call chains. When an HTTP gateway imposes a 10-second overall deadline and downstream services have no awareness of the remaining budget, a 9-second upstream call leaves a 1-second budget for all subsequent services — causing cascading timeouts that manifest as cryptic 503 or 504 errors with no correlation to the true root cause. Exploratory charters for deadline propagation verify that: (a) timeout headers (`Grpc-Timeout`, `X-Request-Deadline`, or custom `X-Upstream-Deadline`) are forwarded through every service hop, (b) partial-result states are surfaced cleanly rather than returning a half-populated response, and (c) the UI distinguishes between a true service failure and a deadline-exceeded condition.

**TypeScript: Deadline propagation oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/deadline-propagation-oracle.ts
// Fires a request chain with a shrinking deadline and verifies that each
// hop propagates the remaining budget and that the UI surfaces a distinct
// "request timed out" message rather than a generic error.

import { type APIRequestContext, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface DeadlineScenario {
  gatewayUrl: string;
  /** Total deadline in milliseconds — start small to force propagation failures */
  budgetMs: number;
  /** Header name used by your gateway for remaining deadline */
  deadlineHeader: string;
  expectedTimeoutMessage: RegExp;
}

export interface DeadlineOracleResult {
  scenario: string;
  deadlineHeaderForwarded: boolean;
  uiShowsTimeoutMessage: boolean;
  partialResponseBody: string | null;
  rawStatus: number;
  durationMs: number;
}

export async function runDeadlinePropagationOracle(
  request: APIRequestContext,
  page: Page,
  scenario: DeadlineScenario
): Promise<DeadlineOracleResult> {
  const start = Date.now();
  const response = await request.get(scenario.gatewayUrl, {
    headers: { [scenario.deadlineHeader]: String(scenario.budgetMs) },
    timeout: scenario.budgetMs + 2000,
  });
  const durationMs = Date.now() - start;

  const rawStatus = response.status();
  const body = await response.text().catch(() => null);
  const deadlineHeaderForwarded =
    response.headers()[scenario.deadlineHeader.toLowerCase()] !== undefined;

  // Check UI layer for correct error presentation
  let uiShowsTimeoutMessage = false;
  if (rawStatus === 504 || rawStatus === 408) {
    await page.reload();
    const errorText = await page.locator('[role="alert"], .error-banner').textContent().catch(() => '');
    uiShowsTimeoutMessage = scenario.expectedTimeoutMessage.test(errorText ?? '');
  }

  return {
    scenario: `${scenario.gatewayUrl} @ ${scenario.budgetMs}ms budget`,
    deadlineHeaderForwarded,
    uiShowsTimeoutMessage,
    partialResponseBody: rawStatus !== 200 ? body : null,
    rawStatus,
    durationMs,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Essential for microservice architectures with cascading synchronous calls, especially after adding new service hops or moving from monolith to service-oriented designs. Particularly important for checkout, payment, and data-export flows where partial results cause data inconsistency. Do NOT use this charter to simulate load-test traffic — it is testing propagation semantics for a single request, not throughput. Named alternative: Istio's request timeout policy can enforce deadline propagation at the infrastructure layer, but it does not verify the UI's error presentation or partial-response handling which the charter covers. [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — Audit Log Completeness Charter  [official]

Regulatory frameworks (GDPR, SOX, HIPAA, ISO 27001) require that security-relevant actions be written to immutable audit logs. Exploratory charters for audit log completeness verify that: every write action (create, update, delete, permission change, data export) generates a log entry, the log entry captures the correct actor identity (not the service account), the timestamp is in UTC with sub-second precision, and log entries cannot be deleted or altered by application-tier users. Silent log gaps — actions that succeed without producing a log entry — are the most dangerous class of defect in compliance-sensitive products.

**TypeScript: Audit log completeness oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/audit-log-oracle.ts
// Performs a series of application actions and then queries the audit log API
// to verify that every action produced a corresponding log entry with the
// required fields (actor, action, resourceId, timestamp, ipAddress).

import { type APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface AuditableAction {
  label: string;
  perform: (request: APIRequestContext) => Promise<{ resourceId: string }>;
}

export interface AuditLogEntry {
  actor: string;
  action: string;
  resourceId: string;
  timestamp: string; // ISO-8601 UTC
  ipAddress: string;
}

export interface AuditLogResult {
  action: string;
  resourceId: string;
  logEntryFound: boolean;
  missingFields: string[];
  timestampIsUtc: boolean;
  latencyMs: number;
}

export async function verifyAuditLogCompleteness(
  request: APIRequestContext,
  auditLogEndpoint: string,
  actions: AuditableAction[],
  authHeader: Record<string, string>
): Promise<AuditLogResult[]> {
  const results: AuditLogResult[] = [];

  for (const action of actions) {
    const actionStart = Date.now();
    const { resourceId } = await action.perform(request);
    const latencyMs = Date.now() - actionStart;

    // Allow brief propagation delay for async log writers
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 500));

    const logResponse = await request.get(
      `${auditLogEndpoint}?resourceId=${encodeURIComponent(resourceId)}`,
      { headers: authHeader }
    );
    const entries: AuditLogEntry[] = (await logResponse.json()).entries ?? [];
    const matching = entries.find((e) => e.resourceId === resourceId);

    const requiredFields: (keyof AuditLogEntry)[] = ['actor', 'action', 'resourceId', 'timestamp', 'ipAddress'];
    const missingFields = matching
      ? requiredFields.filter((f) => !matching[f])
      : requiredFields;

    const timestampIsUtc = matching
      ? /Z$|[+-]00:00$/.test(matching.timestamp)
      : false;

    results.push({
      action: action.label,
      resourceId,
      logEntryFound: !!matching,
      missingFields,
      timestampIsUtc,
      latencyMs,
    });
  }

  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Mandatory for any product with compliance obligations (GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, financial services). Most critical after adding new data-modifying endpoints, permission-management flows, or bulk-export features — these are the most commonly logged yet most frequently missed action types. Do NOT use this charter to performance-test the audit log pipeline (high-volume write throughput is a load test concern). Named alternative: Static code analysis with custom rules can flag "write without audit call" patterns at the function level, but it cannot verify the log entry schema or the actor identity claim captured at runtime. [official]

---

### Pattern 3 — Dark Mode and Theme Switching Visual Correctness Charter  [community]

Applications supporting `prefers-color-scheme` media queries or manual theme toggles often ship visual defects that appear only in the non-default theme: hardcoded hex colors that bypass the CSS variable system, images with no dark-mode alternative that become invisible on dark backgrounds, and focus rings that vanish because the light-theme focus color has insufficient contrast against dark backgrounds. These defects are systematically missed by CI pipelines that snapshot only the default (light) theme.

**TypeScript: Theme switching visual oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/theme-switching-oracle.ts
// Captures screenshots of key routes in both light and dark themes,
// then checks WCAG contrast ratios for foreground/background pairs
// using the luminance formula. Flags any element where contrast < 4.5:1 (AA).

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import * as path from 'path';

export interface ThemeOracleConfig {
  routes: string[];
  outputDir: string;
  contrastThreshold: number; // 4.5 for WCAG AA, 3.0 for WCAG AA large text
}

function relativeLuminance(r: number, g: number, b: number): number {
  const toLinear = (c: number) => {
    const s = c / 255;
    return s <= 0.03928 ? s / 12.92 : Math.pow((s + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
  };
  return 0.2126 * toLinear(r) + 0.7152 * toLinear(g) + 0.0722 * toLinear(b);
}

export async function captureThemeEvidence(
  context: BrowserContext,
  config: ThemeOracleConfig
): Promise<{ route: string; theme: 'light' | 'dark'; screenshotPath: string }[]> {
  const evidence: { route: string; theme: 'light' | 'dark'; screenshotPath: string }[] = [];
  const page: Page = await context.newPage();

  for (const theme of ['light', 'dark'] as const) {
    await context.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: theme });

    for (const route of config.routes) {
      await page.goto(route, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

      // Also toggle the manual theme switch if present
      const themeToggle = page.locator('[data-testid="theme-toggle"], [aria-label*="theme" i]');
      if (await themeToggle.count() > 0) {
        const currentTheme = await page.evaluate(() =>
          document.documentElement.getAttribute('data-theme') ?? ''
        );
        if ((theme === 'dark') !== currentTheme.includes('dark')) {
          await themeToggle.click();
          await page.waitForTimeout(300);
        }
      }

      const screenshotPath = path.join(
        config.outputDir,
        `${theme}-${route.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '_')}.png`
      );
      await page.screenshot({ path: screenshotPath, fullPage: true });
      evidence.push({ route, theme, screenshotPath });
    }
  }

  await page.close();
  return evidence;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Theme switching charters are most valuable for design-system migrations and for products where dark mode was retrofitted rather than designed in from the start. Essential before launches targeting developer or creative professional audiences (who overwhelmingly use dark mode). Do NOT use screenshot comparison alone as the oracle — perceived correctness in a screenshot does not verify contrast ratios; use the luminance formula or a dedicated tool like axe for colour contrast verification. Named alternative: Storybook's dark-mode addon provides per-component theme preview, but it does not cover route-level integration defects where components interact under a shared theme context. [community]

---

### Pattern 4 — CSP (Content Security Policy) Violation Oracle Charter  [official]

Content Security Policy headers define the set of origins from which the browser may load scripts, styles, images, and fonts. Misconfigured CSP causes two distinct failure classes: (a) legitimate resources are blocked by an overly restrictive policy, breaking features silently; and (b) the policy is so permissive (`unsafe-inline`, `unsafe-eval`, or wildcards) that it provides no protection. Exploratory charters for CSP verify correct enforcement by monitoring the browser console for CSP violation events and by checking the policy header against known dangerous directives.

**TypeScript: CSP violation oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/csp-violation-oracle.ts
// Navigates a set of routes and collects all CSP violation events
// from the browser console. Also inspects the Content-Security-Policy
// response header for unsafe directives that indicate a policy weakness.

import { type Page, type Response } from '@playwright/test';

export interface CspViolation {
  route: string;
  blockedUri: string;
  directive: string;
  sourceFile: string;
  lineNumber: number;
}

export interface CspPolicyAudit {
  route: string;
  rawPolicy: string;
  unsafeDirectives: string[];
  hasMissingDirectives: string[];
}

const UNSAFE_DIRECTIVE_PATTERNS = [
  'unsafe-inline',
  'unsafe-eval',
  "'unsafe-hashes'",
  'data:',
  '*',
];

const REQUIRED_DIRECTIVES = ['default-src', 'script-src', 'object-src', 'base-uri'];

export async function auditCspOnRoutes(
  page: Page,
  routes: string[]
): Promise<{ violations: CspViolation[]; policyAudits: CspPolicyAudit[] }> {
  const violations: CspViolation[] = [];
  const policyAudits: CspPolicyAudit[] = [];

  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    const text = msg.text();
    if (msg.type() === 'error' && text.includes('Content Security Policy')) {
      const blockedMatch = text.match(/blocked.*?["']([^"']+)["']/i);
      const directiveMatch = text.match(/directive.*?["']([^"']+)["']/i);
      violations.push({
        route: page.url(),
        blockedUri: blockedMatch?.[1] ?? 'unknown',
        directive: directiveMatch?.[1] ?? 'unknown',
        sourceFile: '',
        lineNumber: 0,
      });
    }
  });

  for (const route of routes) {
    let cspHeader = '';
    page.once('response', (response: Response) => {
      cspHeader = response.headers()['content-security-policy'] ?? '';
    });

    await page.goto(route, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

    if (cspHeader) {
      const unsafeDirectives = UNSAFE_DIRECTIVE_PATTERNS.filter((p) =>
        cspHeader.includes(p)
      );
      const hasMissingDirectives = REQUIRED_DIRECTIVES.filter((d) =>
        !cspHeader.includes(d)
      );
      policyAudits.push({
        route,
        rawPolicy: cspHeader,
        unsafeDirectives,
        hasMissingDirectives,
      });
    }
  }

  return { violations, policyAudits };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: CSP charter is mandatory for any application with a security compliance requirement (PCI-DSS, SOC 2) and highly recommended after introducing any new third-party script (analytics, chat, A/B testing). Most critical after moving to a new CDN or script delivery infrastructure. Do NOT use this charter to validate CORS — CSP and CORS are orthogonal controls; a separate cross-origin resource charter covers CORS header misconfiguration. Named alternative: Google's CSP Evaluator (online tool) analyses a policy string statically; the charter covers runtime enforcement and the interaction between CSP and dynamically loaded third-party content that static analysis cannot predict. [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — Service Worker Update and Cache Eviction Charter  [community]

Progressive Web Apps rely on service workers for offline capability and performance caching. Service worker update bugs are among the most difficult to discover in CI: when a new service worker is available, the browser activates it only after all tabs using the old worker are closed. Applications that do not prompt users to reload on new worker availability can serve stale assets for days. Cache eviction bugs occur when the service worker's cache versioning logic incorrectly retains old API response shapes after a breaking schema change.

**TypeScript: Service worker update oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/service-worker-oracle.ts
// Verifies that a service worker update is detected and that the application
// prompts the user to reload when a new worker is waiting. Also verifies that
// cached API responses are invalidated correctly when the cache version changes.

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface ServiceWorkerAuditResult {
  workerRegistered: boolean;
  workerState: string;
  updatePromptVisible: boolean;
  staleApiResponseDetected: boolean;
  cacheKeys: string[];
  scriptUrl: string;
}

export async function auditServiceWorker(
  context: BrowserContext,
  appUrl: string,
  updateTriggerSelector: string
): Promise<ServiceWorkerAuditResult> {
  const page: Page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto(appUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

  // Inspect service worker state via JS evaluation
  const workerInfo = await page.evaluate(async () => {
    const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistration();
    if (!reg) return { registered: false, state: 'none', scriptUrl: '' };
    const worker = reg.active ?? reg.installing ?? reg.waiting;
    return {
      registered: true,
      state: worker?.state ?? 'unknown',
      scriptUrl: reg.active?.scriptURL ?? '',
    };
  });

  // List cache keys to verify versioning
  const cacheKeys: string[] = await page.evaluate(async () => {
    const keys = await caches.keys();
    return keys;
  });

  // Check for stale API shapes by comparing a known field across cached and live responses
  let staleApiResponseDetected = false;
  const cachedApiResponse = await page.evaluate(async () => {
    const cacheName = (await caches.keys())[0];
    if (!cacheName) return null;
    const cache = await caches.open(cacheName);
    const keys = await cache.keys();
    const apiKey = keys.find((k) => k.url.includes('/api/'));
    if (!apiKey) return null;
    const resp = await cache.match(apiKey);
    return resp ? resp.json() : null;
  });

  if (cachedApiResponse !== null) {
    staleApiResponseDetected = typeof cachedApiResponse.schemaVersion === 'undefined';
  }

  // Check if an update prompt is visible (after simulated update)
  await page.evaluate(() => navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistration().then((r) => r?.update()));
  await page.waitForTimeout(1000);
  const updatePromptVisible =
    (await page.locator(updateTriggerSelector).count()) > 0;

  await page.close();
  return {
    workerRegistered: workerInfo.registered,
    workerState: workerInfo.state,
    updatePromptVisible,
    staleApiResponseDetected,
    cacheKeys,
    scriptUrl: workerInfo.scriptUrl,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Service worker charters are essential for PWAs shipping to mobile users where update notification failures leave users on stale code for weeks. Most critical after changing the service worker's cache strategy or after a backend API breaking change where the old schema must not be served from cache. Do NOT run this charter in headless mode with `--disable-service-workers` — that flag suppresses the exact behaviour you are testing. Named alternative: Workbox's built-in update flow provides standardised update prompting; the charter verifies that whatever update flow is implemented (Workbox-based or hand-rolled) actually prompts users correctly in the browser. [community]

---

### Pattern 6 — Stale Closure and Async State Consistency Charter  [community]

React and Vue applications using hooks or the Composition API are vulnerable to stale closure bugs: an event handler captures a variable from an old render cycle, and when the handler fires (after a user action or setTimeout), it reads outdated state. These bugs are invisible in fast unit tests and only manifest under realistic interaction timing. The most damaging form is a stale closure over a form's `isDirty` flag: a user edits a form, triggers an async validation, and the validation callback fires with the pre-edit state — silently discarding the edit.

**TypeScript: Stale closure detection harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/stale-closure-harness.ts
// Instruments the page to detect stale closures by injecting a global counter
// that increments on every state update and comparing the render cycle number
// captured by an event handler against the current cycle number when it fires.
// A mismatch indicates the handler captured a stale closure.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface StaleClosureObservation {
  event: string;
  handlerRenderCycle: number;
  currentRenderCycle: number;
  isStale: boolean;
  potentialImpact: string;
}

export async function installStaleClosureDetector(page: Page): Promise<void> {
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    (window as any).__renderCycle = 0;
    const originalSetState = (window as any).React?.Component?.prototype?.setState;
    if (originalSetState) {
      (window as any).React.Component.prototype.setState = function (...args: any[]) {
        (window as any).__renderCycle++;
        return originalSetState.apply(this, args);
      };
    }
  });
}

export async function captureStaleClosureEvents(
  page: Page,
  interactions: Array<{ label: string; action: (page: Page) => Promise<void> }>
): Promise<StaleClosureObservation[]> {
  const observations: StaleClosureObservation[] = [];

  await installStaleClosureDetector(page);

  for (const interaction of interactions) {
    const cycleBeforeAction: number = await page.evaluate(
      () => (window as any).__renderCycle ?? 0
    );

    await interaction.action(page);

    await page.waitForTimeout(500); // Allow async handlers to settle
    const cycleAfterAction: number = await page.evaluate(
      () => (window as any).__renderCycle ?? 0
    );

    // If no render occurred after an interaction that should trigger re-render,
    // suspect stale closure preventing state update
    const isStale = cycleAfterAction === cycleBeforeAction;
    observations.push({
      event: interaction.label,
      handlerRenderCycle: cycleBeforeAction,
      currentRenderCycle: cycleAfterAction,
      isStale,
      potentialImpact: isStale
        ? 'Handler may be reading stale state — verify form/list data consistency after this interaction'
        : 'State updated as expected',
    });
  }

  return observations;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Stale closure charters are highest-value for applications with complex async form flows: multi-step wizards, inline editing with auto-save, and collaborative editing features where two users edit concurrently. Most critical after React hook refactors that change dependency arrays. Do NOT treat "zero render cycles detected" as definitive proof of a stale closure — some interactions correctly produce no re-render (read-only interactions); cross-validate with manual form-state inspection. Named alternative: React DevTools' component inspector can show stale props/state visually; the charter provides automated coverage across multiple interaction sequences that would take hours to verify manually. [community]

---

### Pattern 7 — Webhook Replay and Idempotency Charter  [official]

Webhook delivery systems (Stripe, GitHub, Twilio, Shopify) retry webhooks on failure — typically 3–5 times over 24 hours. Applications that process webhooks without idempotency keys create duplicate records: duplicate order fulfilments, duplicate emails, duplicate subscription upgrades. Exploratory charters for webhook idempotency verify that: replaying the same event ID twice produces the same application state as receiving it once, the idempotency check uses the event's provider-assigned ID rather than payload hash, and the processing result is stored and returned on replay rather than re-executing the handler.

**TypeScript: Webhook replay idempotency oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/webhook-idempotency-oracle.ts
// Sends the same webhook payload twice (simulating provider retry) and verifies
// that the application's resulting state is identical after both deliveries —
// meaning no duplicate record was created on the second delivery.

import { type APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';
import * as crypto from 'crypto';

export interface WebhookReplayScenario {
  webhookEndpoint: string;
  eventType: string;
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  idempotencyKey: string;
  /** How to verify idempotency: returns the count of records matching the event */
  countRecordsForEvent: (request: APIRequestContext) => Promise<number>;
  signingSecret?: string;
}

function buildStripeSignature(payload: string, secret: string): string {
  const timestamp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  const sig = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', secret)
    .update(`${timestamp}.${payload}`)
    .digest('hex');
  return `t=${timestamp},v1=${sig}`;
}

export async function runWebhookIdempotencyOracle(
  request: APIRequestContext,
  scenario: WebhookReplayScenario
): Promise<{ countAfterFirst: number; countAfterSecond: number; isIdempotent: boolean }> {
  const body = JSON.stringify({
    ...scenario.payload,
    id: scenario.idempotencyKey,
    type: scenario.eventType,
  });

  const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Idempotency-Key': scenario.idempotencyKey,
  };

  if (scenario.signingSecret) {
    headers['Stripe-Signature'] = buildStripeSignature(body, scenario.signingSecret);
  }

  // First delivery
  await request.post(scenario.webhookEndpoint, { headers, data: body });
  const countAfterFirst = await scenario.countRecordsForEvent(request);

  // Replay — simulates provider retry
  await request.post(scenario.webhookEndpoint, { headers, data: body });
  const countAfterSecond = await scenario.countRecordsForEvent(request);

  return {
    countAfterFirst,
    countAfterSecond,
    isIdempotent: countAfterFirst === countAfterSecond,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Webhook idempotency charters are mandatory for any integration with external event-delivery systems (Stripe, GitHub Actions, Shopify, Twilio) before going live. Most critical when adding new event handlers, changing database write logic in existing handlers, or migrating webhook processors to a new queue infrastructure. Do NOT test idempotency by replaying the same HTTP call in rapid succession — proper idempotency testing must include a delay that reflects the provider's retry window (minutes, not milliseconds), because some implementations use short-lived deduplication windows. Named alternative: Stripe's Webhooks dashboard provides retry simulation for registered endpoints; the charter provides integration-level idempotency testing that can run in any environment including local development and staging. [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — API Versioning and Deprecation Warning Charter  [official]

APIs evolve through versioning schemes (URL path versioning `/v1/`, `/v2/`; header versioning `Accept: application/vnd.api+json; version=2`; query param versioning `?api_version=2026-01`). Exploratory charters for API versioning verify: deprecated versions return `Sunset` and `Deprecation` response headers with correct dates, version-negotiation fallback works when the client sends an unsupported version, and breaking changes in newer versions are not silently applied to requests specifying an older version. Silent version coercion — where the server upgrades a v1 request to v2 semantics without signaling the change — is the most dangerous defect.

**TypeScript: API version negotiation oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/api-version-oracle.ts
// Tests API version negotiation by sending requests with different version
// identifiers and verifying that the correct response schema, deprecation
// headers, and error codes are returned for each version.

import { type APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface VersionScenario {
  label: string;
  endpoint: string;
  versionHeader: string;
  versionValue: string;
  expectedSchemaFields: string[];
  shouldHaveSunsetHeader: boolean;
}

export interface VersionOracleResult {
  label: string;
  status: number;
  versionEchoed: string | null;
  sunsetHeader: string | null;
  deprecationHeader: string | null;
  allExpectedFieldsPresent: boolean;
  missingFields: string[];
  isSilentlyCoerced: boolean;
}

export async function runVersionNegotiationOracle(
  request: APIRequestContext,
  scenarios: VersionScenario[]
): Promise<VersionOracleResult[]> {
  const results: VersionOracleResult[] = [];

  for (const scenario of scenarios) {
    const response = await request.get(scenario.endpoint, {
      headers: { [scenario.versionHeader]: scenario.versionValue },
    });

    const status = response.status();
    const headers = response.headers();
    const body = status < 400 ? await response.json().catch(() => ({})) : {};

    const missingFields = scenario.expectedSchemaFields.filter(
      (f) => body[f] === undefined
    );

    // Detect silent coercion: if the server echoes a different version than requested
    const versionEchoed =
      headers['api-version'] ?? headers['x-api-version'] ?? null;
    const isSilentlyCoerced =
      versionEchoed !== null && versionEchoed !== scenario.versionValue;

    results.push({
      label: scenario.label,
      status,
      versionEchoed,
      sunsetHeader: headers['sunset'] ?? null,
      deprecationHeader: headers['deprecation'] ?? null,
      allExpectedFieldsPresent: missingFields.length === 0,
      missingFields,
      isSilentlyCoerced,
    });
  }

  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: API versioning charters are essential before deprecating any API version that has external consumers, and before releasing a version that introduces breaking schema changes. Most critical for public APIs and internal platform teams serving multiple product teams. Do NOT run this charter only on the latest version — the most valuable part is verifying that old versions continue to behave exactly as documented until their sunset date. Named alternative: Postman Monitors can run versioned request collections on a schedule; the charter provides exploratory-style investigation of version boundary behavior that is difficult to express as a static collection. [official]

---

### Pattern 9 — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Misconfiguration Charter  [official]

CORS misconfiguration is the most common API security defect that passes functional testing: a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on a credentialed endpoint allows any origin to send authenticated requests, and an overly permissive `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` exposes mutation endpoints to cross-site request forgery. Exploratory charters for CORS verify: preflight OPTIONS responses include correct allowed-origins, credentials-bearing requests from the correct origin are accepted, requests from unexpected origins are rejected, and wildcard ACAO headers are never combined with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

**TypeScript: CORS misconfiguration oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/cors-oracle.ts
// Sends preflight OPTIONS requests from both allowed and disallowed origins
// and verifies that the CORS headers correctly reflect the expected policy.
// Flags the dangerous wildcard + credentials combination.

import { type APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface CorsScenario {
  endpoint: string;
  method: string;
  allowedOrigin: string;
  disallowedOrigin: string;
  requiresCredentials: boolean;
}

export interface CorsOracleResult {
  endpoint: string;
  origin: string;
  preflightStatus: number;
  allowedOriginHeader: string | null;
  allowedMethodsHeader: string | null;
  allowCredentialsHeader: string | null;
  wildcardWithCredentials: boolean;
  accessGrantedToDisallowedOrigin: boolean;
}

export async function runCorsOracle(
  request: APIRequestContext,
  scenario: CorsScenario
): Promise<CorsOracleResult[]> {
  const results: CorsOracleResult[] = [];

  for (const origin of [scenario.allowedOrigin, scenario.disallowedOrigin]) {
    const preflight = await request.fetch(scenario.endpoint, {
      method: 'OPTIONS',
      headers: {
        Origin: origin,
        'Access-Control-Request-Method': scenario.method,
        'Access-Control-Request-Headers': 'Content-Type, Authorization',
      },
    });

    const headers = preflight.headers();
    const acao = headers['access-control-allow-origin'] ?? null;
    const acac = headers['access-control-allow-credentials'] ?? null;
    const acam = headers['access-control-allow-methods'] ?? null;

    const wildcardWithCredentials = acao === '*' && acac === 'true';
    const accessGrantedToDisallowedOrigin =
      origin === scenario.disallowedOrigin &&
      (acao === '*' || acao === origin);

    results.push({
      endpoint: scenario.endpoint,
      origin,
      preflightStatus: preflight.status(),
      allowedOriginHeader: acao,
      allowedMethodsHeader: acam,
      allowCredentialsHeader: acac,
      wildcardWithCredentials,
      accessGrantedToDisallowedOrigin,
    });
  }

  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: CORS charters are essential before any API goes public and after every change to API gateway configuration, reverse proxy rules, or CDN origin settings. Most critical for APIs that combine authentication cookies or tokens with cross-origin access. Do NOT limit the charter to the preflight response alone — also verify the actual response headers on simple (non-preflighted) GET requests, because some servers only apply CORS headers to preflighted requests. Named alternative: OWASP's CORS misconfiguration test guide provides a manual checklist; the charter provides automated regression coverage across all API endpoints rather than spot-checking selected endpoints manually. [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — Session Token Rotation and Fixation Charter  [official]

Session fixation attacks allow an attacker to pre-set a session token value before authentication, then read the authenticated session after the victim logs in. Applications that do not rotate session tokens on privilege escalation (login, sudo re-authentication, role elevation) are vulnerable. Exploratory charters for session token rotation verify: the session token changes after successful login, the session token changes after password change, old tokens are invalidated after rotation, and tokens have appropriate entropy and do not contain user-decodable information.

**TypeScript: Session token rotation oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/session-rotation-oracle.ts
// Records the session token before and after login, password change,
// and role elevation, then verifies that the old token is invalidated
// and that the new token has sufficient entropy.

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface RotationCheckpoint {
  label: string;
  tokenBefore: string | null;
  tokenAfter: string | null;
  rotated: boolean;
  oldTokenInvalidated: boolean;
  entropyBits: number;
}

function estimateEntropyBits(token: string): number {
  const uniqueChars = new Set(token.split('')).size;
  return Math.log2(uniqueChars) * token.length;
}

export async function checkSessionTokenRotation(
  context: BrowserContext,
  page: Page,
  cookieName: string,
  steps: Array<{
    label: string;
    action: (page: Page) => Promise<void>;
    verifyOldTokenInvalidated?: (page: Page, oldToken: string) => Promise<boolean>;
  }>
): Promise<RotationCheckpoint[]> {
  const checkpoints: RotationCheckpoint[] = [];

  for (const step of steps) {
    const cookiesBefore = await context.cookies();
    const tokenBefore =
      cookiesBefore.find((c) => c.name === cookieName)?.value ?? null;

    await step.action(page);
    await page.waitForTimeout(300);

    const cookiesAfter = await context.cookies();
    const tokenAfter =
      cookiesAfter.find((c) => c.name === cookieName)?.value ?? null;

    const rotated = tokenBefore !== tokenAfter && tokenAfter !== null;

    let oldTokenInvalidated = false;
    if (rotated && tokenBefore && step.verifyOldTokenInvalidated) {
      oldTokenInvalidated = await step.verifyOldTokenInvalidated(page, tokenBefore);
    }

    checkpoints.push({
      label: step.label,
      tokenBefore,
      tokenAfter,
      rotated,
      oldTokenInvalidated,
      entropyBits: tokenAfter ? estimateEntropyBits(tokenAfter) : 0,
    });
  }

  return checkpoints;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Session rotation charters are mandatory for any application with authentication, especially after changes to the authentication middleware, session management library, or cookie configuration. Most critical for applications supporting elevated-privilege modes (admin views, payment flows, two-factor authentication). Do NOT assume that using a well-known auth library (Passport.js, NextAuth, Supabase Auth) means session rotation is handled correctly — configuration mistakes are the most common source of session fixation defects in production. Named alternative: OWASP's ASVS Level 2 session management requirements provide a comprehensive static checklist; the charter provides runtime verification that the application actually rotates tokens in a browser session, which static analysis cannot verify. [official]

---

### Pattern 11 — Background Sync and Offline Queue Fidelity Charter  [community]

Applications using the Background Sync API or a manual offline queue (IndexedDB + service worker sync) must reliably replay queued actions when connectivity is restored. Common defects include: the sync handler fires but the request body is missing required headers (auth token expired during offline window), the queue processes items out of order when multiple actions were queued, and duplicate sync attempts occur when the user manually retriggers sync by going online and offline in rapid succession.

**TypeScript: Offline queue fidelity harness**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/offline-queue-harness.ts
// Simulates offline → action → online cycles and verifies that
// queued actions are replayed exactly once, in order, with valid
// auth credentials and correct request bodies.

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface QueuedAction {
  label: string;
  perform: (page: Page) => Promise<void>;
}

export interface SyncFidelityResult {
  actionsQueued: number;
  actionsReplayed: number;
  duplicateReplays: number;
  orderPreserved: boolean;
  authHeaderPresentOnReplay: boolean;
  syncLatencyMs: number;
  replayedRequests: Array<{ url: string; method: string; hasAuthHeader: boolean }>;
}

export async function runOfflineQueueFidelityTest(
  context: BrowserContext,
  page: Page,
  actions: QueuedAction[],
  syncTriggerSelector: string
): Promise<SyncFidelityResult> {
  const replayedRequests: SyncFidelityResult['replayedRequests'] = [];
  const seenUrls = new Map<string, number>();

  // Go offline
  await context.setOffline(true);
  await page.waitForTimeout(200);

  // Perform all actions while offline — they should be queued
  for (const action of actions) {
    await action.perform(page);
  }

  // Capture all outbound requests on reconnect
  page.on('request', (req) => {
    const url = req.url();
    seenUrls.set(url, (seenUrls.get(url) ?? 0) + 1);
    replayedRequests.push({
      url,
      method: req.method(),
      hasAuthHeader:
        req.headers()['authorization'] !== undefined ||
        req.headers()['cookie'] !== undefined,
    });
  });

  const syncStart = Date.now();
  await context.setOffline(false);

  // Trigger sync if app requires explicit user action (e.g., "Sync now" button)
  if (syncTriggerSelector) {
    const trigger = page.locator(syncTriggerSelector);
    if (await trigger.count() > 0) await trigger.click();
  }

  await page.waitForTimeout(2000);
  const syncLatencyMs = Date.now() - syncStart;

  const duplicateReplays = Array.from(seenUrls.values()).filter((c) => c > 1).length;
  const orderPreserved = replayedRequests.length >= actions.length;
  const authHeaderPresentOnReplay = replayedRequests.every((r) => r.hasAuthHeader);

  return {
    actionsQueued: actions.length,
    actionsReplayed: replayedRequests.length,
    duplicateReplays,
    orderPreserved,
    authHeaderPresentOnReplay,
    syncLatencyMs,
    replayedRequests,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Background sync charters are essential for field-worker applications, mobile-first apps, and any application explicitly marketed as "works offline". Most critical after changes to the service worker sync handler, the IndexedDB queue schema, or the authentication token refresh logic. Do NOT use this charter in environments with flaky network simulation — Playwright's `context.setOffline()` provides deterministic offline simulation that is far more reliable than throttling-based approaches. Named alternative: Workbox's Background Sync plugin provides tested queue semantics; the charter verifies that the application's usage of the plugin (or equivalent) handles auth-token rotation and ordering correctly. [community]

---

### Pattern 12 — Time Zone Boundary and DST Transition Charter  [official]

Applications storing, displaying, or scheduling events with time-zone context have a class of defects that only manifest at Daylight Saving Time transitions and across the International Date Line. Common defects: an event created at 01:30 AM on a DST "spring forward" night is stored at an impossible local time; a scheduled report set to run "daily at 00:00 UTC-5" runs twice or skips on DST transition nights; date arithmetic that uses local time rather than UTC to calculate durations produces off-by-one-hour errors for dates spanning DST transitions.

**TypeScript: DST boundary oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/dst-boundary-oracle.ts
// Uses Playwright's page.clock() API to freeze time at DST boundary
// moments and verifies that event storage, display, and scheduling
// handle the transition correctly.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface DstBoundaryScenario {
  label: string;
  /** UTC millisecond timestamp for the moment just before the DST transition */
  justBeforeTransitionUtcMs: number;
  /** Expected local offset before transition (e.g., -18000000 for UTC-5) */
  offsetBeforeMs: number;
  /** Expected local offset after transition (e.g., -14400000 for UTC-4) */
  offsetAfterMs: number;
  eventInputSelector: string;
  eventDisplaySelector: string;
}

export interface DstOracleResult {
  scenario: string;
  eventStoredUtcMs: number | null;
  eventDisplayedText: string;
  displayMatchesExpected: boolean;
  ambiguousTimeHandled: boolean;
}

export async function runDstBoundaryOracle(
  page: Page,
  baseUrl: string,
  scenarios: DstBoundaryScenario[]
): Promise<DstOracleResult[]> {
  const results: DstOracleResult[] = [];

  for (const scenario of scenarios) {
    // Freeze clock just before DST transition
    await page.clock.setSystemTime(new Date(scenario.justBeforeTransitionUtcMs));
    await page.goto(baseUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

    // Attempt to input a time that falls in the ambiguous hour
    const ambiguousLocalMs = scenario.justBeforeTransitionUtcMs + 30 * 60 * 1000;
    const ambiguousInput = new Date(ambiguousLocalMs).toISOString().slice(0, 16);

    await page.locator(scenario.eventInputSelector).fill(ambiguousInput);
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
    await page.waitForTimeout(300);

    // Advance clock past the transition
    await page.clock.fastForward(60 * 60 * 1000);

    const displayText = await page
      .locator(scenario.eventDisplaySelector)
      .textContent()
      .catch(() => '');

    // A correct implementation shows the event at the unambiguous UTC-equivalent time
    const displayMatchesExpected = displayText !== null && displayText.length > 0;

    // Check if the app shows any disambiguation UI (expected for ambiguous inputs)
    const ambiguousTimeHandled =
      (await page.locator('[data-testid="tz-disambiguation"]').count()) > 0 ||
      displayText?.includes('UTC') === true;

    results.push({
      scenario: scenario.label,
      eventStoredUtcMs: ambiguousLocalMs,
      eventDisplayedText: displayText ?? '',
      displayMatchesExpected,
      ambiguousTimeHandled,
    });
  }

  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: DST boundary charters are mandatory for calendar, scheduling, and event-management applications. Most critical when supporting users in time zones with DST transitions (most US, EU, Australian zones). Do NOT test DST behaviour by changing the OS timezone in CI — that affects the entire test environment; Playwright's `page.clock()` API provides scoped, deterministic time control that is far more reliable. Named alternative: The `date-fns-tz` and `Temporal` libraries handle DST-safe arithmetic; the charter verifies that the application uses these correctly at the UI and storage layers rather than defaulting to `Date.getTime()` arithmetic. [official]

---

### Pattern 13 — Internationalization Number and Currency Format Charter  [community]

Financial applications and e-commerce platforms display prices, percentages, and quantities in locale-specific formats. The `Intl.NumberFormat` API is the correct tool but is frequently bypassed with ad hoc string formatting. Common defects: negative numbers displayed as `(-5.00)` in locales that expect `-5,00`; currency symbols appended rather than prepended for some locales (`5.00 €` vs `€5.00`); thousand separators omitted for numbers above 9,999; and percentage formatting that adds a space before `%` in French (which is typographically correct but breaks `parseFloat` on the returned string if it is re-ingested by the API).

**TypeScript: Intl number format oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/intl-number-oracle.ts
// Verifies that numbers, currencies, and percentages are displayed correctly
// across a matrix of locales by comparing the page's rendered text against
// the expected output from Intl.NumberFormat.

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface NumberFormatScenario {
  locale: string;
  currency: string;
  testValues: Array<{
    raw: number;
    type: 'currency' | 'percent' | 'decimal';
    selector: string;
  }>;
}

export interface NumberFormatResult {
  locale: string;
  currency: string;
  testValue: number;
  type: string;
  expected: string;
  rendered: string;
  match: boolean;
}

export async function runIntlNumberFormatOracle(
  context: BrowserContext,
  pageUrl: string,
  scenarios: NumberFormatScenario[]
): Promise<NumberFormatResult[]> {
  const results: NumberFormatResult[] = [];
  const page: Page = await context.newPage();

  for (const scenario of scenarios) {
    await context.clearCookies();

    // Set locale via Playwright context (applies Accept-Language header)
    const localeContext = await context.browser()!.newContext({
      locale: scenario.locale,
      timezoneId: 'UTC',
    });
    const localePage = await localeContext.newPage();

    await localePage.goto(pageUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

    for (const tv of scenario.testValues) {
      const formatter =
        tv.type === 'currency'
          ? new Intl.NumberFormat(scenario.locale, {
              style: 'currency',
              currency: scenario.currency,
            })
          : tv.type === 'percent'
          ? new Intl.NumberFormat(scenario.locale, { style: 'percent' })
          : new Intl.NumberFormat(scenario.locale);

      const expected = formatter.format(tv.raw);
      const rendered = (
        await localePage.locator(tv.selector).textContent().catch(() => '')
      )?.trim() ?? '';

      results.push({
        locale: scenario.locale,
        currency: scenario.currency,
        testValue: tv.raw,
        type: tv.type,
        expected,
        rendered,
        match: rendered.includes(expected) || expected.includes(rendered),
      });
    }

    await localeContext.close();
  }

  await page.close();
  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Number format charters are essential before international launches and after any change to number or currency display logic. Most critical for e-commerce, financial services, and reporting dashboards. Do NOT rely on visual inspection alone — identical-looking numbers can differ in non-breaking spaces and invisible Unicode characters that only automated comparison detects. Named alternative: ICU conformance tests verify `Intl.NumberFormat` engine correctness; the charter verifies that the application applies the correct formatter to each data type rather than using raw string interpolation. [community]

---

### Pattern 14 — Speculative Execution and Prefetch Side Effect Charter  [community]

Modern browsers and frameworks (Next.js App Router, Astro, Nuxt 3) speculatively prefetch pages when links enter the viewport or on hover. This creates a class of defects invisible in sequential testing: a prefetch request triggers a server-side side effect (incrementing a page view counter, creating a draft record, or initiating an analytics event), so a user who hovers over a link but never clicks it produces the same server-side effect as a user who navigates. Applications relying on "page loaded = user intent" analytics or "any GET = safe" assumptions are affected.

**TypeScript: Speculative prefetch side effect oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/prefetch-side-effect-oracle.ts
// Monitors network requests during hover interactions to identify
// prefetch requests that trigger state-changing server operations.
// Compares server-side counters before and after a hover-only session.

import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export interface PrefetchSideEffectResult {
  hoverTarget: string;
  prefetchRequestsFired: number;
  prefetchUrls: string[];
  serverCounterBefore: number;
  serverCounterAfter: number;
  sideEffectDetected: boolean;
  sideEffectDescription: string;
}

export async function auditPrefetchSideEffects(
  page: Page,
  hoverTargets: Array<{ selector: string; label: string }>,
  getServerCounter: (page: Page) => Promise<number>
): Promise<PrefetchSideEffectResult[]> {
  const results: PrefetchSideEffectResult[] = [];

  for (const target of hoverTargets) {
    const prefetchUrls: string[] = [];

    // Intercept and record prefetch/prerender requests
    page.on('request', (req) => {
      const purpose = req.headers()['purpose'] ?? req.headers()['sec-purpose'] ?? '';
      if (purpose.includes('prefetch') || purpose.includes('prerender')) {
        prefetchUrls.push(req.url());
      }
    });

    const counterBefore = await getServerCounter(page);

    // Hover without clicking
    await page.locator(target.selector).hover();
    await page.waitForTimeout(1500); // Allow prefetch to fire

    const counterAfter = await getServerCounter(page);
    const sideEffectDetected = counterAfter > counterBefore;

    results.push({
      hoverTarget: target.label,
      prefetchRequestsFired: prefetchUrls.length,
      prefetchUrls,
      serverCounterBefore: counterBefore,
      serverCounterAfter: counterAfter,
      sideEffectDetected,
      sideEffectDescription: sideEffectDetected
        ? `Server counter incremented ${counterAfter - counterBefore} time(s) during hover — verify whether this is intentional`
        : 'No server-side side effect detected during hover',
    });
  }

  return results;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Prefetch side-effect charters are most valuable for applications with server-side analytics event tracking, draft-creation on view, or recommendation systems that record user intent from page loads. Most critical when adding link prefetching to a Next.js App Router, Nuxt, or Astro application. Do NOT block all prefetching as the remediation — prefetching is a significant performance feature; the correct fix is to ensure GET handlers do not produce state-changing side effects (consistent with HTTP semantics). Named alternative: Google Analytics DebugView can show duplicate page_view events from prefetches; the charter provides systematic discovery across all hover-target links in a flow rather than passive post-hoc analysis. [community]

---

### Pattern 15 — Third-Party Font and Icon Loading Fallback Charter  [community]

Web fonts and icon fonts (Google Fonts, Font Awesome, Material Icons) load from CDNs under `preconnect` and `link[rel=stylesheet]` tags. When the CDN is unreachable (corporate firewall, regional block, CDN outage), the application renders with browser fallback fonts or — worse — empty icon buttons with no accessible text alternative. This transforms usable UI into an inaccessible, visually broken experience. FOIT (Flash of Invisible Text) during slow CDN responses causes cumulative layout shift that harms Core Web Vitals.

**YAML: Third-party font fallback charter**

```yaml
# charters/font-fallback-exploration.yaml
charterId: CHR-font-fallback-2026-05-14-01
mission:
  explore: "third-party font and icon CDN loading with network failure simulation"
  using: >
    Playwright route interception to block Google Fonts and CDN subdomains,
    FOIT measurement via PerformanceObserver, icon button keyboard navigation,
    and page.accessibility.snapshot() for icon-only button label verification
  toDiscover: >
    Whether the application renders usably with no web fonts loaded,
    whether icon-only buttons retain accessible labels via aria-label or title
    attributes, and whether FOIT exceeds 3 seconds on CDN timeout

priorityAreas:
  - Icon buttons with no visible text label (navigation, toolbar, action menus)
  - Heading typography with font-weight or letter-spacing dependent on Google Fonts
  - Brand logomarks embedded as icon font glyphs rather than SVG

fallbackMatrix:
  - scenario: google_fonts_blocked
    blockedPatterns:
      - "https://fonts.googleapis.com/**"
      - "https://fonts.gstatic.com/**"
    expectedFallback: "system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif"
    acceptableCls: 0.1

  - scenario: icon_cdn_blocked
    blockedPatterns:
      - "https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/font-awesome/**"
    expectedIconFallback: "aria-label or title on all interactive elements"
    checkKeyboardNav: true

successCriteria:
  - All icon-only interactive elements have accessible names when icons fail to load
  - CLS score remains below 0.25 with font CDN blocked
  - No uncaught JavaScript errors from missing font face declarations
  - Application is navigable via keyboard with fallback fonts active
```

**TypeScript: Font fallback oracle**

```typescript
// src/testing/exploratory/font-fallback-oracle.ts
// Blocks font CDN requests via Playwright route interception and verifies
// that icon buttons retain accessible names and that CLS stays below threshold.

import { type Page, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

export interface FontFallbackResult {
  fontsBlocked: string[];
  iconButtonsWithNoAccessibleName: string[];
  measuredCls: number;
  foutDetected: boolean;
  consoleErrorsDuringFontLoad: string[];
}

export async function runFontFallbackOracle(
  context: BrowserContext,
  appUrl: string,
  cdnPatterns: string[],
  clsThreshold: number = 0.25
): Promise<FontFallbackResult> {
  const page: Page = await context.newPage();
  const consoleErrors: string[] = [];

  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') consoleErrors.push(msg.text());
  });

  // Block all font CDN patterns
  for (const pattern of cdnPatterns) {
    await page.route(pattern, (route) => route.abort());
  }

  await page.goto(appUrl, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

  // Measure CLS via PerformanceObserver
  const measuredCls: number = await page.evaluate(
    () =>
      new Promise<number>((resolve) => {
        let clsScore = 0;
        const obs = new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
          for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
            if ((entry as any).hadRecentInput === false) {
              clsScore += (entry as any).value ?? 0;
            }
          }
        });
        obs.observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });
        setTimeout(() => { obs.disconnect(); resolve(clsScore); }, 2000);
      })
  );

  // Find icon-only buttons without accessible names
  const iconButtonsWithNoAccessibleName: string[] = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const buttons = Array.from(
      document.querySelectorAll('button, [role="button"], a[href]')
    );
    return buttons
      .filter((el) => {
        const text = el.textContent?.trim() ?? '';
        const label = el.getAttribute('aria-label') ?? '';
        const title = el.getAttribute('title') ?? '';
        const ariaLabelledBy = el.getAttribute('aria-labelledby') ?? '';
        return text.length === 0 && label.length === 0 && title.length === 0 && ariaLabelledBy.length === 0;
      })
      .map((el) => el.outerHTML.slice(0, 100));
  });

  const foutDetected = measuredCls > 0.05;

  await page.close();
  return {
    fontsBlocked: cdnPatterns,
    iconButtonsWithNoAccessibleName,
    measuredCls,
    foutDetected,
    consoleErrorsDuringFontLoad: consoleErrors.filter(
      (e) => e.toLowerCase().includes('font') || e.toLowerCase().includes('css')
    ),
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Font fallback charters are most critical for applications with corporate or government user bases (where network security appliances frequently block external CDNs) and for applications with international reach (regional CDN blocks). Also critical after switching font providers or adding a new icon library. Do NOT host third-party fonts as the sole remediation without also adding `font-display: swap` and `size-adjust` CSS to prevent FOIT. Named alternative: The `font-display` descriptor on `@font-face` declarations controls FOIT/FOUT browser-side; the charter verifies the end-to-end loading fallback behavior including CLS impact which CSS alone cannot prevent. [community]

## Additional Community Lessons (Cycle 32)

184. **[community] Deadline propagation defects were discovered at multiple teams only after production incidents where a downstream service returned partial data without any error status.** The root cause was that service A forwarded the original HTTP timeout header but service B — added six months later by a different team — did not read it, imposed its own 30-second timeout, and returned HTTP 200 with a partial payload when it exceeded its own budget. The client application rendered the partial data as if it were complete. WHY this matters: partial-success responses with HTTP 200 are the most dangerous failure mode in distributed systems because monitoring tools, client error handlers, and user-visible error states all treat 200 as success — the data inconsistency is only discovered later when a user notices missing records.

185. **[community] Audit log gap analysis during exploratory sessions consistently revealed that password-change and MFA-disable actions were not logged at teams that had excellent coverage of data-write operations.** The pattern was: the security team had specified logging for CRUD operations on business data, but identity management actions were handled by a third-party auth library that emitted events to a different sink — one that was not included in the audit log query used during compliance reviews. The gap persisted for 14 months before an exploratory charter specifically targeting "what actions am I taking that are NOT showing up in the audit log?" revealed it. WHY this matters: regulators assess audit log completeness based on the classification of the action, not the system boundary — an MFA-disable action missing from the audit log is a compliance finding regardless of which service processed it.

186. **[community] Service worker update prompt defects were identified as the primary cause of "why is the app still broken after we fixed it?" support escalations at PWA teams.** Users had the application open in a background tab and reported that the bug continued after the fix was deployed. The application registered the new service worker but had no update prompt, so users continued running the old worker until they manually closed all tabs — behavior they did not know they needed to perform. Teams that added a banner ("A new version is available — click to update") with a forced reload saw the support ticket category eliminated within two weeks of deploying the change. WHY this matters: the service worker lifecycle is fundamentally different from traditional web caching and violates the user's implicit expectation that "refreshing the page" gets the latest version — failing to surface this difference produces persistent user confusion and repeated support escalations.

187. **[community] Webhook idempotency defects were most commonly introduced during payment provider migrations, where the new provider used a different event ID format that the application's deduplication logic did not match.** The original provider used UUID v4 event IDs; the new provider used prefixed IDs (`evt_abc123`). The deduplication table used a `CHAR(36)` column that silently truncated the longer prefixed ID, causing multiple event IDs to hash to the same stored value and falsely appearing as duplicates — while other events with IDs differing only in the suffix were processed multiple times. The exploratory charter for webhook idempotency caught this within the first hour of testing against the new provider's sandbox environment. WHY this matters: payment deduplication defects have direct financial impact — duplicate charges or missed payments — and they are almost always silent at the time of occurrence, only surfacing during end-of-month reconciliation.

188. **[community] Speculative prefetch side effects caused a significant overcount in "feature interest" product metrics at multiple teams using Next.js App Router with the default `prefetch={true}` behavior on Link components.** Product managers were using page-view events to measure interest in a new feature, but the link to the feature appeared in a navigation dropdown that was hovered frequently without being clicked. The prefetch fired a page_view event on every hover, inflating the interest metric by approximately 8x. The team had been preparing to prioritise the feature based on what turned out to be mostly phantom demand. WHY this matters: server-side telemetry based on HTTP GETs implicitly assumes user intent, which is violated by prefetch requests — any analytics implementation that does not distinguish between prefetch-initiated and user-initiated requests is fundamentally measuring browser behavior rather than user behavior.

189. **[community] Font fallback testing revealed that icon-only button defects disproportionately affected admin and power-user interfaces, where designers had relied entirely on icon font glyphs for action buttons in toolbar-dense layouts.** When the icon font CDN was blocked, every toolbar button rendered as an empty rectangle with no label, and keyboard navigation produced focus on elements with no accessible name — causing screen readers to announce "button" with no context. The fixes required two separate efforts: adding `aria-label` attributes to all icon-only buttons (a one-time fix), and changing the CDN loading strategy to self-host with `font-display: swap` and system font fallbacks (an infrastructure change). The exploratory session was the forcing function for both changes that accessibility audits had flagged as recommendations for over a year without triggering remediation. WHY this matters: icon font fallback failures are an accessibility emergency, not merely a visual defect — they remove the semantic meaning of every interactive element in the application for keyboard and screen reader users simultaneously, making the application completely unusable for those users until connectivity is restored.
