**220. Axe-Core Incremental Accessibility Regression Charter** [official]

**Description**: Running a full-page axe-core scan at the end of a feature session is a common pattern, but it surfaces dozens of pre-existing violations alongside any newly introduced ones, making it impossible to determine whether the current session introduced new regressions. The incremental pattern captures a baseline axe snapshot at session start against a known stable route, then diffs violation fingerprints after the feature under exploration is exercised. Only net-new violations (present after but not before) are treated as session findings. This approach transforms accessibility exploration from a guilt-by-association audit into a targeted regression detector that a tester can act on immediately without triage noise. The delta approach also makes the session result actionable for developers, who can ignore pre-existing debt and focus on what their change broke.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

interface AxeViolation { id: string; nodes: { target: string[] }[] }

function fingerprint(violations: AxeViolation[]): Set<string> {
  const keys = new Set<string>();
  for (const v of violations) {
    for (const node of v.nodes) {
      keys.add(`${v.id}::${node.target.join(',')}`);
    }
  }
  return keys;
}

test('Axe incremental regression — checkout form', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const baselineResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();
  const baselineKeys = fingerprint(baselineResults.violations);

  // Navigate to the feature under exploration
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /cart/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /checkout/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /checkout/i })).toBeVisible();

  const featureResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();
  const featureKeys = fingerprint(featureResults.violations);

  const newViolations = [...featureKeys].filter(k => !baselineKeys.has(k));
  expect(newViolations, `New axe violations introduced by feature:\n${newViolations.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for any feature session involving form elements, dialogs, or dynamic content injection. The baseline must be captured from a route unaffected by the feature under test — if the entire app shares a navigation header that the feature changes, narrow the axe scan with `.include()` to exclude shared components. Do NOT use the full incremental pattern in cold-start exploratory sessions where no stable baseline exists; in that case, capture the full violation set and file pre-existing ones as known issues in the session sheet. Requires `npm install -D @axe-core/playwright` with a pinned version. [official]

---

**221. Network Fault Injection Charter — HTTP Error Cascade Exploration** [official]

**Description**: Web applications frequently handle 200 OK responses correctly while silently breaking on 429 Too Many Requests, 503 Service Unavailable, or partial response payloads. Playwright's `page.route()` lets a tester inject synthetic HTTP faults at any point in a user journey without modifying backend configuration. The charter works through a fault catalogue: 4xx authentication failures, 5xx server errors, empty response bodies with 200 OK status, truncated JSON, and extremely slow responses (via `delay` in `route.fulfill`). Each fault is injected against a different API endpoint in turn to map which service failures cascade visually into the UI and which are silently swallowed. The session produces a fault tolerance map — a table showing which endpoints have graceful error states and which produce blank screens or unhandled exceptions.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const FAULT_CATALOGUE = [
  { status: 429, body: '{"error":"rate_limited"}',   description: 'Rate limit 429' },
  { status: 503, body: '{"error":"unavailable"}',    description: 'Service unavailable 503' },
  { status: 200, body: '',                            description: 'Empty 200 body' },
  { status: 200, body: '{"incomplete":',              description: 'Truncated JSON with 200' },
] as const;

test.describe('API fault injection — product listing endpoint', () => {
  for (const fault of FAULT_CATALOGUE) {
    test(`Products API: ${fault.description}`, async ({ page }) => {
      const uncaughtErrors: string[] = [];
      page.on('console', m => { if (m.type() === 'error') uncaughtErrors.push(m.text()); });

      await page.route('**/api/products**', route =>
        route.fulfill({ status: fault.status, body: fault.body, contentType: 'application/json' })
      );

      await page.goto('/products');

      // Application must show a graceful error state, not a blank page
      const gracefulState = page.locator('[data-testid="error-banner"], [data-testid="empty-state"]');
      await expect(gracefulState).toBeVisible({ timeout: 8000 });

      // No uncaught JS exceptions should be emitted
      const uncaught = uncaughtErrors.filter(e => /uncaught|cannot read/i.test(e));
      expect(uncaught, `Uncaught errors with fault "${fault.description}": ${uncaught.join('; ')}`).toHaveLength(0);
    });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use early in a feature's life cycle — before real backend fault scenarios are available — and before each major release to verify error handling is intact. Fault injection reveals error handling gaps faster than any other single pattern because most developers test only the happy path. `page.route()` intercepts page-level fetch but not service-worker-initiated fetch; use `context.route()` when the application proxies API calls through a service worker. Do NOT use injected delays as a substitute for real performance profiling — the delay is not realistic network latency distribution. [official]

---

**222. Soft Assertion Sweep Charter — Multi-Defect Surface Coverage** [official]

**Description**: Playwright's `expect.soft()` accumulates assertion failures without terminating the test, making it possible to complete an entire user flow and surface all defects in a single run rather than stopping at the first failure. In exploratory sessions this is especially valuable for "sweep" charters: the tester scripts the entire user journey using soft assertions for all non-critical checks, allowing the session to produce a complete defect inventory in one pass. Hard assertions are reserved only for preconditions without which later steps are meaningless (e.g., login must succeed before profile checks can run). Soft assertion results in the Playwright HTML reporter display all accumulated failures together, giving the tester a comprehensive view of session findings without rerunning the test twelve times.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Profile page soft-assertion sweep', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('[name="email"]', 'test@example.com');
  await page.fill('[name="password"]', 'password123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
  // Hard assertion: must be logged in before profile checks make sense
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);

  await page.goto('/profile');

  // Soft assertions — accumulate failures without aborting the session
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /profile/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByLabel(/display name/i)).toBeEditable();
  await expect.soft(page.getByLabel(/email/i)).toHaveValue('test@example.com');
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('img', { name: /avatar/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('button', { name: /save changes/i })).toBeEnabled();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('link', { name: /change password/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.locator('[data-testid="last-login"]')).toContainText(/2026/);
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('button', { name: /delete account/i })).toBeVisible();
  // All soft failures are surfaced together in the HTML report session output
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for sweep charters covering stable, well-understood flows where the goal is defect inventory rather than deep investigation of a single area. Soft assertions lower the information density per run — every failure gets equal visibility regardless of severity, so the tester must triage the output. After the sweep, convert discovered defects into hard assertions in scripted regression tests so future regressions surface immediately. Do NOT use soft assertions throughout production regression suites — they degrade as a feedback mechanism when failures accumulate silently and go un-reviewed across CI runs. [official]

---

**223. Custom Test Annotation-Driven Session Evidence Charter** [official]

**Description**: Playwright's custom annotation API (`test.info().annotations.push({ type, description })`) enables testers to attach structured metadata to each test as the session runs, creating a machine-readable session sheet embedded in the HTML report. During exploratory sessions, annotations serve as the real-time note-taking layer: each observation (a surprising behavior, a potential defect, a risk area identified) is pushed with a structured type (`'observation'`, `'risk'`, `'defect-candidate'`, `'follow-on-charter'`). After the session, the HTML report doubles as the session sheet, with all observations accessible alongside the test timeline. This eliminates the split between "run the test" and "write the session notes" — the notes are generated as a byproduct of execution.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

function note(type: 'observation' | 'risk' | 'defect-candidate' | 'follow-on-charter', description: string) {
  test.info().annotations.push({ type, description });
}

test('Checkout flow — annotation-driven exploratory session', async ({ page }) => {
  note('observation', 'Session start: checkout flow with expired promo code');

  await page.goto('/cart');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /cart/i })).toBeVisible();
  note('observation', '[00:01] Cart loaded correctly with 2 items in basket');

  await page.getByTestId('promo-code-input').fill('EXPIRED2023');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /apply/i }).click();

  const errorMsg = page.getByTestId('promo-error');
  try {
    await expect(errorMsg).toBeVisible({ timeout: 3000 });
    const text = await errorMsg.textContent();
    if (!text?.toLowerCase().includes('expired')) {
      note('defect-candidate', `Promo error message vague: "${text}" — does not mention "expired"`);
    } else {
      note('observation', `[00:02] Error message quality OK: "${text}"`);
    }
  } catch {
    note('defect-candidate', '[00:02] No error message appeared after applying expired promo — silent failure');
  }

  note('follow-on-charter', 'Explore: promo code edge cases — whitespace-only, SQL injection, concurrent apply');
  note('risk', 'Risk: promo validation may be client-side only — confirm server validation exists');
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use when you want the session sheet and test execution to be a single artefact. The annotation approach requires scripting the session flow (or at minimum key checkpoints), which adds structure but reduces the pure-exploration freedom of entirely unscripted sessions. Best applied to "structured exploration" sessions where the happy-path flow is known and the goal is to probe around it. Do NOT use annotations as a substitute for a proper defect filing workflow — annotations are session evidence, not bug tickets, and they disappear when the HTML report is regenerated. [official]

---

**224. Tagged Regression Suite Coverage Mapping Charter** [official]

**Description**: Playwright's `--grep` flag and `@tag` annotation system enable testers to map which tests cover which exploratory charter areas, and to run only the subset relevant to a session's scope. Before a session, running `npx playwright test --grep @checkout` shows which scripted tests already cover the area, allowing the exploratory session to focus on coverage gaps rather than duplicating existing automation. After a session, newly discovered defects that lack existing scripted coverage are tagged `@exploratory-uncovered` to track the exploration-to-automation debt explicitly in the codebase. The session charter explicitly lists which `@tags` it extends and which gaps it reveals.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Pre-session command: npx playwright test --grep @checkout
// This test documents an exploratory-uncovered area: address validation with non-ASCII characters

test('@checkout @exploratory-uncovered Address validation — non-ASCII characters', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/address');
  await page.getByLabel(/street/i).fill('123 Ñoño Ávenue');
  await page.getByLabel(/city/i).fill('São Paulo');
  await page.getByLabel(/postal code/i).fill('01310-100');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /save address/i }).click();

  // Oracle: the address must round-trip correctly without encoding corruption
  await page.goto('/profile/addresses');
  const saved = page.getByTestId('address-display').first();
  await expect(saved).toContainText('Ñoño');
  await expect(saved).toContainText('São Paulo');
});

test('@checkout @exploratory-uncovered Postal code format — country-dependent validation', async ({ page }) => {
  const cases = [
    { country: 'Germany', postal: '10115',    expectValid: true },
    { country: 'UK',      postal: 'SW1A 1AA', expectValid: true },
    { country: 'Japan',   postal: '100-0001', expectValid: true },
    { country: 'Germany', postal: 'SW1A 1AA', expectValid: false },
  ];
  for (const c of cases) {
    await page.goto('/checkout/address');
    await page.getByLabel(/country/i).selectOption(c.country);
    await page.getByLabel(/postal/i).fill(c.postal);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /validate|next/i }).click();
    const result = page.getByTestId('postal-validation-result');
    await expect(result).toContainText(c.expectValid ? /valid/i : /invalid/i);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use during exploratory sessions in areas with existing scripted test suites to avoid duplicating coverage and to target genuine gaps. The `@exploratory-uncovered` convention requires team discipline to retire tags once scripted tests are written for the defects found. Do NOT apply tags retroactively to hundreds of existing tests as a one-time audit — begin with new sessions and evolve the tag convention incrementally so the coverage debt remains accurate and actionable. [official]

---

**225. Response Time SLA Assertion Charter — Client-Perceived Latency Oracle** [official]

**Description**: Most exploratory sessions ignore network timing, but Playwright exposes `response.timing()` — a full resource timing breakdown including DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, and time-to-first-byte — making it possible to assert response-time SLAs as part of exploratory flow without a separate performance tool. The pattern treats a latency threshold as a correctness oracle: if the product SLA guarantees sub-300ms API responses, a 2-second response is a defect even if the response is functionally correct. This is especially valuable in exploratory sessions on new features where no performance baselines have been established yet — the first session creates the baseline and immediately surfaces outliers.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const SLA_MS: Record<string, number> = {
  'api/products':  500,
  'api/cart':      300,
  'api/checkout': 1000,
};

test('Response time SLA oracle — product and cart API calls', async ({ page }) => {
  const breaches: { url: string; duration: number; sla: number }[] = [];

  page.on('response', async response => {
    const url = response.url();
    const matchedEntry = Object.entries(SLA_MS).find(([pattern]) => url.includes(pattern));
    if (!matchedEntry) return;
    const [, sla] = matchedEntry;
    const timing = response.timing();
    const duration = timing.responseEnd - timing.requestStart;
    if (duration > sla) {
      breaches.push({ url, duration, sla });
      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: 'latency-breach',
        description: `${url} took ${duration.toFixed(0)}ms — SLA=${sla}ms`,
      });
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/products');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /cart/i }).click();
  await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  expect(breaches, `SLA breaches detected:\n${JSON.stringify(breaches, null, 2)}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use during feature sessions when the feature makes API calls whose latency affects perceived UX quality. Response timing from `response.timing()` reflects client-perceived latency including TLS and DNS — often a more user-relevant metric than server processing time alone. Do NOT set tight SLAs (< 100ms) in shared CI environments where compute contention inflates durations; calibrate thresholds against p95 production metrics. Avoid asserting timing on third-party resources (analytics, CDN assets) that the team cannot control. [official]

---

**226. Interaction-State Rollback Oracle Charter** [community]

**Description**: Many multi-step UI flows lack a reliable rollback path: the user navigates forward, triggers a side effect (reservation created, payment initiated, file uploaded), then navigates back using the browser Back button or the application's own back link. The rollback oracle checks that navigating backward after a partial side effect leaves the system in a consistent, non-corrupt state. The most common defects in this category are orphaned server-side records created before payment completion, cart quantity drift when navigating back and re-adding items, and file upload partial states that block future uploads. The charter explicitly maps forward-and-back sequences as a first-class exploration target because most development testing covers only the forward path.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Rollback oracle — cart quantity after back navigation mid-checkout', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).first().click();
  const cartCount = page.getByTestId('cart-item-count');
  await expect(cartCount).toHaveText('1');

  // Proceed to checkout and partially fill the form
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /checkout/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/checkout/);
  await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill('test@example.com');

  // Navigate back before completing — rollback oracle
  await page.goBack();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/products/);

  // Cart should still contain exactly 1 item — not 0 (dropped) or 2 (duplicated)
  await expect(cartCount).toHaveText('1');

  // Navigate forward again — form state should be preserved (browser form restoration)
  await page.goForward();
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/email/i)).toHaveValue('test@example.com');

  // In-app "Back" link should behave identically to browser back button
  await page.goto('/products');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /checkout/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /back to cart/i }).click();
  await expect(cartCount).toHaveText('1');
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for any multi-step flow with server-side state creation at an intermediate step: checkouts, booking flows, multi-page forms, file upload wizards. Back-navigation defects are among the most frequently filed production bugs for e-commerce flows yet are almost never covered by scripted tests. Note that `page.goBack()` uses the browser history stack while in-app back links may use `router.push('/cart')` — these are different navigation mechanisms that can behave differently; test both. Do NOT assume a correct `goBack()` result means the application's in-app back link works the same way. [community]

---

**227. Clipboard Read/Write Security and Content Oracle Charter** [community]

**Description**: The Web Clipboard API has specific security constraints: clipboard access requires a user gesture in standard contexts and is restricted in cross-origin iframes. Applications that copy sensitive data (API keys, passwords, payment card numbers) to the clipboard expose users to data exfiltration if a malicious extension or script intercepts clipboard events. The charter explores three dimensions: (1) sensitive data is not copied to the clipboard without explicit user intent (no passive clipboard write on page load); (2) clipboard writes produce the correct plain-text value rather than HTML-encoded garbage or partial content; (3) clipboard access is not attempted inside a cross-origin iframe that would silently fail and leave the user confused by a non-functional copy button.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Clipboard oracle — API key copy button writes correct plain text', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await context.grantPermissions(['clipboard-read', 'clipboard-write']);

  await page.goto('/settings/api-keys');
  const keyDisplay = page.getByTestId('api-key-display');
  await expect(keyDisplay).toBeVisible();

  // Capture the displayed key before clicking copy
  const displayedKey = (await keyDisplay.textContent()) ?? '';

  // Security check: clipboard must not be written before user gesture
  const preClickClipboard = await page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.readText());
  expect(preClickClipboard).not.toBe(displayedKey.trim());

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /copy api key/i }).click();

  // Clipboard must match the displayed value exactly
  const clipboardContent = await page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.readText());
  expect(clipboardContent.trim()).toBe(displayedKey.trim());

  // Verify plain text — no HTML tags in clipboard content
  expect(clipboardContent).not.toMatch(/<[^>]+>/);

  // Confirm visual feedback (e.g., "Copied!" tooltip or button label change)
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /copied/i })).toBeVisible({ timeout: 2000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for any feature that exposes sensitive credentials, tokens, or user data with a copy-to-clipboard affordance. Clipboard permission grants (`context.grantPermissions`) are Chromium-specific in Playwright; Firefox and WebKit have different clipboard security models. The pre-click clipboard check detects passive clipboard writes (a real security risk) but requires that the clipboard was not already populated with the same value from a prior test — ensure test isolation by either clearing the clipboard before the test or using a unique key value per run. Do NOT assume clipboard tests cover third-party extension interception — they only test the application's own behavior. [community]

---

**228. Deep-Link and URL State Fidelity Charter** [community]

**Description**: Applications that encode state in the URL — filters, pagination, selected tabs, modal open states, search terms — must faithfully reconstruct that state when the URL is opened in a fresh browser session. This is the "shareability guarantee": a URL shared in a chat should produce the same view as the URL was generated from. The charter captures URLs at various application states (filter applied, specific tab active, search results page, modal open), clears all cookies and storage, then navigates to each URL to verify exact state reconstruction. Defects include filter state lost on fresh load, wrong tab selected, modal URL opening to modal-closed state, and search term present in the URL bar but absent from the search field.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Deep-link fidelity — filter and pagination state reconstruction', async ({ page, browser }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Apply filter and advance to page 2
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /category/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('option', { name: /electronics/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /next page/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/category=electronics/);
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/page=2/);
  const capturedUrl = page.url();

  // Reconstruct state in a fully isolated context — no cookies, no localStorage
  const freshContext = await browser.newContext({ storageState: undefined });
  const freshPage = await freshContext.newPage();
  await freshPage.goto(capturedUrl);

  // Verify exact state reconstruction
  await expect(freshPage.getByTestId('active-filter')).toContainText(/electronics/i);
  await expect(freshPage.getByTestId('pagination-current')).toHaveText('2');
  await expect(freshPage.getByTestId('product-grid')).toBeVisible();
  // Verify unauthenticated deep-link redirect (if feature requires auth)
  expect(freshPage.url()).not.toMatch(/\/login/);

  await freshContext.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use whenever the application uses URL-based state management (React Router `useSearchParams`, Vue Router query, Next.js dynamic routes). Deep-link fidelity bugs are disproportionately reported by power users who bookmark filtered views or share URLs across team channels. Creating a fresh `browser.newContext()` with `storageState: undefined` is the gold standard for isolation — avoid using `page.reload()` in the same context as it may preserve localStorage. Do NOT test deep links only against authenticated state — also verify the unauthenticated deep-link redirect path, since many teams forget to implement or test the `returnTo` redirect after login. [community]

---

**229. Timezone and Daylight Saving Time Boundary Charter** [community]

**Description**: Web applications that display, compare, or schedule times fail predictably at DST transitions — in the hour that is skipped (spring forward) or repeated (fall back). Playwright's `page.clock()` API enables the browser clock to be frozen and advanced across DST boundary moments without waiting for them to occur naturally. The charter uses `page.clock.setFixedTime()` to position the clock just before each boundary, then `page.clock.fastForward()` to step across it, verifying that the application correctly updates time displays, relative timestamps ("2 hours ago"), and scheduled event times. It also cross-checks that server-returned UTC timestamps are correctly interpreted by the browser's `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in the emulated timezone context.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const DST_BOUNDARIES = [
  { label: 'US/Eastern spring forward', iso: '2026-03-08T06:59:00.000Z' }, // 1:59 AM ET
  { label: 'US/Eastern fall back',      iso: '2026-11-01T05:59:00.000Z' }, // 1:59 AM ET
  { label: 'UTC midnight crossing',     iso: '2026-05-14T23:59:00.000Z' },
] as const;

test.describe('DST boundary oracle', () => {
  for (const { label, iso } of DST_BOUNDARIES) {
    test(`Time display: ${label}`, async ({ page }) => {
      // Freeze the browser clock just before the boundary
      await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date(iso));
      await page.goto('/dashboard');

      const timeDisplay = page.getByTestId('current-time-display');
      await expect(timeDisplay).toBeVisible();
      const before = await timeDisplay.textContent();

      // Advance 2 minutes across the DST boundary
      await page.clock.fastForward(2 * 60 * 1000);
      await page.reload();
      const after = await timeDisplay.textContent();

      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: 'dst-boundary-observation',
        description: `${label}: before="${before}" after="${after}"`,
      });

      // Time display must not go backwards or freeze
      expect(after).not.toBe(before);
    });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for any application that handles scheduling, calendar events, reminders, JWT expiry display, or relative timestamps like "X minutes ago." DST boundary defects are among the hardest to reproduce without clock manipulation — they occur twice a year on specific dates. `page.clock()` is available since Playwright v1.45 with `setFixedTime`, `fastForward`, and `runFor`. Do NOT rely solely on setting the Node.js `TZ` environment variable for DST testing — `TZ=America/New_York` affects the server process timezone but not the browser's `Intl` locale; the browser context timezone must be configured via `timezoneId` in the browser context options for full coverage. [community]

---

**230. Form Auto-Save and Draft Recovery Charter** [community]

**Description**: Long forms (article editors, multi-step onboarding wizards, complex configuration forms) often implement auto-save or draft recovery to prevent data loss. The charter explores whether auto-save is reliable, whether recovery is presented in the correct scenario (tab close, session timeout, network disconnect), and whether stale drafts from a previous completed session are correctly invalidated after explicit submission. The most impactful defect class is the "phantom draft": a recovery prompt appears for a form that was already submitted, misleading the user into thinking their previous submission failed. A second class is "silent auto-save failure": the save indicator says "Saved" but the network request failed, and the user discovers the data is gone only on next visit.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Draft recovery oracle — article editor', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/articles/new');
  await page.getByLabel(/title/i).fill('Draft recovery test article');
  await page.getByLabel(/body/i).fill('Article body that must survive navigation away.');

  // Wait for the auto-save indicator to confirm persistence
  const autoSaveIndicator = page.getByTestId('autosave-indicator');
  await expect(autoSaveIndicator).toContainText(/saved/i, { timeout: 10000 });

  // Simulate abandonment: navigate away without submitting
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);

  // Return to the editor — draft recovery must be offered
  await page.goto('/articles/new');
  const recoveryBanner = page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /restore draft/i })
    .or(page.getByTestId('draft-recovery-banner'));
  await expect(recoveryBanner).toBeVisible({ timeout: 6000 });

  // Accept the recovery and verify content is restored exactly
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /restore/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/title/i)).toHaveValue('Draft recovery test article');
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/body/i)).toHaveValue('Article body that must survive navigation away.');

  // Submit the form — confirm that no recovery prompt appears on the NEXT visit
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /publish|submit/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/articles\/\d+|articles\/[a-z0-9-]+/);
  await page.goto('/articles/new');
  await expect(recoveryBanner).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: 3000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for any feature with a long-form editing flow: CMS editors, configuration wizards, multi-step registrations. Auto-save and draft recovery are among the most user-visible reliability features and among the most commonly broken by schema migrations or IndexedDB refactors. Draft storage implementations vary (localStorage, IndexedDB, server-side drafts API) — the charter approach is identical regardless, but diagnostics when it fails differ. Do NOT use this charter as a substitute for testing offline resilience — the network-interrupted auto-save scenario requires explicit `context.setOffline(true)` beyond what this pattern covers. [community]

---

**231. Incremental Scroll and Progressive Load Integrity Charter** [official]

**Description**: Infinite scroll and virtual-list patterns replace traditional pagination with dynamic content loading triggered by the user reaching the bottom of the viewport. The charter verifies three invariants: (1) no duplicate items appear across scroll positions; (2) the total item count converges to the server-reported total after all pages are loaded; (3) scroll position is preserved after navigating to a detail view and returning via the browser Back button. Playwright's `page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight))` combined with response interception provides deterministic scroll-and-load cycles without relying on flaky `networkidle` waits that break on infinite scroll feeds.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Infinite scroll integrity oracle — feed items', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/feed');
  const seenIds = new Set<string>();
  const duplicates: string[] = [];

  let previousHeight = 0;
  const MAX_ITERATIONS = 10;

  for (let i = 0; i < MAX_ITERATIONS; i++) {
    const items = page.getByTestId('feed-item');
    const count = await items.count();

    for (let j = 0; j < count; j++) {
      const id = await items.nth(j).getAttribute('data-id') ?? `unknown-${j}`;
      if (seenIds.has(id)) duplicates.push(`Iteration ${i}: duplicate id="${id}"`);
      seenIds.add(id);
    }

    // Scroll to trigger next page load
    await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight));
    await page.waitForTimeout(700); // allow loading state to clear

    const newHeight = await page.evaluate(() => document.body.scrollHeight);
    if (newHeight === previousHeight) break; // no new content loaded — end of feed
    previousHeight = newHeight;
  }

  expect(duplicates, `Duplicate feed items detected:\n${duplicates.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);

  // Cross-check loaded count against server-reported total
  const totalDisplay = page.getByTestId('total-item-count');
  if (await totalDisplay.isVisible()) {
    const serverTotal = parseInt(await totalDisplay.innerText(), 10);
    expect(seenIds.size).toBeLessThanOrEqual(serverTotal);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for feeds, product catalogs, comment threads, and any virtual-list component. Duplicate detection requires server-assigned stable IDs in the DOM (`data-id` attributes); if absent, use text-content fingerprinting as a fallback (less reliable due to non-unique items). `page.waitForTimeout(700)` is an explicit delay that introduces flakiness risk — prefer intercepting the paginated API response and waiting for a `.not.toBeVisible()` check on the loading spinner instead. Do NOT use this pattern as a performance benchmark — measure virtual list render time with the Performance API if render speed is the concern. [official]

---

**232. Multi-Step Wizard State Preservation Under Interruption Charter** [community]

**Description**: Multi-step registration, configuration, and onboarding wizards accumulate state across several screens. The charter probes whether wizard state survives interruption events: opening a new tab, a token refresh mid-step, or a session timeout while the user is on step 3. Each interruption type corrupts wizard state in a different way: token refresh may reset the React context holding wizard data; session timeout may redirect to login and discard the `returnTo` URL for the wizard's current step; switching tabs may trigger a security re-authentication challenge that clears previously entered values. The charter documents which interruption types are handled versus which cause silent data loss, creating a fault-tolerance map for the feature.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Wizard state preservation — session timeout mid-wizard', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/onboarding/step-1');
  await page.getByLabel(/company name/i).fill('ACME Corp');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /next/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/step-2/);

  await page.getByLabel(/industry/i).selectOption('Technology');
  await page.getByLabel(/team size/i).selectOption('11-50');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /next/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/step-3/);

  // Simulate session expiry by clearing auth state
  await page.context().clearCookies();

  // Trigger any action requiring auth to expose the expired session state
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /next/i }).click();

  if (page.url().includes('login')) {
    // Graceful: redirected to login with return URL pointing back to wizard
    expect(page.url()).toMatch(/return_to.*onboarding/i);
    test.info().annotations.push({ type: 'observation', description: 'Session expiry redirects to login with return_to wizard URL — correct' });
  } else {
    // Inline re-auth: verify step 2 data was preserved in state
    await expect(page.getByLabel(/industry/i)).toHaveValue('Technology');
    test.info().annotations.push({ type: 'observation', description: 'Inline session refresh — step 2 data preserved correctly' });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for onboarding flows and multi-step setup wizards where abandonment due to interruption represents a meaningful conversion loss. Session timeout simulation via cookie clearing is a blunt instrument that simulates the most common production scenario (JWT expiry during a long form) but does not reproduce graceful server-side timeout with a proper challenge flow. For more realistic simulation, use `page.clock.fastForward()` to advance past the JWT expiry time and then trigger a request. Do NOT assume wizard step data is always stored client-side — some implementations persist each step to the server on Next click, which fundamentally changes the recovery model and failure modes. [community]

---

**233. Accessibility Axe Scan After Dynamic Content Injection Charter** [official]

**Description**: Axe-core scans run at page load catch static accessibility violations, but many modern applications inject content dynamically: modals, drawers, toast notifications, autocomplete dropdowns, and inline validation errors are all rendered after user interaction. The charter runs targeted axe scans immediately after each dynamic content injection event, using `AxeBuilder.include()` scoped to the injected element's container to avoid noise from the unchanged rest of the page. This catches the category of defects that static scanning misses: modal dialogs without `aria-labelledby`, toast notifications without a live region `role="status"`, and validation errors not connected to their input field via `aria-describedby`.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('Axe scan after dynamic injection — modal and toast', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings');

  // Trigger the "Delete account" confirmation modal
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /delete account/i }).click();
  const modal = page.getByRole('dialog');
  await expect(modal).toBeVisible();

  // Scan only the modal container — exclude the rest of the page
  const modalResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .include('[role="dialog"]')
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa'])
    .analyze();
  expect(
    modalResults.violations.map(v => `${v.id}: ${v.description}`),
    'Modal axe violations'
  ).toEqual([]);

  // Dismiss the modal, trigger a success toast
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /cancel/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /save settings/i }).click();
  const toast = page.getByRole('status').or(page.getByRole('alert'));
  await expect(toast).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 });

  // Scan only the toast element
  const toastResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .include('[role="status"], [role="alert"]')
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa'])
    .analyze();
  expect(
    toastResults.violations.map(v => `${v.id}: ${v.description}`),
    'Toast axe violations'
  ).toEqual([]);
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for any feature session that involves UI components injected after user interaction — modals, flyouts, toasts, and inline validation messages. Scoping with `.include()` is essential: a full-page scan after every interaction accumulates redundant violations from unchanged parts of the page, drowning out actionable findings. Requires `npm install -D @axe-core/playwright` with a pinned version to avoid rule changes between minor axe-core updates affecting session-to-session comparability. Do NOT treat passing axe scans as a complete accessibility guarantee — axe detects approximately 30–40% of WCAG violations; manual keyboard and screen reader testing is required for the remainder. [official]

---

**234. Stale Element Resilience Under Skeleton Loading Charter** [community]

**Description**: Many modern applications render skeleton screens — placeholder loading states — while real content is fetched. The skeleton and the real content often occupy the same DOM container, causing locators resolved against the skeleton element to become stale when real content replaces the skeleton node. This creates intermittent test failures that only manifest in CI (where pages load slower) and not locally: the locator finds the skeleton card, real content arrives and replaces the DOM, and the subsequent assertion against the stale skeleton reference throws `ElementNotFound` or `StaleElementReference`. The charter systematically exercises every skeleton loading state in the application, verifying that locator patterns correctly wait for real content rather than racing with the loading state.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Skeleton loading resilience — product cards replace skeleton correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  // Introduce a controlled API delay to ensure skeleton is visible during the test
  await page.route('**/api/products**', async route => {
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 600));
    await route.continue();
  });

  await page.goto('/products');

  // Skeleton placeholder must be visible during loading
  const skeletonCards = page.locator('[data-testid="skeleton-card"]');
  await expect(skeletonCards.first()).toBeVisible({ timeout: 2000 });

  // Wait for real content — use a stable non-loading attribute, not the skeleton locator
  const productCards = page.locator('[data-testid="product-card"]:not([data-loading])');
  await expect(productCards.first()).toBeVisible({ timeout: 8000 });

  // Skeletons must be fully gone after real content arrives
  await expect(skeletonCards).toHaveCount(0);
  const productCount = await productCards.count();
  expect(productCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // Interact only with real content after skeleton is cleared
  await productCards.first().getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-item-count')).toHaveText('1');
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use for any application page that uses skeleton loading patterns — product grids, feed items, dashboard widgets, and table rows. The `:not([data-loading])` attribute selector requires the application to toggle a `data-loading` attribute when real content loads; if no such attribute exists, use `page.waitForResponse('**/api/products**')` followed by `productCards.first().waitFor({ state: 'visible' })` as the transition signal. Do NOT introduce artificial delays into production-facing routes — confine the delay injection to the test environment using a dedicated test route prefix (`/api/test/**`) or Playwright's route pattern scoped to non-production origins. [community]

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 40)

**G1. `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` returns `true` for elements hidden behind a `pointer-events: none` overlay — the element is technically visible in the DOM but unreachable by user interaction.**
Teams discovered that elements covered by a loading overlay with `pointer-events: none` (rather than `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`) were considered visible by Playwright's `toBeVisible()` check, but any attempt to click or type into them would succeed silently against the overlay and never reach the underlying element. Tests passed the visibility assertion and then silently did nothing during the interaction step, producing false-positive test results. WHY this matters: `pointer-events: none` is used extensively in design system loading states and skeleton screens to block interaction without removing elements from the visual layer; Playwright's visibility definition — based on CSS display, visibility, and opacity — does not account for pointer-event blocking, so every exploratory session in a feature that uses overlay loading states must include explicit verification that the element is not only visible but also interactable via `locator.click()` with a short timeout rather than a pre-click `toBeVisible()` assertion.

**G2. `page.selectOption()` on a `<select>` element does not trigger `React`'s synthetic `onChange` event in all React versions — causing React-controlled select components to visually change but not update state.**
Several teams found that after using `page.selectOption()` to change a dropdown value in a React 17 application, the displayed value changed but the form submission still used the original value. React's synthetic event system intercepts native `change` events differently across versions, and Playwright's `selectOption()` uses the native DOM `change` event which does not always bubble through React's event delegation. WHY this matters: the gap between `page.selectOption()` setting the DOM `value` attribute and React updating its controlled component state is invisible in the test because the selected visual state looks correct; the fix is to use `locator.click()` to open a custom select or to verify the selected value persists after clicking a dependent element (such as a submit button that triggers React's reconciliation loop), and this distinction should be documented explicitly in any project using React 17 or earlier.

**G3. `page.waitForSelector()` resolves as soon as the selector matches in the DOM, even if the matched element is inside a `display: contents` wrapper — causing assertions on the element's bounding box to return zero dimensions.**
When developers use `display: contents` on a layout wrapper (a valid CSS technique for removing a wrapper from the box model while keeping its children), child elements matched by `page.waitForSelector()` are "attached and visible" by Playwright's definition but have no independently computed bounding box of their own — the bounding box belongs to their children. WHY this matters: `display: contents` is increasingly used in design systems to flatten layout hierarchies without affecting accessibility trees, but it creates a class of locator edge cases where `.boundingBox()` returns null or zero values for elements that are unambiguously visible to the user; exploratory sessions must add a `getBoundingClientRect()` check via `page.evaluate()` to verify that elements expected to be clickable actually have a non-zero rendered area, rather than relying solely on `toBeVisible()`.

**G4. Playwright's `locator.fill()` clears the existing field value before typing, but `locator.pressSequentially()` does not — silently producing concatenated values when used to "update" a pre-populated field.**
Teams migrating from `locator.type()` (deprecated) to `locator.pressSequentially()` discovered that their update-field tests now produced concatenated values (e.g., setting a name field pre-populated with "Alice" to "Bob" resulted in "AliceBob" rather than "Bob") because `pressSequentially()` simulates keystrokes without first clearing the field. The failure was invisible in sessions where the field happened to be empty. WHY this matters: the `type()` deprecation migration is commonly done with a find-and-replace that does not account for the behavioral difference between clearing-then-filling (`fill()`) and appending-keystrokes (`pressSequentially()`); the correct migration rule is to use `fill()` for setting a field to a known value and `pressSequentially()` only for simulating incremental keyboard input (such as triggering autocomplete after each character), and this distinction must be codified in the project's Playwright style guide before the migration.

**G5. `expect(page).toHaveURL(/pattern/)` passes immediately when the URL matches the pattern, even if the application then performs a client-side redirect within the same navigation — causing subsequent locator operations to target the wrong final URL.**
Teams using single-page applications with post-login redirect chains found that `toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` passed as soon as the URL contained "dashboard" during the transition, but the React Router or Vue Router continued to redirect the user to `/dashboard/onboarding` or `/dashboard/setup` based on user state. Subsequent steps that assumed the final URL was `/dashboard` targeted elements that did not exist on the actual final page. WHY this matters: `toHaveURL()` with a regex pattern matches the current URL at the first instant the pattern is satisfied, not the stable final URL; the fix is to assert against the exact final URL string (`toHaveURL('/dashboard/onboarding')`) or to wait for a page-specific landmark element that only exists on the intended destination before proceeding, ensuring that exploratory sessions on post-authentication redirect flows always verify the complete redirect chain rather than just an intermediate URL.
