**250. Shadow DOM Piercing and Slot Content Exploration Charter** [official]

**Description**: Web components encapsulate their internal DOM inside a shadow root, making standard Playwright locators fail unless the framework correctly exposes roles and labels through the shadow boundary. Playwright's locators pierce open shadow roots automatically when using accessibility-based queries (`getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByText`), but CSS selectors passed to `page.locator()` stop at the shadow boundary unless the author uses `>>` piercing combinators. The exploration charter targets web components — custom elements like `<my-button>`, `<app-dialog>`, slot-projected content, and composed ARIA trees — verifying that role-based queries work, that focus is reachable via Tab, and that slotted content does not escape sanitisation. This is particularly important in design-system-driven apps where all interactive surfaces are custom elements registered in a shared package.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Shadow DOM oracle — custom element accessibility and slot projection', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/demo');

  // Playwright pierces open shadow roots with getByRole automatically
  const customButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit order/i });
  await expect(customButton).toBeVisible();
  await expect(customButton).toBeEnabled();

  // Verify keyboard focus reaches the shadow-hosted element
  await customButton.focus();
  const hasFocus = await customButton.evaluate(el => document.activeElement === el
    || el.shadowRoot?.activeElement !== null);
  expect(hasFocus).toBe(true);

  // Check that slotted content is visible and not duplicated
  const slottedHeading = page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order summary/i });
  await expect(slottedHeading).toBeVisible();
  const headingCount = await slottedHeading.count();
  expect(headingCount).toBe(1); // slot projection should not clone nodes visually

  // Record whether the custom element exposes a role in the accessibility tree
  const ariaRole = await customButton.evaluate(el => el.getAttribute('role'));
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: ariaRole ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Custom button aria role: ${ariaRole ?? 'none — relying solely on shadow-root semantics'}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions targeting any page that registers custom elements or uses a web-component design system (Lit, FAST, Spectrum). Playwright's automatic shadow-piercing with accessibility locators is reliable for open shadow roots but does NOT pierce closed shadow roots (`{ mode: 'closed' }`); closed roots are inaccessible by design and require the component author to expose a testing API. Always confirm shadow mode before investing exploration time — `el.shadowRoot !== null` returns `null` for closed roots, which should itself be flagged as an accessibility concern because closed roots also break assistive technologies. [official]

---

**251. Drag-and-Drop Boundary and Drop-Target Rejection Exploration Charter** [community]

**Description**: Drag-and-drop interfaces often implement custom `dragover` and `drop` event handlers that enforce business rules — a card can only be dropped into a compatible column, a file can only be dropped on a designated upload zone, and a row can only be reordered within its own list. These drop-target rejection paths are almost never tested in scripted suites because they require synthesising multi-step pointer sequences. Playwright's `locator.dragTo()` API encapsulates the full pointer-event sequence (pointerdown, drag, dragenter, dragover, drop, dragend) in a single call, making it practical to attempt drops on valid and invalid targets in the same session and observe whether the rejection is surfaced to the user with a visual indicator and whether the dragged item is returned to its original position. The charter uses a matrix of source × target combinations to systematically cover both permitted and rejected drop paths.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('DnD boundary oracle — drop-target rejection and recovery', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/kanban');

  const todoCard    = page.locator('[data-column="todo"] [data-card]').first();
  const doneColumn  = page.locator('[data-column="done"] [data-droptarget]');
  const todoColumn  = page.locator('[data-column="todo"] [data-droptarget]');
  const invalidZone = page.locator('header'); // not a valid drop target

  // Record initial position for later comparison
  const initialColumn = await todoCard.evaluate(el =>
    el.closest('[data-column]')?.getAttribute('data-column'));

  // Attempt a VALID drop: todo → done
  await todoCard.dragTo(doneColumn);
  const afterValidDrop = await page.locator('[data-column="done"] [data-card]').count();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: afterValidDrop > 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Valid drop to done column: card count = ${afterValidDrop}`,
  });

  // Restore by dragging back
  const doneCard = page.locator('[data-column="done"] [data-card]').first();
  await doneCard.dragTo(todoColumn);

  // Attempt an INVALID drop: card → header
  await todoCard.dragTo(invalidZone);
  const columnAfterInvalid = await todoCard.evaluate(el =>
    el.closest('[data-column]')?.getAttribute('data-column'));

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: columnAfterInvalid === initialColumn ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Card after invalid drop: column = ${columnAfterInvalid} (expected ${initialColumn})`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for kanban boards, tree reordering, file upload zones, and any list-reordering interface. `locator.dragTo()` synthesises pointer events which works for HTML5 drag-and-drop; applications using JavaScript-only DnD libraries (react-beautiful-dnd, dnd-kit) may use pointer events exclusively — these respond correctly to `dragTo`. However, applications using the HTML5 Drag and Drop API on Firefox can behave differently from Chromium; always run DnD exploration sessions on both Chromium and Firefox projects. Keyboard-accessible DnD (ARIA sortable pattern with Space/Arrow key interaction) requires a separate charter scoped to `page.keyboard.press()` interactions and is not covered by `dragTo`. [community]

---

**252. Clipboard Write and Read Isolation Oracle Charter** [community]

**Description**: Modern web applications increasingly use `navigator.clipboard.writeText()` and `navigator.clipboard.readText()` to implement copy-to-clipboard and paste-from-clipboard workflows. These APIs are gated by the `clipboard-read` and `clipboard-write` permissions, and in headless Playwright contexts the clipboard is isolated from the OS clipboard — meaning `page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.readText())` reads only from Playwright's virtual clipboard, not from system content. The charter explores copy/paste flows for share links, code snippets, API keys, and form pre-fill from clipboard, verifying that content is not truncated, does not contain invisible control characters from the UI rendering layer, and that sensitive fields (passwords, tokens) never copy their plain-text value into the clipboard. The session also explores pasting oversized content (> 64 KB) into text inputs and form fields.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Clipboard oracle — copy link correctness and oversized-paste safety', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Grant clipboard permissions explicitly for this context
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    permissions: ['clipboard-read', 'clipboard-write'],
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/share');

  // Test copy-to-clipboard on a share link button
  const copyButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /copy link/i });
  await copyButton.click();

  const clipboardContent = await page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.readText());
  expect(clipboardContent).toMatch(/^https?:\/\//);

  // Oracle: no invisible characters (zero-width spaces, soft hyphens)
  const invisibleChars = /[​‌‍­﻿]/;
  expect(clipboardContent).not.toMatch(invisibleChars);

  // Oversized paste safety: inject 100 KB of text into a bio field
  const bioField = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /bio/i });
  if (await bioField.count() > 0) {
    const bigText = 'A'.repeat(100_000);
    await page.evaluate(([sel, content]) => {
      navigator.clipboard.writeText(content);
    }, [null, bigText]);
    await bioField.focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('Control+v');
    const pastedValue = await bioField.inputValue();
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-info',
      description: `Bio field after 100 KB paste: ${pastedValue.length} chars accepted`,
    });
  }

  await context.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions where copy functionality is a primary sharing mechanism (invite links, embed codes, API keys, referral codes). The virtual clipboard in Playwright is per-BrowserContext and does not interact with the OS clipboard — this is correct for isolation purposes but means you cannot test pasting content that was copied from another application (a common real-world scenario for power users). For that specific scenario, use `page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.writeText('...'))` to pre-seed the clipboard with the content you want to simulate pasting. [community]

---

**253. Progressive Web App Install Prompt and Offline-First Cache Charter** [official]

**Description**: PWAs surface a browser-managed install prompt (`BeforeInstallPromptEvent`) that applications can defer and display on a custom UI trigger. Test suites virtually never exercise the install prompt path because it requires meeting heuristic criteria (HTTPS, service worker, valid manifest) and the browser controls the prompt timing. This charter uses Playwright's Service Worker interception and browser event monitoring to verify three things: that the manifest is valid and correctly linked, that the service worker registers without console errors, and that core routes remain navigable after the network is severed (`context.setOffline(true)`). The offline-first portion of the session also checks that the offline fallback page is served and that stale cached content does not display misleading live-data indicators (e.g., "showing last updated 0 seconds ago" when offline).

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('PWA oracle — manifest validity, SW registration, offline fallback', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // 1. Manifest validity
  await page.goto('/');
  const manifestLink = page.locator('link[rel="manifest"]');
  await expect(manifestLink).toHaveCount(1);
  const manifestHref = await manifestLink.getAttribute('href') ?? '/manifest.json';

  const manifestResp = await page.request.get(manifestHref);
  expect(manifestResp.ok()).toBe(true);
  const manifest = await manifestResp.json();
  expect(manifest).toHaveProperty('name');
  expect(manifest).toHaveProperty('icons');
  expect(Array.isArray(manifest.icons) && manifest.icons.length > 0).toBe(true);

  // 2. Service worker registration without errors
  const swErrors: string[] = [];
  page.on('console', msg => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') swErrors.push(msg.text());
  });
  await page.reload();
  await page.waitForFunction(() => navigator.serviceWorker?.controller !== null, { timeout: 8000 })
    .catch(() => null); // not all pages require SW — treat as optional

  // 3. Offline fallback
  await context.setOffline(true);
  const offlineResp = await page.reload().catch(() => null);
  const bodyText = await page.locator('body').textContent().catch(() => '');
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: bodyText.length > 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Offline body text length: ${bodyText.length} chars (0 = no offline fallback)`,
  });
  await context.setOffline(false);

  if (swErrors.length > 0) {
    test.info().annotations.push({ type: 'observation-gap', description: `SW console errors: ${swErrors.join('; ')}` });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for any application that ships a `manifest.json` and a service worker — especially finance, healthcare, and field-service tools where users may work intermittently offline. `context.setOffline(true)` cuts all network at the Chromium DevTools Protocol level, which correctly simulates a true offline state; however, the PWA install prompt itself (`BeforeInstallPromptEvent`) cannot be triggered programmatically via Playwright because it is controlled by browser heuristics. Verify install-prompt UI by manually confirming heuristic criteria are met in a real browser session rather than trying to automate it. [official]

---

**254. Web Vitals Regression Oracle Charter — CLS, LCP, and INP** [official]

**Description**: Core Web Vitals (CWV) — Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — are performance metrics that directly affect Google Search ranking and user experience. CLS measures unexpected layout shifts during load; LCP measures when the largest visible content element finishes rendering; INP measures the latency of the worst-case interaction in a session. These metrics degrade silently when new CSS, images, or fonts are added without performance review. This charter uses Playwright's `page.evaluate()` to read PerformanceObserver entries for CLS and LCP, and the `event-timing` API for INP-like interaction measurements, asserting against threshold values that match Google's "good" CWV bands. Running this in sessions after significant UI changes gives early warning of regressions before Lighthouse or CrUX data catches up.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Core Web Vitals oracle — CLS and LCP regression detection', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

  // LCP: ≤ 2500 ms = "good" per Google
  const lcp = await page.evaluate((): Promise<number> =>
    new Promise(resolve => {
      new PerformanceObserver(list => {
        const entries = list.getEntries();
        resolve(entries[entries.length - 1]?.startTime ?? Infinity);
      }).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });
      setTimeout(() => resolve(Infinity), 5000);
    })
  );

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: lcp <= 2500 ? 'observation-pass' : lcp <= 4000 ? 'observation-gap' : 'observation-fail',
    description: `LCP: ${lcp.toFixed(0)} ms (good ≤ 2500, needs improvement ≤ 4000, poor > 4000)`,
  });

  // CLS: ≤ 0.1 = "good" per Google
  const cls = await page.evaluate((): Promise<number> =>
    new Promise(resolve => {
      let total = 0;
      new PerformanceObserver(list => {
        for (const e of list.getEntries()) {
          if (!(e as PerformanceEntry & { hadRecentInput?: boolean }).hadRecentInput) {
            total += (e as PerformanceEntry & { value: number }).value;
          }
        }
      }).observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });
      setTimeout(() => resolve(total), 3000);
    })
  );

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: cls <= 0.1 ? 'observation-pass' : cls <= 0.25 ? 'observation-gap' : 'observation-fail',
    description: `CLS: ${cls.toFixed(4)} (good ≤ 0.10, needs improvement ≤ 0.25, poor > 0.25)`,
  });

  expect(lcp, 'LCP must be within "needs improvement" threshold').toBeLessThan(4000);
  expect(cls, 'CLS must be within "needs improvement" threshold').toBeLessThan(0.25);
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions after adding above-the-fold images, hero banners, font loading changes, or CSS-animation introductions. PerformanceObserver in Playwright's isolated browser context does not reflect real-user network conditions — LCP values will be faster than field data (CrUX) because there is no network latency for cached assets in the test environment. Use these measurements as relative regression detectors (comparing before/after a change on the same machine) rather than absolute pass/fail against real-user thresholds. For INP, automating actual interaction-timing measurement requires real pointer-event sequences and the `event-timing` entry type, which is available in Chromium but not all browsers; scope INP exploration to Chromium projects. [official]

---

**255. Internationalization Number, Date, and Currency Formatting Oracle Charter** [official]

**Description**: Applications that display numbers, dates, times, and currency amounts must format them according to the active locale — a price formatted as `$1,234.56` in `en-US` must appear as `1.234,56 $` in `de-DE` and `¥1,235` in `ja-JP` (no decimal). These formatting rules are implemented via `Intl.NumberFormat` and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in modern JavaScript, but backend-rendered values, hardcoded format strings, and timezone conversions frequently produce locale-mismatched output. This charter uses Playwright's `BrowserContext` `locale` and `timezoneId` options to run the same user flows under multiple locales, capturing formatted values and comparing them against `Intl` reference formatters to detect mismatches. This surfaces the extremely common defect where locale switching changes the UI language but not the data formatting.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const LOCALES = [
  { locale: 'en-US', timezone: 'America/New_York', decimalSep: '.', groupSep: ',' },
  { locale: 'de-DE', timezone: 'Europe/Berlin',   decimalSep: ',', groupSep: '.' },
  { locale: 'ja-JP', timezone: 'Asia/Tokyo',       decimalSep: '.', groupSep: ',' },
];

for (const { locale, timezone, decimalSep } of LOCALES) {
  test(`i18n number/date oracle — ${locale}`, async ({ browser }) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ locale, timezoneId: timezone });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await page.goto('/account/summary');

    // Capture a displayed monetary value
    const priceText = await page.getByTestId('account-balance').textContent() ?? '';
    const hasCorrectDecimal = priceText.includes(decimalSep);

    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: hasCorrectDecimal ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
      description: `[${locale}] Balance "${priceText}" uses decimal separator "${decimalSep}": ${hasCorrectDecimal}`,
    });

    // Capture a displayed date and verify it contains expected locale calendar tokens
    const dateText = await page.getByTestId('last-activity-date').textContent().catch(() => '');
    const yearStr = new Date().getFullYear().toString();
    expect(dateText, `Date must contain the current year in locale ${locale}`).toContain(yearStr);

    await ctx.close();
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for any application that localises currency, dates, phone numbers, or addresses. The BrowserContext `locale` option sets the browser's `navigator.language` and `Accept-Language` header — this is sufficient for frontend formatting but does NOT change what the server returns if the server derives locale from a user preference stored in a database. In those architectures, the charter must also set the user's language preference via the application's settings UI before exploring formatted values, otherwise the server will return default-locale data regardless of browser locale. [official]

---

**256. Auth Token Expiry and Silent Refresh Boundary Charter** [community]

**Description**: Applications that use short-lived JWT access tokens paired with long-lived refresh tokens implement a silent refresh mechanism — before the access token expires, the application exchanges the refresh token for a new access token without requiring the user to log in again. This boundary is rarely tested because it occurs on a time schedule (15–60 minutes into a session) that is impractical to wait for. This charter uses Playwright's `page.clock()` API to fast-forward time past the token expiry threshold, then triggers an authenticated API call to observe whether the silent refresh fires correctly, whether the original request is retried after refresh, and whether the user is redirected to the login page when the refresh token is also expired. The session also explores concurrent tab behaviour — two tabs may both attempt to refresh simultaneously, causing a refresh-token race condition.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Auth token expiry oracle — silent refresh and expired-refresh-token redirect', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('test@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/, { timeout: 8000 });

  // Freeze clock at current time, then advance 61 minutes to expire a 60-min access token
  await page.clock.install();
  await page.clock.fastForward(61 * 60 * 1000);

  // Trigger an authenticated action that requires a valid access token
  let refreshCallFired = false;
  await context.route('**/auth/refresh**', async route => {
    refreshCallFired = true;
    await route.continue();
  });

  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /profile/i }).click();

  // Give the silent refresh up to 5 seconds to fire and the page to load
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle', { timeout: 8000 }).catch(() => null);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: refreshCallFired ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Silent refresh fired after clock advance: ${refreshCallFired}`,
  });

  // Verify user is still authenticated (not redirected to /login)
  const currentUrl = page.url();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: !currentUrl.includes('/login') ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `URL after token expiry: ${currentUrl}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for any SPA that uses JWT access tokens with refresh tokens (OAuth 2.0, Cognito, Auth0, custom JWTs). `page.clock.install()` + `page.clock.fastForward()` advances JavaScript timers and `Date.now()` inside the browser context — it does NOT change the system clock or the clock seen by the server. Applications that validate token expiry server-side by comparing `exp` claim against server time will still reject the token at the original expiry time regardless of the browser clock advance. For those applications, intercept and rewrite the token's `exp` field via `context.route()` to simulate expiry, or use a dedicated short-lived test token issued by the auth server. [community]

---

**257. Keyboard Shortcut Registry Conflict and Global Handler Interference Charter** [community]

**Description**: Rich web applications register global keyboard shortcuts (`document.addEventListener('keydown', ...)`) for power-user actions — quick navigation, command palettes, save commands. These global handlers frequently conflict with browser defaults, OS-level shortcuts, and with each other when multiple components register the same key combination. The conflict is invisible in automated tests that focus on single components in isolation because the global handler is only active on the full-page context. This charter registers a listener for all keydown events at the document level, then systematically fires a matrix of modifier combinations (Ctrl, Alt, Shift, Meta × letter keys and F1–F12) and captures which handlers fire, which browser defaults are suppressed, and whether any shortcut causes navigation away from the current page.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Keyboard shortcut oracle — global handler conflict matrix', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/app');

  // Inject a keydown spy before anything else fires
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    (window as any).__shortcutLog = [];
    document.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
      (window as any).__shortcutLog.push({
        key: e.key,
        ctrl: e.ctrlKey,
        alt: e.altKey,
        shift: e.shiftKey,
        meta: e.metaKey,
        prevented: e.defaultPrevented,
      });
    }, { capture: true });
  });

  const shortcuts = [
    ['Control+s'], ['Control+z'], ['Control+/'], ['Alt+ArrowLeft'],
    ['Control+k'], ['F1'], ['F5'], ['Control+Shift+p'],
  ];

  for (const [combo] of shortcuts) {
    await page.keyboard.press(combo);
    await page.waitForTimeout(150); // allow async handlers to settle
  }

  const log: Array<{ key: string; prevented: boolean; ctrl: boolean }> =
    await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__shortcutLog);

  const browserDefaultsSuppressed = log.filter(e => e.prevented);
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `${browserDefaultsSuppressed.length} shortcut(s) suppress browser default: ${
      browserDefaultsSuppressed.map(e => `${e.ctrl ? 'Ctrl+' : ''}${e.key}`).join(', ')
    }`,
  });

  // Flag F5 suppression as a potential issue (prevents reload, surprises users)
  const f5Suppressed = log.find(e => e.key === 'F5' && e.prevented);
  if (f5Suppressed) {
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-gap',
      description: 'F5 default (page reload) is suppressed by application — verify this is intentional',
    });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for command-palette applications, rich document editors, IDEs-in-browser, and any dashboard with declared keyboard shortcut guides. The keydown spy approach captures all handler registrations fired at the document level but does not detect shortcuts registered exclusively on specific focused elements (a component that listens only when it holds focus will not appear in the global log unless that component is focused during the charter). Run this charter after focusing a few different interactive components to widen coverage. The `capture: true` option ensures the spy sees events before any component handler can call `stopPropagation()`. [community]

---

**258. File Upload Mime-Type and Extension Spoofing Boundary Charter** [security]

**Description**: File upload endpoints commonly validate files by checking the `Content-Type` header or the filename extension, rather than reading magic bytes from the file content itself. This allows an attacker to rename a malicious file (e.g., a PHP script renamed to `report.pdf`) or spoof the MIME type in the multipart request header to bypass client-side or server-side extension checks. This charter explores the file upload surface by attempting uploads with mismatched type/extension pairs, oversized files, files with path-traversal sequences in their names (`../../etc/passwd`), zero-byte files, and files with non-ASCII characters in their names. The session also verifies that the server's rejection messages do not reveal internal file system paths or upload directory structure.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';
import fs from 'fs';
import os from 'os';

test('File upload boundary oracle — MIME spoofing and name injection', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/documents/upload');

  const tmpDir = os.tmpdir();
  const cases = [
    { name: 'report.pdf',           content: '<?php echo shell_exec($_GET["cmd"]); ?>', label: 'PHP-in-PDF name' },
    { name: 'dotdot_passwd.txt',    content: 'path traversal test',                    label: 'path traversal name' },
    { name: 'empty.pdf',            content: '',                                        label: 'zero-byte file' },
    { name: 'resume_nonascii.pdf',  content: 'non-ascii filename content',             label: 'non-ASCII filename' },
  ];

  for (const c of cases) {
    const tmpPath = path.join(tmpDir, c.name);
    fs.writeFileSync(tmpPath, c.content);

    const fileInput = page.locator('input[type="file"]');
    await fileInput.setInputFiles(tmpPath);

    const submitBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: /upload|submit/i });
    if (await submitBtn.count() > 0) await submitBtn.click();

    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle', { timeout: 5000 }).catch(() => null);

    const pageText = await page.locator('body').textContent() ?? '';
    const leaksPath = /\/var\/www|\/tmp\/|C:\\/.test(pageText);
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: leaksPath ? 'observation-gap' : 'observation-pass',
      description: `[${c.label}] Server path leaked in response: ${leaksPath}`,
    });

    fs.unlinkSync(tmpPath);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for any application that accepts user-submitted files, regardless of declared purpose. This charter deliberately probes security-relevant boundaries — coordinate with the security team before running in non-isolated test environments. The `setInputFiles()` approach sets the file via the browser file input, which sends the file with the browser's detected MIME type (based on extension), not the spoofed MIME type an attacker would craft in a raw HTTP request. For true MIME-type spoofing (sending `image/jpeg` with a PHP file body), use Playwright's `page.route()` to intercept the multipart upload and rewrite the `Content-Type` part header before it reaches the server. [security]

---

**259. Error Boundary and Suspense Fallback Recovery Exploration Charter** [community]

**Description**: React applications (and similar component-tree frameworks) wrap sections of the UI in error boundaries that catch thrown errors and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole page. The error boundary's reset logic — allowing the user to "try again" — is a separate code path that is almost never tested. This charter uses Playwright to simulate conditions that cause specific components to throw: injecting malformed props via URL parameters, injecting network errors that cause async data to reject, and using `page.evaluate()` to throw directly inside a component's render cycle. The session then verifies that the fallback UI is displayed, that the fallback provides actionable recovery steps, that clicking "try again" triggers a re-render (not a full page reload), and that the error does not propagate past the intended boundary.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Error boundary oracle — fallback display and recovery re-render', async ({ page }) => {
  // Inject a failing API response to trigger data-fetch error boundary
  await page.route('**/api/user/profile**', route =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 500, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }) })
  );

  await page.goto('/profile');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Oracle 1: an error boundary fallback must be visible
  const errorBoundary = page.getByRole('alert').or(page.getByTestId('error-boundary'));
  await expect(errorBoundary).toBeVisible({ timeout: 6000 });

  // Oracle 2: the fallback must contain actionable text
  const fallbackText = await errorBoundary.textContent() ?? '';
  const isActionable = /try again|reload|contact support/i.test(fallbackText);
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: isActionable ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Error boundary fallback text: "${fallbackText.slice(0, 120)}" — actionable: ${isActionable}`,
  });

  // Oracle 3: clicking retry does not navigate away — it re-renders in-place
  await page.unrouteAll(); // remove the fault injection
  const retryButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /try again|retry/i });
  if (await retryButton.count() > 0) {
    const urlBefore = page.url();
    await retryButton.click();
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle', { timeout: 5000 }).catch(() => null);
    expect(page.url()).toBe(urlBefore); // must not redirect to /login or /error
    test.info().annotations.push({ type: 'observation-pass', description: 'Retry is in-place re-render, not redirect' });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for React, Vue, and Svelte applications with component-level error boundaries or Suspense wrappers. The `page.route()` fault-injection approach is the cleanest way to force error boundary activation because it does not require knowledge of component internals. The `page.unrouteAll()` before clicking retry is critical — without it, the retry request will also return a 500 and the recovery path cannot be verified. If the application uses Suspense for lazy-loaded routes, the same charter applies: inject a network error on the dynamic import request and verify the Suspense error fallback activates rather than leaving the user on a blank page. [community]

---

**260. Mobile Viewport Gesture and Touch-Action CSS Property Oracle Charter** [official]

**Description**: Mobile browsers support touch gestures (pinch-to-zoom, swipe-to-navigate, pull-to-refresh) that are deliberately disabled in many web apps by the `touch-action` CSS property or the `<meta name="viewport" content="user-scalable=no">` attribute. Disabling pinch-to-zoom fails WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text) and WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.12, and is considered a mobile accessibility defect. Conversely, applications that set `touch-action: none` globally to prevent scroll conflicts with custom gesture handlers may inadvertently disable swipe navigation between wizard steps. This charter sets the Playwright viewport to a common mobile resolution, emulates touch inputs via `locator.tap()` and multi-touch events, and audits `touch-action` CSS values and `viewport` meta content for WCAG compliance.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect, devices } from '@playwright/test';

test('Mobile touch oracle — touch-action audit and pinch-zoom compliance', async ({ browser }) => {
  const ctx = await browser.newContext({
    ...devices['iPhone 15'],
    hasTouch: true,
  });
  const page = await ctx.newPage();
  await page.goto('/');

  // WCAG 1.4.4: viewport must not forbid user scaling
  const viewportMeta = await page.locator('meta[name="viewport"]').getAttribute('content') ?? '';
  const forbidsZoom = /user-scalable\s*=\s*no/i.test(viewportMeta)
    || /maximum-scale\s*=\s*1[^0-9.]/i.test(viewportMeta);
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: forbidsZoom ? 'observation-gap' : 'observation-pass',
    description: `Viewport meta: "${viewportMeta}" — forbids zoom (WCAG 1.4.4 violation): ${forbidsZoom}`,
  });

  // Audit touch-action on scroll containers
  const touchActionViolations: string[] = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const violations: string[] = [];
    document.querySelectorAll('[class*="scroll"], [class*="container"], main, section').forEach(el => {
      const ta = getComputedStyle(el).touchAction;
      if (ta === 'none') violations.push(`${el.tagName}${el.id ? '#' + el.id : ''}: touch-action:none`);
    });
    return violations.slice(0, 10);
  });

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: touchActionViolations.length === 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `touch-action:none found on ${touchActionViolations.length} element(s): ${touchActionViolations.join('; ')}`,
  });

  // Verify tap interaction works on primary CTA
  const cta = page.getByRole('button').first();
  if (await cta.count() > 0) await cta.tap();

  await ctx.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions targeting any application with a declared mobile UI. Playwright's `devices` presets include correct screen dimensions, device pixel ratio, user-agent, and touch capability for dozens of real devices — always prefer a named device preset over manually setting viewport + hasTouch to avoid inconsistent DPR values. The `touch-action:none` audit is a heuristic sweep, not an exhaustive WCAG test — elements set to `touch-action:none` for legitimate purposes (canvas drawing, custom gesture components) are expected and should be reviewed in context rather than automatically flagged as defects. [official]

---

**261. Long-Running Background Job Status Polling and Timeout Oracle Charter** [community]

**Description**: Features that initiate long-running server-side jobs (bulk exports, report generation, data migrations, AI inference) return immediately with a job ID and expect the client to poll a status endpoint until the job reaches a terminal state. The client-side polling logic frequently contains defects: no maximum retry count (infinite loop on stalled jobs), no exponential backoff (thundering herd on server recovery), silent timeout (job stays "processing" indefinitely), and failure to surface partial results or error details from the terminal state. This charter uses Playwright's `page.route()` to control the job status endpoint response sequence — simulating progress, a stuck-processing state, and a terminal failure — and observes how the UI reacts at each stage.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Background job oracle — stuck-processing timeout and terminal failure UI', async ({ page }) => {
  let pollCount = 0;

  // Simulate: first 3 polls return "processing", 4th returns terminal failure
  await page.route('**/api/jobs/**', async route => {
    pollCount++;
    const body = pollCount < 4
      ? { status: 'processing', progress: Math.min((pollCount / 4) * 100, 75) }
      : { status: 'failed', error: 'Export quota exceeded', details: 'Max 10,000 rows per export' };
    await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify(body), contentType: 'application/json' });
  });

  await page.goto('/reports');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /export|generate report/i }).click();

  // Wait for terminal failure state with a reasonable timeout
  const failureAlert = page.getByRole('alert').or(page.getByTestId('job-error'));
  await expect(failureAlert).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15000 });

  const failureText = await failureAlert.textContent() ?? '';
  const isSpecific = /quota|10.000|10,000|row/i.test(failureText);
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: isSpecific ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Job failure message: "${failureText.slice(0, 150)}" — shows specific cause: ${isSpecific}`,
  });

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Total polls before terminal state: ${pollCount}`,
  });

  // Verify no infinite polling continues after terminal state
  const pollCountAfterTerminal = pollCount;
  await page.waitForTimeout(3000);
  expect(pollCount).toBe(pollCountAfterTerminal); // polling must stop after terminal state
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for bulk operations, AI-powered features with async inference, report generation, and any data-intensive workflow that shows a progress indicator. The route interception approach lets you control the exact sequence of status transitions deterministically — far more reliable than waiting for a real job to complete or fail. The assertion that poll count does not grow after terminal state is a critical oracle that catches the "infinite polling loop" defect, which is one of the most impactful background-job bugs both for user experience (spinner never goes away) and for server load (100 idle users silently hammering a status endpoint). [community]

---

**262. Notification Permission and Browser Push Subscription Exploration Charter** [community]

**Description**: Applications that use the Notifications API and Web Push must request the `notifications` permission, register a push subscription with a server, and handle the user granting, denying, and later revoking the permission. The default Playwright context state is permission-denied for notifications — meaning the permission prompt never appears during tests, and push subscription flows are never exercised. This charter explicitly grants and denies the notification permission at the BrowserContext level to verify both paths: the subscribe flow, the confirmation UI after granting, and the graceful degradation UI shown when the permission is denied. The session also verifies that the application correctly handles the "default" (neither granted nor denied) state and does not aggressively re-prompt users who have not yet made a choice.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Notification permission oracle — grant, deny, and revoke handling', async ({ browser }) => {
  // --- DENY PATH ---
  const deniedCtx = await browser.newContext({ permissions: [] });
  const deniedPage = await deniedCtx.newPage();
  await deniedPage.goto('/settings/notifications');

  const enableToggle = deniedPage.getByRole('switch', { name: /enable.*notification|push.*notification/i });
  if (await enableToggle.count() > 0) {
    await enableToggle.click();
    const deniedMsg = deniedPage.getByText(/notifications.*blocked|permission.*denied|enable in browser/i);
    const deniedVisible = await deniedMsg.isVisible({ timeout: 3000 }).catch(() => false);
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: deniedVisible ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
      description: `Deny path: graceful degradation message shown: ${deniedVisible}`,
    });
  }
  await deniedCtx.close();

  // --- GRANT PATH ---
  const grantedCtx = await browser.newContext({ permissions: ['notifications'] });
  const grantedPage = await grantedCtx.newPage();

  let subscribeCallFired = false;
  await grantedCtx.route('**/push/subscribe**', async route => {
    subscribeCallFired = true;
    await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ subscribed: true }) });
  });

  await grantedPage.goto('/settings/notifications');
  const grantedToggle = grantedPage.getByRole('switch', { name: /enable.*notification|push.*notification/i });
  if (await grantedToggle.count() > 0) {
    await grantedToggle.click();
    await grantedPage.waitForTimeout(2000);
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: subscribeCallFired ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
      description: `Grant path: push subscription API called: ${subscribeCallFired}`,
    });
  }
  await grantedCtx.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for PWAs, chat applications, e-commerce apps with order-status push alerts, and any application with a notification subscription flow. The BrowserContext-level permission grant does not trigger the browser's native permission prompt — it directly sets the permission state, which is correct for testing the application's response to a granted/denied state but does not test the permission-request UI itself (the browser's modal prompt). Testing the actual permission prompt appearance requires running a non-headless browser session with `headless: false` and manually interacting with the OS-level dialog — schedule a manual exploratory session for this specific sub-area. [community]

---

**263. Form Autosave and Dirty-State Indicator Oracle Charter** [community]

**Description**: Long-form entry surfaces (profile editors, document editors, multi-step onboarding) often implement autosave to prevent data loss. The autosave mechanism should: debounce saves (not save on every keystroke), show a "saving…" / "saved" indicator with accessible text, handle save failures gracefully, and correctly mark the form as "dirty" (unsaved changes exist) to trigger a beforeunload warning if the user navigates away without saving. This charter tests the full lifecycle: inducing a dirty state, verifying the indicator, forcing a save failure, verifying the failure UI, then successfully saving and verifying the indicator returns to "saved". The beforeunload path is also explored by attempting page navigation after making changes without saving.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Autosave oracle — dirty state, save indicator, failure recovery, beforeunload', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/profile/edit');

  // 1. Dirty state: make a change
  const nameField = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /display name|full name/i });
  await nameField.fill('Autosave Test User ' + Date.now());

  // 2. Autosave indicator should appear within debounce window (~2 s)
  const savingIndicator = page.getByText(/saving\.\.\.|auto.?saving/i)
    .or(page.getByRole('status').filter({ hasText: /saving/i }));
  await expect(savingIndicator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 });

  // 3. Saved indicator should follow
  const savedIndicator = page.getByText(/saved|changes saved|up to date/i);
  await expect(savedIndicator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 8000 });

  // 4. Force a save failure mid-session
  await page.route('**/api/profile**', route =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 503, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Service unavailable' }) })
  );
  await nameField.fill('Failure trigger ' + Date.now());
  const failureIndicator = page.getByText(/save.*fail|could not save|error saving/i)
    .or(page.getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: /save/i }));
  await expect(failureIndicator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 8000 });
  await page.unrouteAll();

  // 5. beforeunload: navigate away after dirty change without saving
  await nameField.fill('Unsaved change');
  page.on('dialog', dialog => {
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-pass',
      description: `beforeunload dialog shown: "${dialog.message().slice(0, 80)}"`,
    });
    dialog.dismiss();
  });
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /dashboard|home/i }).click().catch(() => null);
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for document editors, CMS content editors, profile management pages, and any wizard step where partial completion should survive a page reload. The `page.on('dialog')` handler intercepts `beforeunload` dialogs — in Playwright, `beforeunload` dialogs are only fired in non-headless mode by default; in headless mode the page navigates immediately. To test `beforeunload` behaviour in headless mode, add `page.on('dialog', ...)` before any navigation AND set `page.waitForEvent('dialog')` — the dialog fires but is auto-dismissed unless a handler is registered. [community]

---

**264. WebSocket Message Ordering and Out-of-Order Delivery Oracle Charter** [official]

**Description**: Real-time features (collaborative editors, live feeds, chat, trading dashboards) depend on WebSocket messages arriving and being applied in the order they were sent. However, applications frequently apply messages in the order they are received — which can differ from send order when messages are queued, batched, or re-sent after a connection drop. This charter uses Playwright's `page.routeWebSocket()` API to intercept WebSocket frames, inject deliberate out-of-order delivery (swap message sequences), and inject duplicate messages to verify that the client-side reconciliation logic handles sequence IDs, vector clocks, or optimistic-update reversals correctly. The session surfaces the class of defect where a live feed temporarily shows stale data after a reconnect or where collaborative edit conflicts are silently discarded.

**TypeScript Example**:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('WebSocket ordering oracle — out-of-order and duplicate message injection', async ({ page }) => {
  const capturedMessages: string[] = [];
  const injectedOutOfOrder: string[] = [];

  await page.routeWebSocket('**/ws/feed**', ws => {
    const server = ws.connectToServer();

    let msgBuffer: string[] = [];
    let bufferTimeout: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null = null;

    server.onMessage(msg => {
      const data = typeof msg === 'string' ? msg : JSON.stringify(msg);
      capturedMessages.push(data);

      // Buffer pairs of messages and deliver them in swapped order
      msgBuffer.push(data);
      if (bufferTimeout) clearTimeout(bufferTimeout);
      bufferTimeout = setTimeout(() => {
        if (msgBuffer.length >= 2) {
          const [first, second, ...rest] = msgBuffer;
          injectedOutOfOrder.push(`swapped: ${second} before ${first}`);
          ws.send(second); // deliver second first
          ws.send(first);  // then first
          rest.forEach(m => ws.send(m));
        } else {
          msgBuffer.forEach(m => ws.send(m));
        }
        msgBuffer = [];
      }, 100);
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/live-feed');
  await page.waitForTimeout(5000); // let messages flow

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Captured ${capturedMessages.length} WS messages; injected ${injectedOutOfOrder.length} out-of-order deliveries`,
  });

  // Oracle: check feed item count for stability after out-of-order injection
  const feedItems = await page.locator('[data-testid="feed-item"]').allTextContents();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Feed item count after out-of-order injection: ${feedItems.length}`,
  });

  // Duplicate message injection: resend the first captured message
  if (capturedMessages.length > 0) {
    const feedCountBefore = feedItems.length;
    await page.evaluate(
      ([url, msg]) => {
        const ws = new WebSocket(url as string);
        ws.onopen = () => { ws.send(msg as string); ws.close(); };
      },
      ['wss://localhost/ws/feed', capturedMessages[0]]
    );
    await page.waitForTimeout(1500);
    const feedCountAfter = await page.locator('[data-testid="feed-item"]').count();
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: feedCountAfter === feedCountBefore ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
      description: `Feed item count after duplicate injection: before=${feedCountBefore}, after=${feedCountAfter} (idempotent: ${feedCountAfter === feedCountBefore})`,
    });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff / when to use**: Use in sessions for collaborative editing tools, live pricing feeds, chat applications, and any real-time feature with server-push architecture. `page.routeWebSocket()` requires Playwright v1.48+ and operates at the WebSocket frame level — it intercepts raw frames before the application sees them, making it the correct tool for delivery-order testing. The route handler receives `ws` (client-side connection) and `server` (server-side connection) separately, allowing bidirectional interception. Note that `routeWebSocket()` only intercepts WebSocket connections initiated after the route is registered — navigating to the page before calling `routeWebSocket()` means the initial connection is not intercepted; always call `page.routeWebSocket()` before `page.goto()`. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 42)

**G1. `page.clock.install()` does not affect `setTimeout` callbacks that were scheduled before `install()` was called — advancing the clock only controls timers registered after the clock is installed.**
Teams using `page.clock.install()` to test JWT expiry and session timeout flows discovered that timers set up during the application's initial bootstrap (e.g., a refresh-timer created in an auth context constructor before the page fully loaded) were not controlled by the Playwright clock. Advancing the clock via `page.clock.fastForward()` moved `Date.now()` forward but the pre-installed timers fired on real wall time, causing the test to either time out waiting for a token-expiry event that never fired, or to observe it firing at an unpredictable real-world time rather than at the clock-advanced moment. WHY this matters: the safest pattern is to call `page.clock.install()` before `page.goto()` using `page.clock.install({ time: new Date() })`, which installs the synthetic clock before any application code runs so that all timers — including bootstrap ones — are registered against the synthetic clock from the very first tick; retrofitting clock control onto a partially-loaded application is unreliable and the ordering mistake is silent.

**G2. `page.routeWebSocket()` intercepts only connections opened after the route is registered — WebSocket connections initiated during the `DOMContentLoaded` phase are missed if `goto()` is called first.**
QA teams building WebSocket message-order and fault-injection charters found that registering the WebSocket route after `page.goto()` caused the route to never fire, because the application's WebSocket connection was established during the page load sequence before the route handler was registered. The test ran to completion without any interception, giving a false-positive result — no injected faults, no captured messages, but no failures either. WHY this matters: this is the WebSocket equivalent of calling `page.route()` for HTTP requests after the requests have already been made; the fix is always to register `page.routeWebSocket()` before `page.goto()`, and if you need to verify that the route fired at all, add a counter inside the route handler and assert `count > 0` before making any observations.

**G3. `locator.dragTo()` synthesises a pointer-event-based drag sequence but does not fire `mouseenter`/`mouseleave` events on intermediate elements — applications that use hover-based drop-zone highlighting during a drag will not highlight correctly, and `dragover` listeners that rely on `mouseenter` to activate will not fire.**
Drag-and-drop charter sessions discovered that visual drop-zone highlighting (a blue border that appears when a card is hovering over a valid column) never activated during Playwright's synthesised drag, even though the drag completed successfully. The application used `mouseenter` on the column element to add the highlight class — but `locator.dragTo()` does not dispatch `mouseenter` on intermediate targets during the drag path, only the final `drop` event on the target. WHY this matters: this creates a gap between what automated exploration observes and what a real user experiences; for sessions where the drag-hover feedback is itself part of the UX being explored, supplement `locator.dragTo()` with explicit `page.mouse.move()` calls along the drag path to trigger `mouseenter`/`mouseleave`, which more faithfully replicates the real drag experience.

**G4. `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with a RegExp pattern matches immediately when the pattern matches the current URL — if the application performs a redirect chain (A → B → C), the assertion can pass on URL B before the final destination C is reached, and subsequent assertions then run on an intermediate page.**
Teams testing post-login redirect flows with a three-step redirect chain found that `await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` passed as soon as the browser reached `/dashboard/loading` — an intermediate redirect step — and subsequent assertions about dashboard content failed intermittently because the page was still in a loading state. WHY this matters: a stricter pattern (e.g., `toHaveURL('/dashboard')` with an exact string rather than a regex) reduces the match window, and `page.waitForURL('/dashboard', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' })` is more appropriate when the goal is to wait for the full redirect chain to complete and the page to finish loading before making content assertions.

**G5. Using `context.setOffline(true)` in a test that shares a BrowserContext with other tests will leave all subsequent tests in that context in an offline state — the offline flag persists until `setOffline(false)` is explicitly called.**
Teams running offline-exploration charters in a shared BrowserContext discovered that tests following the offline charter were intermittently failing with network errors that appeared completely unrelated to offline testing. Inspection of the Playwright context state revealed that a previous offline test had called `context.setOffline(true)` and then failed before reaching the `setOffline(false)` cleanup line. WHY this matters: `setOffline` is a BrowserContext-level setting that persists for the lifetime of the context, not a per-page setting; the safest pattern is to either create a dedicated BrowserContext for offline tests (`browser.newContext()`) and close it after the test, or to use a `try/finally` block that guarantees `setOffline(false)` is called even when the test body throws — using a Playwright fixture that wraps setup/teardown is the most reliable approach for context state that must be guaranteed to revert.

## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 265 — Soft-Assertion Accumulation Oracle Charter [official]

Exploratory testing sessions that verify multiple UI invariants in a single pass benefit from Playwright's `expect.soft()` API, which continues execution after an assertion failure and accumulates all violations before the session ends. Rather than stopping at the first broken state, a soft-assertion charter walks through an entire user flow — filling a form, submitting, navigating to a results page, and checking every visible element — and emits a single structured report of every gap found. This is especially valuable for regression sweeps on dense pages (dashboards, data tables, checkout summaries) where a single real-user interaction surfaces a dozen observable states. The charter concludes by asserting `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` to produce a clean pass/fail signal that CI can act on, while the accumulated soft-failure messages provide the detailed exploration log. Teams should be careful not to write charters whose entire value depends on soft assertions never failing — the goal is observation breadth, not silently swallowing regressions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Soft-assertion accumulation oracle — dashboard invariant sweep', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Accumulate all observations without stopping at the first gap
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Welcome/ })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('metrics-panel')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('recent-activity')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'View all activity' })).toBeEnabled();

  // Navigate deeper — soft failures above don't halt exploration
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Reports' }).click();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Reports/ })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('date-range-picker')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export' })).toBeEnabled();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('chart-container')).toBeVisible();

  // Annotate the full error list before the final gate
  const errors = test.info().errors;
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: errors.length === 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Soft-assertion sweep found ${errors.length} gap(s) across dashboard and reports pages`,
  });

  // Hard gate: fail the test if any soft assertions failed
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Soft assertions are only available with Playwright's built-in test runner — they cannot be used with `expect` from an external library such as `chai` or `jest`. Additionally, `expect.soft()` marks the overall test as failed but continues execution, which means subsequent actions may operate on a page in an unexpected state; for charters that depend on earlier state (e.g., navigating into a feature that only appears when a header is visible), guard each navigation with a hard assertion before the soft sweep to avoid cascading false observations.

---

### Pattern 266 — ARIA Snapshot Charter for Accessibility Tree Drift Detection [official]

Playwright's `locator.ariaSnapshot()` method captures the accessibility tree of a subtree as a YAML-like string representation, providing a compact oracle for whether the semantic structure of a component has drifted between builds. Unlike visual screenshot comparisons that fail on cosmetic CSS changes, ARIA snapshots fail only when the role hierarchy, accessible names, states, or values change — making them ideal for exploratory sessions that focus on whether interactive components remain correctly described to assistive technologies. An ARIA snapshot charter captures the tree of a complex widget (a navigation menu, a data grid, a date-picker dialog), stores it as a golden reference, and uses `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` to detect structural regressions. This charter is particularly valuable for teams who ship third-party component library upgrades and need to verify that the upgrade did not silently change the role tree of any interactive widget. The session should also capture the snapshot with keyboard focus placed on different elements within the widget to verify that focus-dependent `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, and `aria-activedescendant` values are correctly reflected in the tree.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('ARIA snapshot charter — navigation menu structural drift detection', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const navLocator = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' });

  // Capture baseline snapshot and annotate for the exploration log
  const snapshot = await navLocator.ariaSnapshot();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `ARIA snapshot captured:\n${snapshot}`,
  });

  // Assert against golden snapshot — fails if role tree drifts
  await expect(navLocator).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Main":
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Home"
        - listitem:
          - link "Products"
        - listitem:
          - link "About"
  `);

  // Verify focus-dependent aria-expanded state on a submenu trigger
  const submenuTrigger = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Products' });
  await submenuTrigger.focus();
  await submenuTrigger.press('Enter');
  await page.waitForTimeout(300);

  const expandedSnapshot = await navLocator.ariaSnapshot();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `ARIA snapshot after expanding submenu:\n${expandedSnapshot}`,
  });

  // The expanded button should now reflect aria-expanded=true
  await expect(submenuTrigger).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.ariaSnapshot()` and `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` were introduced in Playwright v1.49; earlier versions do not support them. The YAML representation is browser-computed, so the exact format depends on the browser's accessibility tree implementation — Chrome, Firefox, and WebKit may produce subtly different representations for the same HTML, and snapshot golden files are not cross-browser portable. Store separate golden files per browser project if your test matrix spans multiple browsers. For components where accessible names are generated dynamically (e.g., from user data), use the `{ ref: /pattern/ }` partial-match syntax rather than exact strings to avoid brittle snapshots that break on realistic data.

---

### Pattern 267 — page.addInitScript Determinism Charter for Randomness and UUID Seeding [official]

Applications that generate UUIDs, random colours, or probabilistic feature flags at page load produce non-deterministic UI states that break deterministic exploratory assertions. Playwright's `page.addInitScript()` injects a script into the page's JavaScript execution environment before any application code runs — surviving navigations — making it the correct hook for replacing non-deterministic globals with test-controlled fakes. This charter installs a seeded `Math.random` replacement and a deterministic `crypto.randomUUID` stub before the first `goto()`, then verifies that every generated identifier in the page matches the expected deterministic sequence. The session is particularly useful for testing collaborative editing tools, kanban boards, and form builders where new card IDs, block IDs, or session tokens are generated client-side and displayed in the DOM — the charter allows the explorer to make precise assertions about generated values without relying on dynamic matchers.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('addInitScript determinism charter — seeded Math.random and crypto.randomUUID', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install deterministic stubs before any application code runs
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    let seed = 0;
    // Seeded linear-congruential RNG — deterministic, not cryptographically secure
    Math.random = () => {
      seed = (seed * 1664525 + 1013904223) & 0xffffffff;
      return (seed >>> 0) / 0xffffffff;
    };

    // Replace crypto.randomUUID with an incrementing deterministic stub
    let uuidCounter = 0;
    Object.defineProperty(window.crypto, 'randomUUID', {
      value: () => `00000000-0000-0000-0000-${String(++uuidCounter).padStart(12, '0')}`,
      writable: true,
      configurable: true,
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/board');

  // Add a new card and verify the generated ID is deterministic
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add card' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Card title').fill('Test card');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();

  const newCard = page.locator('[data-card-id]').first();
  const cardId = await newCard.getAttribute('data-card-id');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Generated card ID under seeded UUID stub: ${cardId}`,
  });

  // Assert deterministic value — always the same across runs
  expect(cardId).toBe('00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.addInitScript()` executes in the page's JavaScript context, not in Node.js — it cannot access test-local variables directly. Pass data into the init script only via serialisable arguments (the second parameter to `addInitScript(fn, arg)`) and verify that the argument is fully JSON-serialisable before passing it, as non-serialisable values (functions, Maps, class instances) will cause a silent serialisation failure and the init script will not receive the expected values. Also note that the execution order when both `browserContext.addInitScript()` and `page.addInitScript()` are used is not defined by the Playwright spec — if you depend on ordering between two init scripts, merge them into a single script.

---

### Pattern 268 — HAR Recording and Selective Replay Charter for API Dependency Isolation [official]

Applications with deep backend dependencies are difficult to explore deterministically because real API responses change between runs — prices update, stock levels change, user recommendations shift. Playwright's HAR (HTTP Archive) recording and replay workflow records a real network session into a `.har` file and then replays it in subsequent exploration sessions, providing a frozen snapshot of API responses that the frontend sees. This charter first runs in record mode (`update: true`) to capture real responses, then executes the same exploration in replay mode (`update: false`) to verify that the frontend behaves identically against the recorded data. A HAR charter is particularly valuable for exploring complex data-driven features (search result pages, pricing calculators, recommendation engines) where the real backend cannot be controlled from the test and where manual mocking of dozens of endpoints would be impractical. The session should deliberately vary which endpoints are allowed to bypass the HAR (by using `url` filters) to identify which API calls are essential to a feature's correctness versus which are ancillary.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_PATH = path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures', 'product-search.har');

// Run once with UPDATE=true to record, then flip to false to replay
const RECORD_MODE = process.env.UPDATE_HAR === 'true';

test('HAR replay charter — product search API dependency isolation', async ({ page }) => {
  if (RECORD_MODE) {
    // Record: let real requests flow and capture to HAR
    await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH, { update: true, url: '**/api/**' });
  } else {
    // Replay: serve all API calls from the recorded HAR
    await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH, { update: false, url: '**/api/**', notFound: 'fallback' });
  }

  await page.goto('/search?q=laptop');

  const resultCount = await page.locator('[data-testid="search-result"]').count();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Search result count in ${RECORD_MODE ? 'RECORD' : 'REPLAY'} mode: ${resultCount}`,
  });

  // Oracle: result count should be consistent between record and replay runs
  expect(resultCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // Explore sort functionality against the frozen dataset
  await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Sort by' }).selectOption('price-asc');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  const prices = await page.locator('[data-testid="product-price"]').allTextContents();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Prices after sort-ascending (first 5): ${prices.slice(0, 5).join(', ')}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** HAR files encode real response bodies, including any PII or authentication tokens present in the original capture session — before committing HAR files to version control, audit them for sensitive data and consider using `route.fulfill()` with manually crafted fixtures instead when the responses contain user data. The `notFound: 'fallback'` option allows unmatched requests to reach the real network, which can cause non-determinism; prefer `notFound: 'abort'` for strict isolation and adjust as needed when the application makes requests that were not captured in the original HAR session.

### Pattern 269 — Trace Recording and Post-Session Action Timeline Charter [official]

Playwright's trace recording captures a complete timeline of every action, DOM snapshot, network request, and console message in a compressed archive that can be replayed and inspected in the Playwright Trace Viewer. An exploratory session that records a trace provides post-hoc evidence of every interaction step and the exact DOM state before and after each action — making it the canonical artifact for defect reproduction. This charter configures tracing at the BrowserContext level (`context.tracing.start()`), performs an exploratory walk through a high-risk flow, stops the trace with `context.tracing.stop({ path })`, and attaches it to the test report via `testInfo.attach()`. The session then uses the trace viewer to manually review DOM snapshots at each action step and verify that the application's visual state matches the expected state at every transition. Teams running nightly regression suites should use `trace: 'on-first-retry'` in `playwright.config.ts` to capture traces only for failing tests, balancing storage cost against investigation value.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

test('Trace recording charter — checkout flow post-session action timeline', async ({ browser, page }, testInfo) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const tracePage = await context.newPage();

  // Start tracing before any navigation
  await context.tracing.start({
    screenshots: true,
    snapshots: true,   // DOM snapshots for "before/after" diffs in trace viewer
    sources: true,     // Link actions to source code lines
  });

  await tracePage.goto('/cart');
  await tracePage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
  await tracePage.getByLabel('Email').fill('tester@example.com');
  await tracePage.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await tracePage.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await tracePage.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
  await tracePage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();

  // Wait for confirmation and capture observations
  await tracePage.waitForSelector('[data-testid="order-confirmation"]');
  const orderNumber = await tracePage.getByTestId('order-number').textContent();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Order confirmed: ${orderNumber}`,
  });

  // Stop tracing and attach the archive to the test report
  const tracePath = path.join(testInfo.outputDir, 'checkout-trace.zip');
  await context.tracing.stop({ path: tracePath });
  await testInfo.attach('checkout-trace', { path: tracePath, contentType: 'application/zip' });

  expect(orderNumber).toMatch(/^ORD-\d+$/);
  await context.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Full trace recording with `snapshots: true` stores a complete DOM snapshot before and after every action, which can grow very large (10–100 MB per test) for long exploratory sessions involving many navigations or complex DOM trees. For nightly regression suites, use `trace: 'on-first-retry'` in the config rather than programmatic `context.tracing.start()` to avoid capturing traces for tests that pass on the first run. When tracing is enabled, test execution is measurably slower because the browser must serialise DOM snapshots synchronously — budget an extra 20–40% wall-clock time for traced runs compared to untraced runs when planning CI pipeline budgets.
