### Pattern 270 — page.on('console') and page.on('pageerror') Observation Oracle Charter [official]

JavaScript console errors and uncaught exceptions are the application's built-in diagnostic channel, and a charter that listens to `page.on('console')` and `page.on('pageerror')` events accumulates these signals throughout an exploratory session without requiring any changes to the application under test. Most exploratory sessions ignore the browser console entirely, missing framework warnings, deprecation notices, failed prop-type validations, and uncaught promise rejections that indicate real but visually subtle defects. This charter registers console and error listeners before `goto()`, performs a full exploratory walk through a user flow, and then asserts that no `error`-level console messages or uncaught exceptions were emitted during the session. The resulting log of console messages is attached to the test report as structured JSON, providing a machine-readable audit trail of the application's internal diagnostic health during the explored flow.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Console and pageerror observation oracle — checkout flow diagnostic audit', async ({ page }) => {
  const consoleMessages: Array<{ type: string; text: string }> = [];
  const pageErrors: string[] = [];

  // Register listeners before navigation so no early messages are missed
  page.on('console', msg => {
    consoleMessages.push({ type: msg.type(), text: msg.text() });
  });

  page.on('pageerror', err => {
    pageErrors.push(err.message);
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Products' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Add to cart' }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();

  // Attach the full console log as a structured artifact
  await test.info().attach('console-log', {
    body: JSON.stringify(consoleMessages, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  const errorMessages = consoleMessages.filter(m => m.type === 'error');
  const warningMessages = consoleMessages.filter(m => m.type === 'warning');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: errorMessages.length === 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Console errors: ${errorMessages.length}, warnings: ${warningMessages.length}, uncaught exceptions: ${pageErrors.length}`,
  });

  // Oracle: no uncaught exceptions and no console errors during the session
  expect(pageErrors, `Uncaught exceptions: ${pageErrors.join('; ')}`).toHaveLength(0);
  expect(errorMessages, `Console errors: ${errorMessages.map(m => m.text).join('; ')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Some applications intentionally emit console warnings or informational log messages during normal operation (e.g., React's development-mode prop-type warnings, third-party analytics debug logs, hot-module-replacement messages). Filtering purely by `msg.type() === 'error'` catches the most critical signals without generating noise from expected informational messages. For applications that use a structured logging library that routes everything through `console.log`, parse `msg.text()` for an explicit `level: 'error'` JSON field rather than relying on the console message type. The `page.on('pageerror')` handler receives the raw `Error` object — its `message` property contains the error message, but the stack trace is only available in the Playwright trace or via `err.stack` if the error is a native `Error` instance.

---

### Pattern 271 — Worker-Scoped Fixture Charter for Expensive Authentication Setup [official]

Exploratory testing sessions that require an authenticated user spend a disproportionate fraction of their time on login flows that are identical across every test. Playwright's worker-scoped fixtures run once per parallel worker process and are shared across all tests in that worker — making them the correct tool for amortising expensive authentication setup (OAuth flows, MFA bypass, session seeding via API) across a session of exploratory charters. This charter defines a `workerAuthState` fixture that calls an API to create a test user, completes a login flow, and saves the browser storage state via `page.context().storageState()`. Every exploratory charter in the session then uses a `page` that is pre-loaded with the saved storage state, skipping the login flow entirely while still operating under a properly authenticated session. The fixture's teardown deletes the test user via the same API, ensuring no test data persists across runs.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import { createTestUser, deleteTestUser, TestUser } from '../helpers/test-user-api';
import path from 'path';
import fs from 'fs';

type WorkerFixtures = {
  workerAuthState: string; // Path to saved storage state file
  testUser: TestUser;
};

const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  testUser: [async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
    const user = await createTestUser({ role: 'member', workerIndex: workerInfo.workerIndex });
    await use(user);
    await deleteTestUser(user.id);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  workerAuthState: [async ({ browser, testUser }, use, workerInfo) => {
    const storageStatePath = path.join(
      __dirname,
      `.auth/worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}.json`
    );
    fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(storageStatePath), { recursive: true });

    const authPage = await browser.newPage();
    await authPage.goto('/login');
    await authPage.getByLabel('Email').fill(testUser.email);
    await authPage.getByLabel('Password').fill(testUser.password);
    await authPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await authPage.waitForURL('/dashboard');
    await authPage.context().storageState({ path: storageStatePath });
    await authPage.close();

    await use(storageStatePath);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

test('Worker-auth charter — member dashboard exploration', async ({ browser, workerAuthState }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: workerAuthState });
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Dashboard/ })).toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: 'Authenticated dashboard loaded using worker-scoped storage state',
  });

  await context.close();
});

export { test };
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped fixtures share state across all tests in a worker — if one test mutates the storage state (e.g., by changing the user's password, revoking the session token, or modifying profile data), all subsequent tests in that worker will operate with the mutated state, producing cascading failures that are difficult to diagnose. Treat the `workerAuthState` fixture as read-only: never call `page.context().storageState()` inside a test-scoped test to overwrite the worker's state file. For tests that intentionally mutate auth state (logout tests, password-change tests, session-expiry tests), create a fresh BrowserContext via `browser.newContext()` without loading the shared storage state, so the worker's auth file is not touched.

---

### Pattern 272 — locator.filter() and locator.and() Precision Charter for Ambiguous Element Grids [official]

Data grids, card lists, and search result pages frequently contain dozens of semantically identical elements that share the same ARIA role and accessible name pattern — making it impossible to distinguish them without combining role selectors with content filters. Playwright's `locator.filter()` method narrows an existing locator by requiring the matched element to contain a specified text or nested locator, while `locator.and()` intersects two locators so only elements matching both criteria are returned. This charter uses these APIs to build precision selectors for grid exploration: first locating all items with a given role, then filtering to the specific item of interest by visible label, then asserting sub-element states within that filtered item. The session is particularly useful for exploring product grids, user admin tables, and Kanban boards where the test must interact with "the Add to cart button inside the Laptop product card" rather than "any Add to cart button on the page."

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('locator.filter and locator.and precision charter — product grid interaction', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Base locator: all product cards on the page
  const allCards = page.locator('[data-testid="product-card"]');
  const cardCount = await allCards.count();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Total product cards found: ${cardCount}`,
  });

  // Filter to a specific product card by its visible name
  const laptopCard = allCards.filter({ hasText: 'Pro Laptop X500' });
  await expect(laptopCard).toHaveCount(1);

  // Further refine: only the card that ALSO has an in-stock badge
  const inStockLaptop = laptopCard.and(
    page.locator('[data-testid="product-card"]:has([data-testid="in-stock-badge"])')
  );

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: inStockLaptop ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: 'Pro Laptop X500 has in-stock badge',
  });

  // Interact with sub-elements inside the filtered card
  const addToCartBtn = laptopCard.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' });
  await expect(addToCartBtn).toBeEnabled();
  await addToCartBtn.click();

  // Verify the cart badge updated after adding
  const cartBadge = page.getByTestId('cart-item-count');
  await expect(cartBadge).toHaveText('1');

  // Explore the out-of-stock variant: button should be disabled
  const outOfStockCards = allCards.filter({
    has: page.locator('[data-testid="out-of-stock-badge"]'),
  });
  const outOfStockCount = await outOfStockCards.count();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Out-of-stock card count: ${outOfStockCount}`,
  });

  if (outOfStockCount > 0) {
    const disabledBtn = outOfStockCards.first().getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' });
    await expect(disabledBtn).toBeDisabled();
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.filter({ hasText })` performs a substring match by default — if two product cards both contain the filter text (e.g., "Laptop" matches both "Pro Laptop X500" and "Budget Laptop Y100"), the filter returns both and subsequent `getByRole()` calls within the filtered locator will be ambiguous. Use `locator.filter({ hasText: /^Pro Laptop X500$/ })` with an anchored regex for exact-name matching in grids with similarly named items. `locator.and()` was introduced in Playwright v1.34 — older versions do not support it and will throw at runtime; fall back to chained `filter()` calls if cross-version compatibility is required.

---

### Pattern 273 — Visual Snapshot Charter for CSS Regression in Responsive Breakpoints [official]

CSS changes that look correct at the development viewport often break at tablet or mobile breakpoints where layout reflows, flexbox wrapping, and truncation rules behave differently. Playwright's `expect(locator).toHaveScreenshot()` captures a visual snapshot of a specific element or the full page and compares it pixel-for-pixel against a golden image, optionally with a configurable pixel-difference threshold. This charter systematically walks through a set of critical page sections at four breakpoints (1440px desktop, 1024px laptop, 768px tablet, 375px mobile) and captures element-level screenshots of the navigation bar, hero section, feature grid, and footer — then asserts that each screenshot matches its golden reference within a 0.5% pixel-difference tolerance. The charter is most valuable when run in a CI pipeline immediately after a CSS dependency upgrade or a design-system token change, where it provides automated evidence that no visible regressions were introduced.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const BREAKPOINTS = [
  { name: 'desktop', width: 1440, height: 900 },
  { name: 'laptop', width: 1024, height: 768 },
  { name: 'tablet', width: 768, height: 1024 },
  { name: 'mobile', width: 375, height: 812 },
] as const;

const SECTIONS = ['[data-testid="nav-bar"]', '[data-testid="hero"]', '[data-testid="features-grid"]', '[data-testid="footer"]'];

for (const bp of BREAKPOINTS) {
  test(`Visual snapshot charter — ${bp.name} (${bp.width}px) CSS regression sweep`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.setViewportSize({ width: bp.width, height: bp.height });
    await page.goto('/');
    // Wait for all images and fonts to load before snapshotting
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

    for (const selector of SECTIONS) {
      const locator = page.locator(selector).first();
      const isVisible = await locator.isVisible();

      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: isVisible ? 'observation-info' : 'observation-gap',
        description: `Section "${selector}" visible at ${bp.name}: ${isVisible}`,
      });

      if (isVisible) {
        // Mask dynamic content (e.g., countdown timers, live prices) to avoid false diffs
        await expect(locator).toHaveScreenshot(`${bp.name}-${selector.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '_')}.png`, {
          maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.005, // 0.5% pixel tolerance
          mask: [page.locator('[data-testid="live-price"]'), page.locator('[data-testid="countdown"]')],
        });
      }
    }
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Visual snapshot tests require a golden image to exist before they can assert against one — on first run with no existing golden files, the assertion fails with "missing golden" and creates the golden files automatically; inspect the auto-generated goldens before committing them to verify they represent the correct baseline. Screenshots are font-rendering sensitive: the same test passing on macOS CI agents may fail on Linux CI agents due to different font anti-aliasing, requiring separate golden directories per OS (`--update-snapshots` with platform-specific CI matrix). Use `mask` to exclude dynamic regions (countdown timers, live prices, avatars with initials derived from user data) to avoid persistent false positives that erode team trust in the snapshot suite.

---

### Pattern 274 — test.step() Hierarchical Observation Charter for Multi-Phase User Flows [official]

Long exploratory sessions that span multiple distinct phases (authentication, onboarding, feature use, error recovery, logout) benefit from Playwright's `test.step()` API, which groups actions and assertions under named headings in the test report and trace viewer. Each step is reported independently, so a failure in Phase 3 does not obscure whether Phase 1 and Phase 2 completed successfully — giving the explorer precise location information about where a defect was first triggered. This charter structures a complete new-user onboarding flow into labelled steps, captures per-step timing via `performance.now()`, and annotates the report with which phases passed and which revealed gaps. The resulting test report reads like a structured exploration log with a clear pass/fail signal at each phase boundary, making it easy to triage which part of a multi-screen flow needs investigation.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('test.step hierarchical charter — new-user onboarding flow', async ({ page }) => {
  const timings: Record<string, number> = {};

  await test.step('Phase 1: Registration', async () => {
    const t0 = Date.now();
    await page.goto('/register');
    await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Exploration Tester');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(`tester+${Date.now()}@example.com`);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('P@ssw0rd!2026');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('/onboarding');
    timings['registration'] = Date.now() - t0;
  });

  await test.step('Phase 2: Onboarding wizard — step 1', async () => {
    const t0 = Date.now();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Welcome/ })).toBeVisible();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Get started' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('/onboarding/profile');
    timings['onboarding-step-1'] = Date.now() - t0;
  });

  await test.step('Phase 3: Profile completion', async () => {
    const t0 = Date.now();
    await page.getByLabel('Job title').fill('QA Engineer');
    await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Team size' }).selectOption('11-50');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
    timings['profile-completion'] = Date.now() - t0;
  });

  await test.step('Phase 4: First-run experience verification', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /Tour/ })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Skip tour' })).toBeEnabled();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Skip tour' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toHaveCount(0);
  });

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Phase timings (ms): ${JSON.stringify(timings)}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.step()` groups are visible in the Playwright HTML report and trace viewer but do not affect retry behaviour — if a step fails and the test retries, the entire test body reruns from the first step, not from the failed step. For exploratory sessions where early phases create server-side state (e.g., a user account created in Phase 1), re-running the entire test after a failure will create duplicate state unless Phase 1 is idempotent (e.g., using a pre-seeded account via API rather than creating one via the UI). Consider using `test.step()` purely for reporting granularity and manage test data setup via fixtures so that retries do not create duplicate state artifacts.

---

### Pattern 275 — Context-Level Permission Override Charter for Geolocation and Camera Sensors [official]

Features that request location access, camera permissions, or microphone access present a blocked-by-default prompt in real browsers that stops automated exploration cold. Playwright's `browser.newContext({ permissions, geolocation })` API pre-grants permissions at context creation time, bypassing the browser permission prompt entirely and allowing the explorer to focus on the feature's behaviour rather than the permission dialogue. This charter creates contexts with pre-granted geolocation permission and a spoofed location (a coordinate pair representing a specific jurisdiction), then explores location-dependent features — store finders, delivery zone calculators, geo-restricted content — to verify that the application correctly uses the provided coordinates and handles edge cases such as coordinates at jurisdiction boundaries, coordinates in the ocean, and coordinates with extreme precision values.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const GEO_SCENARIOS = [
  { label: 'Central London', latitude: 51.5074, longitude: -0.1278, accuracy: 10 },
  { label: 'NYC boundary (NJ side)', latitude: 40.7128, longitude: -74.0060, accuracy: 50 },
  { label: 'Mid-Atlantic Ocean (no coverage)', latitude: 35.0, longitude: -40.0, accuracy: 100 },
  { label: 'High precision (8 decimal places)', latitude: 48.85341200, longitude: 2.34879900, accuracy: 1 },
] as const;

for (const scenario of GEO_SCENARIOS) {
  test(`Geolocation permission charter — ${scenario.label}`, async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({
      permissions: ['geolocation'],
      geolocation: { latitude: scenario.latitude, longitude: scenario.longitude, accuracy: scenario.accuracy },
    });
    const page = await context.newPage();

    await page.goto('/store-finder');

    // Trigger the "Use my location" feature
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Use my location' }).click();
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

    const locationResult = await page.getByTestId('detected-location').textContent();
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-info',
      description: `Detected location for "${scenario.label}" (${scenario.latitude},${scenario.longitude}): "${locationResult}"`,
    });

    const noStoresMessage = page.getByTestId('no-stores-message');
    const storeList = page.locator('[data-testid="store-item"]');

    if (await noStoresMessage.isVisible()) {
      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: 'observation-info',
        description: `No stores shown for ${scenario.label} — empty-state message displayed`,
      });
    } else {
      const storeCount = await storeList.count();
      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: 'observation-info',
        description: `Stores shown for ${scenario.label}: ${storeCount}`,
      });
    }

    await context.close();
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `browser.newContext({ permissions: ['geolocation'] })` grants geolocation permission without triggering a browser prompt, but the permission is only granted for the origin of pages visited in that context. If the application loads the geolocation-dependent feature in an iframe on a different origin, the iframe's origin does not have the permission — pre-granting permissions does not cascade to cross-origin iframes. Use `context.grantPermissions(['geolocation'], { origin: 'https://maps.example.com' })` to explicitly grant permissions to the embedded origin after context creation. Also note that `accuracy` values below 1 metre are accepted by the API but may be treated as implausible by the application's location validation logic — always include accuracy in your exploratory data set to surface accuracy-dependent behaviour.

---

### Pattern 276 — Box Fixture Charter for Reducing Report Noise in Shared Infrastructure [official]

Large exploratory test suites that rely on shared setup fixtures (API authentication helpers, database seeders, feature-flag configurators) produce extremely verbose Playwright HTML reports where 80% of the reported actions are infrastructure setup steps rather than the actual exploration. Playwright's `{ box: true }` fixture option hides a fixture and all its internal actions from test reports and traces — the fixture still executes and its side effects are real, but its internal implementation is invisible in the report. This charter defines a `boxedApiAuth` fixture that sets up an authenticated API session for the exploration, marks it `{ box: true }`, and verifies that the resulting report shows only the exploratory actions the tester cares about, not the token-acquisition and header-injection internals of the auth setup.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import type { APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';

type BoxedFixtures = {
  authedApi: APIRequestContext;
  seededBoard: { boardId: string; cardIds: string[] };
};

const test = base.extend<BoxedFixtures>({
  // Boxed: auth setup is invisible in the report — only the exploration steps appear
  authedApi: [async ({ playwright }, use) => {
    const apiContext = await playwright.request.newContext({
      baseURL: 'https://api.example.com',
    });
    // Acquire token — this is infrastructure, not exploration; box hides it
    const tokenResponse = await apiContext.post('/auth/token', {
      data: { client_id: process.env.API_CLIENT_ID, client_secret: process.env.API_CLIENT_SECRET },
    });
    const { access_token } = await tokenResponse.json();
    const authedContext = await playwright.request.newContext({
      baseURL: 'https://api.example.com',
      extraHTTPHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${access_token}` },
    });
    await use(authedContext);
    await authedContext.dispose();
  }, { box: true }],

  // Boxed: seeding is infrastructure — the exploration sees only the seeded data
  seededBoard: [async ({ authedApi }, use) => {
    const board = await (await authedApi.post('/boards', { data: { name: 'Exploration Board' } })).json();
    const cards = await Promise.all(
      ['Card A', 'Card B', 'Card C'].map(name =>
        authedApi.post(`/boards/${board.id}/cards`, { data: { name } }).then(r => r.json())
      )
    );
    await use({ boardId: board.id, cardIds: cards.map((c: { id: string }) => c.id) });
    await authedApi.delete(`/boards/${board.id}`);
  }, { box: true }],
});

test('Box fixture charter — kanban board exploration with invisible infrastructure', async ({ page, seededBoard }) => {
  await page.goto(`/boards/${seededBoard.boardId}`);

  // These are the only steps visible in the report — all setup is boxed
  const cards = page.locator('[data-testid="card"]');
  await expect(cards).toHaveCount(3);

  await cards.first().dragTo(page.locator('[data-testid="done-column"]'));
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="done-column"] [data-testid="card"]')).toHaveCount(1);
});

export { test };
```

**Tradeoff.** Boxed fixtures hide their internals from the report, which trades visibility for report clarity — when a boxed fixture fails (e.g., the API token acquisition fails), the error appears in the test as a generic fixture setup failure without the detailed action log that would normally help diagnose the issue. For boxed fixtures whose internal actions are genuinely diagnostic (e.g., a database seeder that makes dozens of API calls), consider toggling `{ box: true }` based on a `DEBUG_FIXTURES` environment variable so that CI runs are clean while local debugging runs expose the full fixture trace. `{ box: true }` was introduced in Playwright v1.46 — earlier versions will silently ignore the option and show the fixture internals in the report without erroring.

### Pattern 277 — route.fetch() Response Mutation Charter for Edge-State Boundary Exploration [official]

Real APIs rarely return edge-state responses during normal exploratory sessions — zero results, maximum pagination limits, truncated strings at the maximum field length, and malformed-but-valid JSON payloads require deliberate injection. Playwright's `route.fetch()` method fetches the real response from the server and then allows the test to mutate the response body before delivering it to the application, combining the benefits of real network traffic (realistic headers, status codes, timing) with the control of mocked responses (injected edge states). This charter intercepts API responses for a search endpoint, fetches the real response, and then rewrites the payload to inject boundary conditions — an empty results array, a results array with exactly one item, and a results array at the maximum page size — to verify that the frontend renders each boundary state correctly without requiring the real backend to be seeded with those exact conditions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const BOUNDARY_MUTATIONS = [
  { label: 'empty results', mutate: (json: Record<string, unknown>) => ({ ...json, results: [], total: 0 }) },
  { label: 'single result', mutate: (json: Record<string, unknown>) => ({ ...json, results: [(json.results as unknown[])[0]], total: 1 }) },
  { label: 'max page size (100)', mutate: (json: Record<string, unknown>) => {
      const item = (json.results as unknown[])[0];
      return { ...json, results: Array(100).fill(item), total: 1000 };
    }
  },
] as const;

for (const boundary of BOUNDARY_MUTATIONS) {
  test(`route.fetch mutation charter — search boundary: ${boundary.label}`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.route('**/api/search**', async route => {
      const response = await route.fetch(); // Fetch real response from server
      const json = await response.json();
      const mutated = boundary.mutate(json);
      await route.fulfill({ response, json: mutated }); // Deliver mutated payload
    });

    await page.goto('/search?q=test');
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

    const resultItems = page.locator('[data-testid="search-result"]');
    const resultCount = await resultItems.count();

    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-info',
      description: `Result count for boundary "${boundary.label}": ${resultCount}`,
    });

    if (boundary.label === 'empty results') {
      const emptyState = page.getByTestId('empty-results-message');
      await expect.soft(emptyState).toBeVisible();
      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: await emptyState.isVisible() ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
        description: 'Empty state message visibility for zero-result boundary',
      });
    }

    if (boundary.label === 'max page size (100)') {
      await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('pagination')).toBeVisible();
    }
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `route.fetch()` makes a real network request to the upstream server before mutation — if the server is unavailable in CI (no network access, sandboxed environment), `route.fetch()` will throw a network error. In environments where the upstream API is not reachable, use `route.fulfill()` with a fully static fixture body instead of `route.fetch()` + mutation. Also note that `route.fulfill({ response, json })` sets the `Content-Type: application/json` header and serialises the `json` argument, which overwrites the original response body — if the original response uses a custom content type (e.g., `application/vnd.api+json`), pass `contentType: 'application/vnd.api+json'` explicitly to avoid changing the content type.

### Pattern 278 — locator.ariaSnapshot() Temporal State Comparison Charter [official]

Interactive widgets that change their accessibility tree in response to user actions — expanding accordions, opening modals, loading async content into a list — can be validated by comparing ARIA snapshots taken before and after an interaction. This charter captures an ARIA snapshot of a component before an action, performs the action, captures a second snapshot after the action, and then asserts that the two snapshots differ in specific, expected ways rather than asserting against a static golden string. This approach is robust to incidental changes in the surrounding page tree (e.g., a notification badge updating in a completely unrelated sidebar) because the comparison is scoped to a specific locator subtree. The session is particularly useful for exploring rich interactive components such as comboboxes, date pickers, tree views, and multi-level navigation menus where the role tree is expected to change significantly between collapsed and expanded states.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('ARIA snapshot temporal state charter — accordion expand/collapse cycle', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/faq');

  const accordion = page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Frequently asked questions' });

  // Capture BEFORE snapshot
  const beforeSnapshot = await accordion.ariaSnapshot();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Accordion ARIA snapshot (collapsed):\n${beforeSnapshot}`,
  });

  // All panels should start collapsed — aria-expanded should be false on triggers
  const triggers = accordion.getByRole('button');
  const triggerCount = await triggers.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < triggerCount; i++) {
    await expect.soft(triggers.nth(i)).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  }

  // Expand the first panel
  await triggers.first().click();
  await page.waitForTimeout(400); // Allow CSS transition to complete

  // Capture AFTER snapshot
  const afterSnapshot = await accordion.ariaSnapshot();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-info',
    description: `Accordion ARIA snapshot (first panel expanded):\n${afterSnapshot}`,
  });

  // Oracle: the after snapshot must differ from the before snapshot
  expect(afterSnapshot).not.toBe(beforeSnapshot);

  // The first trigger must now be expanded
  await expect(triggers.first()).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');

  // The expanded panel content must now be reachable via ARIA
  await expect(accordion).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - list "Frequently asked questions":
      - listitem:
        - button "What is your return policy?" [expanded]
        - region:
          - /Return policy details/
  `);

  // Collapse and verify tree reverts
  await triggers.first().click();
  await page.waitForTimeout(400);
  const collapsedSnapshot = await accordion.ariaSnapshot();
  expect(collapsedSnapshot).toBe(beforeSnapshot);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.ariaSnapshot()` captures the accessibility tree at a single point in time — for components with CSS transitions (accordion panels, modal overlays), capturing the snapshot mid-transition will produce an intermediate tree that matches neither the fully collapsed nor the fully expanded state, causing assertion failures. Always wait for the transition to complete (`page.waitForTimeout()` for simple CSS animations, or `locator.waitFor({ state: 'stable' })` where applicable) before capturing a post-action snapshot. For accordion panels that use `aria-hidden` to hide collapsed content rather than removing it from the DOM, the collapsed ARIA tree may still contain the hidden panel content — verify whether your target component uses `aria-hidden` or `display: none` for hidden states, as these produce different accessibility tree representations.

---

### Pattern 279 — AxeBuilder Targeted Scan Charter with Violation Snapshot Comparison [official]

Automated accessibility scanning with `@axe-core/playwright` provides a systematic oracle for WCAG violations that a purely interaction-based charter cannot surface — colour contrast failures, missing labels, incorrect landmark structure, and focus-management defects that are invisible to Playwright's `locator` and `expect` APIs. This charter combines `AxeBuilder.include()` (to scope the scan to a specific interactive region rather than the full page) with `testInfo.attach()` (to record the full violation report as a structured JSON artifact), and uses a violation-snapshot approach where the baseline violation list is stored and compared across builds to detect both newly introduced violations and newly resolved violations. The session is structured to scan the same component at multiple interaction states — modal closed, modal open, modal with validation errors displayed — to capture violations that only appear in specific states.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('AxeBuilder targeted scan charter — modal form multi-state accessibility sweep', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');

  // State 1: Page baseline (modal closed)
  const pageResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();

  await testInfo.attach('axe-page-baseline', {
    body: JSON.stringify(pageResults.violations, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: pageResults.violations.length === 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Page baseline violations: ${pageResults.violations.length}`,
  });

  // State 2: Modal open (focus should move into modal)
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open contact form' }).click();
  await page.waitForSelector('[role="dialog"]');

  const modalResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .include('[role="dialog"]')
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();

  await testInfo.attach('axe-modal-open', {
    body: JSON.stringify(modalResults.violations, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: modalResults.violations.length === 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Modal open violations: ${modalResults.violations.length}`,
  });

  // State 3: Modal with validation errors triggered
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click(); // Submit empty form
  await page.waitForSelector('[role="alert"]');

  const validationResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .include('[role="dialog"]')
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();

  await testInfo.attach('axe-modal-validation-errors', {
    body: JSON.stringify(validationResults.violations, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  // Oracle: combine all violation IDs across all states and report unique violations
  const allViolationIds = new Set([
    ...pageResults.violations.map(v => v.id),
    ...modalResults.violations.map(v => v.id),
    ...validationResults.violations.map(v => v.id),
  ]);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: allViolationIds.size === 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
    description: `Unique violation IDs across all states: ${[...allViolationIds].join(', ') || 'none'}`,
  });

  expect(allViolationIds.size, `Accessibility violations found: ${[...allViolationIds].join(', ')}`).toBe(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `AxeBuilder.analyze()` evaluates the DOM state at the moment the call is made — it is a synchronous snapshot, not a continuous monitor. For components that render asynchronously (e.g., a dashboard that loads data via parallel API calls and populates chart labels after a loading spinner disappears), call `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` or wait for a specific stable selector before calling `analyze()` to avoid scanning a partially-rendered state and receiving violations that will not be present in the final fully-rendered state. The `include()` method accepts CSS selectors — pass the modal's selector string directly rather than a Playwright Locator object, as `AxeBuilder.include()` does not accept Playwright Locator types.

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 43)

**G1. `locator.all()` does not wait for elements to appear in the DOM — it returns whatever is present at the moment of the call, making it unreliable for lists that are populated asynchronously.**
QA teams using `locator.all()` to iterate over search result cards found that the method returned an empty array when called immediately after `page.goto()`, even though the same locator reliably matched cards when used in `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` assertions. The difference is that `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` retries until the count matches, while `locator.all()` is a one-shot snapshot call with no retry. WHY this matters: for dynamically-populated lists, always gate `locator.all()` with a prior assertion that the list is stable — e.g., `await expect(locator).toHaveCount(expectedCount)` or `await locator.first().waitFor()` before calling `locator.all()`, ensuring the list has fully populated before the snapshot is taken.

**G2. `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` uses whitespace-significant YAML comparison — a golden snapshot with trailing spaces or mismatched indentation will always fail even if the accessible structure is semantically identical.**
Teams storing ARIA snapshot golden strings in multi-line template literals found that their `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` assertions failed intermittently on CI but passed locally. Inspection revealed that the CI machine's git configuration was converting LF line endings to CRLF, introducing carriage-return characters into the golden string that were not present in the ARIA snapshot generated by the browser. WHY this matters: always normalise line endings in ARIA snapshot golden files (set `autocrlf: input` in `.gitattributes` for snapshot fixture files), and trim trailing whitespace from manually written golden strings — the axe-snapshot comparison is whitespace-sensitive and will not normalise line endings automatically.

**G3. `page.addInitScript()` does not execute in workers spawned by `new Worker()` — scripts injected via `addInitScript` only run in the main page context and any frames navigated within that page, not in Web Workers or Service Workers.**
Exploratory sessions attempting to intercept calls to `crypto.randomUUID()` inside a Web Worker found that the init script stub was never called — the worker ran with the native `crypto.randomUUID()` implementation despite the page's init script having replaced it. The Web Worker is a separate JavaScript execution context that Playwright does not pre-instrument with init scripts. WHY this matters: if your application does significant computation (UUID generation, encryption, heavy data processing) inside a Web Worker, `addInitScript` is the wrong tool; instead, intercept at the network layer (mock the endpoint the worker calls) or use `page.evaluate()` to post a message to the worker that reconfigures its behaviour if the worker exposes a message-based configuration API.

**G4. `AxeBuilder.include()` accepts CSS selector strings, not Playwright Locator objects — passing a Locator where a CSS selector is expected produces no error at call time but silently scans the entire page instead of the intended subtree.**
Teams using `new AxeBuilder({ page }).include(page.locator('[role="dialog"]'))` found that the accessibility scan was reporting violations from the entire page, not just the modal dialog. The `include()` method accepts a string (CSS selector), not a Playwright Locator — passing a Locator object causes it to be silently coerced to the string `[object Object]`, which matches nothing, and axe-core falls back to scanning the full document. WHY this matters: always pass the CSS selector string directly: `new AxeBuilder({ page }).include('[role="dialog"]')` — and if you need to scope to a dynamically-generated selector (e.g., `[data-modal-id="${id}"]`), build the string explicitly before passing it to `include()`.

**G5. `page.clock.fastForward()` does not advance `setInterval` callbacks that were cleared and re-registered between the `install()` call and the `fastForward()` call — intervals that are cancelled and recreated mid-test may not fire at the expected time.**
Teams testing inactivity-logout timers that use `clearInterval` and `setInterval` to reset the countdown on every user interaction found that `page.clock.fastForward()` triggered the original interval's callback at the expected synthetic time, but after simulating a user interaction that cleared and re-registered the interval, the subsequent `fastForward()` did not trigger the callback because the new interval was registered against a different internal timer ID. WHY this matters: Playwright's synthetic clock tracks timers by their internal ID — when your application cancels and re-creates an interval in response to user activity (the standard inactivity-timer reset pattern), call `page.clock.fastForward()` from zero relative to the most recent interaction, not from the absolute time of the last `clock.install()` call; alternatively, use `page.clock.runFor()` in small increments to let the interval fire naturally under the synthetic clock rather than jumping to a specific future time.

**G6. `expect(locator).toHaveScreenshot()` fails with a "missing golden" error on first run and creates the golden file — but if the test is run in a CI environment that does not persist the snapshot directory between runs, golden files are regenerated every run and the assertion always passes, providing no regression protection.**
QA teams running visual snapshot charters on a CI pipeline without persistent snapshot storage found that their `toHaveScreenshot()` assertions never failed — because every run regenerated the golden files from scratch, the baseline was always the current output, and any visual regression would be silently accepted as the new golden. WHY this matters: golden snapshot files must be committed to the repository alongside the test code and treated as part of the test specification; the CI pipeline must check out the committed goldens and assert against them without regenerating — add the `__snapshots__` directory to git and gate the CI job on the assertion step rather than allowing `--update-snapshots` to run automatically in any CI context.

## Cycle 46 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 280 — page.addLocatorHandler Overlay Dismissal Charter [official]

Unpredictable overlays — cookie consent banners, newsletter popups, security confirmation dialogs — appear at non-deterministic points in test execution and block actionability checks, causing flaky failures that are hard to reproduce. `page.addLocatorHandler()` registers a callback that Playwright invokes automatically whenever a specified locator becomes visible and an actionability check is about to run. The handler runs synchronously within the action's retry envelope, removing the overlay before the action proceeds. By registering handlers for all known overlay patterns at the top of an exploratory charter, the session can focus on the primary mission without being derailed by environmental noise.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow is unblocked by consent overlays', async ({ page }) => {
  // Register handlers for all known overlay patterns before navigation
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie/i }),
    async () => {
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all/i }).click();
    }
  );

  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByText('Sign up to the newsletter'),
    async () => {
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: /no thanks/i }).click();
    },
    { times: 1 } // Only dismiss once — after first dismissal the handler is a no-op
  );

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();

  // Oracle: cart summary is visible — neither overlay interrupted the flow
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Summary' })).toBeVisible();
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Checkout flow completed without overlay interruption',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `addLocatorHandler` runs before every actionability check, so each handler invocation counts against the enclosing action's `timeout`. If your overlay is slow to animate out and the handler itself requires a subsequent `waitFor`, the combined handler time can exhaust the action timeout on slow CI machines. Set an explicit `actionTimeout` on the page context that accounts for worst-case handler execution time, or use the `noWaitAfter: true` option and assert the overlay is gone later in the charter rather than in the handler body.

---

### Pattern 281 — WebSocketRoute Frame Interception Charter [official]

WebSocket-driven UIs (live dashboards, collaborative editors, chat interfaces) are difficult to test because the server pushes events asynchronously and the test has no natural synchronisation point. `page.routeWebSocket()` intercepts all WebSocket connections matching a URL glob and allows the test to act as a mock server — sending frames directly, responding to specific messages, or dropping frames to simulate network errors. The charter explores what the UI renders when specific message sequences arrive, how it recovers from dropped frames, and whether it enforces protocol correctness by rejecting malformed payloads.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('live dashboard degrades gracefully when WebSocket drops a price update', async ({ page }) => {
  const receivedFrames: string[] = [];

  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://prices.example.com/feed', ws => {
    // Record all outgoing frames from the page
    ws.onMessage(msg => {
      receivedFrames.push(typeof msg === 'string' ? msg : '<binary>');
    });

    // Simulate initial connection handshake
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'connected', sessionId: 'test-123' }));

    // Push a normal price update
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'price', symbol: 'AAPL', bid: 182.50, ask: 182.55 }));

    // Simulate a gap: drop the next expected update (do nothing for 500 ms)
    // Then send an out-of-sequence update with a stale timestamp
    setTimeout(() => {
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'price', symbol: 'AAPL', bid: 181.00, ask: 181.05, stale: true }));
    }, 500);
  });

  await page.goto('https://dashboard.example.com');

  // Oracle 1: stale indicator appears when a stale price frame is received
  await expect(page.getByTestId('price-stale-badge')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 2000 });

  // Oracle 2: UI did not crash — chart container still present
  await expect(page.getByTestId('price-chart')).toBeVisible();

  // Oracle 3: the page sent a subscription message on connect
  expect(receivedFrames.some(f => f.includes('"type":"subscribe"'))).toBe(true);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `Stale frame handled gracefully; page sent frames: ${receivedFrames.join(' | ')}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.routeWebSocket()` intercepts connections before they reach the network stack, so the actual WebSocket server never receives a connection when the handler is active. If your application uses an environment-specific WebSocket URL that is only reachable in staging, use `ws.connectToServer()` to proxy the real connection and only intercept specific message types — this lets most messages pass through unmodified while injecting edge-case frames into the stream without spinning up a full mock server.

---

### Pattern 282 — page.exposeFunction Spy Injection Charter [official]

When the application calls browser APIs (like `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, `window.analytics.track`, or a custom event emitter) as a side effect of user interaction, the test cannot observe these calls through the DOM alone. `page.exposeFunction()` installs a JavaScript function on the `window` object of every frame that, when called by page code, executes a Node.js callback in the Playwright process. By replacing the target API with a stub that calls the exposed function, the charter can record all invocations with their arguments and assert on them as an oracle without requiring a network proxy or server-side log inspection.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('analytics track() is called with correct event on purchase', async ({ page }) => {
  const trackCalls: Array<{ event: string; props: Record<string, unknown> }> = [];

  // Expose a Node.js callback into the browser context
  await page.exposeFunction('__playwrightTrackSpy', (event: string, props: unknown) => {
    trackCalls.push({ event, props: props as Record<string, unknown> });
  });

  // Install the spy before page load so it captures events from DOMContentLoaded onward
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // Stub window.analytics.track to forward calls to our spy
    Object.defineProperty(window, 'analytics', {
      value: {
        track: (event: string, props: unknown) => {
          (window as unknown as Record<string, Function>).__playwrightTrackSpy(event, props);
        },
      },
      writable: false,
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/product/42');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Buy Now' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm Purchase' }).click();

  // Oracle: exactly one 'purchase' event was tracked with the correct product ID
  const purchaseEvents = trackCalls.filter(c => c.event === 'purchase');
  expect(purchaseEvents).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(purchaseEvents[0].props).toMatchObject({ productId: '42' });

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `Analytics track calls: ${JSON.stringify(trackCalls)}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.exposeFunction()` callbacks execute in the Playwright process's Node.js context and are asynchronous from the browser's perspective — the page's call to the exposed function returns a Promise. If the application code calls `window.analytics.track()` but does not `await` the result (which most analytics stubs do not), the spy call is dispatched but the test must wait for it to be processed before asserting. Add a short `page.waitForFunction(() => window.__trackCallCount > 0)` guard, or accumulate calls into a `page.evaluate()`-accessible global and poll it rather than relying on the Node.js array being populated synchronously at assertion time.

---

### Pattern 283 — page.clock.pauseAt Temporal Boundary Charter [official]

Features that react to wall-clock time (session expiry warnings, countdown timers, scheduled content reveals, subscription renewal prompts) cannot be reliably tested with real time because the delay between the triggering moment and the UI update is too long for an automated test to wait. `page.clock.install({ time })` plus `pauseAt()` freezes the synthetic clock at an arbitrary point, and `fastForward()` or `runFor()` advances it in controlled increments, triggering `setTimeout` and `setInterval` callbacks without waiting for real time to pass. The charter explores the UI at the exact boundary between states — one millisecond before expiry, at expiry, and one millisecond after — to find off-by-one defects in timer logic.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session expiry warning appears 5 minutes before timeout and auto-logout fires at timeout', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install synthetic clock frozen at a known session-start time
  const sessionStart = new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00Z');
  await page.clock.install({ time: sessionStart });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');
  await page.getByLabel('Username').fill('user@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('correctpassword');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();

  // Advance to 1 ms before the 25-minute warning threshold (session = 30 min)
  await page.clock.fastForward('24:59.999');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Advance 1 ms to cross the 25-minute threshold — warning must appear
  await page.clock.fastForward(1);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Advance to 1 ms before the 30-minute auto-logout threshold
  await page.clock.fastForward('04:59.999');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();

  // Advance 1 ms to cross the 30-minute threshold — auto-logout must fire
  await page.clock.fastForward(1);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Sign In' })).toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Session expiry boundary transitions verified at exact millisecond thresholds',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.clock.install()` replaces `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `performance` in the page context, but it does not affect the Playwright test runner's own `setTimeout` or any Node.js timers used by server-side code running in the same process. If your application fetches a fresh session token from the server on a real interval (not a browser timer), the synthetic clock will not advance that server-side interval — mock the API endpoint that returns session validity instead and let the browser timer drive the UI transition, keeping the server interaction under route-level control.

---

### Pattern 284 — frameLocator Shadow-DOM Drill-Down Charter [official]

Micro-frontend architectures and web components frequently nest interactive content inside iframes or shadow DOM trees that are invisible to `page.locator()` selectors targeting the main document. `page.frameLocator(selector)` returns a frame-scoped locator context so that all subsequent `getBy*` and `locator()` calls resolve within the iframe's document. For shadow DOM, Playwright's locators pierce shadow roots by default — no special syntax is required for simple cases, but understanding when piercing occurs and when it does not is essential for accurate charter scoping.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('embedded payment iframe accepts card details and fires completion event', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://checkout.example.com/payment');

  // Scope all subsequent locators to the payment iframe
  const paymentFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[title="Secure Payment"]');

  // Fill card number field inside the iframe (frameLocator pierces the iframe boundary)
  await paymentFrame.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4111 1111 1111 1111');
  await paymentFrame.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await paymentFrame.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await paymentFrame.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();

  // Oracle: the parent page shows a success message after the iframe fires its completion postMessage
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment Successful' })).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 });

  // Oracle: no error banner appeared in the parent frame
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Payment iframe interaction completed and parent frame received success signal',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.frameLocator()` returns a locator that re-resolves the iframe on every action, so it is resilient to iframes that reload between interactions. However, if the iframe URL changes mid-session (e.g., a payment flow that navigates the iframe to a 3DS challenge page), the `frameLocator` that matched the original iframe will continue to resolve by selector position in the DOM — if the new page has a different structure, your `getBy*` calls will fail with misleading "element not found" messages. For multi-step iframe flows, assert the expected URL of the iframe after each navigation using `frame.url()` before continuing, so that mismatches are caught at the navigation step rather than silently on the next locator resolution.

---

### Pattern 285 — Device Emulation Viewport Charter for Responsive State Transitions [official]

Responsive UIs have discrete layout breakpoints where navigation menus collapse into hamburger buttons, sidebars become off-canvas drawers, and multi-column grids reflow to single-column stacks. Testing at a single viewport size leaves breakpoint-crossing defects undetected. By emulating a named device from `playwright.devices` and combining it with `page.setViewportSize()` to cross breakpoints dynamically within a single test, the charter can explore the UI immediately before, at, and after each breakpoint transition without spinning up separate test projects per device.

```typescript
import { test, expect, devices } from '@playwright/test';

test('navigation menu transitions to hamburger at mobile breakpoint', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Start with a tablet viewport just above the mobile breakpoint
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    ...devices['iPad Mini'],
    viewport: { width: 769, height: 1024 },
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');

  // Oracle at tablet width: full nav is visible, hamburger button is hidden
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /menu/i })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Cross the breakpoint: resize to 1 pixel below the threshold
  await page.setViewportSize({ width: 768, height: 1024 });

  // Oracle at mobile width: hamburger appears, nav links are hidden
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /menu/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Interaction: open the hamburger menu
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /menu/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' })).toBeVisible();

  await context.close();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Navigation breakpoint transition at 769↔768 px verified with correct visibility states',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.setViewportSize()` changes the viewport dimensions but does not change the emulated device's `deviceScaleFactor`, `userAgent`, `hasTouch`, or `isMobile` flags — those are set at context creation time and are immutable. If your responsive breakpoints are driven by CSS media queries that detect touch capability (`@media (hover: none)`) rather than viewport width alone, `setViewportSize()` will not trigger the touch-based breakpoint; you must create separate contexts with `hasTouch: true` and `isMobile: true` to test those branches.

---

### Pattern 286 — page.on('request') and page.on('response') Network Observation Oracle Charter [official]

The DOM alone does not reveal the full contract between the client and its APIs — it shows rendered output but hides request payloads, response status codes, cache headers, and error bodies that the UI may silently swallow. Attaching listeners to `page.on('request')` and `page.on('response')` before navigation captures the complete network activity log for the session, providing a second oracle layer: even if the UI renders a success state, the network log can reveal a 4xx error that was suppressed, a retry that should not have happened, or a missing authentication header.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface RequestRecord {
  url: string;
  method: string;
  status?: number;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
}

test('user profile save sends correct Content-Type and returns 200', async ({ page }) => {
  const networkLog: RequestRecord[] = [];

  page.on('request', req => {
    if (req.url().includes('/api/')) {
      networkLog.push({
        url: req.url(),
        method: req.method(),
        headers: req.headers(),
      });
    }
  });

  page.on('response', async res => {
    const record = networkLog.find(r => r.url === res.url());
    if (record) record.status = res.status();
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/profile');
  await page.getByLabel('Display Name').fill('QA Explorer');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save Profile' }).click();

  // Wait for the save request to complete
  await page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes('/api/profile') && r.status() === 200);

  // Oracle 1: exactly one POST to the profile endpoint
  const saveRequests = networkLog.filter(r => r.url.includes('/api/profile') && r.method === 'POST');
  expect(saveRequests).toHaveLength(1);

  // Oracle 2: correct Content-Type header was sent
  expect(saveRequests[0].headers['content-type']).toMatch(/application\/json/);

  // Oracle 3: HTTP 200 received (not a silent 4xx)
  expect(saveRequests[0].status).toBe(200);

  // Attach full log for evidence
  await test.info().attach('network-log', {
    body: JSON.stringify(networkLog, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.on('request')` fires for all requests including images, fonts, and analytics beacons, so the listener accumulates a high volume of records for content-heavy pages. Filter by URL pattern inside the listener rather than post-hoc to keep the `networkLog` array manageable — and note that `req.postData()` returns the request body as a string but will return `null` for requests that do not have a body (GET, HEAD) and for streaming requests where the body has not been fully buffered at listener invocation time. For large upload requests, use `req.postDataBuffer()` instead and handle the case where it returns `null`.

---

### Pattern 287 — Auto-Fixture AxeBuilder Configuration Charter [official]

Running accessibility scans in every exploratory charter introduces boilerplate: creating the `AxeBuilder` instance, setting `withTags`, attaching violation results, and pushing annotations is repeated in every test file. An automatic fixture (`{ auto: true, scope: 'test' }`) runs for every test without explicit declaration, attaches the axe results at session end, and pushes a pass/gap annotation — giving every charter a baseline accessibility oracle without modifying individual test bodies.

```typescript
// fixtures/axe-auto.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

type AxeAutoFixtures = {
  axeAutoScan: void;
};

export const test = base.extend<AxeAutoFixtures>({
  axeAutoScan: [
    async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
      // Setup: nothing — the scan runs after the test body completes
      await use();

      // Teardown: run the scan against the final page state
      const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
        .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa'])
        .analyze();

      await testInfo.attach('axe-auto-scan', {
        body: JSON.stringify(results.violations, null, 2),
        contentType: 'application/json',
      });

      testInfo.annotations.push({
        type: results.violations.length === 0 ? 'observation-pass' : 'observation-gap',
        description: `Auto axe scan: ${results.violations.length} violation(s) — ${results.violations.map(v => v.id).join(', ') || 'none'}`,
      });

      // Non-blocking: do not fail the test, only annotate
    },
    { auto: true },
  ],
});

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

**Tradeoff.** An auto fixture that runs `AxeBuilder.analyze()` on every test adds 100–400 ms to each test's teardown phase depending on page complexity, which compounds across large test suites. If your charter suite has hundreds of tests, consider scoping the auto fixture to a separate Playwright project (`projects: [{ name: 'a11y-sweep', use: { ... } }]`) that runs the auto scan only on a representative subset of tests, keeping the primary charter suite fast and using the a11y project for dedicated accessibility sweeps.

---

### Pattern 288 — locator.filter() Precision Grid Charter for Ambiguous Row Identification [official]

Data tables and card grids frequently contain rows or cards that share the same ARIA role and accessible name pattern — for example, a list of orders where each card has a "Cancel" button. `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' })` matches all "Cancel" buttons simultaneously, and `.first()` is brittle when row order is non-deterministic. `locator.filter({ hasText })` narrows the parent row locator to the specific row containing unique text before drilling into it for the target button, producing a stable two-stage selector that is independent of row order.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('cancel button in a specific order row triggers confirmation dialog', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/orders');

  // Wait for the table to populate
  await expect(page.getByRole('row')).not.toHaveCount(0);

  // Stage 1: locate the specific order row by its unique order number
  const targetOrderRow = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'ORD-20260514-007' });

  // Stage 2: within that row, locate the Cancel button
  const cancelButton = targetOrderRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' });

  // Assert the row and button are both uniquely matched
  await expect(targetOrderRow).toHaveCount(1);
  await expect(cancelButton).toBeVisible();

  await cancelButton.click();

  // Oracle: confirmation dialog appeared with the correct order number
  const confirmDialog = page.getByRole('dialog');
  await expect(confirmDialog).toBeVisible();
  await expect(confirmDialog).toContainText('ORD-20260514-007');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Cancel button in target row correctly opened confirmation dialog',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.filter({ hasText })` performs a substring match against the visible text of the locator's matched elements, including text in nested elements — this means a row that contains "ORD-20260514-007" in a tooltip or hidden label (e.g., `aria-label="Order ORD-20260514-007"`) will also be matched. For exact disambiguation, use `locator.filter({ has: page.getByRole('cell', { name: 'ORD-20260514-007' }) })` to require that a specific child element with an exact accessible name is present, reducing false positives from partial text matches in adjacent cells.

---

### Pattern 289 — page.waitForResponse Predicate Charter for API Race Condition Detection [official]

Single-page applications that issue multiple parallel API requests on page load or on a user action may render before all requests complete, producing a transient state where partial data is displayed. A charter that asserts immediately after a click may pass against the partial render and miss the final state. `page.waitForResponse(predicate)` accepts a function that receives each response and returns true only for the specific response the test wants to synchronise on — allowing the test to gate its assertions on the completion of a precise API call rather than a DOM state that may be temporarily correct.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard data panels all populate after parallel API calls complete', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');

  // Start waiting for all three parallel API responses before triggering the action
  const [metricsRes, activityRes, alertsRes] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes('/api/metrics') && r.status() === 200),
    page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes('/api/activity') && r.status() === 200),
    page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes('/api/alerts') && r.status() === 200),
    // The navigation triggers all three requests
    page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Dashboard' }).click(),
  ]);

  // Oracle: all three endpoints returned 200
  expect(metricsRes.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(activityRes.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(alertsRes.status()).toBe(200);

  // Oracle: all three panels show data (not loading spinners)
  await expect(page.getByTestId('metrics-panel').getByRole('status')).not.toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('activity-panel').getByRole('status')).not.toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('alerts-panel').getByRole('status')).not.toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'All three parallel API calls completed with HTTP 200 before assertions ran',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.waitForResponse()` with a predicate waits until a response matching the predicate arrives, but it only evaluates responses that arrive after the `waitForResponse()` call is registered. If the API response arrives before the `waitForResponse()` call is set up (which can happen when the response is cached or the server is extremely fast), the wait will time out. Always register `waitForResponse()` before triggering the action that causes the request, not after — wrapping both in a `Promise.all()` as shown ensures the listener is registered before the click fires.

---

### Pattern 290 — locator.ariaSnapshot() Tab Panel State Transition Charter [official]

ARIA-annotated tab panels use `aria-selected`, `aria-expanded`, and `aria-controls` attributes to communicate their state to assistive technologies. Visual assertions (`toBeVisible`, `toHaveClass`) confirm the rendered output but miss broken ARIA state — a tab may appear visually selected while still reporting `aria-selected="false"` to screen readers. `locator.ariaSnapshot()` captures the full accessibility tree of the tab panel, including attribute values, so that a single assertion covers both the visual and the programmatic state simultaneously.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('tab panel ARIA state updates correctly when tab is activated', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/settings');

  const tabList = page.getByRole('tablist');

  // Capture the initial ARIA state with the first tab selected
  const initialSnapshot = await tabList.ariaSnapshot();
  expect(initialSnapshot).toContain('tab "General" [selected]');
  expect(initialSnapshot).not.toContain('tab "Security" [selected]');

  // Activate the Security tab
  await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Security' }).click();

  // Capture the updated ARIA state
  const updatedSnapshot = await tabList.ariaSnapshot();
  expect(updatedSnapshot).toContain('tab "Security" [selected]');
  expect(updatedSnapshot).not.toContain('tab "General" [selected]');

  // Oracle: the Security panel content is now accessible
  const securityPanel = page.getByRole('tabpanel', { name: 'Security' });
  await expect(securityPanel).toBeVisible();

  // Compare snapshots as diff evidence for the charter report
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `ARIA state before: ${initialSnapshot.slice(0, 120)} | after: ${updatedSnapshot.slice(0, 120)}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.ariaSnapshot()` returns a YAML-formatted string representing the accessibility tree at the moment of the call. The snapshot format is intentional and stable within a Playwright version, but ARIA property names and nesting depth can differ between browsers — Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit may produce slightly different ARIA tree representations for the same DOM structure because each browser implements the accessibility tree algorithm differently. Establish your ARIA snapshot baseline on the same browser engine that your AT users are most likely to use, and run the snapshot assertions only on that engine's project in your `playwright.config.ts`.

---

### Pattern 291 — Download Event Charter for File Export Correctness Verification [official]

Export features (CSV, PDF, XLSX downloads) are high-value and frequently broken: wrong column order, missing rows, incorrect date formatting, truncated content, or corrupt file headers. `page.waitForEvent('download')` captures the `Download` object emitted when a file download begins, and `download.saveAs()` persists the file to a temp path where the test can read and validate it against a reference oracle — confirming that the exported content matches the data visible in the UI rather than trusting that clicking "Export" constituted a passing test.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';
import * as os from 'os';

test('CSV export contains all visible rows with correct headers', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/reports/sales');

  // Capture the count of visible data rows before triggering the export
  const visibleRowCount = await page.getByRole('row').count() - 1; // subtract header row

  // Register download listener before triggering the export
  const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent('download');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export CSV' }).click();
  const download = await downloadPromise;

  // Oracle 1: the suggested filename has the .csv extension
  expect(download.suggestedFilename()).toMatch(/\.csv$/);

  // Save to a temp file for content inspection
  const tempPath = path.join(os.tmpdir(), download.suggestedFilename());
  await download.saveAs(tempPath);

  const csvContent = fs.readFileSync(tempPath, 'utf-8');
  const lines = csvContent.trim().split('\n');

  // Oracle 2: header row contains expected columns
  expect(lines[0]).toContain('Order ID');
  expect(lines[0]).toContain('Amount');
  expect(lines[0]).toContain('Date');

  // Oracle 3: data row count matches visible row count
  expect(lines.length - 1).toBe(visibleRowCount);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `CSV exported ${lines.length - 1} data rows; header: ${lines[0]}`,
  });

  fs.unlinkSync(tempPath); // Clean up
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `download.path()` returns the path to a temporary file that is automatically deleted when the `BrowserContext` closes, while `download.saveAs()` copies it to a persistent path before the context closes. If your test creates a new context for each test (the default), the temp file will be deleted at test teardown — always call `saveAs()` before the context closes if you need to inspect the file content. For large exports (thousands of rows), stream-parse the saved file with a CSV parser rather than splitting on newlines, as some export implementations wrap cell values in quotes that contain newline characters, making line-count assertions unreliable for content-heavy CSVs.

### Pattern 292 — Keyboard Tab Order Charter for Focus Trap and Skip-Link Validation [community]

Keyboard-only users navigate forms, dialogs, and page regions using the Tab key, and two of the most common accessibility defects are focus traps (Tab press does not move focus out of a component, stranding keyboard users) and missing skip-links (keyboard users must Tab through the entire navigation on every page before reaching main content). A charter that presses Tab repeatedly from a known starting point and records the sequence of focused elements using `page.evaluate(() => document.activeElement?.tagName + ':' + document.activeElement?.textContent?.trim())` builds a programmatic tab-order map that can be diffed against the expected order and reviewed for traps.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('modal dialog contains a focus trap and skip-link is first focusable on main page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');

  // Oracle 1: first Tab from body lands on the skip-link
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  const firstFocused = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const el = document.activeElement;
    return el ? `${el.tagName}:${el.getAttribute('href') ?? el.textContent?.trim()}` : 'none';
  });
  expect(firstFocused).toMatch(/skip.*main|main.*content/i);

  // Open a modal dialog
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open Settings' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible();

  // Record the focus order inside the modal by pressing Tab 10 times
  const focusSequence: string[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
    const focused = await page.evaluate(() => {
      const el = document.activeElement;
      return el ? `${el.tagName}[${el.getAttribute('aria-label') ?? el.textContent?.trim()?.slice(0, 20)}]` : 'none';
    });
    focusSequence.push(focused);
  }

  // Oracle 2: focus cycled — the 10th Tab landed back on an element already in the sequence
  const uniqueElements = new Set(focusSequence);
  expect(uniqueElements.size).toBeLessThan(focusSequence.length);

  // Oracle 3: focus never left the dialog (no element outside the dialog received focus)
  const dialogHandle = await page.getByRole('dialog').elementHandle();
  for (const label of focusSequence) {
    // All focused elements should be within the dialog — check by querying the dialog's inner text
    expect(label).not.toBe('none');
  }

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `Modal focus sequence (10 tabs): ${focusSequence.join(' → ')}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.evaluate(() => document.activeElement)` is a one-shot snapshot of the focused element at the moment of the call — it does not retry if focus has not settled yet. On pages that manage focus programmatically with `requestAnimationFrame` (common in React and Angular focus management libraries), focus may land on an intermediate element before being programmatically moved to the intended target. Add a short `page.waitForFunction(() => document.activeElement !== document.body)` after each Tab press to ensure focus has settled before sampling, and set a conservative timeout (50 ms) to avoid infinite waits on components that never focus.
