### Pattern 293 — route.fulfill() Edge-State Oracle Charter for Error Response Handling [official]

Applications that rely on API responses must gracefully handle HTTP error codes (400, 401, 403, 404, 429, 500, 503) and network-level failures. In a live environment these states are difficult to reliably trigger, but `page.route()` combined with `route.fulfill()` lets the charter inject any HTTP status, body, and headers in response to matching requests. By systematically exercising each error response class for each API dependency, the charter maps how the UI degrades — whether it shows a friendly error message, retries silently, or crashes with an unhandled exception.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const errorScenarios = [
  { status: 401, body: { error: 'Unauthorized' }, expectedUI: /sign in|unauthorized/i },
  { status: 403, body: { error: 'Forbidden' }, expectedUI: /permission|access denied/i },
  { status: 429, body: { error: 'Too Many Requests' }, expectedUI: /rate limit|try again/i },
  { status: 503, body: { error: 'Service Unavailable' }, expectedUI: /unavailable|service/i },
];

for (const scenario of errorScenarios) {
  test(`dashboard handles HTTP ${scenario.status} from /api/dashboard gracefully`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.route('**/api/dashboard', route => {
      route.fulfill({
        status: scenario.status,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify(scenario.body),
      });
    });

    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

    // Oracle 1: no unhandled JavaScript error was thrown
    const pageErrors: string[] = [];
    page.on('pageerror', err => pageErrors.push(err.message));

    // Oracle 2: a user-facing error message matching the scenario is displayed
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert').or(page.getByRole('status'))).toContainText(scenario.expectedUI);

    // Oracle 3: no JavaScript exceptions were thrown during the error render
    expect(pageErrors).toHaveLength(0);

    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-pass',
      description: `HTTP ${scenario.status} handled: UI showed matching error message; no JS exceptions`,
    });
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.route()` intercepts requests at the network layer within the Playwright context — it does not intercept requests made by Service Workers or Web Workers unless those workers were also set up within the same browser context. If your application uses a Service Worker to cache API responses, `route.fulfill()` may never be reached because the Service Worker serves the cached response before the request reaches the network layer. Unregister the Service Worker in a `page.addInitScript()` block before the route handler fires, or use `context.addInitScript()` to clear the service worker registration on every page load during the charter session.

---

### Pattern 294 — Geolocation and Permission Context Charter for Location-Dependent UI [official]

Features that branch on the user's geographic location (store locators, regional pricing, GDPR consent flows, language detection) require the test to control the browser's reported position and permission state. A `BrowserContext` created with `geolocation` and `permissions: ['geolocation']` pre-grants the permission at context creation time, bypassing the browser permission prompt that would otherwise block the test. Combining multiple geolocation coordinates with different permission states (granted, denied, prompt) allows the charter to explore all branches of the location-detection logic in a single session.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('store locator with geolocation', () => {
  test('shows local stores when geolocation is granted', async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({
      geolocation: { latitude: 48.8566, longitude: 2.3522 }, // Paris, France
      permissions: ['geolocation'],
    });
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/find-a-store');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Use My Location' }).click();

    // Oracle: Paris-area stores appear in the results
    await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Nearby Stores' })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toContainText(/Paris|75\d{3}/);

    await context.close();
  });

  test('shows manual entry prompt when geolocation is denied', async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({
      // No geolocation option — deny the permission
    });
    await context.grantPermissions([]); // Explicitly grant nothing
    const page = await context.newPage();

    // Override the permission to denied state for geolocation
    await context.setGeolocation(null as unknown as { latitude: number; longitude: number });
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/find-a-store');

    // Trigger location request — permission will be denied
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Use My Location' }).click();

    // Oracle: manual entry form appears as fallback
    await expect(page.getByLabel('Enter your postcode or city')).toBeVisible();

    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-pass',
      description: 'Geolocation denied gracefully — manual entry fallback shown',
    });

    await context.close();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `context.setGeolocation()` updates the geolocation mid-test — all subsequent calls to the Geolocation API within that context return the new coordinates. However, if your application caches the geolocation result in memory after the first `getCurrentPosition()` call (a common optimisation to avoid repeated permission prompts), `setGeolocation()` updates the browser's position but the cached value in the application's memory will not change until the cache is invalidated. To test dynamic position updates (e.g., a map that tracks a moving user), either mock the application's geolocation caching layer with `page.addInitScript()` to prevent caching, or reload the page after calling `setGeolocation()` to clear the cache.

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 46)

**G7. `page.frameLocator()` resolves the iframe on every action call, but if the iframe's `src` attribute changes between actions (e.g., a multi-step payment flow that navigates the iframe to a 3DS challenge page), the locator continues to match by CSS selector position — not by URL — so `getBy*` calls inside the re-navigated iframe silently target the new page's DOM, producing misleading "element not found" errors when the new page has a different structure.**
QA teams automating a checkout flow that embedded Stripe's 3DS challenge in an iframe found that `paymentFrame.getByLabel('OTP Code')` failed with "element not found" despite the OTP input being visually present. The frame locator was resolving correctly to the iframe element, but the iframe had navigated from `stripe.com/checkout` to `stripe.com/3ds-challenge` between the two interactions. WHY this matters: always assert `page.frameLocator(selector).owner().evaluate(el => el.contentWindow.location.href)` before each set of iframe interactions to confirm the iframe is on the expected URL, and treat iframe navigation as a new "phase" in the charter requiring fresh locator validation.

**G8. `page.routeWebSocket()` stops forwarding frames to the real server as soon as an `onMessage` handler is registered — there is no automatic passthrough, and forgetting to call `ws.connectToServer()` means the real server never receives the page's subscription messages, causing the UI to hang indefinitely waiting for data that will never arrive.**
Teams mocking a subset of WebSocket messages for a live trading dashboard found that registering an `onMessage` handler to intercept specific price-update frames caused all other message types (heartbeats, subscription acknowledgements) to be silently dropped. The real server's connection was never established because `connectToServer()` was not called, and the application's ping/pong keepalive logic timed out after 30 seconds, closing the connection. WHY this matters: if you need to intercept only specific message types, always call `const server = ws.connectToServer()` first to establish the real connection, then forward all non-intercepted messages with `server.send(message)` inside the `onMessage` handler, intercepting only the messages your charter specifically targets.

**G9. `page.exposeFunction()` installs the function on every frame in the page, including iframes from third-party origins — but cross-origin iframes run in a separate security context where the `window` object is not directly accessible, and the exposed function will not be callable from within a cross-origin iframe's JavaScript.**
A QA team attempting to spy on analytics calls made by a third-party widget loaded in a cross-origin iframe found that calls to `window.__spy()` from within the iframe were blocked by the browser's same-origin policy, even though `page.exposeFunction('__spy', ...)` was called before navigation. The function was installed on the top-level page's `window`, but the cross-origin iframe's `window` is a separate, isolated context that Playwright cannot instrument directly. WHY this matters: for cross-origin iframes, use `page.on('request')` or `page.route()` to intercept the network requests that the iframe makes as a side effect of the analytics call — this is the only reliable way to observe side effects of code running in a cross-origin context without modifying the iframe's source.

**G10. `page.clock.fastForward()` accepts a duration string like `'01:30'` (one minute 30 seconds) or a millisecond integer, but passing a string that looks like a wall-clock time (e.g., `'10:30:00'`) is parsed as a duration (10 hours, 30 minutes, 0 seconds), not as an absolute time — silently advancing the clock by 10+ hours instead of jumping to 10:30 AM.**
Teams writing session-expiry tests found that `await page.clock.fastForward('09:00:00')` (intending to jump to 9 AM) instead advanced the clock by 9 hours, triggering session expiry warnings that were not expected until a small increment forward. The string format for `fastForward()` is always `HH:MM:SS` representing an elapsed duration from the current synthetic time, not an absolute target time. WHY this matters: to jump to an absolute clock time, use `page.clock.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-14T09:00:00Z'))` after `install()`, or pass millisecond integers to `fastForward()` computed as `targetTime.getTime() - currentSyntheticTime.getTime()`, never a wall-clock time string.

**G11. `download.path()` returns `null` if the download is still in progress when the call is made — there is no built-in "wait for download to complete" mechanism, and calling `download.path()` before the download finishes produces a null path that is silently passed to `fs.readFileSync()`, causing an unhandled `TypeError: path must be a string` that obscures the real issue.**
Teams testing large file exports (10,000+ row CSVs) found that `download.path()` returned `null` when called immediately after `await downloadPromise` resolved, because `waitForEvent('download')` resolves when the browser initiates the download, not when it completes. The download was still being streamed from the server when `path()` was called. WHY this matters: always use `await download.saveAs(targetPath)` instead of `download.path()` for inspecting downloaded content — `saveAs()` waits for the download to complete before copying the file to the target path, guaranteeing the full content is available; `path()` returns the browser's temp file path without waiting for completion.

**G12. `locator.filter({ hasText })` performs a case-sensitive substring match in most Playwright versions before v1.50 — teams that upgraded from an older version and expected case-insensitive matching found their filter assertions started failing after the version upgrade changed the default matching behaviour.**
A QA team with an existing charter that used `locator.filter({ hasText: 'cancelled' })` to find rows with "Cancelled" status found their tests started failing after a Playwright upgrade because the application had changed "Cancelled" to "CANCELLED" in the status badge. The filter had been working due to case-insensitive matching in the older version, masking the coupling between the filter string and the exact rendered text. WHY this matters: always use `{ hasText: /cancelled/i }` (a RegExp with the `i` flag) when the filter is intended to be case-insensitive, rather than relying on implicit matching behaviour that may change between Playwright versions — the RegExp form is explicit, version-stable, and self-documenting.

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 295 — toMatchAriaSnapshot Structural Regression Charter [official]

`toMatchAriaSnapshot()` (introduced in Playwright v1.49) validates the entire accessible tree of a component or page against a YAML template, catching structural regressions that purely visual snapshot tests miss. Unlike `toHaveText()` or `toHaveRole()` which probe individual elements, this assertion encodes the hierarchical ARIA contract of a UI region in one readable artefact. The YAML template supports exact name strings, RegExp patterns (`/pattern/`), and partial matching (omitting child nodes that are not relevant to the charter). When a component's ARIA structure diverges — e.g., a `list` becomes a `grid`, or a `button` is demoted to a `link` — the failure message shows a structural diff, not just a missing element. This is the canonical charter pattern for landmark navigation, menu trees, and wizard step indicators.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Navigation landmark ARIA contract', () => {
  test('primary nav has stable accessible structure', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com');

    // Wait for navigation to be fully hydrated
    const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Primary' });
    await expect(nav).toBeVisible();

    // Snapshot encodes the exact ARIA tree — any structural change fails the test
    await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - navigation "Primary":
        - list:
          - listitem:
            - link "Home"
          - listitem:
            - link "Products"
          - listitem:
            - link /Deals.*/
          - listitem:
            - link "Account"
    `);

    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-pass',
      description: 'Primary nav ARIA structure is stable — list/listitem/link hierarchy intact',
    });
  });

  test('mobile nav collapses to disclosure widget', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.setViewportSize({ width: 375, height: 812 });
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com');

    // At mobile width, nav switches to a disclosure button + region
    await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Primary' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - navigation "Primary":
        - button "Menu" [expanded=false]
    `);

    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Menu' }).click();

    await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Primary' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - navigation "Primary":
        - button "Menu" [expanded=true]
        - list:
          - listitem:
            - link "Home"
          - listitem:
            - link "Products"
    `);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` uses order-sensitive, hierarchical comparison by default: adding a new nav item or reordering items will fail the test even if no existing items were removed. Use RegExp patterns for dynamic labels (e.g., `/Cart \(\d+\)/`) and omit child nodes you do not care about by ending the list early — Playwright treats an incomplete child list as a "contains" assertion rather than an exact match when the parent role does not specify `/children: equal`. The tradeoff against `toHaveText()` or `toHaveRole()` spot checks is that ARIA snapshot tests are more brittle to benign structural additions but provide far stronger regression coverage when the accessible tree is a contractual guarantee (e.g., a component library's public API).

---

### Pattern 296 — expect.soft Multi-Oracle Charter for Form Validation [official]

Soft assertions (`expect.soft()`) allow a charter to accumulate all failing conditions in a single test run rather than halting at the first failure, which is especially valuable when exploring form validation states where multiple fields may be simultaneously invalid. A standard `expect()` call throws immediately on failure, meaning a test that checks 10 form field errors will surface only the first mismatch per run; `expect.soft()` collects all failures and reports them together in the test result. This pattern is best applied to checklists — situations where the full list of issues matters more than knowing one exists. Terminate a soft-assertion block with `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` to convert accumulated soft failures into a hard stop at the end of the charter phase.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout form shows correct validation messages for all empty fields', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout');

  // Submit with all fields empty to trigger all validation messages simultaneously
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();

  // Soft assertions: collect ALL missing validations in one run
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('First name is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Last name is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Email address is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Delivery address is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Payment method is required')).toBeVisible();

  // Assert that the submit button is disabled after failed submission
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' })).toBeDisabled();

  // Assert the page has not navigated away
  await expect.soft(page).toHaveURL(/checkout/);

  // Hard stop: if any soft assertion failed, terminate and surface the full list
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `All ${7} checkout validation messages visible simultaneously`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Soft assertions do not retry — they evaluate the DOM at the moment they are called and do not benefit from Playwright's auto-retry mechanism. This means soft assertions placed too early (before an async validation message animation completes) will silently record a false negative. Always `await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toBeVisible()` with a hard assertion to anchor the validation state before switching to soft assertions for the individual field checks. The benefit is that the full list of simultaneous failures is surfaced in a single test run, dramatically reducing the round-trip cost of exploratory form validation charters.

---

### Pattern 297 — routeFromHAR Offline Replay Charter for Third-Party API Dependencies [official]

`page.routeFromHAR()` replays a previously recorded HTTP Archive against a URL glob pattern, allowing charters that depend on volatile third-party APIs (payment providers, mapping services, shipping calculators) to run deterministically without live network access. In `update: true` mode the HAR file is created or refreshed against the real network; in `update: false` (or omitted) mode every request matching the glob is served from the recorded file. The HAR format captures status codes, response headers, and body verbatim, making it possible to test edge-state scenarios by manually editing the JSON body of a specific captured response. Unlike `page.route()` + `route.fulfill()`, HAR replay does not require maintaining mock data inline in the test — the recorded file is the source of truth and can be committed to version control.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_PATH = path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/hars/shipping-calculator.har');

test.describe('Shipping calculator — offline HAR replay', () => {
  test('displays DHL Express rates from recorded HAR', async ({ page }) => {
    // Replay all requests to the shipping API from the HAR file
    await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH, {
      url: '*/**/api/v2/shipping/**',
      update: false, // strict replay — no live network calls
    });

    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/cart');
    await page.getByLabel('Postcode').fill('10115');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Calculate Shipping' }).click();

    // Oracle: HAR contains a DHL Express rate of €9.90 for postcode 10115
    await expect(page.getByText('DHL Express')).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('shipping-price-dhl-express')).toHaveText('€9.90');

    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-pass',
      description: 'Shipping rates rendered correctly from HAR replay — no live API call made',
    });
  });

  test('shows error state when API returns 503 (manually edited HAR)', async ({ page }) => {
    // A separate HAR with the shipping response body replaced with 503
    const errorHar = path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/hars/shipping-calculator-503.har');
    await page.routeFromHAR(errorHar, { url: '*/**/api/v2/shipping/**' });

    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/cart');
    await page.getByLabel('Postcode').fill('10115');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Calculate Shipping' }).click();

    // Oracle: application shows graceful degradation message
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Shipping rates temporarily unavailable');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** HAR replay matches POST requests by body payload as well as URL — if the application sends a POST body with a dynamic `sessionId` or `correlationId` field, the HAR will fail to match because the recorded payload differs from the live test's payload. Use `page.route()` + `route.fulfill()` instead for endpoints whose request bodies contain dynamic fields, or preprocess the HAR file to remove those fields using a `recordHarUrlFilter` during recording. The advantage of HAR over inline mocks is that the entire HTTP contract (including headers like `Content-Type`, `Cache-Control`, and cookies set by `Set-Cookie`) is preserved faithfully, catching bugs caused by incorrect header handling that inline `route.fulfill()` mocks might miss.

---

### Pattern 298 — expect.poll Async Condition Charter for Eventually-Consistent State [official]

`expect.poll()` converts a synchronous predicate into a retrying assertion, polling the predicate function on a configurable interval until it returns a value that satisfies the matcher or the timeout expires. It is the correct tool for conditions that cannot be expressed as a Playwright locator assertion — for example, checking the state of a server-side process via a REST API, waiting for an email to appear in a test mailbox service, or polling a background job queue endpoint. Unlike `page.waitForFunction()` which evaluates JavaScript inside the browser, `expect.poll()` runs in the Node.js test process, making it suitable for calls to `page.request.get()` or Node-side SDKs. The polling interval defaults to 100 ms but can be increased for expensive operations.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('background PDF export job completes within 30 seconds', async ({ page, request }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/reports');

  // Trigger the export job — the API returns a job ID immediately
  const triggerResponse = await page.request.post('/api/exports', {
    data: { format: 'pdf', reportType: 'monthly-sales', month: '2026-04' },
  });
  expect(triggerResponse.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  const { jobId } = await triggerResponse.json();

  // Poll the job status endpoint until the job is complete or 30s elapses
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const statusResponse = await request.get(`/api/exports/${jobId}/status`);
      if (!statusResponse.ok()) return 'error';
      const body = await statusResponse.json();
      return body.status; // 'pending' | 'processing' | 'complete' | 'failed'
    },
    {
      message: `Export job ${jobId} did not complete within 30 seconds`,
      timeout: 30_000,
      intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000, 5_000], // back-off: check frequently then slow down
    },
  ).toBe('complete');

  // Now fetch the download link and verify the file is accessible
  const downloadResponse = await request.get(`/api/exports/${jobId}/download`);
  expect(downloadResponse.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  expect(downloadResponse.headers()['content-type']).toContain('application/pdf');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `PDF export job ${jobId} completed and download URL returned valid PDF`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.poll()` does not share Playwright's actionability model — it will not automatically wait for the page to be in a stable state between polling calls. If the polling function performs a `page.request` call that triggers a navigation or changes DOM state as a side effect, those side effects accumulate without cleanup. Prefer `expect.poll()` exclusively for read-only status-check endpoints; for conditions that require interaction (e.g., refreshing the page to see updated server state), use `expect.toPass()` instead, which retries an entire async block including `page.reload()` and locator assertions together.

---

### Pattern 299 — Worker-Scoped Authentication Fixture Charter for Expensive Login Flows [official]

Playwright's worker-scoped fixtures run once per worker process and are shared across all tests in that worker, making them the correct scope for expensive setup such as authentication flows that involve TOTP, OAuth redirects, or captcha bypass. A worker-scoped `authenticatedPage` fixture that calls `page.goto('/login')`, fills credentials, and saves `storageState` to a per-worker temp file avoids re-executing the login flow for every test. Combined with Playwright's `--workers` parallelisation, this pattern can reduce a 500-test suite's total setup time by 80% compared to test-scoped login. The key invariant is that the fixture must save `storageState` to a file and restore it via `browser.newContext({ storageState })` for each test, not share a mutable `page` object across tests.

```typescript
// fixtures/auth.ts
import { test as base, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';
import os from 'os';
import fs from 'fs';

type AuthFixtures = {
  workerStorageState: string;       // path to the saved storage state (worker-scoped)
  authedContext: BrowserContext;    // pre-authenticated context (test-scoped)
};

export const test = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  // Worker-scoped: runs once per worker, shared by all tests on that worker
  workerStorageState: [
    async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
      const storageStatePath = path.join(
        os.tmpdir(),
        `auth-worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}.json`,
      );

      if (!fs.existsSync(storageStatePath)) {
        // First test on this worker — perform full login and save state
        const loginPage = await browser.newPage();
        await loginPage.goto('https://shop.example.com/login');
        await loginPage.getByLabel('Email').fill(`qa-worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}@example.com`);
        await loginPage.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.QA_PASSWORD!);
        await loginPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();
        await expect(loginPage).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);
        await loginPage.context().storageState({ path: storageStatePath });
        await loginPage.close();
      }

      await use(storageStatePath);
    },
    { scope: 'worker' }, // critical: worker scope, not test scope
  ],

  // Test-scoped: each test gets a fresh context with pre-loaded auth state
  authedContext: async ({ browser, workerStorageState }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: workerStorageState });
    await use(context);
    await context.close();
  },
});

export { expect };
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped fixtures are not automatically reset between tests — if one test in the worker corrupts the shared state (e.g., the authenticated user's account is deleted or their session is invalidated by a test), all subsequent tests on the same worker will fail with misleading authentication errors rather than the actual defect. Always use separate test-scoped `authedContext` fixtures derived from the worker-scoped `storageState` file, never share a mutable `page` or `context` object between tests. If your test suite includes tests that mutate user state (change password, delete account), assign those to a dedicated Playwright project with `workers: 1` to prevent cross-contamination.

---

### Pattern 300 — page.on('console') Error Listener Charter for Silent JavaScript Failures [official]

Registering a `page.on('console')` listener before navigation captures all console messages emitted by the page's JavaScript, including `console.error()` calls that indicate caught-but-logged errors which produce no visible UI change. Many production React/Vue applications catch promise rejections and API errors silently, logging them to the console while rendering a stale or empty UI — a pattern that is invisible to locator-based assertions but surfaces immediately when console output is monitored. The charter pattern is to register the listener, perform the user journey, and then assert at the end that no `type === 'error'` messages were emitted. Filtering to `error` type prevents test noise from informational logs.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product listing page emits no console errors on initial load and filter interaction', async ({ page }) => {
  const consoleErrors: string[] = [];

  // Register listener before navigation — captures errors from initial JS evaluation
  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') {
      consoleErrors.push(`[${msg.type()}] ${msg.text()}`);
    }
  });

  // Also capture unhandled page errors (uncaught exceptions)
  const pageErrors: Error[] = [];
  page.on('pageerror', (err) => pageErrors.push(err));

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Products' })).toBeVisible();

  // Interact: apply a filter that triggers an API call
  await page.getByLabel('Category').selectOption('Electronics');
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toBeVisible();

  // Interact: sort — another API round-trip
  await page.getByLabel('Sort by').selectOption('price-asc');
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toBeVisible();

  // Oracle: no console errors emitted during the entire journey
  expect(
    consoleErrors,
    `Console errors detected:\n${consoleErrors.join('\n')}`,
  ).toHaveLength(0);

  expect(
    pageErrors,
    `Uncaught page errors:\n${pageErrors.map((e) => e.message).join('\n')}`,
  ).toHaveLength(0);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'No console errors or uncaught exceptions during product listing journey',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.on('console')` captures all frames' console output, including third-party analytics scripts, ad networks, and browser extensions injected by other Playwright tests that share a browser context. In a suite that runs multiple tests against the same browser context, console errors from a previous test's lingering async operations (e.g., a cancelled `fetch()`) may appear in the current test's listener. Always register the listener inside a fresh test-scoped context or use `page.off('console', handler)` during teardown. Additionally, some frameworks (e.g., React in development mode) emit `console.error` for prop-type warnings that are not runtime errors — add an allowlist of known-benign patterns using `if (msg.text().includes('Warning:')) return` to prevent false positives from obscuring real errors.

---

### Pattern 301 — expect.toPass Retry-Block Charter for Flaky Multi-Step Sequences [official]

`expect.toPass()` retries an entire async function block — including interactions and assertions — until it passes without throwing or the timeout expires. This is the correct pattern for exploratory charters that involve an inherently unstable intermediate state: for example, a WebSocket-driven dashboard that requires the server to emit a specific event before the UI renders, or a polling-based refresh button that may need clicking multiple times before the server has processed the background job. Unlike `waitForFunction()` (browser-side evaluation) or `expect.poll()` (Node-side predicate without interaction), `expect.toPass()` can contain full Playwright interactions and retrying assertions in the same block.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('live order status updates to Dispatched after fulfilment processing', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/orders/ORD-20260514-001');

  // The fulfilment system processes the order asynchronously — status may lag by up to 60 s
  await expect(async () => {
    // Reload to get fresh server state (some apps don't push real-time updates)
    await page.reload();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-status-badge')).toHaveText('Dispatched');
  }).toPass({
    timeout: 60_000,    // total retry budget
    intervals: [2_000], // reload every 2 s
  });

  // Once status is confirmed, assert secondary state: tracking number is now shown
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Tracking Number')).not.toBeEmpty();
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: /Track Your Parcel/i })).toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Order status transitioned to Dispatched with tracking number visible',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.toPass()` retries the entire block, including any side-effect interactions inside it (in the example above, `page.reload()`). If the block contains a destructive action — clicking a "Pay Now" button that charges a card — retrying it will trigger the action multiple times, potentially charging the card several times or creating duplicate records. Only use `expect.toPass()` for idempotent interaction sequences. For non-idempotent flows, use `expect.poll()` to poll a read-only status endpoint, and perform the one-time action once before the poll block begins.

---

### Pattern 302 — page.addInitScript Invariant Injection Charter for Pre-Hydration State [official]

`page.addInitScript()` runs a script in every frame before any page scripts execute — it fires before the application's JavaScript bundle, before framework hydration, and before any `DOMContentLoaded` listeners. This timing makes it the correct tool for injecting test invariants that must be visible to the application from the very first `window` evaluation: feature flags stored in `window.__config`, A/B test variants, `localStorage` pre-seeding, or mocking a global dependency like `window.analytics`. Unlike `page.evaluate()` (which runs after the page has loaded and the application may have already read `localStorage`), `addInitScript()` guarantees the injected value is present before the application reads it.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout page renders with pre-seeded cart items from localStorage', async ({ page }) => {
  // Inject localStorage state before any application script runs
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    const cartItems = [
      { sku: 'WIDGET-100', qty: 2, price: 29.99 },
      { sku: 'GADGET-200', qty: 1, price: 149.00 },
    ];
    localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(cartItems));
    localStorage.setItem('cart_currency', 'EUR');
  });

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout');

  // Oracle: cart is pre-populated without requiring any prior navigation to /products
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-item-count')).toHaveText('3 items');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-subtotal')).toHaveText('€208.98');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Checkout rendered with pre-seeded cart from localStorage — no prior navigation needed',
  });
});

test('feature flag killswitch disables express checkout button', async ({ page }) => {
  // Inject a feature flag before the application reads window.__config
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    Object.defineProperty(window, '__config', {
      value: { features: { expressCheckout: false } },
      writable: false,
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout');

  // Oracle: express checkout button is absent when the feature flag is false
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Express Checkout' })).not.toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to Payment' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.addInitScript()` scripts cannot import Node.js modules or reference variables from the outer test scope — the function is serialised and evaluated in the browser context, so closures over test variables will throw a `ReferenceError`. Pass data as serialised arguments using `page.addInitScript(({ cartItems }) => { localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(cartItems)) }, { cartItems })` — Playwright serialises the second argument and makes it available as the script's parameter. Additionally, scripts registered with `addInitScript()` persist for the lifetime of the page context, including after `page.reload()`, which can cause unexpected state bleed if a test chain reloads the page and the script re-applies stale data.

---

### Pattern 303 — locator.pressSequentially Typing Speed Charter for Input Debounce Validation [official]

`locator.pressSequentially()` types a string character-by-character with a configurable `delay` between keystrokes, faithfully simulating a human typing at a specific speed. This is distinct from `locator.fill()` which sets the entire value in a single DOM event, bypassing the keydown/keypress/keyup cycle that many input validators and debounced search fields depend on. Exploratory charters for autocomplete dropdowns, live search fields, password strength meters, and username availability checks should use `pressSequentially()` to trigger the actual debounce behaviour rather than filling the field atomically. The `delay` parameter (in milliseconds per character) controls whether the debounce timer fires between characters.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('username availability check fires after debounce and shows correct states', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/register');

  const usernameField = page.getByLabel('Choose a username');
  const availabilityIndicator = page.getByTestId('username-availability');

  // Type slowly enough that the debounce fires mid-typing (debounce = 400 ms)
  // delay: 50 ms/char — each character fires keyup, triggering the availability check
  await usernameField.pressSequentially('john', { delay: 50 });

  // Wait for the in-flight state to appear (debounce fires after 400 ms of silence)
  await expect(availabilityIndicator).toHaveText('Checking...');
  await expect(availabilityIndicator).toHaveText('Username taken', { timeout: 5_000 });

  // Clear and type a unique username
  await usernameField.selectText();
  await usernameField.pressSequentially('john_unique_2026', { delay: 50 });

  await expect(availabilityIndicator).toHaveText('Checking...');
  await expect(availabilityIndicator).toHaveText('Available!', { timeout: 5_000 });

  // Assert the form is submittable only when username is available
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create Account' })).toBeEnabled();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Debounced username availability check transitions through Checking → Available correctly',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `pressSequentially()` with a `delay` will increase test execution time proportional to the string length — typing a 20-character username at 100 ms/char adds 2 seconds per call. For charters where the typing speed is irrelevant and only the final value matters (e.g., a simple text input with no debounce logic), `locator.fill()` is faster and should be preferred. Reserve `pressSequentially()` explicitly for charters targeting debounce, keystroke-level event handling, character-by-character validation (e.g., password strength meters that update on each keystroke), or input mask libraries that consume raw key events.

---

### Pattern 304 — page.request API-Layer Probe Charter for Backend State Verification [official]

`page.request` exposes a `fetch`-like API that runs in the browser context with all cookies and authentication headers automatically included from the current page session. This makes it the correct tool for probing backend state as an oracle after a UI action — confirming that a submitted form actually persisted to the database, checking that a deletion cascade completed, or reading the server's canonical representation of a resource to compare against the UI's rendered value. Unlike a separate `request` fixture that starts a new session, `page.request` shares the authenticated session with the open page, so authenticated API calls succeed without re-providing credentials.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('address book update persists correctly to the API', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/account/addresses');

  // UI action: edit the first address
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit', exact: true }).first().click();
  await page.getByLabel('Street address').fill('42 New Street');
  await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Berlin');
  await page.getByLabel('Postcode').fill('10115');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save Address' }).click();

  // Wait for the confirmation toast to confirm the UI accepted the change
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Address updated');

  // API-layer oracle: fetch the address directly from the REST API to confirm persistence
  const addressesResponse = await page.request.get('/api/v1/account/addresses');
  expect(addressesResponse.ok()).toBeTruthy();

  const addresses = await addressesResponse.json();
  const updatedAddress = addresses.find(
    (a: { street: string }) => a.street === '42 New Street',
  );

  expect(updatedAddress, 'Updated address not found in API response').toBeDefined();
  expect(updatedAddress.city).toBe('Berlin');
  expect(updatedAddress.postcode).toBe('10115');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Address update confirmed via UI and validated against REST API response',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.request` calls are subject to the browser's same-origin policy for cookies — if your application uses `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` session cookies, cross-origin API calls made via `page.request` will not include those cookies, and the request will fail with a 401. In that case, use the test-level `request` fixture (which runs outside the browser sandbox) combined with explicitly-stored `storageState` to make authenticated server-side API calls. For same-origin APIs, `page.request` is the simpler and more reliable option because it inherits the full browser session automatically.

---

### Pattern 305 — Dialog Auto-Handler Charter for Alert/Confirm/Prompt Coverage [official]

`page.on('dialog')` registers a handler that fires whenever the browser shows a native dialog (`window.alert`, `window.confirm`, `window.prompt`, or `beforeunload`). Without a registered handler, dialogs block all subsequent Playwright actions indefinitely, causing timeouts that mask the actual behaviour under test. The charter pattern registers a handler before triggering the action that causes the dialog, captures the dialog's message for assertion, and then accepts or dismisses it based on what the charter is verifying. For `beforeunload` dialogs specifically, the handler must be registered before navigation away from the page.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('delete account confirmation dialog shows correct message and cancels safely', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/account/settings');

  // Register the dialog handler BEFORE the action that triggers the dialog
  const dialogMessages: string[] = [];
  page.once('dialog', async (dialog) => {
    dialogMessages.push(dialog.message());
    // Cancel the deletion — oracle: the account still exists after cancel
    await dialog.dismiss();
  });

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete My Account' }).click();

  // Verify the dialog message was the expected confirmation text
  expect(dialogMessages).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(dialogMessages[0]).toContain('permanently delete your account');
  expect(dialogMessages[0]).toContain('cannot be undone');

  // Oracle: still on the settings page — deletion was cancelled
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/account\/settings/);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Account Settings' })).toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Delete dialog shown with correct message; dismiss returns user to settings',
  });
});

test('beforeunload dialog fires when leaving a form with unsaved changes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/account/profile');
  await page.getByLabel('Display Name').fill('Unsaved Change');

  let beforeUnloadFired = false;
  page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => {
    if (dialog.type() === 'beforeunload') {
      beforeUnloadFired = true;
      await dialog.accept(); // allow navigation to proceed
    }
  });

  // Navigate away — should trigger beforeunload
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/account/orders');

  expect(beforeUnloadFired, 'beforeunload dialog was not fired for unsaved changes').toBe(true);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.once('dialog')` registers a one-time handler that is removed after the first dialog event. If a sequence of actions triggers two successive dialogs (e.g., a confirm followed by an alert acknowledgement), `page.once()` will handle the first and the second will block the test. Use `page.on('dialog')` (persistent handler) in charters that might trigger multiple dialogs, and track the sequence with an array of captured dialog objects. Be aware that Playwright automatically dismisses unhandled dialogs in headless mode after a short timeout, which means a missing handler may produce a flaky test that occasionally passes (dialog auto-dismissed) and occasionally times out (dialog blocks next action) depending on timing.

---

### Pattern 306 — Parameterised Test Charter for Multi-Locale Currency Rendering [official]

Playwright's `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` combined with a data-driven array loop produces a suite of parallel test instances that each exercise one configuration — the canonical pattern for locale and currency rendering charters. Rather than copy-pasting the same assertions for `en-GB`, `de-DE`, `fr-FR`, and `ja-JP`, a single parameterised charter encodes the expected decimal separator, currency symbol position, and thousands grouping for each locale and asserts all variants in one commit. Each parameterised instance is an independent Playwright test worker, so failures in one locale do not block others.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const LOCALE_CASES = [
  { locale: 'en-GB', currency: 'GBP', price: '£1,299.00', symbol: '£', separator: ',' },
  { locale: 'de-DE', currency: 'EUR', price: '1.299,00 €', symbol: '€', separator: '.' },
  { locale: 'fr-FR', currency: 'EUR', price: '1 299,00 €', symbol: '€', separator: ' ' },
  { locale: 'ja-JP', currency: 'JPY', price: '¥1,299',    symbol: '¥', separator: ',' },
  { locale: 'ar-SA', currency: 'SAR', price: '1,299.00 ر.س', symbol: 'ر.س', separator: ',' },
] as const;

for (const { locale, currency, price, symbol } of LOCALE_CASES) {
  test(`product price renders correctly for ${locale} (${currency})`, async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({
      locale,
      // Set timezone consistent with locale to avoid date-related rendering differences
      timezoneId: locale.startsWith('ja') ? 'Asia/Tokyo' : 'Europe/London',
    });
    const page = await context.newPage();

    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products/widget-pro');

    const priceLocator = page.getByTestId('product-price');
    await expect(priceLocator).toBeVisible();

    // Assert the full formatted price string
    await expect(priceLocator).toHaveText(price);

    // Assert currency symbol is present (locale-aware position check)
    const priceText = await priceLocator.textContent();
    expect(priceText).toContain(symbol);

    test.info().annotations.push({
      type: 'observation-pass',
      description: `${locale}: price rendered as "${price}" — symbol and separators correct`,
    });

    await context.close();
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Each parameterised test creates and tears down its own `BrowserContext`, adding roughly 200–400 ms of overhead per locale variant. For suites with 20+ locales, this overhead compounds; consider grouping locale variants into a single test with soft assertions (`expect.soft()`) per locale if the overhead is prohibitive. The advantage of fully separate parameterised tests is that each locale appears as its own named test in the report, making it immediately obvious which locales are failing without reading assertion diffs. Use the parameterised form when locale failures are expected to be rare (regression suite) and the grouped soft-assertion form during active internationalisation development when multiple locales may fail simultaneously.

---

### Pattern 307 — page.clock.setSystemTime Charter for Session Expiry and Token Renewal Boundaries [official]

`page.clock.install()` followed by `page.clock.setSystemTime()` replaces the browser's native time APIs (`Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `performance.now`) with synthetic equivalents that the test controls. This is the only reliable way to test time-sensitive behaviour such as JWT expiry, "session idle timeout" warnings, or countdown timers — polling real time with `page.waitForTimeout()` makes tests slow and brittle, while injecting a synthetic clock allows the test to jump to the exact moment of interest in milliseconds. The `install()` call must happen before `page.goto()` to ensure the application reads the synthetic time during its initial hydration.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session idle timeout warning appears after 14 minutes and logs out at 15 minutes', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install the clock BEFORE navigation so the app reads synthetic time from the start
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-05-14T09:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();

  // Jump to 14 minutes — idle timeout warning should appear
  await page.clock.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-14T09:14:00Z'));
  // Also advance timers to fire the setInterval that drives the idle check
  await page.clock.runFor(1_000); // fire any 1-second interval-based checks

  await expect(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Session Expiring Soon' }),
  ).toBeVisible({ timeout: 3_000 });
  await expect(page.getByTestId('session-countdown')).toContainText('1 minute');

  // Advance to exactly 15 minutes — session should expire
  await page.clock.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-14T09:15:00Z'));
  await page.clock.runFor(1_000);

  // Oracle: user is redirected to login with an expiry message
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/login/);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Your session has expired');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Idle timeout warning at 14 min and automatic logout at 15 min confirmed via synthetic clock',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.clock.setSystemTime()` updates the synthetic clock value but does not automatically fire pending timers — `setTimeout(() => logout(), 900_000)` registered at page load will not fire until `page.clock.runFor(900_000)` or `page.clock.fastForward(900_000)` is also called. `setSystemTime()` changes what `Date.now()` returns; `runFor()`/`fastForward()` advances the timer queue. If your application uses `setTimeout`-based session expiry (fire a callback after N ms), use `page.clock.fastForward()`. If it uses `Date`-comparison-based expiry (check `Date.now() > expiresAt` on every render cycle), `setSystemTime()` plus a single `runFor(100)` to trigger the next render cycle is sufficient. Mixing both approaches in the same application requires both calls.

---

### Pattern 308 — Component-Test mount() Charter for Isolated Unit-Level UI Contracts [official]

Playwright's experimental `@playwright/experimental-ct-*` packages expose a `mount()` fixture that renders a single component in a real browser without loading the full application. This enables charters that verify a component's accessible contract, event emission, and visual state in complete isolation from routing, authentication, and global state — making defects unambiguous and reproducible. The `mount()` fixture returns a `Locator` pointing at the component root, so all standard Playwright assertions and interactions apply without modification. Component tests run in Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit via Vite bundling, providing true cross-browser component coverage without E2E overhead.

```typescript
// tests/components/ProductCard.spec.tsx  (React example)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import { ProductCard } from '../../src/components/ProductCard';

test('ProductCard renders product name, price, and add-to-cart button', async ({ mount }) => {
  const product = {
    id: 'WIDGET-100',
    name: 'Pro Widget',
    price: 29.99,
    currency: 'EUR',
    inStock: true,
  };

  const component = await mount(<ProductCard product={product} />);

  // Accessible name assertions
  await expect(component.getByRole('heading', { level: 3 })).toHaveText('Pro Widget');
  await expect(component.getByTestId('price')).toHaveText('€29.99');
  await expect(component.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' })).toBeEnabled();
});

test('ProductCard shows out-of-stock state and disables add-to-cart button', async ({ mount }) => {
  let addedToCart = false;

  const component = await mount(
    <ProductCard
      product={{ id: 'WIDGET-100', name: 'Pro Widget', price: 29.99, currency: 'EUR', inStock: false }}
      onAddToCart={() => { addedToCart = true; }}
    />,
  );

  await expect(component.getByRole('button', { name: /out of stock/i })).toBeDisabled();
  await expect(component.getByRole('button', { name: /out of stock/i })).toHaveAttribute(
    'aria-disabled',
    'true',
  );

  // Verify the callback is not invoked even if the button is programmatically clicked
  await component.getByRole('button').click({ force: true });
  expect(addedToCart).toBe(false);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Component tests cannot test integration concerns: routing, global state management (Redux/Zustand stores), authenticated API calls, or multi-component interactions that depend on a shared context provider. The `beforeMount` hook allows injecting providers (router, i18n, theme), but any provider that makes network calls will require `page.route()` mocking to keep the component test isolated. The payoff is determinism and speed — component tests run in under 200 ms per case without a full app startup, making them suitable for TDD loops and CI pre-commit hooks. Use component tests for UI contract coverage (rendered output, accessibility attributes, event callbacks) and reserve E2E charters for integration and flow coverage.

---

### Pattern 309 — HAR update: true Record-and-Replay Charter for API Contract Freezing [official]

Combining `routeFromHAR(path, { update: true })` on first run with `routeFromHAR(path, { update: false })` on subsequent runs implements a "record once, replay forever" pattern: the first test run against the live API captures all responses to a HAR file, and every subsequent run replays from that file, making the suite independent of API availability while still producing realistic response data. This is distinct from hand-authored mocks: the HAR contains the actual server's response headers, cookies, and timing data, making it a faithful snapshot of the API contract at the moment of recording. CI pipelines can use `update: false` exclusively; developers refresh the HAR when the API contract intentionally changes.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_FILE = path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/hars/product-search.har');

// Set UPDATE_HAR=true in the environment to re-record against the live API
const UPDATE_MODE = process.env.UPDATE_HAR === 'true';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_FILE, {
    url: '*/**/api/search/**',
    update: UPDATE_MODE,
    updateContent: 'embed', // store response bodies inside the HAR, not as separate files
  });
});

test('product search returns relevant results for "widget"', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  await page.getByLabel('Search products').fill('widget');
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');

  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Search Results' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(10);
  // Oracle: first result is the expected top-ranked product
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toContainText('Pro Widget');

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `Search results rendered correctly (HAR ${UPDATE_MODE ? 're-recorded' : 'replayed'})`,
  });
});

test('product search with no results shows empty state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  await page.getByLabel('Search products').fill('xyznonexistentproduct');
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');

  await expect(page.getByText('No products found')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Browse All Products' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `updateContent: 'embed'` option stores base64-encoded response bodies directly inside the HAR JSON, which keeps the fixture self-contained but significantly increases the file size for binary responses (images, PDFs). For APIs that return large binary payloads, use `updateContent: 'attach'` to store response bodies as separate sidecar files referenced by the HAR. Additionally, HAR files capture `Set-Cookie` response headers including `HttpOnly` cookies — committing HAR files that contain real session tokens or API keys to version control is a security risk; always record against a dedicated QA environment that uses non-sensitive test credentials, or strip authentication headers from the HAR before committing using a post-processing script.

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 47)

**G13. `locator.pressSequentially()` does not trigger the browser's built-in autofill or password manager suggestions — Chrome's autofill fires on `focus` plus a synthetic `input` event with a specific `isTrusted: true` flag, which Playwright cannot replicate because `isTrusted` is always `false` for programmatically dispatched events, meaning tests that depend on autofill populating a second field (e.g., address autofill filling city/state/postcode from street) will silently leave those fields empty while passing all assertions on the street field itself.**
A QA team testing an address form found that typing into the street address field via `pressSequentially()` never triggered the browser's address autofill, leaving the city and postcode fields empty. The test passed because assertions only checked the street field. WHY this matters: for charters that must test autofill interactions, use `page.addInitScript()` to pre-populate `localStorage` with the address data and verify the form hydrates from that state, or use `route.fulfill()` to mock the Places autocomplete API that the form's address lookup widget calls — never rely on the browser's native autofill in automated tests since `isTrusted: false` prevents it from firing.

**G14. `expect(locator).toHaveAttribute('disabled', '')` passes for a `<button disabled>` element but fails for a `<button disabled="disabled">` element in some browser rendering engines because the DOM normalises the `disabled` attribute value differently across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit — in Chromium, `button.getAttribute('disabled')` returns `''` for a boolean attribute, but in Firefox it may return `'disabled'`, meaning attribute-value assertions are inherently cross-browser fragile.**
Teams running cross-browser suites found that `toHaveAttribute('disabled', '')` passed in Chromium but failed in Firefox for the same `<button disabled>` element. The boolean attribute `disabled` has no specified value in HTML, and browsers normalise the serialised attribute value differently. WHY this matters: always use `toBeDisabled()` instead of `toHaveAttribute('disabled', ...)` for boolean HTML attributes — `toBeDisabled()` uses Playwright's actionability model which checks the element's computed disabled state via the accessibility tree, not the raw attribute string, and is therefore browser-agnostic and stable across all three engine families.

**G15. `page.routeFromHAR()` fails silently when the HAR file contains responses whose `Content-Encoding: gzip` header is present but the body was stored uncompressed in the HAR — this happens when the HAR was recorded with a proxy that decompressed the response before writing it to disk. The browser receives an uncompressed body with a `Content-Encoding: gzip` header and attempts to decompress it, producing corrupted JSON that the application silently ignores, causing the UI to show an empty state with no visible error.**
A QA team using Charles Proxy to record their HAR found that their product listing page showed 0 results when replaying the HAR in Playwright, despite the HAR containing valid JSON product data. The proxy had decompressed the gzip response but preserved the original `Content-Encoding: gzip` header. WHY this matters: when recording HAR files, always verify the Content-Encoding header matches the actual body encoding by inspecting the HAR JSON directly — if the body is valid UTF-8 JSON but the header says `gzip`, remove the `Content-Encoding` header from the HAR entry manually, or use `npx playwright open --save-har` (which records directly via the browser's DevTools protocol and preserves encoding correctly) instead of a proxy-based recorder.

**G16. `page.clock.install()` called after `page.goto()` does not retroactively reset timers that the application registered during the initial page load — `setTimeout(() => showIdleWarning(), 900_000)` registered at hydration time has already been enqueued in the real timer queue, and `page.clock.install()` replaces `setTimeout` for future calls but cannot cancel or re-enqueue the already-registered timer, meaning the idle warning will fire at the real-time interval, not the synthetic one.**
Teams testing idle session warnings found that calling `page.clock.install()` after navigating to the dashboard had no effect on the idle timer — the warning still appeared after the real 15 minutes rather than after the synthetic fast-forward. The idle timer had been registered at hydration time before `clock.install()` replaced `setTimeout`. WHY this matters: always call `page.clock.install({ time: ... })` before `page.goto()` — the docs explicitly state this requirement — and if existing test setup code calls `goto()` in a `beforeEach` fixture before your clock setup, refactor the fixture to accept a `url` parameter so the clock is installed first, then `goto()` is called second inside the test body.

**G17. `expect.soft()` assertions are evaluated lazily in Playwright's assertion pipeline — if you place a `expect.soft()` call inside a `test.step()` block, the soft failure is recorded against the step, but the step itself is marked as failed while execution continues into the next step, creating a report where a later step is shown as "passed" even though it was reached only because a prior step's soft assertion was not hard-stopping. Reviewing the report without expanding all steps can give a false impression that the entire test passed through all phases successfully.**
A QA team using `test.step()` for charter phase labelling found that their Step 2 "Form Submission" step was marked as passed in the HTML report even though Step 1 "Field Population" had recorded a soft failure for a missing validation message. The soft failure was correctly listed in the test's error count, but the step-level pass/fail indicator in the collapsed report view suggested Step 2 had been reached with a clean state. WHY this matters: for charters that use `test.step()` structuring, place the `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` hard stop at the end of each step, not just at the end of the entire test — this converts any accumulated soft failures into a step-level hard stop before the next phase begins, keeping the step-level pass/fail indicators honest.

**G18. `page.on('dialog')` must be registered before the interaction that triggers the dialog — Playwright resolves dialogs on the event loop tick they are emitted, and if no handler is registered at that tick, the dialog is auto-accepted (in Chromium) or auto-dismissed (in Firefox and WebKit) silently, with no error and no indication that a dialog was shown. Tests relying on the dialog to block navigation (e.g., `beforeunload` preventing accidental form abandonment) will pass even when the application has a bug that disables the `beforeunload` handler, because the dialog was never actually triggered.**
Teams testing `beforeunload` form protection found that their tests passed on CI (Chromium headless) even after a developer removed the `beforeunload` event listener, because the test was registering the dialog handler after `page.goto(targetUrl)` was already in flight — the `beforeunload` event had already fired and been auto-accepted before the handler was registered. WHY this matters: always register `page.on('dialog')` at the very start of the test, before any navigation or interaction. For `beforeunload` specifically, set a flag in the handler and assert `expect(beforeUnloadFired).toBe(true)` after the navigation completes — if the handler never fires, the flag remains false and the charter correctly surfaces the missing protection.

**G19. `expect(component).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` in component tests (`@playwright/experimental-ct-*`) snapshots the component's subtree only — it does not include portal-rendered elements such as modals, tooltips, and dropdown menus that the component mounts via `ReactDOM.createPortal()` or Vue's `Teleport` into `document.body` outside the component root. Asserting the presence of a portal-rendered dropdown via `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` on the component locator will always fail because the dropdown's DOM node is outside the component's subtree.**
Teams writing component tests for a `<Select>` dropdown that used `ReactDOM.createPortal()` to render its menu in `document.body` found that `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` on the `<Select>` root never showed the menu items, even after clicking the trigger. The ARIA snapshot was correct for the trigger button but showed no children for the expanded state. WHY this matters: for portal-rendered elements, use `expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` (targeting the entire page document) instead of targeting the component locator, or use `page.getByRole('listbox')` to locate the portal-rendered menu directly. If the component is intended to be tested in isolation, refactor it to accept a `menuContainer` prop that defaults to `document.body` but can be overridden to the component root in tests.
