## Cycle 48 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 310 — page.addLocatorHandler() Overlay Auto-Dismiss Charter for Sticky UI Blockers [official]

Cookie banners, chat widgets, newsletter pop-ups, and survey overlays appear asynchronously during exploratory sessions and block otherwise-valid interactions. `page.addLocatorHandler()` registers a callback that fires automatically whenever a matching locator is visible, dismissing the overlay before Playwright retries the blocked action. This is architecturally superior to inserting explicit dismissal steps into every test: the handler runs transparently in the background, keeps the charter focused on the feature under investigation, and prevents flakiness caused by non-deterministic overlay timing. The handler fires at most once per matching locator visibility event, so it does not create infinite dismiss loops.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Register a handler that auto-dismisses the cookie consent banner
  // whenever it appears during any action in this session
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie/i }),
    async (overlay) => {
      await overlay.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all|reject all/i }).first().click();
      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: 'overlay-dismissed',
        description: 'Cookie consent banner auto-dismissed by locator handler',
      });
    },
  );

  // Also dismiss any survey/feedback widget that appears mid-session
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByTestId('feedback-widget'),
    async (widget) => {
      await widget.getByRole('button', { name: /close|dismiss/i }).click();
    },
  );
});

test('checkout flow completes without overlay interference', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/cart');
  // Overlays may appear at any point; the handlers above dismiss them automatically
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('test@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Shipping Address' })).toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Checkout flow completed; overlays were handled transparently',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.addLocatorHandler()` is not a substitute for testing the overlay itself — it is a session hygiene tool that prevents overlays from contaminating charters focused on other features. If the charter's mission includes verifying consent banner behaviour (GDPR compliance, reject-all persistence), do not register a handler; instead, test the banner explicitly in a dedicated charter. Additionally, the handler's callback must be idempotent because Playwright may call it multiple times if the overlay reappears. Handlers registered in `beforeEach` propagate to every test in the suite; register them in the test body if only specific charters need them to avoid unexpected side effects on tests that intentionally verify overlay interactions.

---

### Pattern 311 — expect.extend() Custom Domain Matcher Charter for Business-Rule Oracles [official]

Playwright's `expect.extend()` API allows registering custom assertion matchers that encapsulate domain-specific oracle logic. Rather than scattering complex conditional checks throughout session harnesses, custom matchers express business rules as named, reusable assertions: `expect(priceText).toBeFormattedCurrency('EUR')`, `expect(orderStatus).toBeValidTransitionFrom('pending')`. This makes charters self-documenting, produces clear failure messages, and allows multiple teams to share a library of domain oracles without duplicating logic.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/customMatchers.ts
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Extend Playwright's expect with business-rule matchers
expect.extend({
  toBeFormattedCurrency(received: string, currencyCode: string) {
    // Validates format like "€29.99" or "USD 1,234.56"
    const patterns: Record<string, RegExp> = {
      EUR: /^€\d{1,3}(,\d{3})*\.\d{2}$/,
      USD: /^\$\d{1,3}(,\d{3})*\.\d{2}$/,
      GBP: /^£\d{1,3}(,\d{3})*\.\d{2}$/,
    };
    const pattern = patterns[currencyCode];
    if (!pattern) {
      return { pass: false, message: () => `Unknown currency code: ${currencyCode}` };
    }
    const pass = pattern.test(received.trim());
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `Expected "${received}" NOT to be a valid ${currencyCode} formatted price`
          : `Expected "${received}" to match ${currencyCode} format (e.g. ${currencyCode === 'EUR' ? '€29.99' : '$29.99'})`,
    };
  },

  toBeValidOrderStatus(received: string, expectedFrom: string) {
    const validTransitions: Record<string, string[]> = {
      pending:    ['processing', 'cancelled'],
      processing: ['shipped', 'cancelled'],
      shipped:    ['delivered', 'returned'],
      delivered:  [],
      cancelled:  [],
    };
    const allowed = validTransitions[expectedFrom] ?? [];
    const pass = allowed.includes(received);
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `Expected "${received}" NOT to be a valid transition from "${expectedFrom}"`
          : `Expected "${received}" to be one of [${allowed.join(', ')}] from state "${expectedFrom}", got "${received}"`,
    };
  },
});

// tests/order-status-charter.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import './fixtures/customMatchers';

test('order status transitions are valid after dispatch', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://admin.example.com/orders/ORD-0042');
  const status = await page.getByTestId('order-status').textContent() ?? '';
  const price  = await page.getByTestId('order-total').textContent() ?? '';

  expect(status.trim()).toBeValidOrderStatus('processing');
  expect(price.trim()).toBeFormattedCurrency('EUR');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom matchers in `expect.extend()` are synchronous by default. If the oracle logic requires async operations (e.g., an API call to verify a backend state), the matcher function must return a `Promise`, which Playwright supports but which adds complexity: the matcher must be declared `async` and the `message` function must still be synchronous (it receives the resolved state as a closure). Keep matchers focused on value-level assertions rather than side effects; use `test.step()` blocks for the async setup preceding the assertion. Also note that custom matchers are not automatically available in all test files — they must be imported or registered in a global setup file via `import './customMatchers'` in `playwright.config.ts`'s `require` array.

---

### Pattern 312 — page.on('requestfinished') Timing Oracle Charter for API Latency Budgets [official]

Exploratory testing sessions that include performance-as-quality charters can use Playwright's `page.on('requestfinished')` event to collect real API latency observations during normal interaction flows. Unlike synthetic performance tests that benchmark in isolation, this pattern captures latency in the context of realistic user journeys — including the overhead of authentication headers, cookie payloads, and concurrent requests triggered by component mount effects.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface RequestTiming {
  url: string;
  method: string;
  status: number;
  durationMs: number;
}

test('dashboard API calls complete within latency budget during load', async ({ page }) => {
  const timings: RequestTiming[] = [];
  const LATENCY_BUDGET_MS = 500; // SLA: all API calls under 500 ms

  page.on('requestfinished', async (request) => {
    const response = await request.response();
    if (!response) return;
    if (!request.url().includes('/api/')) return;

    const timing = request.timing();
    const durationMs = timing.responseEnd - timing.requestStart;

    timings.push({
      url:        new URL(request.url()).pathname,
      method:     request.method(),
      status:     response.status(),
      durationMs: Math.round(durationMs),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');
  // Wait for the page to fully settle (all deferred requests complete)
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Attach all timing observations to the session report
  test.info().attach('api-timings', {
    body:        Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(timings, null, 2)),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  const violations = timings.filter((t) => t.durationMs > LATENCY_BUDGET_MS);
  expect.soft(violations, `API calls exceeding ${LATENCY_BUDGET_MS}ms budget`).toHaveLength(0);

  if (violations.length > 0) {
    test.info().annotations.push({
      type:        'latency-violation',
      description: violations.map((v) => `${v.method} ${v.url}: ${v.durationMs}ms`).join('; '),
    });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `request.timing()` returns the DevTools Protocol timing object, which reports time relative to the start of the request context, not wall-clock time. The `responseEnd - requestStart` delta gives total round-trip time from the browser's perspective, including DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, and transfer time. This is an end-to-end latency measurement from the client's perspective, which is what users experience, but it is not a server-side processing time measurement. For diagnosing slow APIs, correlate the `requestfinished` timing with server-side spans in your observability platform using the `X-Request-ID` or trace ID header that the server returns in the response. Do not use `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` as the termination condition if the page has polling requests or streaming connections — it will never resolve. Use a fixed `page.waitForTimeout(2000)` or a specific `page.waitForResponse()` sentinel instead.

---

### Pattern 313 — browserContext.tracing Granular Snapshot Charter for Defect Evidence Capture [official]

Playwright's built-in tracing API (`browserContext.tracing.start()/stop()`) captures a full session artifact including DOM snapshots, network requests, console messages, and action timeline. For exploratory sessions, wrapping individual charter phases in discrete trace segments — rather than capturing one monolithic trace for the entire session — produces focused, smaller trace files that are faster to open in the Trace Viewer and directly correspond to the charter's Z-goal. The `snapshots: true` option stores DOM state at every action, enabling pixel-accurate replay of what the tester saw at each step.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const TRACE_DIR = path.join(process.cwd(), 'traces');

test('checkout Phase 1: address form with international postal codes', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page    = await context.newPage();

  // Phase 1 trace: address form exploration
  await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true, sources: true });
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout/address');
  await page.getByLabel('Country').selectOption('DE');
  await page.getByLabel('Postal Code').fill('10115');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
  const phase1Path = path.join(TRACE_DIR, `address-phase1-${Date.now()}.zip`);
  await context.tracing.stop({ path: phase1Path });

  test.info().attach('trace-phase1-address', {
    path:        phase1Path,
    contentType: 'application/zip',
  });

  // Phase 2 trace: payment form exploration
  await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true });
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment' })).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  const phase2Path = path.join(TRACE_DIR, `payment-phase2-${Date.now()}.zip`);
  await context.tracing.stop({ path: phase2Path });

  test.info().attach('trace-phase2-payment', {
    path:        phase2Path,
    contentType: 'application/zip',
  });

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
  await context.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Storing `sources: true` in trace options embeds the test source code in the trace file, which is valuable for correlating a DOM snapshot with the exact line of the session harness that produced it. However, this also means trace files may contain sensitive information if the source code includes hardcoded credentials, API keys, or internal hostnames. For shared or public CI environments, use `sources: false` and rely on the action timeline labels for correlation instead. Additionally, very long sessions with `snapshots: true` produce large trace files (50–200 MB for a 10-minute session) — use per-phase tracing to keep individual trace files under 20 MB for practical Trace Viewer performance.

---

### Pattern 314 — page.waitForResponse() Sentinel Charter for Async Mutation Confirmation [official]

Exploratory charters investigating form submissions, data saves, and multi-step workflows need to confirm that backend mutations complete before asserting application state. `page.waitForResponse()` with a URL predicate and status check provides a deterministic, race-condition-free oracle that replaces fragile UI-polling patterns. By interleaving the wait with the triggering action via `Promise.all()`, the charter captures the response before any UI update that might scroll the evidence out of view.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('profile update persists correctly to backend and refreshes UI', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/profile/edit');

  // Stage the waitForResponse before the triggering click to avoid race conditions
  const [response] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForResponse(
      (resp) =>
        resp.url().includes('/api/users/') &&
        resp.request().method() === 'PATCH' &&
        resp.status() === 200,
    ),
    (async () => {
      await page.getByLabel('Display Name').fill('Jane Explorer');
      await page.getByLabel('Bio').fill('QA engineer exploring the unknown');
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save Changes' }).click();
    })(),
  ]);

  // Oracle 1: backend accepted the mutation
  const responseBody = await response.json();
  expect(responseBody).toMatchObject({
    displayName: 'Jane Explorer',
    bio:         'QA engineer exploring the unknown',
  });

  // Oracle 2: UI reflects the saved state without a page reload
  await expect(page.getByTestId('profile-display-name')).toHaveText('Jane Explorer');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/saved|updated/i);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `Profile PATCH returned 200; UI updated without reload. Response ID: ${responseBody.id}`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.waitForResponse()` has a default timeout of 30 seconds (configurable via `timeout` option). For slow backend endpoints, this is usually sufficient, but for charters exploring slow administrative workflows (bulk import, report generation), increase the timeout explicitly or use `page.waitForResponse(predicate, { timeout: 120_000 })`. The predicate-based overload (passing a function rather than a URL string) is more resilient than string matching because it can check both URL and method in a single expression, preventing false matches when multiple endpoints share a URL prefix. Note that `page.waitForResponse()` resolves as soon as the response headers arrive, not when the full response body is buffered — call `await response.json()` or `await response.body()` after the `waitForResponse` resolves to read the body, and handle the resulting `Promise` appropriately.

---

### Pattern 315 — Playwright Tags and grep Filtering Charter for Risk-Tiered Session Execution [official]

Playwright's test tag system (`test('@smoke')`, `test('@regression')`, `test('@risk-high')`) combined with the `--grep` CLI flag enables risk-tiered charter execution: exploratory sessions can be segmented by risk level so that a quick pre-deployment check runs only `@smoke` charters, while a full release sign-off run executes all `@risk-high` and `@regression` charters. Tags are first-class annotations in the HTML report, making risk tier visible alongside pass/fail status in CI dashboards.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Risk-tiered tags applied to exploratory charter tests
// Run smoke only:      npx playwright test --grep @smoke
// Run high-risk only:  npx playwright test --grep @risk-high
// Exclude flaky:       npx playwright test --grep-invert @flaky

test('@smoke @risk-high checkout completes for authenticated user', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Checkout' })).toBeVisible();
});

test('@regression @risk-medium guest checkout address validation rejects invalid postal codes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Postal Code').fill('INVALID');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/invalid postal code/i);
});

test('@risk-low @cosmetic product image alt text is present on category page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  const images = page.getByRole('img');
  const imageCount = await images.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < imageCount; i++) {
    await expect(images.nth(i)).toHaveAttribute('alt', /.+/);
  }
});

// Charter runner configuration: playwright.config.ts
// projects: [
//   { name: 'smoke', grep: /@smoke/ },
//   { name: 'risk-high', grep: /@risk-high/ },
//   { name: 'full', grep: /.*/ },
// ]
```

**Tradeoff.** Playwright's tag system uses string matching, not a structured taxonomy — there is no enforcement that a test has exactly one risk tier tag, or that mutually exclusive tags (e.g., `@risk-high` and `@risk-low`) are not applied simultaneously. Teams need a naming convention and a linting rule (enforced via a custom ESLint rule or a `check:tags` npm script) to maintain tag discipline at scale. Also note that the `--grep` flag uses regex matching against the full test title string including tags, so a tag like `@smoke` will inadvertently match a test titled `"@smokeless form should reject empty fields"` — use a word-boundary pattern in the project `grep` config (`/\@smoke\b/`) rather than a bare prefix match.

---

### Pattern 316 — locator.and() Compound Selector Charter for Dense UI Disambiguation [official]

In data-dense UIs such as data tables, admin panels, and dashboards, multiple elements share the same role and similar accessible names. `locator.and(otherLocator)` creates a compound locator that matches elements satisfying both conditions simultaneously, providing precise disambiguation without resorting to XPath or CSS class selectors. This is semantically cleaner than chaining `.filter()` calls and produces more readable failure messages.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('admin table: active user row shows correct role badge', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://admin.example.com/users');

  // Without .and(): ambiguous — multiple rows may have an "Edit" button
  // page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' })

  // With .and(): narrows to the "Edit" button inside a row that also contains "jane@example.com"
  const janeRow   = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'jane@example.com' });
  const editBtn   = janeRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' });
  const activeTag = janeRow.getByRole('status').and(page.getByText('Active'));

  await expect(activeTag).toBeVisible();
  await expect(editBtn).toBeEnabled();

  // Compound locator: a button that is both labeled "Delete" AND has aria-pressed="false"
  const notPressedDelete = page
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })
    .and(page.locator('[aria-pressed="false"]'));

  await expect(notPressedDelete.first()).toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Jane row has Active badge; Edit button enabled; Delete button not in pressed state',
  });
});

test('dashboard: warning card that is also dismissible', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  // Find a card that is both a warning AND has a dismiss button as a child
  const dismissibleWarning = page
    .getByRole('alert')
    .and(page.locator('[data-severity="warning"]'))
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('button', { name: /dismiss/i }) });

  const count = await dismissibleWarning.count();
  if (count > 0) {
    await dismissibleWarning.first().getByRole('button', { name: /dismiss/i }).click();
    await expect(dismissibleWarning.first()).not.toBeVisible();
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.and()` requires both locators to resolve to elements in the same DOM subtree — it performs an intersection of two locator match sets. If the two locators match elements at different levels of the DOM tree (e.g., a row-level locator AND a cell-level locator), the intersection will be empty and the compound locator will time out. Use `.filter({ has: ... })` for parent-child relationships (find an ancestor that contains a descendant matching the filter) and `.and()` for same-element multi-attribute matching (find a single element satisfying two independent criteria). Mixing the two is valid: `page.getByRole('row').filter({ has: page.getByText('jane') }).and(page.locator('[data-status="active"]'))` finds a row containing "jane" that also has `data-status="active"` on the row element itself.

---

### Pattern 317 — test.step() Structured Phase Labelling Charter for Debrief-Ready Session Reports [official]

Wrapping distinct charter phases in named `test.step()` blocks transforms Playwright's HTML report into a structured session sheet. Each step appears as a collapsed timeline entry with its own duration, pass/fail indicator, and attached annotations — mirroring the SBTM session sheet structure without requiring a separate documentation artefact. The `box: true` option in `test.step()` simplifies the error location in the report to the step call site rather than the line within the step, keeping failure messages terse for human reviewers.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('SBTM Charter: password reset flow end-to-end', async ({ page }) => {
  // Phase 1: trigger reset
  await test.step('Phase 1 — Trigger password reset from login page', async () => {
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/login');
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Forgot password?' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Reset Password' })).toBeVisible();
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('tester@example.com');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send Reset Link' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/check your email/i);
    test.info().annotations.push({ type: 'phase-1-pass', description: 'Reset email sent confirmation displayed' });
  });

  // Phase 2: simulate email link click via direct URL (token from API seeding)
  await test.step('Phase 2 — Follow reset link and set new password', async () => {
    // In a real session, seed the reset token via API; here we simulate with a test token
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/reset-password?token=TEST_TOKEN_FROM_SEED');
    await page.getByLabel('New Password').fill('SecureP@ss2026!');
    await page.getByLabel('Confirm Password').fill('SecureP@ss2026!');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Set Password' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/password updated/i);
  }, { box: true }); // box: true — errors report at the step level, not individual line

  // Phase 3: confirm login with new password
  await test.step('Phase 3 — Confirm login with new password succeeds', async () => {
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('tester@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('SecureP@ss2026!');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /dashboard|welcome/i })).toBeVisible();
    test.info().annotations.push({ type: 'phase-3-pass', description: 'Login with new password succeeded' });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.step()` is a reporting construct, not a transaction boundary — if a step fails, Playwright halts the test at the failing assertion and does not roll back any browser state. Steps cannot be independently retried; only the entire test can be retried via `retries`. For session harnesses that need to continue past a step failure to gather more evidence, use `expect.soft()` within the step body and place a `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` hard-stop gate at the start of each subsequent step. The `box: true` flag changes error reporting but does not change execution behaviour — boxed steps still fail at the line of the failing assertion, but the stack trace shown in the HTML report is truncated to the `test.step()` call site, which reduces noise for reviewers who want a phase-level summary rather than a code-level trace.

---

### Pattern 318 — page.route() Request Mutation Charter for Edge-Case Response Exploration [official]

`page.route()` with a `route.fulfill()` or `route.continue({ ...overrides })` call enables charters that explore how the application handles edge-case API responses that are difficult to reproduce against a real backend: empty arrays, maximum-length payloads, deprecated field names, unexpected HTTP status codes, and malformed JSON. This pattern decouples the UI exploration charter from backend availability and allows systematic coverage of error-handling paths that a live API would never serve in a test environment.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product list handles empty search results gracefully', async ({ page }) => {
  // Override the search API to return an empty results array
  await page.route('*/**/api/products/search*', async (route) => {
    const originalResponse = await route.fetch();
    const body = await originalResponse.json();
    // Mutate the response: replace results with an empty array, keep metadata
    await route.fulfill({
      status:  200,
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body:    JSON.stringify({ ...body, results: [], total: 0 }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products?q=widget');
  await expect(page.getByText('No products found')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Clear search' })).toBeVisible();
});

test('dashboard handles 503 from analytics API without crashing', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('*/**/api/analytics/**', (route) =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 503, body: 'Service Unavailable' }),
  );

  const consoleErrors: string[] = [];
  page.on('pageerror', (err) => consoleErrors.push(err.message));

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');
  await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  // Oracle: page renders a degraded-state placeholder, does not crash
  await expect(page.getByTestId('analytics-widget')).toContainText(/unavailable|error loading/i);
  // Oracle: no unhandled JS errors from the analytics widget failure
  expect(consoleErrors.filter((e) => e.includes('Uncaught')), 'Unhandled JS errors from analytics 503').toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `route.fetch()` proxies the request through Playwright's built-in fetch, which does not reuse the browser's authentication cookies or session headers unless `route.fetch({ headers: request.headers() })` is called explicitly. For APIs that require session cookies, always forward the original request headers when mutating via `route.fetch()`. Also note that `page.route()` intercepts requests made directly by the page's JavaScript, but does not intercept requests made by service workers unless service worker interception is enabled explicitly. If the application uses a service worker to cache API responses, register the route before `page.goto()` AND set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the browser context to prevent the cache from serving stale responses to the mutated route.

---

### Pattern 319 — Playwright Config projects Array Multi-Browser Charter for Cross-Engine Regression Parity [official]

Playwright's `projects` array in `playwright.config.ts` allows the same charter suite to run against Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit in a single CI invocation. Cross-browser exploration surfaces rendering divergences, CSS layout bugs, Web API compatibility gaps, and font-rendering differences that only manifest in specific browser engines. Structuring projects around named browser profiles (including mobile emulation) makes the charter portfolio explicit about which browsers are covered at each risk tier.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests/charters',
  fullyParallel: true,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,
  reporter: [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['json', { outputFile: 'results.json' }]],

  use: {
    baseURL:     'https://app.example.com',
    trace:       'on-first-retry',
    screenshot:  'only-on-failure',
    video:       'retain-on-failure',
  },

  projects: [
    // Tier 1: Smoke — Chromium only for speed
    { name: 'chromium-smoke', grep: /@smoke/, use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },

    // Tier 2: Cross-browser — risk-high charters on all three engines
    { name: 'firefox-risk-high',  grep: /@risk-high/, use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] } },
    { name: 'webkit-risk-high',   grep: /@risk-high/, use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] } },
    { name: 'chromium-risk-high', grep: /@risk-high/, use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },

    // Tier 3: Mobile emulation — form and viewport charters
    { name: 'mobile-chrome', grep: /@mobile/, use: { ...devices['Pixel 7'] } },
    { name: 'mobile-safari', grep: /@mobile/, use: { ...devices['iPhone 15'] } },

    // Tier 4: Full regression — all tests on Chromium
    { name: 'chromium-full', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Running all three browser engines multiplies test execution time by approximately 3x. For a charter portfolio with 200 tests at 5 seconds per test, a single-browser run takes ~17 minutes while a three-browser run takes ~50 minutes. Mitigate this by applying `--grep` filtering so that only `@risk-high` and `@regression` charters run cross-browser in CI, while `@smoke` and `@risk-low` charters run Chromium-only. Additionally, some Playwright assertions behave slightly differently across engines: `toHaveAttribute()` for boolean attributes, CSS pseudo-class selectors (`:focus-visible`), and `scrollIntoView()` semantics all have engine-specific quirks. When a charter fails on one engine only, check the Playwright browser-specific behaviour notes in the docs before filing a product defect — the root cause may be a known engine difference rather than an application bug.

---

### Pattern 320 — page.accessibility.snapshot() Deep ARIA Tree Charter for Dynamic Widget Exploration [community]

Playwright's `page.accessibility.snapshot()` returns the full accessibility tree of the page as a structured JSON object, including roles, names, states, and the complete child hierarchy. For exploratory charters targeting complex interactive widgets (rich text editors, tree views, data grids, date pickers), diffing the ARIA tree before and after an interaction provides a structural oracle that catches accessibility regressions invisible to visual screenshots: focus management failures, missing `aria-expanded` state updates, incorrect role assignments after dynamic DOM mutations, and label binding breaks.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('date picker ARIA tree is coherent before and after month navigation', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/book-appointment');

  // Capture ARIA tree before opening the date picker
  const treeBefore = await page.accessibility.snapshot({ root: page.locator('[data-testid="date-picker"]') });

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Choose date' }).click();

  // After open: dialog role must be present
  const treeOpen = await page.accessibility.snapshot({ root: page.locator('[role="dialog"]') });
  expect(treeOpen?.role).toBe('dialog');
  expect(treeOpen?.children?.some((c) => c.role === 'grid')).toBe(true);

  // Navigate to next month
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next month' }).click();

  const treeNextMonth = await page.accessibility.snapshot({ root: page.locator('[role="dialog"]') });
  // Oracle: grid heading changed (month name updated)
  expect(treeNextMonth?.children?.find((c) => c.role === 'heading')?.name).not.toBe(
    treeOpen?.children?.find((c) => c.role === 'heading')?.name,
  );

  test.info().attach('aria-tree-open', {
    body:        Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(treeOpen, null, 2)),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Date picker ARIA tree coherent; grid present; month heading updates on navigation',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.accessibility.snapshot()` uses the browser's accessibility API, which is populated from the DOM's accessible name computation algorithm. In Chromium, the accessibility tree is built lazily and may not reflect very recent DOM mutations — a 100–200 ms `waitFor` after triggering an interaction is sometimes necessary before taking a snapshot. The `root` option limits the snapshot to a subtree, which is faster and produces smaller output than a full-page snapshot, but requires knowing the root element's locator in advance. For charters exploring unknown widget implementations, take a full-page snapshot first to discover the widget's role and name, then refine subsequent snapshots to use the widget as the `root`. Note that `page.accessibility.snapshot()` is considered a lower-level API compared to `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` — for regression testing, prefer the YAML-based snapshot assertion; use `page.accessibility.snapshot()` for programmatic oracle logic that computes differences.

---

### Pattern 321 — Service Worker Registration State Charter for PWA Offline Exploration [community]

Progressive Web Apps register service workers that intercept network requests and serve cached responses. An exploratory charter that explicitly checks the service worker's registration state, cache contents, and offline behaviour provides coverage that end-to-end testing commonly misses: stale cache entries serving outdated content, cache-miss fallback pages that render blank, push notification permission prompts blocking interactions, and background sync queues accumulating failed mutations. Playwright's `page.evaluate()` enables direct inspection of the Service Worker API from within the session harness.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('PWA service worker is registered and cache is populated after first load', async ({ page }) => {
  // Allow service workers (default context blocks them if serviceWorkers: 'block' is set)
  await page.goto('https://pwa.example.com/');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Oracle 1: service worker is registered and active
  const swState = await page.evaluate(async () => {
    const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistration();
    if (!reg) return { registered: false };
    return {
      registered: true,
      scope:      reg.scope,
      state:      reg.active?.state ?? 'none',
    };
  });
  expect(swState.registered).toBe(true);
  expect(swState.state).toBe('activated');

  // Oracle 2: cache storage contains expected shell assets
  const cachedUrls = await page.evaluate(async () => {
    const cacheNames = await caches.keys();
    const allUrls: string[] = [];
    for (const name of cacheNames) {
      const cache  = await caches.open(name);
      const keys   = await cache.keys();
      allUrls.push(...keys.map((r) => new URL(r.url).pathname));
    }
    return allUrls;
  });
  expect(cachedUrls).toContain('/');
  expect(cachedUrls.some((u) => u.endsWith('.js'))).toBe(true);

  // Oracle 3: offline navigation serves cached shell, not a network error
  await page.context().setOffline(true);
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
  await page.context().setOffline(false);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: `SW active at scope ${swState.scope}; ${cachedUrls.length} cached URLs; offline reload served shell`,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.context().setOffline(true)` simulates network unavailability at the Playwright level but does not simulate a true airplane-mode scenario — IndexedDB, localStorage, and service worker cache remain accessible because they are local storage APIs, not network APIs. The service worker's `fetch` event handler still fires for cached resources, so a properly implemented PWA will serve from cache correctly. However, `setOffline()` does not exercise the service worker's background sync queue or push notification service — those require interacting with the browser's push service infrastructure, which cannot be simulated in automated tests without a test push endpoint. For background sync charters, use `page.evaluate()` to register a sync tag directly via `registration.sync.register('test-sync')` and verify the sync handler logic separately from the network simulation.

---

### Pattern 322 — Response Body Schema Diff Charter for API Contract Drift Detection [community]

API contracts drift silently when backend teams add, rename, or remove response fields without coordination. An exploratory charter that captures live API response bodies and compares them against a baseline JSON Schema — stored as a test fixture — provides a lightweight contract testing layer that runs in the same session as UI exploration. Unlike dedicated contract testing tools (Pact, Dredd), this pattern integrates directly into the Playwright harness, requires no broker infrastructure, and produces defect evidence in the same HTML report as the UI observations.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import Ajv from 'ajv';
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

const ajv = new Ajv({ allErrors: true, strict: false });

// Load the stored baseline schema from the fixtures directory
const productSchema = JSON.parse(
  fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/schemas/product.json'), 'utf-8'),
);
const validateProduct = ajv.compile(productSchema);

test('product detail API response matches baseline schema', async ({ page }) => {
  let capturedBody: unknown;

  // Intercept the product detail API call and capture its response body
  page.on('response', async (response) => {
    if (response.url().includes('/api/products/') && response.status() === 200) {
      try {
        capturedBody = await response.json();
      } catch {
        // ignore non-JSON responses
      }
    }
  });

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products/WIDGET-100');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  expect(capturedBody, 'Product API response was not captured').toBeDefined();

  const valid = validateProduct(capturedBody);
  if (!valid) {
    const violations = (validateProduct.errors ?? []).map(
      (e) => `${e.instancePath || '(root)'}: ${e.message}`,
    );
    test.info().attach('schema-violations', {
      body:        Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(violations, null, 2)),
      contentType: 'application/json',
    });
    expect(violations, 'Schema drift detected').toHaveLength(0);
  }

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'observation-pass',
    description: 'Product detail API response matches baseline JSON Schema',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** JSON Schema validation with AJV reports structural violations (missing required fields, wrong types) but cannot detect semantic drift: a field renamed from `price` to `unitPrice` that retains the same type will pass schema validation while breaking every consumer that read `price`. For semantic contract drift, combine schema validation with golden-file snapshot comparison: store a sanitised example response body (with timestamps and IDs normalised to constants) as a fixture and use `expect(normalisedBody).toMatchSnapshot()` alongside the schema check. Also note that `page.on('response')` fires before `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')`; ensure `capturedBody` is read after the network settles to avoid a race where the assertion runs before the response listener fires.

---

### Pattern 323 — Keyboard Shortcut Charter with Modifier Key Combos for Power-User Workflow Coverage [community]

Applications with keyboard shortcut systems (productivity tools, IDEs, design tools, admin dashboards) have shortcut coverage that is routinely absent from scripted test suites because shortcut interactions require multi-key combinations and stateful context awareness. An exploratory charter using `page.keyboard.press()` and `page.keyboard.down()`/`page.keyboard.up()` for held-modifier combinations systematically covers the shortcut matrix and surfaces conflicts (e.g., a browser-level shortcut that shadows an application shortcut), focus-context failures (a shortcut that only works when a specific element is focused), and OS-level interceptions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Shortcut charter: map of keyboard combos to expected outcomes
const SHORTCUT_MATRIX = [
  { keys: 'Control+s',       description: 'Save document',           oracle: /saved|changes saved/i },
  { keys: 'Control+z',       description: 'Undo last action',        oracle: /undo/i },
  { keys: 'Control+Shift+z', description: 'Redo last undone action', oracle: /redo/i },
  { keys: 'Control+/',       description: 'Toggle comment',          oracle: null }, // visual-only
  { keys: 'Escape',          description: 'Close modal/panel',       oracle: null },
] as const;

test('document editor keyboard shortcuts fire expected outcomes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://editor.example.com/documents/new');
  await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  // Ensure the editor canvas has focus before triggering shortcuts
  const editorCanvas = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Document content' });
  await editorCanvas.click();
  await editorCanvas.fill('Hello, World!');

  for (const shortcut of SHORTCUT_MATRIX) {
    await test.step(`Shortcut: ${shortcut.keys} — ${shortcut.description}`, async () => {
      await page.keyboard.press(shortcut.keys);
      if (shortcut.oracle) {
        await expect(page.getByRole('status').or(page.getByRole('alert'))).toContainText(shortcut.oracle);
      }
      // Post-shortcut: ensure the editor canvas is still the focused element
      await expect(editorCanvas).toBeFocused();
      test.info().annotations.push({
        type: 'shortcut-pass',
        description: `${shortcut.keys}: ${shortcut.description} — focus returned to editor`,
      });
    });
  }
});

test('shortcut does not fire when modal is open (focus trap)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://editor.example.com/documents/new');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Settings' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Settings' })).toBeVisible();

  // Control+S inside a modal should NOT save the document (it should do nothing or save form)
  await page.keyboard.press('Control+s');
  // Oracle: document saved notification should NOT appear when modal is focused
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).not.toContainText(/document saved/i);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.keyboard.press()` dispatches keyboard events with `isTrusted: false`, which some applications check to distinguish between synthetic and user-initiated events. If the application's shortcut handler checks `event.isTrusted` (a security measure to prevent malicious scripts from triggering shortcuts), `page.keyboard.press()` will not fire the handler and the charter will produce a false negative. To test these applications, use `page.evaluate()` with `document.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 's', ctrlKey: true, bubbles: true }))` — this also sets `isTrusted: false`, but some applications only check `isTrusted` in the default handler; event listeners registered directly on `document` may still fire. The only reliable way to test `isTrusted`-gated shortcuts is via the CDP `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` command, which is not part of the public Playwright API and is engine-specific.

---

### Pattern 324 — Visual Regression Snapshot Charter with Mask/Threshold for Dynamic Content Stability [community]

Playwright's `toHaveScreenshot()` with the `mask` option allows exploratory visual regression charters to exclude dynamically changing regions (timestamps, live counters, animated elements, ad slots) from the pixel comparison while still asserting visual stability across the static portions of the page. Combined with the `maxDiffPixelRatio` threshold for anti-aliasing tolerance, this pattern provides a practical visual oracle that is resistant to dynamic content noise without requiring full-page masking.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product listing page visual regression — stable layout regions', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Mask dynamic regions: live pricing ticker, "X viewing now" counters, ad banner
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('product-listing-stable.png', {
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.02, // allow 2% pixel difference for anti-aliasing
    mask: [
      page.getByTestId('live-price-ticker'),
      page.locator('[data-dynamic="viewers-count"]'),
      page.getByRole('banner').filter({ has: page.locator('[data-slot="advertisement"]') }),
    ],
    animations: 'disabled', // freeze CSS animations for deterministic capture
    fullPage:   true,
  });

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'visual-oracle-pass',
    description: 'Product listing stable regions match snapshot; dynamic zones masked',
  });
});

test('checkout form visual regression — error state layout', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout');
  // Trigger validation errors by submitting an empty form
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('form', { name: 'Checkout' })).toHaveScreenshot(
    'checkout-error-state.png',
    {
      maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
      animations: 'disabled',
      // Only screenshot the form element, not the full page
    },
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toHaveScreenshot()` is a golden-file assertion: the first run creates the baseline image and always passes; subsequent runs compare against that baseline and fail if the diff exceeds the threshold. This means the initial baseline capture must be done in a controlled state that is genuinely correct — capturing a baseline of a broken UI will make future regressions invisible. Baseline images should be committed to version control and reviewed in PRs like code changes. The `mask` option uses the locator's bounding box to overlay a solid mask colour, so if a masked element changes its layout position or size between runs, the mask may not cover the moved element and the comparison may fail for the wrong reason. Pair visual regression charters with structural (ARIA snapshot) assertions so that a layout shift that moves the element also triggers an ARIA oracle failure, giving two independent signals for the same defect.

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 48)

**G20. `page.addLocatorHandler()` callbacks are not awaited inline with the action that triggered the overlay — the handler fires after Playwright's action retry loop detects that an element is blocked, and if the handler itself throws an unhandled error (e.g., the dismiss button is not found because the overlay variant has changed), the error surfaces as an opaque "locator handler failed" message with no indication of which overlay variant was encountered or which charter step triggered it.**
A team dismissing a cookie consent banner via `page.addLocatorHandler()` encountered test failures after a redesign changed the banner's dismiss button from `role="button"` with name "Accept" to an icon button with `aria-label="Close"`. The handler threw `TimeoutError: getByRole('button', { name: 'Accept' }) not visible`, but the failure message in the HTML report attributed it to the test's main interaction (a `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click()`), making the root cause non-obvious. WHY this matters: always include a `test.info().annotations.push()` call at the start of each `addLocatorHandler()` callback to record which overlay was matched and which dismiss strategy was attempted — this produces a breadcrumb trail in the test report that makes handler failures diagnosable without needing to replay the full session trace.

**G21. `expect.extend()` custom matchers that return `{ pass: true, message: () => '...' }` inside a `not` chain produce the negation failure message from the `message()` function, not an automatically inverted version — developers often write the `message()` function assuming it will only fire in the positive failure case, producing confusing negation failure messages like "Expected value to be valid EUR currency" when the test was actually asserting `expect(price).not.toBeFormattedCurrency('EUR')` and the assertion correctly failed.**
A team using `toBeFormattedCurrency()` in a negative assertion (`expect(rawPrice).not.toBeFormattedCurrency('EUR')`) received the failure message "Expected '€29.99' to match EUR format" when the actual intent was to assert that the raw price was NOT formatted as currency. The `message()` function was written with only the positive failure in mind. WHY this matters: always write the `message()` function to handle both polarities — use the `this.isNot` flag (available in the matcher's `this` context) to switch between "Expected X to be Y" (positive) and "Expected X NOT to be Y" (negative) message templates, making both failure directions diagnosable at a glance.

**G22. `page.waitForResponse()` resolves as soon as the HTTP response status line and headers arrive — calling `await response.json()` immediately after may throw "Response body not available" if the response body is still streaming, particularly for large JSON payloads or streaming NDJSON endpoints where the server sends chunks over multiple TCP segments.**
A team waiting for a bulk-export API response found that `const body = await response.json()` intermittently threw `Error: Response body not available for redirect responses` even though the status was 200 and the content-type was `application/json`. The response body was a 2.4 MB JSON array that arrived in multiple chunks; the `waitForResponse()` resolved after the first chunk, and `json()` was called before the body was fully buffered. WHY this matters: for large response bodies, use `await response.finished()` between the `waitForResponse()` and `response.json()` calls — `response.finished()` resolves only after the full response body has been received and buffered, making it safe to call `json()` or `body()` immediately after.

**G23. The `projects` array `grep` option in `playwright.config.ts` accepts a `RegExp` or `string`, but when using a string, Playwright converts it to a `RegExp` without anchors — a project with `grep: '@smoke'` will match any test whose full title (including all `describe` blocks) contains the substring `'@smoke'`, including test titles like `'non-@smokeable feature should fail gracefully'`. Teams using word-fragment tags like `@s` or `@api` are particularly vulnerable to unintended matches that inflate the project's test count and may include unrelated charters in a risk-tiered run.**
A team setting up a `@smoke` project found it was running 47 tests instead of the expected 12 because several test files used `describe('@smoke-related features')` as their outermost describe block title, which caused every test inside those blocks to match the `'@smoke'` grep regardless of individual test tags. WHY this matters: use anchored regex patterns in the `projects` grep config (`grep: /(?<![a-zA-Z])@smoke(?![a-zA-Z])/`) to enforce word-boundary matching, and adopt a tagging convention that ensures risk-tier tags are unique substrings not found in any describe block titles.

**G24. `toHaveScreenshot()` baselines stored in version control are silently invalidated when the `playwright.config.ts` `use.deviceScaleFactor` or `use.viewport` settings change — Playwright stores the baseline filename without encoding the viewport dimensions or pixel density, so a team that changes from `viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 }` to `viewport: { width: 1920, height: 1080 }` will find all existing baselines silently used for comparison against the new larger viewport, producing massive diff failures with no explanation of why the dimensions changed.**
A team that upgraded from a 1280-wide to a 1920-wide test viewport after a design review found that 100% of their `toHaveScreenshot()` tests failed with "screenshot does not match" errors. The failure images showed only the left portion of the new 1920-wide page compared against the old 1280-wide baseline. Because the filename had not changed, Playwright treated the old narrow baseline as the expected reference for the new wide capture. WHY this matters: whenever `viewport`, `deviceScaleFactor`, or `colorScheme` changes in the Playwright config, delete all existing snapshot baselines and regenerate them with `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` before committing — and document the regeneration in the same commit message as the config change so that future blame archaeology explains why all baselines were replaced simultaneously.

## Cycle 50 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 325 — `locator.filter()` Chained Predicate Charter for List-Item Precision Selection [official]

Playwright's `locator.filter()` method narrows an existing locator by applying secondary predicates — `hasText`, `has`, or `hasNot` — without changing the selector strategy, allowing exploratory charters to target exactly one item from a repeating list widget without resorting to `nth()` index fragility. Chaining multiple `.filter()` calls composes predicates with an implicit AND, making multi-condition selection both readable and robust against list reordering.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('filter chained predicate — select "In Stock" item with a specific label', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  // Narrow the full product card list to cards that are both "In Stock"
  // and carry a "New Arrival" badge — without relying on nth() indices.
  const newArrivalInStock = page
    .getByRole('listitem')                          // all product cards
    .filter({ hasText: /in stock/i })               // only in-stock cards
    .filter({ has: page.getByTestId('badge-new') }); // that also have a "New" badge

  // Assert there is at least one qualifying card and click the first
  await expect(newArrivalInStock.first()).toBeVisible();
  await newArrivalInStock.first().getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/added to cart/i);

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'filter-predicate-pass',
    description: 'Located "In Stock + New Arrival" card via chained filter() without index fragility',
  });
});

test('filter hasNot — skip discontinued products from interaction sweep', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  const activeCards = page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasNot: page.getByTestId('badge-discontinued') });

  for (const card of await activeCards.all()) {
    await expect(card.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' })).toBeEnabled();
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.filter()` with `has` performs an internal sub-query for each candidate element in the outer locator's match set, which can be slower than a single CSS/XPath expression when the outer set is very large (hundreds of items). For very long lists, consider adding a more-specific outer selector before filtering. Additionally, `hasText` matches against the element's `textContent`, not its `innerText`, so hidden text nodes (e.g., `aria-hidden` siblings for icon labels) may cause unexpected matches; use `hasText: /^exact phrase$/` with anchors to tighten the match.

### Pattern 326 — `page.emulateMedia()` Color Scheme and Forced-Colors Charter for Accessibility Rendering Exploration [official]

`page.emulateMedia()` allows exploratory charters to switch CSS media features — including `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion`, and `forced-colors` — without restarting the browser context, enabling a single session to sweep dark mode, reduced-motion, and high-contrast rendering states in rapid succession. This is the primary Playwright mechanism for validating that UI components respond correctly to OS-level accessibility preferences.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const MEDIA_STATES = [
  { colorScheme: 'light' as const,  forcedColors: 'none'   as const, label: 'light-default'   },
  { colorScheme: 'dark'  as const,  forcedColors: 'none'   as const, label: 'dark-mode'        },
  { colorScheme: 'light' as const,  forcedColors: 'active' as const, label: 'forced-colors'    },
] as const;

test('media emulation sweep — theme and forced-colors rendering', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  for (const state of MEDIA_STATES) {
    await test.step(`Emulate: ${state.label}`, async () => {
      await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: state.colorScheme, forcedColors: state.forcedColors });

      // Structural oracle: primary nav should always be visible regardless of theme
      await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' })).toBeVisible();

      // Visual oracle: snapshot each state for side-by-side comparison
      await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(`dashboard-${state.label}.png`, {
        animations: 'disabled',
        maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
        mask: [page.getByTestId('live-clock')],
      });
    });
  }
});

test('reduced-motion emulation — animated onboarding tour skips CSS transitions', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' });
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/onboarding');
  // Transition duration should be 0ms under reduced-motion; tooltip should appear synchronously
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start Tour' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('tooltip').first()).toBeVisible(); // no transition delay
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.emulateMedia()` only affects CSS media features resolved by the browser engine — it does not change the value returned by `window.matchMedia()` for all possible queries in all browser versions simultaneously. Some older implementations cache the initial `prefers-color-scheme` result and do not re-evaluate it dynamically within the same page load; for those cases, navigate to the page after calling `emulateMedia()` rather than calling it mid-session. The `forced-colors: 'active'` emulation renders the Windows High Contrast palette substitutions but does not perfectly replicate every OS-level forced-colors override; manual verification on a real high-contrast OS session is still required for WCAG 1.4.11 compliance sign-off.

---

### Pattern 327 — `browserContext.addCookies()` Pre-Auth State Injection Charter for Login-Wall Bypass [official]

Injecting authentication cookies directly into a `BrowserContext` via `addCookies()` before the first navigation avoids the round-trip through the login UI on every charter session, reducing session setup time from seconds to milliseconds and making the per-feature exploration phase deterministic. Combined with Playwright's `storageState` serialisation, this pattern supports a "one login, many charters" model where a single authenticated state artifact is reused across the entire suite.

```typescript
import { test, expect, chromium, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';

// Typically generated once in a global setup fixture and stored as a JSON file
const AUTH_STATE_PATH = 'playwright/.auth/user.json';

test.use({ storageState: AUTH_STATE_PATH });

test('pre-auth injection — dashboard accessible without login UI', async ({ page }) => {
  // storageState is injected before page creation — navigate directly to protected route
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  // Oracle: authenticated user sees their name, not the login form
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /welcome/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /log in/i })).not.toBeVisible();
});

// Fixture-level approach: inject programmatically and verify cookie presence
test('addCookies manual injection — verify session cookie is present', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context: BrowserContext = await browser.newContext();
  await context.addCookies([
    {
      name:    'session_token',
      value:   process.env.TEST_SESSION_TOKEN ?? 'test-token-abc123',
      domain:  'app.example.com',
      path:    '/',
      httpOnly: true,
      secure:   true,
      sameSite: 'Lax',
    },
  ]);
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-avatar')).toBeVisible();
  await context.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Cookie-based pre-auth bypasses the login UI, which means any defect in the login flow itself (CSRF token handling, redirect-after-login bugs, session fixation vulnerabilities) will never be caught by charters using this pattern. Maintain a separate, explicit login-flow charter that exercises the full credential submission path. Additionally, `storageState` files may contain refresh tokens or long-lived session cookies — treat these files as secrets, exclude them from version control with `.gitignore`, and rotate them regularly in CI pipelines to prevent token leakage.

---

### Pattern 328 — `test.beforeEach()` Network Condition Preset Charter for Slow-Connection Regression [official]

Wrapping `page.context().setNetworkConditions()` (or `browser.newContext()` with `offline: false` and throttling via CDP) inside a `test.beforeEach()` fixture ensures every charter in a suite consistently experiences a specified network profile, making latency-sensitive rendering bugs reproducible in isolation rather than requiring manual DevTools throttling during exploratory sessions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Simulate a "Slow 3G" network profile as defined by Chrome DevTools
const SLOW_3G = {
  offline:             false,
  downloadThroughput:  500 * 1024 / 8,   // 500 kbps download
  uploadThroughput:    500 * 1024 / 8,   // 500 kbps upload
  latency:             400,               // 400ms RTT
};

test.describe('Slow-3G network charter suite', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    // Access the CDP session via the Playwright-internal connection
    const client = await (page.context() as any)._newCDPSession(page);
    await client.send('Network.emulateNetworkConditions', {
      ...SLOW_3G,
      connectionType: 'cellular3g',
    });
  });

  test('product page loads critical content within 5 s on slow 3G', async ({ page }) => {
    const startMs = Date.now();
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products/widget-pro');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5_000 });
    const elapsed = Date.now() - startMs;
    expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(5_000);
    test.info().annotations.push({ type: 'perf', description: `LCP heading visible in ${elapsed}ms on Slow 3G` });
  });

  test('add-to-cart button remains enabled while cart API request is in flight', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products/widget-pro');
    const cartApiResponsePromise = page.waitForResponse('**/api/cart/add');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
    // Oracle: button should show a loading state (aria-busy) but remain visible and not disabled
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' })).toHaveAttribute('aria-busy', 'true');
    await cartApiResponsePromise;
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' })).not.toHaveAttribute('aria-busy');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** CDP-level network throttling is only available in Chromium-based browsers; Firefox and WebKit do not support `Network.emulateNetworkConditions` via CDP, so this pattern produces a Chromium-only test suite by design. For cross-browser slow-network charters, use a network proxy (e.g., `tsproxy`, `toxiproxy`) at the OS level and point the `playwright.config.ts` `proxy` option at it — this approach works across all engines but requires additional infrastructure setup. The CDP session approach also applies throttling globally to all requests in the page context, including analytics and third-party scripts; mask or intercept third-party requests with `page.route()` to prevent their slow responses from polluting the latency budget measurement.

---

### Pattern 329 — `locator.dragTo()` Drag-and-Drop Interaction Charter for Reorder Widget Exploration [official]

`locator.dragTo()` performs a full drag-and-drop sequence (pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup) on a source locator toward a target locator, enabling exploratory charters to verify that reorderable list, kanban board, and file-upload drop-zone widgets respond correctly to drag interactions without requiring raw CDP mouse coordinate arithmetic. The `sourcePosition` and `targetPosition` options allow sub-element drop targeting for widgets with multiple drop zones within a single element.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('kanban board — drag card from "To Do" to "In Progress" column', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/board');
  await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  const todoCard = page.getByTestId('kanban-column-todo').getByRole('listitem').first();
  const inProgressColumn = page.getByTestId('kanban-column-inprogress');

  // Capture card title before drag for oracle assertion after drop
  const cardTitle = await todoCard.getByRole('heading').textContent();

  await todoCard.dragTo(inProgressColumn);

  // Oracle: card now appears in "In Progress" column and is absent from "To Do"
  await expect(inProgressColumn.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: cardTitle! })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('kanban-column-todo').getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: cardTitle! })).not.toBeVisible();
});

test('drag-to reorder — task list item moves up one position', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/tasks');
  const taskItems = page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Task list' }).getByRole('listitem');

  const secondItem = taskItems.nth(1);
  const firstItem  = taskItems.nth(0);
  const secondTitle = await secondItem.textContent();

  // Drag second item above first item — target top edge of first item
  await secondItem.dragTo(firstItem, { targetPosition: { x: 10, y: 5 } });

  // Oracle: second item is now at position 0
  await expect(taskItems.first()).toContainText(secondTitle!.trim());
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.dragTo()` synthesises pointer events, not the legacy `mousedown`/`mousemove`/`mouseup` sequence. Libraries that implement drag-and-drop via `MouseEvent` listeners (e.g., older versions of `react-beautiful-dnd` prior to its pointer-event migration) will not respond to `dragTo()` correctly. For those libraries, use `page.mouse.move()` + `page.mouse.down()` + `page.mouse.move()` + `page.mouse.up()` to simulate the legacy mouse event sequence. Verify which event model the widget uses by inspecting its source code or reading the library's changelog before selecting the interaction strategy for the charter.

---

### Pattern 330 — `expect(locator).toBeHidden()` Disappearance Oracle Charter for Teardown Transition Verification [official]

Asserting that an element has disappeared from the DOM (or become hidden) after a user interaction is as important as asserting its appearance, yet teams often skip it, leaving "ghost" UI elements (loading spinners that never dismiss, error banners that persist, modals that remain open) undetected. `expect(locator).toBeHidden()` and `locator.waitFor({ state: 'hidden' })` provide explicit disappearance oracles that fail fast when teardown transitions stall.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('login loading spinner dismisses after authentication completes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/login');

  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('user@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('correct-password');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();

  // Oracle 1: spinner appears immediately after submit
  const spinner = page.getByRole('progressbar', { name: 'Signing in' });
  await expect(spinner).toBeVisible({ timeout: 1_000 });

  // Oracle 2: spinner DISAPPEARS after auth completes (max 5 s)
  await expect(spinner).toBeHidden({ timeout: 5_000 });

  // Oracle 3: success state is rendered
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /dashboard/i })).toBeVisible();

  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'disappearance-oracle-pass',
    description: 'Login spinner appeared then dismissed within 5 s; dashboard heading visible',
  });
});

test('delete confirmation modal closes after confirm action', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/items');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete item' }).first().click();

  const modal = page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Confirm deletion' });
  await expect(modal).toBeVisible();

  await modal.getByRole('button', { name: 'Yes, delete' }).click();

  // Oracle: modal must close; failure here indicates the close handler is broken
  await expect(modal).toBeHidden({ timeout: 3_000 });
  await expect(page.getByText(/item deleted/i)).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toBeHidden()` returns `true` for both `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, and elements removed from the DOM — it does not distinguish between these three states. If the bug under investigation is specifically about whether an element is removed from the DOM versus merely hidden via CSS (relevant for screen reader exposure and memory leak analysis), use `expect(await page.locator('...').count()).toBe(0)` to assert DOM removal specifically, and `toHaveCSS('display', 'none')` to assert CSS hiding specifically. Using the generic `toBeHidden()` is appropriate for most exploratory charters; prefer the specific assertions only when the hidden-vs-removed distinction is itself the bug hypothesis.

---

### Pattern 331 — `page.route()` Latency Injection Charter for Skeleton-Screen and Loading-State Validation [community]

By combining `page.route()` with a deliberate `setTimeout` delay inside the route handler, exploratory charters can hold a specific API response artificially long enough to observe the application's skeleton screen, loading indicator, and progressive disclosure behaviour — without needing a dedicated staging environment with degraded APIs. This pattern makes loading-state bugs reproducible on demand.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

function delay(ms: number): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

test('product listing skeleton screen renders for 2 s while API is slow', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept the products API and hold it for 2 seconds
  await page.route('**/api/products**', async route => {
    await delay(2_000);
    await route.continue();
  });

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');

  // Oracle 1: skeleton placeholder visible within 200 ms of navigation
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card-skeleton').first()).toBeVisible({ timeout: 200 });

  // Oracle 2: skeleton disappears after API resolves (within 3.5 s total from nav start)
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card-skeleton').first()).toBeHidden({ timeout: 3_500 });

  // Oracle 3: real product cards appear after skeleton dismisses
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card').first()).toBeVisible();
});

test('table pagination controls are disabled while data is loading', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/reports**', async route => {
    await delay(1_500);
    await route.continue();
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/reports');

  const nextPageBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next page' });
  // Oracle: pagination is disabled during load to prevent double-fetch
  await expect(nextPageBtn).toBeDisabled({ timeout: 500 });
  await expect(nextPageBtn).toBeEnabled({ timeout: 3_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Adding `setTimeout` inside `page.route()` handlers increases test duration by the delay amount. In a suite with many charters using this pattern, cumulative delay can significantly extend total run time. Set an upper bound on delays (e.g., 2 s maximum) and use `test.slow()` or adjust `timeout` per-test rather than raising the global timeout. Additionally, the delay applies only to requests matching the route pattern — if the application makes multiple API calls in parallel and only one is delayed, the observed loading state may differ from a production slow-API scenario where all calls are equally throttled. For holistic slow-network simulation, prefer the CDP network throttling approach (Pattern 328).

---

### Pattern 332 — `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with Regex Charter for Post-Navigation Destination Verification [official]

Asserting the URL after a navigation action is a fast, low-cost oracle for verifying that routing logic, redirects, and deep-link parameters behave correctly. Using a `RegExp` with `toHaveURL()` allows charters to assert the structural shape of the destination URL (path prefix, query parameter presence) without hard-coding the full URL including variable segments like UUIDs, timestamps, or environment-specific hostnames.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('successful checkout redirects to order confirmation URL with order ID', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();

  // Oracle: redirects to /orders/<uuid>/confirmation — UUID is dynamic but path shape is not
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(
    /\/orders\/[0-9a-f-]{36}\/confirmation/,
    { timeout: 10_000 },
  );
});

test('unauthenticated access to protected page redirects to login with returnUrl', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/settings/billing');
  // Oracle: redirected to /login with the original path preserved in returnUrl
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login\?returnUrl=%2Fsettings%2Fbilling/, { timeout: 3_000 });
});

test('search page populates q param from search input submission', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');
  await page.getByRole('searchbox', { name: 'Search' }).fill('playwright testing');
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  // Oracle: URL includes the search query as the q parameter
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/[?&]q=playwright\+testing/, { timeout: 3_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toHaveURL()` with a regex matches against the full URL string including protocol, hostname, port, path, and query string. A regex like `/orders/` will match any URL containing the substring "orders", including `https://app.example.com/admin/orders/archive`. Always anchor patterns appropriately (`/\/orders\/[uuid-pattern]\/confirmation/`) to avoid false positives from coincidental substring matches. When the application uses hash-based routing (e.g., `/#/orders/123`), the `#` fragment is included in the URL string and must be part of the regex; do not assume the URL ends at the `?` character.
