### Pattern 333 — `test.describe.parallel()` Shard-Aware Charter Suite for CI Parallelism Exploration [official]

Playwright's `test.describe.parallel()` mode runs tests within the describe block concurrently in the same worker process, while `--shard` CLI option distributes tests across CI jobs. Designing exploratory charters with sharding in mind — ensuring tests are state-independent and side-effect-free — prevents false failures caused by shared server state when the same suite runs across multiple parallel executors.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Explicitly declare parallel execution — each test gets its own browser context
test.describe.parallel('product search exploratory charter suite', () => {

  test('search by category returns filtered results', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products?category=electronics');
    const cards = page.getByTestId('product-card');
    await expect(cards.first()).toBeVisible();
    // Oracle: every visible card has the electronics category label
    for (const card of await cards.all()) {
      await expect(card.getByTestId('category-label')).toContainText(/electronics/i);
    }
  });

  test('empty search query shows all products', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products?q=');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card').first()).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByText(/no products found/i)).not.toBeVisible();
  });

  test('special characters in search do not break the page', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto("https://shop.example.com/products?q=<script>alert('xss')</script>");
    // Oracle: page renders normally, no JS alert fired, heading visible
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toBeVisible();
    page.on('dialog', async dialog => {
      await dialog.dismiss();
      throw new Error('XSS dialog fired — potential injection vulnerability');
    });
  });

  test('pagination state persists on browser back navigation', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products?page=3');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('pagination-current')).toHaveText('3');
    await page.getByTestId('product-card').first().click();
    await page.goBack();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/page=3/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.describe.parallel()` requires that each test is fully isolated — no shared in-process state, no reliance on prior tests having seeded the database, and no assumption about test execution order. If a suite mixes `parallel` and sequential tests in the same file, Playwright will respect the innermost mode annotation, which can produce confusing interleaving. Avoid using `parallel` mode for charters that mutate server-side state (e.g., creating orders, deleting records) unless each test uses a unique user account or tenant ID to prevent state collisions between concurrent executions.

### Pattern 334 — `page.evaluate()` DOM Introspection Charter for Non-Visible State Verification [official]

`page.evaluate()` executes arbitrary JavaScript in the page's context and returns the result to the test process, enabling charters to assert against computed state that is not surfaced in the ARIA tree or visible text — such as CSS custom property values, `data-*` attribute state machines, scroll position, localStorage tokens, or Redux/Zustand store contents via exposed dev globals.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('theme toggle updates CSS custom property --color-bg correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');
  const initialBg = await page.evaluate(() =>
    getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--color-bg').trim()
  );
  expect(initialBg).toBe('#ffffff'); // light mode default

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Toggle dark mode' }).click();

  const darkBg = await page.evaluate(() =>
    getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--color-bg').trim()
  );
  expect(darkBg).toBe('#121212');
});

test('cart item count syncs to localStorage after add-to-cart', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).first().click();

  const cartData = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem('cart');
    return raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : null;
  });
  expect(cartData).not.toBeNull();
  expect(cartData.items).toHaveLength(1);
});

test('scroll position is restored after navigation back', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/long-list');
  await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, 800));
  await page.getByRole('link').first().click();
  await page.goBack();

  const scrollY = await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollY);
  expect(scrollY).toBeGreaterThan(500); // scroll position restored
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.evaluate()` breaks the abstraction boundary between the test process and the browser — it is a direct inspection of implementation details (CSS variables, localStorage keys, internal state shapes) that are more likely to change than the user-visible interface. Overuse of `page.evaluate()` couples the charter suite tightly to implementation details, increasing maintenance cost when the application refactors its state management. Reserve `page.evaluate()` for cases where no public-facing observable (visible text, ARIA role, URL) exposes the state under investigation, and document why a DOM introspection was necessary in a `test.info().annotations.push()` call so future maintainers understand the intent.

---

### Pattern 335 — `test.afterEach()` Screenshot-on-Failure Charter for Automatic Defect Evidence Capture [community]

Attaching a full-page screenshot in `test.afterEach()` when `testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus` provides automatic visual evidence for every failing charter without requiring the tester to reproduce the failure manually. Combined with `testInfo.attachments.push()`, the screenshot appears inline in the Playwright HTML report, making it immediately available during debrief.

```typescript
import { test, expect, TestInfo } from '@playwright/test';

test.afterEach(async ({ page }, testInfo: TestInfo) => {
  if (testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus) {
    const screenshotBuffer = await page.screenshot({ fullPage: true });
    await testInfo.attach('failure-screenshot', {
      body:      screenshotBuffer,
      contentType: 'image/png',
    });
    // Also capture the current URL and page title for context
    testInfo.annotations.push({
      type:        'failure-url',
      description: page.url(),
    });
    testInfo.annotations.push({
      type:        'failure-title',
      description: await page.title(),
    });
  }
});

test('feature works correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/feature');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Activate Feature' }).click();
  // If this assertion fails, afterEach captures the screenshot automatically
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/feature activated/i);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.screenshot()` in `afterEach` adds latency to every failing test — a `fullPage: true` screenshot of a long page can take 200–500ms, which accumulates in suites with many failures during a degraded CI run. For large suites, consider gating the screenshot behind a check for `testInfo.retry === testInfo.project.retries` (i.e., only capture on the final retry, not intermediate retries) to avoid redundant screenshots for flaky-retry runs. Also note that `afterEach` runs even if the browser context was destroyed by a crash or timeout; wrap `page.screenshot()` in a `try/catch` to prevent `afterEach` errors from masking the original test failure.

### Pattern 336 — `locator.selectOption()` and `locator.check()` Multi-State Form Charter for Validation Coverage [official]

Combining `selectOption()` for `<select>` dropdowns, `check()` / `uncheck()` for checkboxes and radio groups, and `fill()` for text inputs in a parameterised form state matrix allows exploratory charters to sweep validation rules across multiple field combination states without duplicating code. Each row in the matrix drives a fresh form submission and asserts the expected validation outcome.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface FormScenario {
  label:               string;
  country:             string;
  subscribeNewsletter: boolean;
  preferredContact:    string;
  expectError:         RegExp | null;
}

const FORM_SCENARIOS: FormScenario[] = [
  { label: 'valid',                 country: 'US', subscribeNewsletter: true,  preferredContact: 'email', expectError: null },
  { label: 'no country selected',   country: '',   subscribeNewsletter: false, preferredContact: 'phone', expectError: /country is required/i },
  { label: 'newsletter + no email', country: 'DE', subscribeNewsletter: true,  preferredContact: 'sms',   expectError: /email required for newsletter/i },
];

for (const scenario of FORM_SCENARIOS) {
  test(`profile form — ${scenario.label}`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/profile/edit');

    if (scenario.country) {
      await page.getByLabel('Country').selectOption(scenario.country);
    }

    if (scenario.subscribeNewsletter) {
      await page.getByLabel('Subscribe to newsletter').check();
    } else {
      await page.getByLabel('Subscribe to newsletter').uncheck();
    }

    await page.getByRole('radiogroup', { name: 'Preferred contact' })
      .getByLabel(scenario.preferredContact, { exact: false }).check();

    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save Profile' }).click();

    if (scenario.expectError) {
      await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(scenario.expectError);
    } else {
      await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/profile saved/i);
    }
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Generating tests from a data array means all scenario tests share the same code path — a bug in the test harness itself (e.g., a wrong locator for the country select) fails all scenarios simultaneously rather than individual ones, making the failure look like a suite-wide issue rather than a single test defect. Validate the harness with at least one known-good scenario that passes in isolation before adding negative test cases. Also, `selectOption()` throws if the option value/label does not exist in the `<select>` element; ensure the scenario values exactly match the rendered option text or value attributes, which may differ between environments if the option list is populated from a backend API.

---

### Pattern 337 — `page.on('console')` and `page.on('pageerror')` Charter for Client-Side Error Monitoring [official]

Attaching `console` and `pageerror` event listeners before navigation captures every browser console warning, error, and uncaught exception that occurs during a charter session, providing a passive defect detection layer that does not require specific assertions about known error messages. This pattern turns every charter into an implicit "no console errors" health check.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('console error monitoring charter', () => {
  test('product page loads without console errors or uncaught exceptions', async ({ page }) => {
    const consoleErrors: string[] = [];
    const pageErrors:    Error[]  = [];

    page.on('console', msg => {
      if (msg.type() === 'error') {
        consoleErrors.push(`[console.error] ${msg.text()}`);
      }
    });

    page.on('pageerror', err => {
      pageErrors.push(err);
    });

    await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products/widget-pro');
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

    // Interact with the page to trigger lazy-loaded components
    await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Reviews' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();

    // Oracle: no console errors or uncaught exceptions during the full session
    expect(consoleErrors, `Console errors:\n${consoleErrors.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
    expect(pageErrors, `Page errors:\n${pageErrors.map(e => e.message).join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
  });

  test('report page console-error allowlist — known third-party script error is excluded', async ({ page }) => {
    const unexpectedErrors: string[] = [];
    const KNOWN_THIRD_PARTY_PATTERN = /Failed to load resource.*analytics\.thirdparty\.com/;

    page.on('console', msg => {
      if (msg.type() === 'error' && !KNOWN_THIRD_PARTY_PATTERN.test(msg.text())) {
        unexpectedErrors.push(msg.text());
      }
    });

    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/reports');
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

    expect(unexpectedErrors).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.on('console')` fires for all console output including intentional developer-mode logging that is suppressed in production builds. Running this charter against a development build will surface numerous `console.log` and `console.warn` calls that are irrelevant to the charter's defect hypothesis; always run console-monitoring charters against a production or production-equivalent build. The `pageerror` event fires for uncaught exceptions but not for caught exceptions that are swallowed with empty `catch {}` blocks — it does not replace error monitoring in the application itself. Combine this charter pattern with application-level error boundary reporting for complete error coverage.

---

### Pattern 338 — `request.postDataJSON()` API Payload Capture Charter for Mutation Verification [official]

Reading the parsed JSON payload of a POST/PUT request via `request.postDataJSON()` inside a `page.on('request')` handler provides an outbound payload oracle — verifying that the browser sends the correct data structure to the API before the server processes it. This catches serialisation bugs (missing fields, incorrect types, wrong nesting) independently of what the server returns.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('add-to-cart API payload includes product ID, quantity, and variant', async ({ page }) => {
  let capturedPayload: Record<string, unknown> | null = null;

  page.on('request', req => {
    if (req.url().includes('/api/cart/add') && req.method() === 'POST') {
      capturedPayload = req.postDataJSON() as Record<string, unknown>;
    }
  });

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/products/widget-pro');
  await page.getByLabel('Colour').selectOption('Red');
  await page.getByLabel('Quantity').fill('2');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();

  await page.waitForResponse('**/api/cart/add');

  // Outbound payload oracle: assert shape before server response is observed
  expect(capturedPayload).not.toBeNull();
  expect(capturedPayload).toMatchObject({
    productId: expect.any(String),
    quantity:  2,
    variant:   expect.objectContaining({ colour: 'Red' }),
  });
});

test('profile update payload does NOT include password field in plain text', async ({ page }) => {
  const sentPayloads: unknown[] = [];
  page.on('request', req => {
    if (req.url().includes('/api/profile') && req.method() === 'PUT') {
      sentPayloads.push(req.postDataJSON());
    }
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/profile/edit');
  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('Alice');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save Profile' }).click();
  await page.waitForResponse('**/api/profile');

  // Security oracle: password must not be included in the profile update payload
  for (const payload of sentPayloads) {
    expect(payload).not.toHaveProperty('password');
    expect(payload).not.toHaveProperty('passwordHash');
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `request.postDataJSON()` returns `null` if the request body is not `application/json` content-type (e.g., `multipart/form-data` for file uploads, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` for legacy forms, or a raw binary body). For non-JSON payloads use `request.postData()` to get the raw string and parse it manually. Additionally, `page.on('request')` fires synchronously before awaiting; if the request is sent before the listener is attached (e.g., due to a very fast redirect on page load), the event may be missed. Attach listeners before calling `page.goto()` to ensure all requests from initial navigation are captured.

---

### Pattern 339 — `expect.soft()` Non-Blocking Assertion Charter for Full-Sweep Defect Inventory [official]

`expect.soft()` marks an assertion as non-fatal — the test continues executing even if the assertion fails, accumulating all soft failures and reporting them together at the end of the test. This makes it ideal for exploratory sweeps where the goal is to inventory every defect on a page in a single session rather than stopping at the first failure.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('homepage full-sweep defect inventory — soft assertions', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Each soft assertion continues even if it fails, accumulating all defects
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('contentinfo')).toBeVisible();

  // Check every nav link has a non-empty href
  const navLinks = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' }).getByRole('link');
  for (const link of await navLinks.all()) {
    const href = await link.getAttribute('href');
    await expect.soft(link, `Nav link "${await link.textContent()}" has empty href`).not.toHaveAttribute('href', '');
    expect.soft(href, `Nav link href should not be null`).not.toBeNull();
  }

  // Check all images have alt text
  const images = page.getByRole('img');
  for (const img of await images.all()) {
    await expect.soft(img, `Image missing alt attribute`).toHaveAttribute('alt', /.*/);
  }

  // Check page title is non-empty
  const title = await page.title();
  expect.soft(title, 'Page title is empty').not.toBe('');

  // Hard assertion at end: if the page didn't load at all, fail definitively
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeAttached();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.soft()` failures are collected and reported at the end of the test, but they do not cause `test.afterEach()` fixtures to receive `testInfo.status === 'failed'` until the test function itself returns — meaning any cleanup or screenshot-on-failure logic in `afterEach` fires after all soft assertions have run. Soft assertions should not be used for assertions that establish preconditions for subsequent test steps: if a soft assertion for "nav is visible" fails but the test continues and tries to click a nav item, the subsequent hard failure will obscure the original soft failure. Use soft assertions only for independent, parallel-observable properties of the same page state.

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 50)

**G25. `locator.filter({ hasText: '...' })` uses `String.prototype.includes()` semantics on the element's `textContent`, not its `innerText` — elements with `::before`/`::after` pseudo-element content injected via CSS are NOT included in `textContent` and will cause `filter()` to silently skip elements whose visible text exists only in CSS-generated content.**
A team filtering product cards by a "Sale" badge found that `filter({ hasText: 'Sale' })` returned zero matches even though every card had a visible "Sale" label. The badge text was injected via `content: "Sale"` on a `::before` pseudo-element, which does not appear in `textContent`. WHY this matters: CSS pseudo-element content is invisible to all Playwright text matchers including `hasText`, `getByText()`, and `toContainText()` — if the application renders meaningful text via CSS `content:`, work with the development team to add a real DOM text node or `aria-label` attribute, or use `toHaveCSS` to assert the computed `content` property value directly.

**G26. `page.route()` handler callbacks registered with `await page.route(pattern, handler)` are not automatically unregistered after the test ends — if a test that adds a route handler times out or crashes before `await page.unroute()` is called, the orphaned handler persists in the browser context and intercepts requests in subsequent tests that share the same context, causing seemingly unrelated later tests to receive mocked or delayed responses.**
A team noticed that tests following a slow-API latency injection charter intermittently received 2-second delays on API calls even though those tests had no `page.route()` calls. The culprit was a timed-out route handler test that never reached its cleanup call. WHY this matters: always register `page.route()` cleanup via `test.afterEach()` or use `page.unrouteAll()` in the `afterEach` hook rather than inlining cleanup at the end of the test body — `afterEach` runs even when the test times out, ensuring route handlers are always cleared.

**G27. `page.evaluate()` serialises its return value using the structured clone algorithm — return values that contain `undefined` properties, `Function` values, DOM nodes, `Symbol` keys, or circular references will be silently dropped or cause `page.evaluate()` to throw "Evaluation failed: Object could not be cloned", with no indication of which property caused the cloning failure.**
A team calling `page.evaluate(() => window.__APP_STATE__)` found that the returned object was missing several properties that were clearly visible in the browser console. The missing properties were functions (action creators attached to the state object by a Redux devtools extension) and `Symbol`-keyed metadata properties — both are non-cloneable and are silently dropped by the structured clone algorithm. WHY this matters: before asserting on `page.evaluate()` return values, serialise the target data to a plain JSON-compatible object inside the browser context using `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))` and return that instead — this surfaces serialisation errors explicitly at the `JSON.stringify` call inside `evaluate()` rather than silently stripping data.

**G28. `toHaveScreenshot()` pixel comparison fails reproducibly on Linux CI runners that use a different font rendering stack (e.g., FreeType without hinting) than the macOS or Windows developer machines where baselines were originally captured — font anti-aliasing differences produce a pixel-level diff on every text-bearing element even when `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.02` is set, causing all visual regression charters to fail on CI despite the UI being visually correct.**
A team that captured screenshot baselines on macOS found that 80% of their visual regression tests failed on the Ubuntu CI runner. Diffing the images showed that every text element had slightly different sub-pixel rendering. WHY this matters: always capture screenshot baselines on the same OS and rendering environment where they will be compared — use a Docker container matching the CI OS for local baseline capture, configure Playwright CI runs to generate baselines on first push using `--update-snapshots` in a dedicated baseline-generation job, and store platform-specific baselines in separate directories using the `snapshotPathTemplate` config option with the `{platform}` token.

**G29. `page.addInitScript()` scripts run before the page's own JavaScript but AFTER the browser's built-in APIs are initialised — if the script under test replaces a global (e.g., `window.fetch = customFetch`) before `DOMContentLoaded`, an `addInitScript()` that tries to spy on `window.fetch` will receive the already-replaced version, not the original browser `fetch`, making the spy's call count reflect only calls routed through the custom implementation and missing any calls made directly to the original `fetch` before the replacement.**
A team adding an `addInitScript()` fetch spy to count API calls found that their spy reported 0 calls on a page that the Network tab confirmed made 12 fetch requests. The application replaced `window.fetch` synchronously in its first script tag; the spy was attached to the already-replaced function, which was never actually called. WHY this matters: for reliable request interception and counting, always prefer `page.on('request')` or `page.route()` over `addInitScript()` fetch spies — `page.on('request')` intercepts at the network layer beneath JavaScript, making it immune to application-level `fetch` replacements and ensuring every outbound request is captured regardless of which JavaScript code path initiates it.

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 340 — `browserContext.route()` Context-Wide API Mock Charter for Cross-Page Contract Verification

`browserContext.route()` intercepts requests across every page opened in the same browser context, making it ideal for exploratory charters that must verify consistent API contract behaviour across multiple views (e.g., a dashboard tab and a detail panel that both call the same endpoint). Unlike `page.route()`, which only intercepts for a single page, context-level routing ensures that a mock or fault injection applies globally without needing to register it on each page individually.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('context-wide API contract charter — 404 propagation across pages', async ({ context }) => {
  // Register mock once at context level — applies to ALL pages in this context
  await context.route('**/api/v2/products**', async route => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 404,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Not Found', code: 'PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND' }),
    });
  });

  const dashboardPage = await context.newPage();
  await dashboardPage.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  const detailPage = await context.newPage();
  await detailPage.goto('https://app.example.com/products/123');

  // Both pages should degrade gracefully on 404
  await expect(dashboardPage.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/no products/i);
  await expect(detailPage.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/product not found/i);

  // Verify neither page shows a loading spinner indefinitely
  await expect(dashboardPage.getByTestId('loading-spinner')).toBeHidden();
  await expect(detailPage.getByTestId('loading-spinner')).toBeHidden();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Context-level routes cannot be selectively scoped to a single page after registration — if the charter later needs a different mock for one page, you must call `context.unroute()` globally and re-register page-specific handlers. For multi-page charters that require divergent mock behaviour per page, use `page.route()` on each page individually and accept the duplication; context-level routes are optimal when uniform fault injection across all pages is the explicit charter goal.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 341 — `route.fetch()` Response Augmentation Charter for Header-Injection and Versioning Exploration

`route.fetch()` performs the real network request inside a route handler and returns the actual server response, which can then be forwarded after selectively modifying headers, status, or body. This pattern is superior to `route.fulfill()` for exploratory charters that need to test how the application handles specific response headers (e.g., `Deprecation`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `Cache-Control`) without fully replacing server behaviour — the real data is preserved while only the metadata is mutated.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('response header augmentation charter — deprecation warning banner', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/v1/**', async route => {
    // Fetch the real response from the server
    const response = await route.fetch();
    const headers = await response.allHeaders();

    // Inject deprecation headers that the real v1 server does not yet send
    await route.fulfill({
      response,
      headers: {
        ...headers,
        'Deprecation': 'true',
        'Sunset': 'Sat, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT',
        'Link': '<https://api.example.com/v2/>; rel="successor-version"',
      },
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/settings');
  // Charter: does the UI surface a deprecation warning when headers indicate v1 is sunset?
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /api deprecation/i })).toBeVisible();
  const link = page.getByRole('link', { name: /migrate to v2/i });
  await expect(link).toBeVisible();
  await expect(link).toHaveAttribute('href', /\/v2\//);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `route.fetch()` makes a real outbound HTTP call from the browser, so it requires network access and adds latency to every intercepted request. If the charter is running in an offline CI environment or against a staging server with strict CORS policies, `route.fetch()` may fail entirely. In those scenarios, capture a real response fixture first using `page.on('response')` in a separate recording session and use `route.fulfill({ body: fixture })` instead. `route.fetch()` is most valuable in developer-mode charters where live server data must be preserved and only specific metadata needs exploration.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 342 — `page.waitForResponse()` Promise-Race Charter for Concurrent Request Ordering Verification

`page.waitForResponse()` returns a promise that resolves to the first response matching a URL pattern or predicate. By creating multiple `waitForResponse` promises before triggering a user action, exploratory charters can assert on the order, timing, and outcome of concurrent API requests that a single UI gesture initiates — a critical pattern for exploring race conditions and request waterfalling in dashboards, infinite scroll, or multi-panel layouts.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('concurrent request ordering charter — dashboard parallel load', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  // Register response waiters BEFORE the action that triggers them
  const metricsPromise = page.waitForResponse(
    resp => resp.url().includes('/api/metrics') && resp.status() === 200
  );
  const alertsPromise = page.waitForResponse(
    resp => resp.url().includes('/api/alerts') && resp.status() === 200
  );
  const activityPromise = page.waitForResponse(
    resp => resp.url().includes('/api/activity') && resp.status() === 200
  );

  // Trigger the refresh action
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh' }).click();

  // Await all three in parallel — Promise.all fails fast if any rejects
  const [metricsResp, alertsResp, activityResp] = await Promise.all([
    metricsPromise,
    alertsPromise,
    activityPromise,
  ]);

  // Charter: all three must succeed (no sequential waterfalling on refresh)
  expect(metricsResp.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(alertsResp.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(activityResp.status()).toBe(200);

  // Confirm UI rendered data from all three requests
  await expect(page.getByTestId('metrics-widget')).not.toBeEmpty();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('alerts-widget')).not.toBeEmpty();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `Promise.all([waitForResponse...])` will hang indefinitely if any of the expected responses never arrives (e.g., the server drops the request silently). Always use `Promise.race([waitForResponse, page.waitForTimeout(5000).then(() => { throw new Error('timeout') })])` or set a test-level `timeout` to prevent tests from blocking the CI queue. Additionally, `waitForResponse` matches the first response — if the same URL is called multiple times (e.g., polling), the promise resolves on the first hit and subsequent calls are not asserted on unless individual promises are created for each expected invocation.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 343 — `AxeBuilder.include()` Scoped Accessibility Charter for Interaction-Revealed Content

`AxeBuilder.include('#selector')` scopes an axe accessibility scan to a specific subtree of the DOM, enabling charters to run targeted WCAG compliance checks on content that is only revealed after user interaction (modal dialogs, dropdown menus, expanded accordion panels, toast notifications). Running a full-page scan misses the accessibility state of these components because they are hidden during page load; a scoped scan after the reveal action catches violations that a baseline scan would never surface.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('scoped accessibility charter — modal dialog WCAG 2.1 AA scan', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/team');

  // Trigger the modal — it only exists in the DOM after click
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Invite Member' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Invite Team Member' })).toBeVisible();

  // Scope the axe scan to the dialog subtree only
  const accessibilityScanResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .include('[role="dialog"]')
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();

  // Attach the full report as an artifact for triage
  expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations, JSON.stringify(
    accessibilityScanResults.violations.map(v => ({
      id: v.id,
      impact: v.impact,
      nodes: v.nodes.map(n => n.target),
    })),
    null,
    2
  )).toEqual([]);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Scoping with `.include()` limits the scan to the specified subtree, which means accessibility violations in the page backdrop (e.g., focus not being trapped within the modal, background content not being `aria-hidden`) will not be detected by the scoped scan. A complete modal accessibility charter requires a second full-page scan to verify `aria-hidden="true"` has been applied to the main content behind the modal and that the focus trap is in effect. Use `.include()` for component-level WCAG verification and a separate untargeted `AxeBuilder` scan for focus trap and background inertness checks.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 344 — `devices['iPhone 15']` Mobile Emulation Charter for Touch-Target and Viewport-Overflow Exploration

`playwright.devices['iPhone 15']` provides a pre-configured device descriptor (viewport, user agent, pixel ratio, touch capability, `isMobile: true`) that activates mobile rendering paths in the browser. Exploratory charters using device emulation can surface touch-target sizing violations (WCAG 2.5.5 requires 44×44 CSS pixels), viewport overflow caused by fixed-width elements, and mobile-specific code paths that only execute when `isMobile` is true — none of which appear in desktop-viewport tests.

```typescript
import { test, expect, devices } from '@playwright/test';

const iPhone15 = devices['iPhone 15'];

test.use({ ...iPhone15 });

test('mobile touch-target charter — checkout flow minimum tap areas', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/checkout');

  // Collect all interactive elements and verify minimum touch target size
  const interactiveEls = page.getByRole('button').or(page.getByRole('link'));
  const allEls = await interactiveEls.all();

  for (const el of allEls) {
    const box = await el.boundingBox();
    if (!box) continue; // hidden elements — skip

    const label = await el.textContent() ?? await el.getAttribute('aria-label') ?? 'unknown';
    expect.soft(
      box.height,
      `Touch target "${label.trim()}" height ${box.height}px is below WCAG 44px minimum`
    ).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(44);
    expect.soft(
      box.width,
      `Touch target "${label.trim()}" width ${box.width}px is below WCAG 44px minimum`
    ).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(44);
  }

  // Charter: verify no horizontal overflow (common mobile regression)
  const bodyWidth = await page.evaluate(() => document.body.scrollWidth);
  const viewportWidth = page.viewportSize()!.width;
  expect(bodyWidth, `Horizontal overflow detected: body ${bodyWidth}px > viewport ${viewportWidth}px`).toBeLessThanOrEqual(viewportWidth);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Playwright's device emulation uses a Chromium browser rendering in a desktop OS environment — it does not simulate iOS Safari's WebKit rendering engine, CSS quirks (`-webkit-` prefixed properties, safe area insets, bounce scrolling), or iOS-specific JavaScript APIs. Touch-target failures found in Playwright device emulation will closely match Android Chrome behaviour but may diverge from Safari on iOS, particularly for fixed positioning, viewport units (`100vh`), and `position: sticky` within scrollable containers. Use Playwright emulation for rapid coverage and supplement with real-device Sauce Labs / BrowserStack sessions for iOS-specific regressions.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 345 — `test.extend()` Authenticated User Fixture Charter for Role-Based Access Boundary Exploration

`test.extend()` creates a custom fixture that provides a pre-authenticated page for a named user role (admin, editor, viewer, guest), enabling exploratory charters to rapidly context-switch between roles and verify that access boundaries are enforced consistently across every protected route. The fixture encapsulates storage state injection and authentication preconditions so charter test bodies focus purely on the boundary under exploration rather than login ceremony.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

type AuthFixtures = {
  adminPage: import('@playwright/test').Page;
  editorPage: import('@playwright/test').Page;
  viewerPage: import('@playwright/test').Page;
};

const test = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  adminPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({
      storageState: path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/auth/admin.json'),
    });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await use(page);
    await ctx.close();
  },
  editorPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({
      storageState: path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/auth/editor.json'),
    });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await use(page);
    await ctx.close();
  },
  viewerPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({
      storageState: path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/auth/viewer.json'),
    });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await use(page);
    await ctx.close();
  },
});

test('role boundary charter — delete button visibility', async ({ adminPage, viewerPage }) => {
  await adminPage.goto('https://app.example.com/documents/456');
  await expect(adminPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toBeVisible();

  await viewerPage.goto('https://app.example.com/documents/456');
  await expect(viewerPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toBeHidden();
});

export { test };
```

**Tradeoff.** Storage-state fixtures captured via `page.context().storageState()` embed session tokens that expire; if the auth server uses short-lived JWTs, fixtures can silently expire between capture and charter execution, causing every role-boundary test to redirect to the login page and appear as a UI regression rather than a fixture staleness issue. Always pair storage-state fixtures with a `beforeAll` freshness check that navigates to a protected route and asserts `page.url()` does not contain `/login` — if it does, re-run `npm run auth:setup` to refresh fixtures before the full charter suite executes.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 346 — `locator.and()` Compound Attribute Charter for Ambiguous Element Disambiguation

`locator.and(otherLocator)` returns a locator that matches elements satisfying both locator conditions simultaneously — it is the Playwright-idiomatic replacement for writing compound CSS attribute selectors or XPath `and` predicates. Exploratory charters use `.and()` to disambiguate pages that render multiple elements with the same role or text label but different semantic states (e.g., two "Submit" buttons where only the enabled one should be clicked) without resorting to fragile index-based selection.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('compound locator charter — enabled submit button disambiguation', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/wizard');

  // Two "Next" buttons exist — one for current step (enabled), one pre-rendered lookahead (disabled)
  const enabledNext = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' })
    .and(page.locator(':not([disabled])'));

  // Verify only one enabled "Next" button is in scope before clicking
  await expect(enabledNext).toHaveCount(1);
  await enabledNext.click();

  // After navigation, enter data to make the submit button enter its "ready" state
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('user@example.com');

  const submitWithData = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })
    .and(page.locator('[data-state="ready"]'));

  await expect(submitWithData).toBeVisible();
  await submitWithData.click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/submitted/i);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `.and()` enforces that both locators match the same element in the same DOM snapshot — it does not perform sequential narrowing. If the second locator uses a broad selector (e.g., `.and(page.locator('div'))`) it will still match all buttons inside `div` ancestors, not restrict the match to buttons that are themselves `div` elements. The most common misuse is treating `.and()` as a "within" scope operator when `.locator().locator()` chaining is the correct approach for ancestor-descendant containment. Use `.and()` strictly for adding attribute/state conditions to the same element, and use chaining for navigating the DOM hierarchy.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 347 — `locator.or()` Optional Dialog Charter for Non-Deterministic Interstitial Handling

`locator.or(otherLocator)` creates a locator that matches elements from either alternative, resolving non-deterministic states where the application may show one of two different UI branches depending on account state, A/B group, or race condition outcome. Exploratory charters use `.or()` to gate progression through a flow when an interstitial (consent dialog, onboarding tip, rate-limit banner) may or may not appear, preventing test flakiness without suppressing the exploration of the interstitial itself.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('optional interstitial charter — cookie consent or main content', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');

  // Either the consent modal or the hero section is the first interactive element
  const consentButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all|accept cookies/i });
  const heroHeading = page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 });

  // Wait for whichever appears first
  await expect(consentButton.or(heroHeading).first()).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });

  // Dismiss consent modal only if it appeared
  if (await consentButton.isVisible()) {
    // Charter: modal has required WCAG focus management
    await expect(page.locator('[role="dialog"]')).toBeFocused().catch(() => {
      console.warn('[CHARTER NOTE] Cookie consent dialog does not receive focus on open');
    });
    await consentButton.click();
    await expect(consentButton).toBeHidden();
  }

  // Charter continues regardless of which branch occurred
  await expect(heroHeading).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `.or()` resolves to the first visible element matching either locator, but `expect(locator.or(...)).toBeVisible()` does not tell you which branch was matched. If the charter logic must branch (e.g., "dismiss the modal if it appeared, then continue"), use `locator.isVisible()` after the `.or()` assertion to detect which branch was taken, as shown above. Do not use `.or()` as a permanent accommodation for a UI non-determinism bug — if the modal's appearance is supposed to be conditional, file a defect for the unpredictable render and track the `.or()` usage as a known debt comment so it can be removed once the root cause is fixed.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 348 — `page.evaluate()` + `MutationObserver` Charter for Asynchronous DOM Mutation Tracking

Injecting a `MutationObserver` via `page.evaluate()` into the page context before triggering an action enables exploratory charters to record every DOM mutation that occurs as a side effect — element additions, attribute changes, text content updates — providing a structural change log that `toBeVisible()` assertions alone cannot capture. This is particularly valuable when chartering real-time collaboration features, live data feeds, or complex animation sequences where intermediate DOM states are transient and invisible to point-in-time assertions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('MutationObserver charter — live chat message arrival tracking', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/chat/room/42');

  // Inject observer BEFORE the action that triggers mutations
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    (window as any).__mutations = [];
    const observer = new MutationObserver(records => {
      for (const record of records) {
        (window as any).__mutations.push({
          type: record.type,
          target: (record.target as Element).tagName,
          addedCount: record.addedNodes.length,
          removedCount: record.removedNodes.length,
          attributeName: record.attributeName,
        });
      }
    });
    observer.observe(document.getElementById('message-list')!, {
      childList: true,
      subtree: true,
      attributes: true,
      characterData: false,
    });
  });

  // Simulate incoming message via custom event (replace with real stimulus in full charter)
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('__test:injectMessage', {
      detail: { text: 'Hello from charter', author: 'bot' },
    }));
  });

  // Poll until at least one mutation is recorded rather than using a fixed delay
  await page.waitForFunction(() => (window as any).__mutations.length > 0, { timeout: 5000 });

  // Read mutation log from page context
  const mutations = await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__mutations);
  expect(mutations.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  const addedNodes = mutations.filter((m: any) => m.type === 'childList' && m.addedCount > 0);
  expect(addedNodes.length, 'Expected at least one message node to be added').toBeGreaterThan(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `MutationObserver` callbacks run asynchronously on the microtask queue — use `page.waitForFunction(() => (window as any).__mutations.length > 0)` to poll until at least one mutation is recorded rather than a hardcoded `waitForTimeout`. Additionally, `page.evaluate()` cannot transfer the `MutationObserver` object itself across the sandbox boundary — all data must be serialised into a plain JSON-compatible structure (as shown with the summary object) before being readable from the test process. The observer remains active for the lifetime of the page and accumulates all mutations indiscriminately; scope `observer.observe()` to the smallest meaningful subtree to avoid performance overhead and noise from unrelated DOM updates.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 349 — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` Sequential State-Dependent Charter for Multi-Step Wizard Exploration

`test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` forces all tests within a `describe` block to run sequentially in a single worker, sharing state across tests — the opposite of Playwright's default parallel isolation. This pattern is appropriate for exploratory charters of stateful multi-step wizards, checkout flows, or onboarding sequences where each step genuinely depends on successful completion of the prior step and independent isolation would require complex state reconstruction in each test.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('checkout wizard charter', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

  let sharedPage: import('@playwright/test').Page;

  test.beforeAll(async ({ browser }) => {
    sharedPage = await browser.newPage();
    await sharedPage.goto('https://app.example.com/checkout');
  });

  test.afterAll(async () => {
    await sharedPage.close();
  });

  test('step 1 — cart review: items and totals are correct', async () => {
    await expect(sharedPage.getByTestId('cart-item-count')).toHaveText('3');
    await expect(sharedPage.getByTestId('cart-total')).toContainText('$');
    await sharedPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Shipping' }).click();
  });

  test('step 2 — shipping: form validation and address entry', async () => {
    await expect(sharedPage).toHaveURL(/\/checkout\/shipping/);
    await sharedPage.getByLabel('Full Name').fill('Jane Doe');
    await sharedPage.getByLabel('Address').fill('123 Main St');
    await sharedPage.getByLabel('City').fill('Springfield');
    await sharedPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to Payment' }).click();
  });

  test('step 3 — payment: card entry and order confirmation', async () => {
    await expect(sharedPage).toHaveURL(/\/checkout\/payment/);
    await sharedPage.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await sharedPage.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await sharedPage.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
    await sharedPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
    await expect(sharedPage.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `mode: 'serial'` sacrifices Playwright's core test isolation guarantee — a failure in step 1 causes all subsequent tests in the block to be marked as skipped, making the failure cascade appear worse than it is in CI reports. More critically, because all tests share a single browser context, a crash in step 2 leaves the context in an undefined state for step 3. Use `mode: 'serial'` only for charters that explicitly model a user journey and cannot be meaningfully decomposed; for regression suites, restructure each step as an isolated test with its own storage-state setup so failures are independent and immediately actionable.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 350 — `page.getByLabel()` Form Binding Charter for `for`/`id` Association Verification

`page.getByLabel('Label Text')` resolves the associated form control by following the HTML label `for`/`id` binding, the `aria-labelledby` association, or the implicit label wrapping pattern — in that priority order. Exploratory charters using `getByLabel()` as the exclusive form-field locator strategy serve double duty: they test functional form behaviour AND validate that every input has a properly associated label, because if the label association is broken, `getByLabel()` will throw and the charter fails with a clear accessibility defect signal rather than a generic "element not found" error.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form label binding charter — registration form accessibility contract', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/register');

  // getByLabel throws if association is broken — this IS the accessibility test
  await page.getByLabel('First Name').fill('Jane');
  await page.getByLabel('Last Name').fill('Doe');
  await page.getByLabel('Email Address').fill('jane.doe@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('S3cur3P@ss!');
  await page.getByLabel('Confirm Password').fill('S3cur3P@ss!');

  // Charter: select options also require accessible labels
  await page.getByLabel('Country').selectOption('US');
  await page.getByLabel('Date of Birth').fill('1990-01-15');

  // Verify all required fields are marked as such
  const requiredFields = ['First Name', 'Last Name', 'Email Address', 'Password'];
  for (const label of requiredFields) {
    const input = page.getByLabel(label);
    const isRequired = await input.getAttribute('required');
    const isAriaRequired = await input.getAttribute('aria-required');
    expect.soft(
      isRequired !== null || isAriaRequired === 'true',
      `Field "${label}" is not marked required`
    ).toBe(true);
  }

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create Account' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/onboarding|\/dashboard/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `getByLabel()` follows the label-to-input binding strictly — if a design uses visually styled placeholder text as a substitute for a visible label (a common anti-pattern), `getByLabel()` will not find the input and the test will fail, correctly surfacing the accessibility violation. However, this means `getByLabel()` cannot be used at all on forms that deliberately use `aria-label` attributes on inputs without corresponding `<label>` elements — in those cases, use `page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Email Address' })` which resolves the accessible name via `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or `title` in addition to `<label>` association.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 351 — `page.on('requestfailed')` Network Failure Charter for Silent Error Swallowing Detection

`page.on('requestfailed')` fires for every request that the browser could not complete — DNS failures, connection resets, TLS errors, CORS rejections before the response arrives, and requests aborted via `route.abort()`. Exploratory charters that register this listener at setup and collect all failed requests during an interaction sequence can detect silent network failures that the UI swallows without surfacing any visible error state — a particularly dangerous class of defect where the application appears to work while important data (analytics, error reporting, feature flags) is silently lost.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('request failure charter — silent failure detection during page load', async ({ page }) => {
  const failedRequests: Array<{ url: string; failure: string | null }> = [];

  page.on('requestfailed', request => {
    const url = request.url();
    // Ignore known non-critical resources (fonts, analytics)
    if (url.includes('fonts.gstatic.com') || url.includes('analytics')) return;
    failedRequests.push({
      url,
      failure: request.failure()?.errorText ?? 'unknown',
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Interact with key features to trigger lazy-loaded requests
  await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Reports' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Settings' }).click();

  // Charter: no non-critical requests should fail silently
  expect(
    failedRequests,
    `Silent network failures detected:\n${failedRequests.map(r => `  ${r.failure}: ${r.url}`).join('\n')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `requestfailed` fires for browser-aborted requests, but not for requests that complete with HTTP error status codes (4xx/5xx) — those fire `page.on('response')` with a non-2xx status. A comprehensive network health charter requires both: `requestfailed` for transport-level failures and a `page.on('response')` listener with `response.status() >= 400` for protocol-level errors. Additionally, `requestfailed` includes requests aborted intentionally by the test via `route.abort()` — always filter by URL when `page.route()` is also in use to avoid false positives from deliberate route abortions.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 352 — `page.getByRole('row')` Table Content Charter for Accessible Data Table Verification

`page.getByRole('row')` locates `<tr>` elements by their implicit ARIA `row` role, enabling structured table traversal without relying on brittle nth-child CSS selectors or column-index arithmetic. Exploratory charters can use role-based row and cell navigation to verify data table semantics (presence of column headers, correct `scope` attributes, sortable column indicators) and data correctness simultaneously — combining functional and accessibility assertions in a single pass.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('data table accessibility charter — users table semantic structure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/admin/users');
  await page.waitForSelector('table');

  const table = page.getByRole('table', { name: /users/i });
  await expect(table).toBeVisible();

  // Charter: column headers must exist and have scope
  const headers = table.getByRole('columnheader');
  await expect(headers).toHaveCount(5); // Name, Email, Role, Status, Joined

  for (const header of await headers.all()) {
    const scope = await header.getAttribute('scope');
    expect.soft(
      scope,
      `Column header "${await header.textContent()}" is missing scope="col"`
    ).toBe('col');
  }

  // Charter: sortable column must expose aria-sort after click
  const nameHeader = table.getByRole('columnheader', { name: /name/i });
  await nameHeader.click();
  await expect(nameHeader).toHaveAttribute('aria-sort', /ascending|descending/);

  // Charter: data rows exist and have correct cell count
  const dataRows = table.locator('tbody').getByRole('row');
  const rowCount = await dataRows.count();
  expect(rowCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  for (const row of await dataRows.all()) {
    const cells = row.getByRole('cell');
    await expect.soft(cells).toHaveCount(5);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `getByRole('row')` returns ALL `<tr>` elements in the table including the header row — scoping to `table.locator('tbody').getByRole('row')` (as shown above) is more explicit and does not require a filter to exclude the header row. The `getByRole('table', { name: /users/i })` requires the table to have an accessible name via `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or a `<caption>` element — if none is present, the locator falls back to the first unnamed table on the page, which is a hidden accessibility defect the charter surfaces. For tables with server-side pagination, always trigger a page load or await a stable row count before iterating rows to avoid asserting on a partially-rendered table.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 353 — `test.slow()` Extended Timeout Charter for Long-Running Background Job Polling

`test.slow()` triples the test's default timeout, signalling to both Playwright and the test report reader that the charter intentionally exercises a slow user-observable path (background job completion, export file generation, email delivery confirmation) without requiring a hardcoded `timeout` value that drifts as server performance varies. Pairing `test.slow()` with `expect(...).toBeVisible({ timeout: N })` provides a self-documenting slow-path charter that does not mask performance regressions — if the operation consistently takes longer than three times the default timeout, the charter surfaces the regression.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('background export charter — CSV generation completion polling', async ({ page }) => {
  // Signal: this charter tests a legitimately slow path (job queue + file gen)
  test.slow();

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/reports');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export to CSV' }).click();

  // Charter: a progress indicator must appear immediately after click
  await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 2000 });

  // Poll for the download link — explicit generous timeout for long-running jobs
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('link', { name: /download.*\.csv/i })
  ).toBeVisible({ timeout: 45_000 });

  // Charter: progress indicator must disappear when download is ready
  await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeHidden();

  // Charter: download link must be functional
  const [download] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('download'),
    page.getByRole('link', { name: /download.*\.csv/i }).click(),
  ]);

  expect(download.suggestedFilename()).toMatch(/\.csv$/);
  const path = await download.path();
  expect(path).not.toBeNull();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.slow()` multiplies the global `timeout` configured in `playwright.config.ts` by 3 — if the global timeout is 30 seconds, `test.slow()` gives the test 90 seconds. This is appropriate for single-use slow-path charters but should never be applied to an entire `describe` block covering multiple tests, as it balloons CI time disproportionately. For charters where the slow operation's expected duration is known and bounded, prefer `test.setTimeout(specificMs)` over `test.slow()` to express the intended bound explicitly and make performance regressions immediately visible when the actual duration crosses the explicit threshold.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 354 — `page.route()` + `route.abort()` Third-Party Script Blocking Charter for Core-Experience Degradation Testing

Blocking all third-party JavaScript domains via `route.abort()` and then exercising the application's core user journey tests whether the application degrades gracefully when CDN-hosted scripts (analytics, chat widgets, consent managers, A/B testing frameworks) are unavailable. This charter pattern catches a class of production outages where a third-party CDN incident causes `TypeError: window.analytics is not defined` to crash the application's own JavaScript initialization sequence.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const THIRD_PARTY_DOMAINS = [
  '**/segment.io/**',
  '**/google-analytics.com/**',
  '**/hotjar.com/**',
  '**/intercom.io/**',
  '**/cdn.optimizely.com/**',
];

test('third-party script failure charter — core flow survives CDN outage', async ({ page }) => {
  const blockedUrls: string[] = [];

  // Block all known third-party domains
  for (const pattern of THIRD_PARTY_DOMAINS) {
    await page.route(pattern, route => {
      blockedUrls.push(route.request().url());
      route.abort('failed');
    });
  }

  // Monitor for JS errors caused by missing third-party globals
  const jsErrors: string[] = [];
  page.on('pageerror', err => jsErrors.push(err.message));

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Charter: the critical path must remain fully functional with all third-party scripts blocked
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('user@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/);
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();

  // Charter: no uncaught JS errors referencing third-party globals
  const thirdPartyErrors = jsErrors.filter(msg =>
    /analytics|hotjar|intercom|optimizely|segment/i.test(msg)
  );
  expect(
    thirdPartyErrors,
    `Third-party JS errors leaked into core app:\n${thirdPartyErrors.join('\n')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `route.abort('failed')` simulates a network-level failure (connection refused), which is subtly different from a script loading with a 404 (resource not found) or a script that loads but throws a runtime exception during initialisation. Some application startup sequences defensively catch network-level failures but not runtime errors from partially-loaded scripts. For comprehensive third-party resilience coverage, run three variants of this charter: one with `abort('failed')`, one with `route.fulfill({ status: 404 })`, and one with `route.fulfill({ body: 'throw new Error("Third-party init failed")' })` to cover all three failure modes.

**Tag:** [official]

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 51)

**G30. `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` incorrectly signals readiness on pages that implement long-polling, WebSocket connections, or periodic `setInterval`-based XHR keep-alive pings — the network is never truly idle, so `networkidle` never resolves and the test times out even though the page is fully rendered and interactive.**
A team chartering a real-time dashboard found that every test using `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` timed out after 30 seconds because the application maintained a persistent WebSocket connection and sent a heartbeat XHR every 5 seconds. Switching to `waitForLoadState('load')` followed by `expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible()` resolved the timeouts immediately. WHY this matters: `networkidle` waits for at least 500ms with no more than 0 in-flight network connections — any persistent connection or polling interval makes this condition impossible to satisfy; prefer `waitForLoadState('load')` combined with a specific application-readiness assertion (e.g., the primary content region becoming visible) over `networkidle` for all applications that use WebSockets, SSE, or polling.

**G31. `locator.fill()` does not trigger the `input` event on React-controlled inputs that use synthetic event handlers in concurrent mode — `fill()` dispatches an `InputEvent` on the DOM, but React's synthetic event system may not flush the state update synchronously, causing the input's value to appear correct in the DOM but the React state to remain stale, leading to form submissions that send the pre-fill default value instead of the filled value.**
A team filling a React 18 concurrent-mode search box with `locator.fill('search term')` found that the API request triggered on form submit always contained an empty query parameter. Inspecting the React DevTools showed the component state had never updated. The fix was to use `locator.pressSequentially('search term', { delay: 50 })` which fires individual `keydown`/`keypress`/`keyup` events that React's synthetic system processes correctly. WHY this matters: `fill()` is optimised for speed and bypasses keyboard events; for React concurrent-mode inputs that depend on keyboard events for state synchronisation, `pressSequentially()` or `locator.click(); await locator.type()` are more reliable, albeit slower, alternatives.

**G32. `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })` matches buttons whose accessible name contains "Submit" as a substring by default — on pages that render both a "Submit for Review" and a "Submit" button, the locator matches both, causing a strict mode violation even though the developer intended to match only the shorter label.**
A team's charter for the document publish flow began failing after a "Submit for Review" secondary action was added to the same toolbar. The fix was `getByRole('button', { name: /^Submit$/ })` — using a regex anchored with `^` and `$` enforces exact full-string matching rather than substring inclusion. WHY this matters: Playwright's `name` option in `getByRole` performs substring matching by default (equivalent to `includes()`); always use a regex with `^` and `$` anchors when the accessible name must be matched exactly and other elements on the page may have longer names that contain the target string as a substring.

**G33. `page.screenshot({ fullPage: true })` on pages with `position: sticky` headers captures the sticky element at its stuck (viewport-top) position in every screenshot tile, resulting in the sticky header appearing multiple times overlaid at regular intervals throughout the full-page screenshot — the screenshot does not show the page as it would appear during a normal scroll, making the artifact misleading for visual regression baselines.**
A team building a full-page screenshot charter for a documentation site found that every screenshot had the sticky navigation bar stamped across the content at 900px intervals. Mitigation requires hiding sticky elements before capturing: `await page.addStyleTag({ content: '[style*="sticky"], .sticky-header { position: static !important; }' })` before calling `screenshot({ fullPage: true })`, then reverting the style tag after capture. WHY this matters: `fullPage: true` composites multiple viewport-height screenshots by scrolling the page programmatically; sticky elements re-render in their stuck position in each tile, duplicating them visually — always normalise sticky positioning before full-page screenshot capture when the goal is a coherent document view.

**G34. `expect(locator).toHaveText(['item1', 'item2', 'item3'])` asserts on the `textContent` of each matched element in DOM order, but DOM order does not always match visual order on pages that use CSS Grid with explicit placement or `flexbox` with the `order` property — the assertion passes even when items are visually reordered by CSS, creating a false-positive that masks a reorder bug where the visual order changed but the DOM order was not updated.**
A team chartering a kanban board's drag-and-drop reorder feature found that `toHaveText()` consistently reported the correct order after a drag operation that visually displayed items in the wrong sequence. The application updated CSS `order` properties instead of reordering DOM nodes. WHY this matters: Playwright's `toHaveText()` and all locator-based text assertions operate on DOM order, not visual/layout order; for charters that must verify visual ordering, extract `getComputedStyle(el).order` via `page.evaluate()` or compare element bounding box Y coordinates using `locator.boundingBox()` to assert on the visually-rendered sequence rather than the DOM sequence.
