## Cycle 52 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 355 — `page.route()` Abort-Variant Resilience Charter for Graceful-Degradation Verification

When a third-party API or back-end microservice is unavailable, the application must degrade gracefully rather than crash or freeze. This pattern uses `page.route()` with `route.abort()` to simulate outages at the network layer during an exploratory session and asserts that user-facing state remains coherent and informative. The charter is distinct from a simple mocked 500 response because `abort()` replicates a connection-refused/timeout at the TCP level, which exercises a different branch of application error handling.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('recommendations service outage — layout remains stable', async ({ page }) => {
  // Simulate the recommendations API being completely unreachable
  await page.route('**/api/recommendations**', route =>
    route.abort('connectionrefused')
  );

  const jsErrors: string[] = [];
  page.on('pageerror', err => jsErrors.push(err.message));

  await page.goto('/home');
  await page.waitForLoadState('load');

  // Oracle 1: primary content region must still be visible
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();

  // Oracle 2: a user-facing fallback message or skeleton must replace the widget
  const recommendationsRegion = page.getByTestId('recommendations-widget');
  await expect(recommendationsRegion).toBeVisible();
  const widgetText = await recommendationsRegion.textContent();
  expect(
    widgetText,
    'Recommendations widget should show fallback, not be blank'
  ).not.toBe('');

  // Oracle 3: no uncaught JS exceptions should reference the aborted call
  expect(jsErrors, `Uncaught JS errors:\n${jsErrors.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `abort('connectionrefused')` is the most severe failure mode; real outages may instead produce 504 Gateway Timeout responses (which take time to arrive). For comprehensive resilience coverage run three variants: `abort('connectionrefused')`, `route.fulfill({ status: 504, body: '' })`, and a delayed fulfill using `setTimeout` inside the route handler to simulate slow degradation. The abort variant is the fastest to execute in CI but covers the least realistic production scenario.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 356 — `expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` Visual Regression Baseline Charter with `stylePath` Noise Suppression

Visual regression baselines are only useful if the comparison is noise-free. Dynamic page elements (timestamps, avatars, ad banners) introduce pixel churn that generates false failures. This pattern establishes a baseline charter using `toHaveScreenshot()` with a `stylePath` CSS file that hides volatile regions, plus `maxDiffPixels` tolerance calibrated to the target component. The charter is structured so that the baseline itself becomes a living artifact reviewed alongside code changes.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// noise-suppressor.css (referenced via stylePath):
//   [data-testid="user-avatar"] { visibility: hidden !important; }
//   [data-testid="timestamp"]   { visibility: hidden !important; }
//   .ad-banner                  { display: none !important; }

test('dashboard summary card — visual baseline (noise-suppressed)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // Wait for data to load so the skeleton is replaced
  await expect(page.getByTestId('summary-card-loaded')).toBeVisible();

  // Charter: element-level screenshot to isolate the component
  const card = page.getByTestId('summary-card');
  await expect(card).toHaveScreenshot('summary-card-baseline.png', {
    stylePath: './visual-suppressor.css',
    maxDiffPixels: 50,
    animations: 'disabled', // freeze CSS animations before capture
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `stylePath` injects a `<style>` tag before capture and removes it afterward, which means the baseline reflects a "hidden noise" rendering that never matches what real users see. If the visual suppressor hides an element that is actually broken (e.g., a broken avatar URL that renders a broken-image icon), the test will not catch it. Always run a separate accessibility charter that checks `<img>` `alt` attributes and `src` validity alongside the visual baseline charter to compensate for this blind spot.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 357 — `page.route()` + `route.fetch()` Response-Latency Injection Charter for Loading-State Exploration

Loading states (spinners, skeletons, progress indicators) are only exercised when responses are slow. In test environments back-ends are typically fast, so loading states are never rendered and bugs in them go undetected. This pattern injects artificial latency by intercepting real requests, waiting, and then forwarding them, forcing the application through its loading-state branch without stubbing the response data.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const LATENCY_MS = 1500; // enough to render the skeleton state

test('invoice list — skeleton loading state is rendered during slow fetch', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/invoices**', async route => {
    // Delay the real response to expose the loading state
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, LATENCY_MS));
    const response = await route.fetch();
    await route.fulfill({ response });
  });

  const navigationPromise = page.goto('/invoices');

  // Charter: skeleton must appear within 200ms of navigation start
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-skeleton')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 500 });
  // Charter: skeleton must disappear after data loads
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-skeleton')).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: LATENCY_MS + 2000 });
  // Charter: real content must replace the skeleton
  await expect(page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Invoices' })).toBeVisible();

  await navigationPromise;
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Injecting latency via `setTimeout` inside a route handler is approximate — the actual delay seen by the browser is `LATENCY_MS` plus the time Playwright takes to invoke the handler. At high parallelism this can fluctuate ±200 ms. For precise latency control, use `page.clock.install()` (v1.45+) in combination with `route.fetch()` so that time-dependent assertions use controlled clock ticks rather than wall-clock timing. The `setTimeout` approach is simpler to set up but produces flakey results under CI load.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 358 — `AxeBuilder.include()` Post-Interaction Accessibility Charter for Dynamically-Revealed Content

Static page scans miss accessibility defects in content revealed only after user interaction: expanded accordions, opened modals, filled error states, and activated tooltips. This pattern runs `AxeBuilder.analyze()` twice per session — once on page load and once after triggering the dynamic content — to catch WCAG violations that would be invisible to a single static scan.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('contact form — error states are accessible after failed submit', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');

  // Baseline scan — clean page
  const baselineScan = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();
  expect(baselineScan.violations).toHaveLength(0);

  // Trigger validation errors by submitting without required fields
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send Message' }).click();

  // Wait for error messages to be injected into the DOM
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toBeVisible();

  // Post-interaction scan scoped to the form to isolate new violations
  const errorStateScan = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .include('#contact-form')
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21aa'])
    .analyze();

  // Attach full results for triage even on pass
  await test.info().attach('axe-error-state-scan', {
    body: JSON.stringify(errorStateScan, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  expect(
    errorStateScan.violations,
    `Post-interaction a11y violations:\n${JSON.stringify(errorStateScan.violations, null, 2)}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Running `AxeBuilder.analyze()` multiple times within a single test adds 500–2000 ms per call depending on DOM size. For large single-page applications with many components, consider scoping each call with `.include()` to the component under test rather than scanning the entire page, and use `.disableRules(['color-contrast'])` selectively for known false-positive rules in third-party widgets you cannot control. The post-interaction scan scope should be kept as narrow as practical to keep session duration acceptable.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 359 — `test.extend()` Worker-Scoped Fixture Charter for Expensive Shared Setup Exploration

Some exploratory sessions require database seeding, OAuth token acquisition, or external service warm-up that takes 5–30 seconds and would be prohibitively slow if repeated per test. Worker-scoped fixtures in Playwright run once per parallel worker process, amortising the setup cost across all tests in that worker. This pattern wraps a shared test database seed in a worker fixture and pairs it with a per-test rollback to ensure session isolation.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = { seededDb: { userId: string; orgId: string } };
type TestFixtures  = { cleanSession: void };

export const test = base.extend<TestFixtures, WorkerFixtures>({
  // Worker-scoped: run once, shared across all tests in this worker
  seededDb: [async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
    const seed = await seedTestDatabase({
      suffix: `worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}`,
    });
    await use(seed);
    await teardownTestDatabase(seed.orgId);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  // Test-scoped: reset state between tests using the shared seed
  cleanSession: async ({ seededDb, page }, use) => {
    await page.goto(`/login?seed=${seededDb.userId}`);
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/);
    await use();
    // Soft-reset: clear session storage and cookies between tests
    await page.evaluate(() => sessionStorage.clear());
    await page.context().clearCookies();
  },
});

test('charter: bulk delete — confirmation modal requires explicit user intent', async ({
  cleanSession,
  seededDb,
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto(`/orgs/${seededDb.orgId}/members`);
  await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Select all' }).check();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete selected' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /delete/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('button', { name: /confirm/i })
  ).toBeEnabled();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped fixtures share state across tests in the same worker, so any test that mutates the shared resource in a way not cleaned up by the per-test teardown will leak state into subsequent tests. This is particularly dangerous when tests run in random order (Playwright's default). Always pair a worker-scoped seed fixture with a per-test cleanup fixture (`cleanSession` above) and ensure the cleanup is comprehensive. If mutation isolation is critical, prefer per-test database seeding even at the performance cost.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 360 — `tracing.startHar()` / `stopHar()` HAR-Based API Contract Charter for Session Replay

HAR (HTTP Archive) files capture every network request and response during a session with full headers, bodies, and timings. This pattern uses Playwright's first-class HAR tracing API to record a complete exploratory session's network traffic, then programmatically validates the HAR against an OpenAPI schema to detect undocumented endpoints, unexpected status codes, and response structure drift between sessions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import Ajv from 'ajv';
import openApiSchema from './openapi.json';

test('checkout flow HAR contract charter', async ({ page, context }) => {
  const harPath = `./har-artifacts/checkout-${Date.now()}.har`;

  // Start HAR recording on the context (captures all pages)
  await context.tracing.startHar({ path: harPath, updateContent: 'attach' });

  // Perform the exploratory session
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();

  await context.tracing.stopHar();

  // Post-session HAR validation
  const har = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(harPath, 'utf-8'));
  const apiEntries = har.log.entries.filter((e: any) =>
    e.request.url.includes('/api/')
  );

  const ajv = new Ajv({ strict: false });
  const issues: string[] = [];
  for (const entry of apiEntries) {
    const url = new URL(entry.request.url);
    const pathKey = url.pathname.replace(/\/\d+/g, '/{id}');
    if (!openApiSchema.paths[pathKey]) {
      issues.push(`Undocumented endpoint: ${entry.request.method} ${pathKey}`);
    }
  }

  expect(issues, `HAR contract violations:\n${issues.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** HAR files grow large quickly — a 10-minute exploratory session on a data-heavy SPA can produce a 50–200 MB HAR file when `updateContent: 'attach'` is used. For long sessions, use `updateContent: 'embed'` (smaller but no body content) or filter routes before recording with `context.route()` to exclude static assets. The HAR oracle is most valuable for API-heavy flows where response body schema drift is the primary risk; for UI-focused sessions the overhead of HAR analysis rarely justifies the file size cost.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 361 — `page.ariaSnapshot()` Structural Regression Charter for Dynamic Component State Transitions

ARIA snapshots capture the accessibility tree as a YAML string that encodes role, name, and ARIA attributes without pixel-level noise. This pattern uses `locator.ariaSnapshot()` to capture component state at each stage of a multi-step interaction (idle → loading → loaded → error), creating a structural oracle that detects regressions in semantic markup without being brittle about visual appearance.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('data table — ARIA structure survives sort and filter operations', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports/transactions');
  const table = page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Transactions' });

  // Baseline structural snapshot
  await expect(table).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - table "Transactions":
      - rowgroup:
        - row:
          - columnheader "Date" [sort=ascending]
          - columnheader "Description"
          - columnheader "Amount"
  `);

  // Sort by Amount — assert sort indicator moves correctly
  await page.getByRole('columnheader', { name: 'Amount' }).click();
  await expect(table).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - table "Transactions":
      - rowgroup:
        - row:
          - columnheader "Date"
          - columnheader "Description"
          - columnheader "Amount" [sort=ascending]
  `);

  // Apply filter — assert table still announces row count to screen readers
  await page.getByLabel('Filter by description').fill('coffee');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Apply filter' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(
    `- status: /\\d+ results/`
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` uses `contain` semantics by default — the template is a subset check, not an exact match. This makes snapshots resilient to new rows being added but means that a column header losing its `sort` attribute would only be caught if the template explicitly asserts the attribute. For critical ARIA properties (sort direction, expanded state, selected state), always include the ARIA attribute in the template with `[attr=value]` syntax. Without this, ARIA snapshot tests give false confidence that accessibility structure is correct when important state attributes have silently been removed.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 362 — `page.evaluate()` + `PerformanceObserver` Core Web Vitals Charter for LCP/CLS/INP Exploration

Performance regressions in Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) directly affect SEO ranking and user experience but are invisible to functional test assertions. This pattern injects a `PerformanceObserver` via `page.evaluate()` early in a session to capture real CWV metrics during the exploratory workflow, then asserts thresholds at session end to catch regressions before they reach production.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface CWVSnapshot {
  lcp: number | null;
  cls: number;
  inp: number | null;
}

async function collectCWV(page: import('@playwright/test').Page): Promise<CWVSnapshot> {
  return page.evaluate(() => {
    return new Promise<CWVSnapshot>(resolve => {
      const metrics: CWVSnapshot = { lcp: null, cls: 0, inp: null };

      new PerformanceObserver(list => {
        const entries = list.getEntries();
        metrics.lcp = entries[entries.length - 1].startTime;
      }).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });

      new PerformanceObserver(list => {
        for (const entry of list.getEntries() as any[]) {
          metrics.cls += entry.value;
        }
      }).observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });

      // Resolve after 3s to allow LCP and CLS to settle
      setTimeout(() => resolve(metrics), 3000);
    });
  });
}

test('product listing page — Core Web Vitals within budget', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  await page.waitForLoadState('load');
  const cwv = await collectCWV(page);

  expect(cwv.lcp ?? Infinity, 'LCP must be under 2500ms (Good threshold)').toBeLessThan(2500);
  expect(cwv.cls, 'CLS must be under 0.1 (Good threshold)').toBeLessThan(0.1);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `PerformanceObserver` in headless Chromium does not account for CPU throttling or network conditions that real users experience on mobile devices. CWV scores captured in a CI headless environment are typically 30–60% better than field data captured by the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX). Use this charter as a regression detection baseline (i.e., "did we regress from last sprint's score?") rather than an absolute quality gate. For absolute production accuracy, compare against CrUX field data using the PageSpeed Insights API as a supplementary oracle.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 363 — `page.addInitScript()` Pre-Navigation Feature-Flag Override Charter for Dark-Launch Boundary Exploration

Dark-launched features are gated behind feature flags that may be unset for test users, making them impossible to reach via normal test flows. `page.addInitScript()` injects JavaScript before any page script runs, enabling reliable flag overrides that survive full-page navigations within the session. This charter pattern systematically explores both flag-on and flag-off states without requiring backend flag management.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const FLAG_OVERRIDES_ON  = { newCheckoutFlow: true,  splitPayment: true  };
const FLAG_OVERRIDES_OFF = { newCheckoutFlow: false, splitPayment: false };

async function withFlagOverride(
  page: import('@playwright/test').Page,
  flags: Record<string, boolean>
) {
  // Inject before ANY page scripts run — survives navigation
  await page.addInitScript(overrides => {
    (window as any).__FEATURE_FLAGS__ = {
      ...(window as any).__FEATURE_FLAGS__,
      ...overrides,
    };
  }, flags);
}

test('charter: new checkout — payment summary shown only when flag is ON', async ({ page }) => {
  await withFlagOverride(page, FLAG_OVERRIDES_ON);
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-summary-v2')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-summary-v1')).not.toBeVisible();
});

test('charter: legacy checkout — old summary shown when flag is OFF', async ({ page }) => {
  await withFlagOverride(page, FLAG_OVERRIDES_OFF);
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-summary-v1')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-summary-v2')).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `addInitScript()` overrides flags in the browser's JavaScript runtime only — it does not affect server-side flag evaluation. If the application uses server-rendered feature gating (e.g., the server decides which HTML to render before the page loads), `addInitScript()` will not override the server's decision. For server-side feature flag exploration, you must either use backend test APIs to toggle flags per test user, or intercept the flag-configuration API endpoint with `page.route()` and return a mocked flag payload.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 364 — `page.waitForFunction()` Long-Poll Convergence Charter for Eventually-Consistent UI State

Some UI states only stabilise after a server-side background job completes — file import processing, AI generation, report compilation. Polling with `page.waitForFunction()` evaluates a JavaScript predicate in the browser context repeatedly until it returns truthy, making it the most reliable mechanism for waiting for eventual consistency without coupling the test to application internals.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('CSV import — all rows processed within 60 seconds', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/import');

  // Upload file
  const [fileChooser] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('filechooser'),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Upload CSV' }).click(),
  ]);
  await fileChooser.setFiles('./fixtures/1000-row-sample.csv');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start Import' }).click();

  // Charter oracle: wait for the progress indicator to show 100%
  await page.waitForFunction(
    () => {
      const el = document.querySelector('[data-testid="import-progress"]');
      return el?.textContent?.includes('100%') || el?.textContent?.includes('Complete');
    },
    undefined,
    { timeout: 60_000, polling: 1000 }
  );

  // Structural assertion after convergence
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /import complete/i })).toBeVisible();
  const rowCount = page.getByTestId('import-row-count');
  await expect(rowCount).toHaveText('1,000 rows imported');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.waitForFunction()` with `polling: 1000` issues a JavaScript evaluation every second, which can interfere with browser performance profiling during an exploratory session and may trigger rate-limiting on applications that track client-side analytics events. For applications where client-side polling is undesirable, prefer `page.waitForResponse()` against the job-status API endpoint instead of DOM polling — it avoids JavaScript execution overhead and respects natural API response timing. The DOM-polling approach is preferable when no stable API endpoint exists for job status.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 365 — `page.on('dialog')` Automatic Dialog Acceptance Charter for Unhandled Confirm/Prompt Detection

Unhandled `window.confirm()`, `window.alert()`, and `window.prompt()` calls freeze Playwright sessions and are a common source of exploratory session timeouts. This pattern registers a dialog listener at the start of every session that records all dialogs and auto-dismisses them, converting session-blocking dialogs from fatal errors into observable signals for the charter.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface DialogRecord {
  type: string;
  message: string;
  url: string;
  timestamp: number;
}

test('settings deletion flow — no unexpected confirm dialogs on cancel', async ({ page }) => {
  const dialogs: DialogRecord[] = [];

  page.on('dialog', async dialog => {
    dialogs.push({
      type: dialog.type(),
      message: dialog.message(),
      url: page.url(),
      timestamp: Date.now(),
    });
    // Accept all dialogs to prevent session freeze; analyse after
    await dialog.accept();
  });

  await page.goto('/settings/account');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete account' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' }).click();

  // Charter: pressing Cancel should not trigger a browser-native confirm
  const unexpectedDialogs = dialogs.filter(d => d.type === 'confirm');
  expect(
    unexpectedDialogs,
    `Unexpected native confirm dialogs:\n${JSON.stringify(unexpectedDialogs, null, 2)}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);

  // Charter: the account settings page should still be accessible after cancel
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/settings\/account/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Auto-accepting all dialogs with `dialog.accept()` masks intentional UX — some dialogs are correct product behaviour (e.g., a confirm before a destructive action). If the charter is specifically exploring a destructive flow, use a conditional handler that rejects (`dialog.dismiss()`) to explore the cancellation path and accepts only when proceeding. Auto-accept is appropriate only for defensive session harnesses that want to prevent freezes during broad exploratory sweeps; targeted charters should handle dialog intent explicitly.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 366 — `locator.filter({ hasText, has })` Contextual Row Finder Charter for Complex List Exploration

Exploratory sessions on list and table UIs need to target specific rows by compound criteria — matching a row that contains both a specific text label and a specific status indicator, without relying on brittle CSS selectors or row indices that shift with data. `locator.filter()` composes predicates on an existing locator match set, enabling human-readable, resilient row selection in charters for CRUD, bulk-edit, and filtering workflows.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice list — overdue invoices have correct action menu options', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/invoices');

  // Find all rows that contain both "Overdue" badge and a specific vendor name
  const overdueAcmeRow = page
    .getByRole('row')
    .filter({ hasText: 'Acme Corp' })
    .filter({ has: page.getByTestId('badge-overdue') });

  await expect(overdueAcmeRow).toHaveCount(1);

  // Open the action menu for that specific row
  await overdueAcmeRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Actions' }).click();

  const menu = page.getByRole('menu');
  await expect(menu).toBeVisible();

  // Charter: overdue invoices must offer a "Send reminder" action
  await expect(menu.getByRole('menuitem', { name: 'Send reminder' })).toBeVisible();
  // Charter: overdue invoices must NOT offer "Mark as paid" from the quick menu
  await expect(menu.getByRole('menuitem', { name: /mark as paid/i })).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Chaining multiple `.filter()` calls narrows the match set but can produce misleadingly-passing tests when the compound predicate accidentally matches zero rows if test data is wrong — `toHaveCount(1)` is essential to assert that the selection is unique before proceeding. Without the count assertion, `overdueAcmeRow.getByRole('button', ...)` on an empty locator will silently pass `not.toBeVisible()` assertions and fail `click()` with a confusing timeout error. Always follow a chained `filter()` with an explicit count or visibility assertion before interacting with the matched element.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 367 — `page.clock.freeze()` Deterministic Time Charter for Expiry and Scheduling Exploration

Time-dependent features — session expiry warnings, scheduled notifications, token refresh windows, coupon expiry — cannot be explored with real clock time without waiting minutes or hours. `page.clock.freeze()` stops the JavaScript clock at a specified timestamp, and `page.clock.fastForward()` advances it by a given millisecond delta, enabling deterministic exploration of time-sensitive branches in seconds.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session expiry — warning banner appears 5 minutes before timeout', async ({ page }) => {
  // Freeze time at a known point: user logged in, session valid for 30 minutes
  const SESSION_START = new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00Z').getTime();
  const SESSION_TTL_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000; // 30 minutes
  const WARNING_THRESHOLD_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000; // 5 minutes before expiry

  await page.clock.install({ time: SESSION_START });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Charter: no warning banner at session start
  await expect(page.getByTestId('session-expiry-warning')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Fast-forward to 25 minutes in (5 minutes before expiry)
  await page.clock.fastForward(SESSION_TTL_MS - WARNING_THRESHOLD_MS);
  await page.waitForTimeout(100); // allow React re-render cycle

  // Charter: warning banner must appear
  await expect(page.getByTestId('session-expiry-warning')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('session-expiry-warning')).toContainText(/5 minutes/);

  // Fast-forward past expiry
  await page.clock.fastForward(WARNING_THRESHOLD_MS + 1000);
  await page.waitForTimeout(100);

  // Charter: session expired — redirect to login
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.clock.install()` only controls the browser's JavaScript clock (`Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`). If the application validates session expiry on the server by comparing the request timestamp against a stored session record, the server will not observe the frozen time and will not expire the session. This charter is therefore only valid for client-driven expiry logic (e.g., a React countdown timer that triggers logout). For server-enforced expiry, you must also mock the session API endpoint to return a 401 at the appropriate time using `page.route()` alongside `page.clock`.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 368 — `test.extend()` Auto-Fixture Trace-on-Failure Charter for Zero-Config Session Evidence

Capturing Playwright traces manually requires remembering to configure tracing in each test. An automatic fixture using `{ auto: true }` intercepts test teardown to start tracing at test begin and attach the trace to `testInfo` only on failure, combining session evidence with zero test boilerplate. This pattern is especially valuable during exploratory sprint cycles where new charters are written rapidly.

```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

export const test = base.extend<{ _autoTrace: void }>({
  _autoTrace: [async ({ context }, use, testInfo) => {
    // Start tracing unconditionally at test begin
    await context.tracing.start({
      screenshots: true,
      snapshots: true,
      sources: true,
    });

    await use(); // run the test

    // Only keep the trace if the test failed or had a timeout
    if (testInfo.status !== 'passed' && testInfo.status !== 'skipped') {
      const tracePath = path.join(
        testInfo.outputDir,
        `trace-${testInfo.title.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}.zip`
      );
      await context.tracing.stop({ path: tracePath });
      await testInfo.attach('session-trace', {
        path: tracePath,
        contentType: 'application/zip',
      });
    } else {
      await context.tracing.stop(); // discard without saving on pass
    }
  }, { auto: true }],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Tracing with `screenshots: true` and `snapshots: true` adds 10–30% overhead to test execution time due to DOM serialisation and screenshot capture at each action. On very long exploratory sessions (10+ minutes of interaction), trace files can reach 500 MB+. For production CI pipelines, configure tracing at the project level with `trace: 'on-first-retry'` rather than using an auto-fixture, which limits trace collection to failing retries. The auto-fixture is most appropriate for short exploratory sessions during sprint development where failure evidence is needed immediately without project-level configuration changes.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 369 — `page.route()` Response-Header Injection Charter for Security Header Exploration

Security headers (`Content-Security-Policy`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Content-Type-Options`) are often set correctly in production but missing in staging or development environments. This pattern injects, removes, or modifies security response headers via `page.route()` to explore how the application behaves when security headers are present, absent, or deliberately misconfigured — without needing access to the back-end server configuration.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('CSP: inline script blocked by strict policy — no uncaught eval errors', async ({ page }) => {
  // Inject a strict Content-Security-Policy that blocks unsafe-inline and eval
  await page.route('**', async route => {
    const response = await route.fetch();
    const headers = response.headers();
    headers['content-security-policy'] =
      "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; object-src 'none'";
    // Remove legacy permissive headers that might override CSP
    delete headers['x-content-security-policy'];
    await route.fulfill({ response, headers });
  });

  const cspViolations: string[] = [];
  // CSP violations are reported as security policy violation events
  await page.exposeFunction('__reportCspViolation', (msg: string) => {
    cspViolations.push(msg);
  });
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    document.addEventListener('securitypolicyviolation', e => {
      (window as any).__reportCspViolation(
        `${e.violatedDirective}: ${e.blockedURI}`
      );
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Charter: core app should function with strict CSP — no violations expected
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
  expect(
    cspViolations,
    `CSP violations under strict policy:\n${cspViolations.join('\n')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Injecting headers via `page.route()` operates at the Playwright network interception layer, which processes headers after the browser's own security model. Chrome ignores some CSP headers injected after redirect chains, and `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` requires a reporting endpoint to collect violations, which this pattern does not provide. The `securitypolicyviolation` DOM event listener is the most portable alternative for violation collection in a Playwright context. For comprehensive security header exploration, supplement this charter with an OWASP ZAP passive scan against the real staging environment where headers are set at the HTTP server level.

**Tag:** [official]

---

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 52)

**G35. `page.route('**', handler)` catch-all route interceptors silently apply to all requests including Playwright's own internal requests (e.g., `playwright.dev` beacon URLs used by test tooling), and when the handler calls `route.fetch()` to forward the request, any fetch error from a non-app URL propagates as an unhandled promise rejection that can destabilise the entire test worker — not just the individual test.**
A team added a catch-all response-header injection route to a global `beforeAll` hook, intending to add security headers to all application responses. Within two hours, flaky test-worker crashes began appearing with the message "Failed to fetch: net::ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED" because `route.fetch()` was being called for Playwright telemetry and browser update check URLs that are blocked by the corporate proxy. The fix was to narrow the route pattern to `**/api/**` or the application's known origin, not `**`. WHY this matters: `page.route('**', ...)` matches every request the browser makes, including browser-internal requests, third-party CDNs, and telemetry pings that are irrelevant to the application under test; always scope route intercept patterns to the application origin or API path prefix to avoid unintended interception of infrastructure traffic that can destabilise the test runner.

**G36. `expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` baselines generated on a developer laptop running macOS with a Retina display are incompatible with baselines generated in a Linux CI container — even with identical viewport sizes and headless mode, sub-pixel anti-aliasing differences cause pixel-diff failures of 5–15% even on unchanged UI, making visual regression tests permanently flakey when baselines and CI environments do not match.**
A team introduced `toHaveScreenshot()` for a design system component library and immediately saw 8–12% pixel-diff failures in every CI run, despite the UI being visually identical. Investigation revealed that macOS Retina displays render at device pixel ratio 2 while the CI Docker container rendered at DPR 1, producing differently-aliased text. The fix was to generate all baselines exclusively in the CI Docker container using `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` and commit those baselines — never from a developer machine. WHY this matters: `toHaveScreenshot()` baselines are environment-specific binary artifacts; the golden rule is "baselines are generated in the same environment where comparisons run" — use a dedicated Docker image for all visual snapshot management and document this constraint in the contributing guide to prevent local baseline commits.

**G37. `locator.filter({ has: page.getByRole(...) })` silently succeeds with an empty locator when the inner `has` predicate locator is resolved in a different `Page` or `BrowserContext` instance than the outer locator — Playwright performs the filter relative to each outer element's subtree, but cross-context locators have no shared DOM, returning zero matches that then pass `not.toBeVisible()` assertions trivially and fail `click()` assertions with confusing messages.**
A team extracted a shared `page.getByRole('badge')` locator into a test helper function that received `page` from a different test context than the one used to build the outer `getByRole('row')` locator. All `.filter({ has: badge })` calls returned empty match sets because the `badge` locator was bound to a different page instance. The fix was to ensure both the outer locator and the `has` locator are constructed from the same `page` instance, which the TypeScript type system does not enforce at compile time. WHY this matters: Playwright locators are bound to the `Page` or `Frame` instance they were created from; mixing locators across page instances in `filter({ has })` or `locator.and()` produces silently-empty match sets — always construct compound locators from a single page instance and add a `toHaveCount(n)` assertion immediately after to catch accidental empty matches before any interaction.

**G38. `page.clock.install()` overrides `Date`, `setTimeout`, and `setInterval` globally in the browser context, but it does not intercept `queueMicrotask()`, `requestAnimationFrame()`, or `Promise` microtask scheduling — application code that uses `requestAnimationFrame`-based animation timers or `Promise.resolve().then()` deferral chains for UI updates will run at real time even when the clock is frozen, causing race conditions where the controlled clock fires a timeout callback before the rAF-driven animation that it depends on has completed.**
A team testing a toast notification that auto-dismissed after 5 seconds used `page.clock.fastForward(5100)` and then immediately asserted `not.toBeVisible()`. The assertion passed inconsistently because the dismissal animation (driven by `requestAnimationFrame` at 60fps) had not completed when the assertion fired — the clock advanced the `setTimeout` correctly but `rAF` callbacks continued on the real clock. The fix was to add `await page.waitForTimeout(500)` (real time) after `fastForward()` to allow rAF-driven animations to settle before asserting. WHY this matters: `page.clock` controls only the JavaScript timer API; animation-frame scheduling and microtask queues operate on the browser's native rendering pipeline which is outside `page.clock`'s scope — always add a short real-time pause after `fastForward()` when the UI under test uses CSS transitions or rAF-driven state changes.

**G39. `test.extend()` fixtures that perform `async` setup inside a `[async, { scope: 'worker' }]` fixture using `await page.goto()` will fail with "Target page, context or browser has been closed" when the worker processes a test file that does not import the `page` fixture — because the worker-scoped fixture is initialised before any page is created, the `page` fixture is not available in the worker scope and Playwright throws a cryptic scope mismatch error that appears to blame the wrong fixture.**
A team attempted to build a worker-scoped authentication fixture that navigated to a login page to acquire a session cookie, passing `{ page }` as a dependency. The fixture compiled successfully but crashed with "page is not defined in worker scope" on any test file that did not directly use the `page` fixture in a test body. The fix was to use the `browser` worker-scoped built-in fixture to create a temporary page for authentication, use it to acquire the session, close it, and pass the resulting `storageState` string to test-scoped fixtures for page creation. WHY this matters: `page` is a test-scoped fixture and cannot be used as a dependency inside worker-scoped fixtures; authentication flows that require a browser page for cookie acquisition must create and dispose their own temporary page via the worker-scoped `browser` fixture, storing only serialisable state (e.g., `storageState` JSON) for handoff to test-scoped fixtures.

### Pattern 370 — `browserContext.route()` vs `page.route()` Scope-Awareness Charter for Popup and Multi-Tab Exploration

When a user action opens a new browser tab or popup window, `page.route()` intercepts only requests from the originating page — the popup page makes its own requests outside that scope. This charter uses `browserContext.route()` to register a single intercept handler covering all pages in the context, including dynamically-opened popups, so that network mocking, latency injection, and abort testing apply uniformly across the full multi-tab user journey.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('popup share-link page loads correctly under rate-limit simulation', async ({
  context, page,
}) => {
  // context-level route covers pages opened via window.open or target="_blank"
  await context.route('**/api/share/**', async route => {
    // simulate a rate-limit response for the share endpoint
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 429,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'rate_limit', retryAfter: 30 }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Trigger action that opens a popup
  const [popup] = await Promise.all([
    context.waitForEvent('page'),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Share' }).click(),
  ]);

  await popup.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  // Verify the popup page handles the 429 gracefully
  await expect(popup.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/rate limit|try again/i);
  // Confirm the originating page is unaffected
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `browserContext.route()` applies to every page in the context, so a mocking rule intended for a popup may inadvertently intercept the same endpoint on the parent page if the parent also calls it. Scope the URL pattern as tightly as possible (e.g., `**/api/share/**` rather than `**/api/**`) and add `page.unroute()` cleanup where needed to avoid bleed-through. For tests where the parent page must hit the real API, create a separate BrowserContext for the popup-isolated scenario.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 371 — `serviceWorkers: 'block'` BrowserContext Charter for Service-Worker-Free Baseline Exploration

Service Workers intercept network requests before Playwright's own route handlers can see them, silently caching responses or serving stale data during a session. This charter creates a dedicated BrowserContext with `serviceWorkers: 'block'` and compares the application behaviour (network calls, response freshness, offline banner display) between the blocked-SW context and a normal context, surfacing SW-induced divergences that would otherwise be invisible to `page.route()`-based oracles.

```typescript
import { test, expect, chromium } from '@playwright/test';

test('product list shows fresh API data without service worker cache interference', async ({}) => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();

  // Context A: service workers blocked — requests reach server directly
  const ctxBlocked = await browser.newContext({ serviceWorkers: 'block' });
  const pageBlocked = await ctxBlocked.newPage();

  // Context B: service workers allowed — may serve cached responses
  const ctxNormal = await browser.newContext();
  const pageNormal = await ctxNormal.newPage();

  const apiCalls: Record<'blocked' | 'normal', number> = { blocked: 0, normal: 0 };

  pageBlocked.on('request', r => {
    if (r.url().includes('/api/products')) apiCalls.blocked++;
  });
  pageNormal.on('request', r => {
    if (r.url().includes('/api/products')) apiCalls.normal++;
  });

  await pageBlocked.goto('/products');
  await pageNormal.goto('/products');

  await pageBlocked.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
  await pageNormal.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // If SW intercepts in normal context, fewer real network requests are expected
  console.log('SW-blocked API calls:', apiCalls.blocked);
  console.log('Normal API calls:', apiCalls.normal);

  // Both pages should render the same product count
  const blockedCount = await pageBlocked.getByRole('listitem').count();
  const normalCount = await pageNormal.getByRole('listitem').count();
  expect(blockedCount, 'Product count divergence: SW may be serving stale data').toBe(normalCount);

  await ctxBlocked.close();
  await ctxNormal.close();
  await browser.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Blocking service workers removes offline-capable PWA features, push notifications, and background sync from the test context, so this charter is intentionally a comparison harness rather than a primary regression suite. Use it during dedicated SW-regression sessions or when investigating cache-related bugs. For environments that require SW-driven auth token injection (e.g., Firebase Auth with a SW), blocking SWs will break authentication; only apply `serviceWorkers: 'block'` when the charter explicitly targets network-path verification.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 372 — `page.emulate({ locale, timezoneId })` Locale-Switch-During-Session Charter for i18n Boundary Exploration

Most i18n test suites verify locale-specific rendering at page load time, but skip the case where a user changes their locale preference mid-session (e.g., via a language switcher) without reloading. This charter uses `page.context().setExtraHTTPHeaders()` plus `page.evaluate()` to simulate a mid-session locale change and verifies that date formats, currency symbols, number separators, and RTL layout all transition correctly without a full page reload.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const LOCALES = [
  { locale: 'de-DE', timezoneId: 'Europe/Berlin', currency: '€', decimalSep: ',' },
  { locale: 'ar-SA', timezoneId: 'Asia/Riyadh',   currency: 'ر.س', decimalSep: '.' },
  { locale: 'en-US', timezoneId: 'America/New_York', currency: '$', decimalSep: '.' },
] as const;

for (const { locale, timezoneId, currency, decimalSep } of LOCALES) {
  test(`invoice page renders correct currency and number format for ${locale}`, async ({
    browser,
  }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ locale, timezoneId });
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('/invoices/123');

    // Verify currency symbol appears in the total price
    const totalCell = page.getByRole('cell', { name: /total/i }).locator('+ td');
    await expect(totalCell).toContainText(currency);

    // Verify number decimal separator matches locale convention
    const priceText = await totalCell.textContent() ?? '';
    const hasCorrectDecimal = priceText.includes(decimalSep);
    expect(hasCorrectDecimal, `Decimal separator mismatch for ${locale}: "${priceText}"`).toBe(true);

    // For RTL locales, verify document direction attribute
    if (locale.startsWith('ar')) {
      const dir = await page.evaluate(() => document.documentElement.dir);
      expect(dir).toBe('rtl');
    }

    await context.close();
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Playwright's `locale` context option sets the `Accept-Language` HTTP header and `navigator.language`, but it does not automatically change the application's UI language if the app uses a client-side i18n library (e.g., i18next, react-intl) that reads `navigator.language` at module initialisation time rather than reactively. For such apps, supplement this charter with a `page.addInitScript()` that overrides `navigator.language` before the i18n library initialises, and verify the language switcher interaction independently.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 373 — `page.frameLocator()` Cross-Frame Interaction Charter for Embedded Widget Exploration

Embedded iframes (payment widgets, chat windows, OAuth consent dialogs) run in separate browsing contexts with their own DOM, and `page.getByRole()` locators silently skip iframe content without raising errors — returning empty matches that produce false-negative `not.toBeVisible()` passes. This charter uses `page.frameLocator()` to pierce the iframe boundary and verify the embedded widget's interactive elements, form submissions, and post-message communication back to the parent page.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Stripe payment widget accepts card number and posts success message to parent', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Locate the Stripe payment iframe by its title attribute
  const stripeFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[title*="Secure payment"]');

  // Interact with elements inside the iframe using the frame locator
  await stripeFrame.getByPlaceholder('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await stripeFrame.getByPlaceholder('MM / YY').fill('12 / 28');
  await stripeFrame.getByPlaceholder('CVC').fill('123');

  // Listen for postMessage from iframe to parent (payment success event)
  const messagePromise = page.waitForEvent('console', {
    predicate: msg => msg.text().includes('payment_success'),
    timeout: 10_000,
  });

  // Click pay button in the parent page (outside the iframe)
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  // Verify postMessage arrived (app must log it to console for this oracle)
  const successMsg = await messagePromise;
  expect(successMsg.text()).toContain('payment_success');

  // Verify parent page navigates to confirmation
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/order-confirmed/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.frameLocator()` works only when the iframe origin matches the test's context (same-origin) or when the test is run against a sandboxed environment where the iframe content is served locally. Cross-origin iframes (e.g., real Stripe Elements loaded from `js.stripe.com`) block Playwright from inspecting their DOM — the correct approach for cross-origin embedded widgets is to replace the real SDK with a test-double that exposes the same postMessage API surface but loads from the application's own origin.

**Tag:** [official]
