### Pattern 374 — `page.on('response')` Streaming Response Oracle Charter for Server-Sent Events and Chunked Transfer Exploration

Server-Sent Events (SSE) and chunked HTTP responses deliver data incrementally, but most network-level assertions only fire on the final response completion. This charter attaches a `page.on('response')` listener and inspects the `response.body()` stream incrementally, verifying that partial data is valid, that the `Content-Type: text/event-stream` header is set correctly, and that the UI updates progressively rather than waiting for the full payload.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface SseChunk {
  event?: string;
  data: string;
  receivedAt: number;
}

test('AI response stream delivers partial tokens progressively to the chat UI', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  const sseChunks: SseChunk[] = [];

  page.on('response', async response => {
    if (!response.url().includes('/api/chat/stream')) return;

    // Verify SSE content type is set correctly
    const ct = response.headers()['content-type'] ?? '';
    expect(ct).toContain('text/event-stream');

    const body = await response.body();
    const text = body.toString('utf-8');

    // Parse SSE format: "data: {...}\n\n"
    const lines = text.split('\n').filter(l => l.startsWith('data:'));
    for (const line of lines) {
      try {
        const payload = JSON.parse(line.slice(5).trim());
        sseChunks.push({ event: payload.event, data: payload.token ?? '', receivedAt: Date.now() });
      } catch { /* incomplete chunk at boundary — expected */ }
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/chat');
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Message' }).fill('Explain REST APIs in one sentence');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click();

  // Wait for the [DONE] sentinel or the stop button to disappear
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Stop' })).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: 30_000 });

  // Assert that streaming occurred (multiple chunks received, not a single dump)
  expect(sseChunks.length, 'Expected >3 SSE chunks for progressive streaming').toBeGreaterThan(3);

  // Verify the rendered output contains meaningful text
  await expect(page.getByRole('article').last()).not.toBeEmpty();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `response.body()` buffers the entire response body in memory even for streaming endpoints — it does not expose a Node.js readable stream for truly incremental processing. For very long AI-generated responses (>1 MB) or infinite-scroll feeds, this can cause the test to wait until the stream closes before any oracle fires. A more incremental approach is to use `page.on('requestfinished')` per-chunk via a chunked mocking harness, or to instrument the application's SSE client with `page.exposeFunction()` callbacks that report each token as it is appended to the DOM.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 375 — `page.evaluate()` + `MutationObserver` DOM-Mutation Charter for Asynchronous UI State Verification

React, Vue, and Angular applications update the DOM asynchronously after state changes, and a `locator.waitFor()` poll can succeed before a multi-step DOM mutation sequence has fully completed. This charter injects a `MutationObserver` into the page before the triggering action and records every attribute/text change on the target subtree, producing a mutation log that reveals intermediate states (e.g., `loading → error → empty` flash states) that are invisible to a simple `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface MutationRecord {
  type: string;
  target: string;
  attributeName: string | null;
  oldValue: string | null;
  newValue: string | null;
  timestamp: number;
}

test('search results transition through loading → results without an error flash', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('/search');

  // Expose a callback so the browser-side observer can push records to Node
  const mutations: MutationRecord[] = [];
  await page.exposeFunction('__recordMutation', (rec: MutationRecord) => {
    mutations.push(rec);
  });

  // Inject MutationObserver before triggering the search
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    const target = document.getElementById('search-results')!;
    const observer = new MutationObserver(records => {
      for (const r of records) {
        (window as any).__recordMutation({
          type: r.type,
          target: (r.target as Element).tagName ?? 'TEXT',
          attributeName: r.attributeName,
          oldValue: r.oldValue,
          newValue: r.type === 'attributes'
            ? (r.target as Element).getAttribute(r.attributeName!) ?? null
            : (r.target as Text).textContent?.slice(0, 80) ?? null,
          timestamp: Date.now(),
        });
      }
    });
    observer.observe(target, { childList: true, attributes: true, subtree: true, attributeOldValue: true });
  });

  await page.getByRole('searchbox').fill('playwright testing patterns');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();

  // Wait for stable end state
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount({ minimum: 1 }, { timeout: 15_000 });

  // Assert no error state was shown during the transition
  const errorStates = mutations.filter(m =>
    m.attributeName === 'data-state' && m.newValue === 'error'
  );
  expect(errorStates, `Unexpected error flash during search: ${JSON.stringify(errorStates)}`).toHaveLength(0);
  console.table(mutations.slice(0, 20)); // Log first 20 mutations for session notes
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `MutationObserver` records are serialised through `page.exposeFunction()`, which imposes a JSON-serialisation overhead per mutation. On pages with high-frequency DOM updates (virtual scroll lists, live data feeds), this can produce thousands of records per second and degrade test performance. Scope the `MutationObserver` to the smallest subtree needed and add a `maxRecords` guard that calls `observer.disconnect()` once a threshold is reached to cap memory usage.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 376 — `page.requestGC()` + `WeakRef` Memory-Leak Charter for Long-Running Session Exploration

Single-page applications that render and destroy components across navigation events can accumulate memory leaks through retained event listener references, uncleaned intervals, or component instances not released by the framework. This charter uses Playwright's `page.requestGC()` (v1.48+) to trigger a garbage collection cycle and then checks a `WeakRef` to a previously-destroyed component, verifying it has been reclaimed. Any non-null `WeakRef.deref()` after GC indicates a retention path.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('modal component is garbage-collected after close, no listener leak', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Register a WeakRef to a component instance before mount
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    // Expose hook so test can store a weak reference to the modal DOM node
    (window as any).__modalWeakRef = null;
    const observer = new MutationObserver(() => {
      const modal = document.querySelector('[role="dialog"]');
      if (modal && !(window as any).__modalWeakRef) {
        (window as any).__modalWeakRef = new WeakRef(modal);
        observer.disconnect();
      }
    });
    observer.observe(document.body, { childList: true, subtree: true });
  });

  // Open and then close the modal
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open Settings' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Close' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Request GC cycle to allow weak references to be cleared
  await page.requestGC();

  // Check if the WeakRef was collected (null deref = no leak)
  const isCollected = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const ref = (window as any).__modalWeakRef;
    return ref === null || ref.deref() === undefined;
  });

  expect(isCollected, 'Modal DOM node was not garbage-collected — possible listener leak').toBe(true);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.requestGC()` sends a hint to the V8 engine to run a major GC cycle, but the JavaScript specification does not guarantee that any particular object will be collected — the engine may defer collection if heap pressure is low. A single negative result (WeakRef still non-null) is not definitive proof of a leak; the charter should be run 3–5 times in sequence with intermediate navigation events to amplify heap pressure before declaring a failure. For production-grade memory leak investigation, supplement this pattern with Chrome DevTools Protocol heap snapshots via `cdpSession.send('HeapProfiler.takeHeapSnapshot')`.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 377 — `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` Auth-State Rotation Charter for Firebase/IndexedDB App Exploration

Applications that use Firebase Auth, Supabase, or other SDKs that persist session tokens in IndexedDB (not cookies or localStorage) are invisible to the default `storageState` capture, meaning `context.storageState()` returns empty auth data and every test re-authenticates from scratch. This charter uses the `{ indexedDB: true }` option (v1.51+) to include IndexedDB contents in the stored state, verifying that mid-session token refresh, concurrent-tab auth sharing, and forced sign-out propagate correctly across contexts.

```typescript
import { test, expect, chromium } from '@playwright/test';
import * as path from 'path';
import * as fs from 'fs';

const STATE_FILE = '/tmp/firebase-auth-state.json';

test.describe.serial('Firebase auth state persistence', () => {
  test('capture IndexedDB auth state after login', async ({}) => {
    const browser = await chromium.launch();
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();

    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('tester@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

    // Wait for Firebase to write auth token to IndexedDB
    await page.waitForFunction(() =>
      indexedDB.databases().then(dbs => dbs.some(db => db.name?.includes('firebaseLocalStorage')))
    );

    // Capture state including IndexedDB
    await context.storageState({ path: STATE_FILE, indexedDB: true });
    await browser.close();

    expect(fs.existsSync(STATE_FILE)).toBe(true);
    const state = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(STATE_FILE, 'utf-8'));
    expect(state.origins.some((o: any) => o.indexedDB?.length > 0)).toBe(true);
  });

  test('restore IndexedDB auth state and access protected route', async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: STATE_FILE });
    const page = await context.newPage();

    // Should access the protected route without re-authenticating
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /dashboard/i })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page).not.toHaveURL(/\/login/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `indexedDB: true` option serialises the entire IndexedDB store to JSON, which can be very large for applications that cache API responses or asset manifests in IndexedDB (e.g., Workbox offline cache). Inspect the captured state file size before committing it to version control — files over 1 MB should be generated in CI on each run rather than checked in. Additionally, Firebase auth tokens expire; if the state file is reused across test runs without regeneration, the token will expire and tests will fail with auth errors that superficially resemble routing bugs.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 378 — `toContainClass()` CSS-State Oracle Charter for Component Visual-State Verification

CSS classes are the primary mechanism through which React/Vue/Angular components communicate visual state (disabled, active, selected, error, loading) to stylesheets. Asserting that a specific class is present or absent after an interaction is more robust than asserting on CSS property values (which require `page.evaluate()`) and more semantically precise than `toHaveAttribute('class', ...)` exact-string matching. This charter uses `expect(locator).toContainClass()` (v1.52+) to verify component state transitions through their CSS class interface.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('cart checkout button progresses through idle → loading → disabled CSS states', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');

  const checkoutBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' });

  // Initial state: button should be enabled (no disabled class)
  await expect(checkoutBtn).not.toContainClass('btn-disabled');
  await expect(checkoutBtn).toContainClass('btn-primary');

  // Intercept the checkout API to add artificial delay for loading state capture
  await page.route('**/api/checkout', async route => {
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 800));
    await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: '123' }) });
  });

  // Trigger checkout
  checkoutBtn.click(); // don't await — check intermediate state

  // Immediately verify loading state CSS class appears
  await expect(checkoutBtn).toContainClass('btn-loading', { timeout: 500 });

  // During loading, the button should also be disabled
  await expect(checkoutBtn).toContainClass('btn-disabled', { timeout: 500 });

  // After completion, loading class should clear
  await expect(checkoutBtn).not.toContainClass('btn-loading', { timeout: 5_000 });
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/order-confirmed/, { timeout: 5_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toContainClass()` asserts on the class attribute's string content, making it sensitive to CSS framework refactoring where a class is renamed (e.g., `btn-loading` becomes `is-loading`). Unlike `toHaveRole()` or `toHaveAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true')`, CSS class assertions are tied to implementation details rather than semantic contracts. Prefer ARIA attribute assertions (`toHaveAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true')`, `toHaveAttribute('aria-busy', 'true')`) for state that maps cleanly to ARIA roles; use `toContainClass()` as a supplementary oracle when ARIA attributes are absent from the component design.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 379 — `page.on('requestfailed')` + `failOnFlakyTests` Flaky-Request Charter for Network Reliability Exploration

A request that fails intermittently under normal load (DNS timeout, connection reset, TLS handshake failure) produces a `requestfailed` event in Playwright that most tests silently ignore because the UI may recover gracefully. This charter attaches a `requestfailed` listener as a session-wide oracle to capture every failed request URL, status, and failure reason, then asserts that no mission-critical endpoints (auth, checkout, data-save) appear in the failure log — surfacing transient network errors that the UI masks with silent retries.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const CRITICAL_ENDPOINTS = ['/api/auth', '/api/checkout', '/api/save', '/api/upload'];

interface FailedRequest {
  url: string;
  method: string;
  failure: string;
  timestamp: number;
}

test('critical API endpoints produce no network failures during checkout flow', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  const failedRequests: FailedRequest[] = [];

  page.on('requestfailed', req => {
    const url = req.url();
    const isCritical = CRITICAL_ENDPOINTS.some(ep => url.includes(ep));
    if (isCritical) {
      failedRequests.push({
        url,
        method: req.method(),
        failure: req.failure()?.errorText ?? 'unknown',
        timestamp: Date.now(),
      });
    }
  });

  // Execute a representative checkout journey
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/order-confirmed/, { timeout: 15_000 });

  expect(
    failedRequests,
    `Critical endpoint failures detected:\n${JSON.stringify(failedRequests, null, 2)}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.on('requestfailed')` only fires for network-layer failures (DNS errors, TCP resets, TLS failures) — it does not fire for HTTP 4xx/5xx responses that represent successful TCP connections but application-level errors. To catch 500 errors on critical endpoints, combine this listener with a `page.on('response')` handler that checks `response.status()` for the same CRITICAL_ENDPOINTS list. Running this charter under a real network with artificial packet loss (e.g., via `tc netem` on Linux) is more revealing than running against a localhost server where network failures are rare.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 380 — `locator.and()` Multi-Criterion Disambiguation Charter for Dense-UI Element Identification

Pages with design systems that reuse the same ARIA role and label across multiple contexts (e.g., multiple "Edit" buttons in a table) produce strict-mode violations when addressed by `getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' })`. Rather than falling back to fragile nth-child selectors or test IDs, this charter uses `locator.and()` to compose two orthogonal criteria — role+name AND a data attribute or ancestor context — into a single strict locator, and documents the composition strategy as a reusable pattern for the session.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('edit button in "Billing" row opens correct account section, not "Shipping"', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('/account/addresses');

  // Strict failure: both rows have an "Edit" button
  // page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' }) → strict mode violation

  // Safe: compose role+name with row ancestor context using locator.and()
  const billingSection = page.getByRole('region', { name: 'Billing address' });
  const editBillingBtn = billingSection.getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' });

  // Alternative with .and() for cross-cutting criteria:
  const editBtnWithTestId = page
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' })
    .and(page.locator('[data-section="billing"]'));

  // Use the ancestor-scoped locator for the interaction
  await editBillingBtn.click();

  // Verify the correct form opened
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Edit billing address' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Edit shipping address' })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Verify the form is pre-populated with billing data, not shipping data
  const city = page.getByRole('dialog').getByLabel('City');
  await expect(city).not.toBeEmpty();

  // Cross-verify: editBtnWithTestId resolves to the same element
  const [a, b] = await Promise.all([
    editBillingBtn.getAttribute('data-testid'),
    editBtnWithTestId.getAttribute('data-testid'),
  ]);
  expect(a).toBe(b);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.and()` requires that both locators be resolved from the same `page` instance (the cross-context caveat from G37 applies here too). The ancestor-scoping approach (`billingSection.getByRole('button', ...)`) is generally preferred because it mirrors how a user would describe the element ("the Edit button in the Billing section") and is more resilient to data-attribute changes. Use `locator.and()` when the two distinguishing criteria cannot be expressed as a parent–child DOM relationship — for example, when the selector criteria span different DOM branches connected only by a shared data attribute.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 381 — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` Concurrent-Session Charter for Race-Condition Exploration

Race conditions in shared-state operations (concurrent form submissions, parallel file uploads, simultaneous shopping cart modifications) are invisible in sequential test suites because operations never overlap. This charter enables `{ mode: 'parallel' }` within a describe block to run two or more test workers simultaneously against the same application instance, triggering concurrent actions and asserting on the combined outcome to detect double-submission, lost-update, and optimistic-lock failures.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Run all tests in this describe block in parallel, in the same worker
test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' });

const BASE_URL = process.env.APP_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000';

test('user A and user B can add to cart concurrently without losing items', async ({
  browser,
}) => {
  // Create two independent browser contexts for concurrent users
  const [ctxA, ctxB] = await Promise.all([
    browser.newContext({ storageState: 'auth/user-a.json' }),
    browser.newContext({ storageState: 'auth/user-b.json' }),
  ]);

  const [pageA, pageB] = await Promise.all([
    ctxA.newPage(),
    ctxB.newPage(),
  ]);

  // Both users navigate to the product simultaneously
  await Promise.all([
    pageA.goto(`${BASE_URL}/product/42`),
    pageB.goto(`${BASE_URL}/product/42`),
  ]);

  // Both add to cart at the same time
  await Promise.all([
    pageA.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click(),
    pageB.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click(),
  ]);

  // Each user's cart should contain exactly one item (no cross-contamination)
  await Promise.all([
    pageA.goto(`${BASE_URL}/cart`),
    pageB.goto(`${BASE_URL}/cart`),
  ]);

  const [cartCountA, cartCountB] = await Promise.all([
    pageA.getByRole('listitem').count(),
    pageB.getByRole('listitem').count(),
  ]);

  expect(cartCountA).toBe(1);
  expect(cartCountB).toBe(1);

  await Promise.all([ctxA.close(), ctxB.close()]);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` requires that each test in the block is fully independent and does not share mutable fixtures (e.g., a single database record that both tests modify). Running concurrent tests against a shared database without row-level locking can produce test data corruption that outlives the test run, polluting subsequent test runs. Always pair this pattern with a dedicated test-data isolation strategy (unique user accounts per test, per-run table prefixes, or a database transaction rollback mechanism) to avoid flakiness cascade from concurrent data mutations.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 382 — `page.evaluate()` + `PerformanceMark` Charter for User-Perceived Interaction Latency Measurement

Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) measure page-load quality, but interaction latency within an already-loaded SPA is not captured by standard CWV tooling. This charter injects `performance.mark()` calls around user interactions (button click to result render) and uses `performance.measure()` to compute the elapsed time as a custom metric, asserting that interaction latency stays within defined thresholds during exploratory sessions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface InteractionTiming {
  name: string;
  startTime: number;
  duration: number;
  withinThreshold: boolean;
}

const LATENCY_THRESHOLDS_MS: Record<string, number> = {
  'search-to-results': 1000,
  'add-to-cart': 300,
  'checkout-form-submit': 2000,
};

async function measureInteraction(
  page: import('@playwright/test').Page,
  name: string,
  action: () => Promise<void>,
  readySignal: () => Promise<void>
): Promise<InteractionTiming> {
  await page.evaluate((n) => performance.mark(`${n}-start`), name);
  await action();
  await readySignal();
  await page.evaluate((n) => performance.mark(`${n}-end`), name);

  const { startTime, duration } = await page.evaluate((n) => {
    const m = performance.measure(n, `${n}-start`, `${n}-end`);
    return { startTime: m.startTime, duration: m.duration };
  }, name);

  return {
    name,
    startTime,
    duration,
    withinThreshold: duration <= (LATENCY_THRESHOLDS_MS[name] ?? Infinity),
  };
}

test('search interaction latency stays within 1 second threshold', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');

  const timing = await measureInteraction(
    page,
    'search-to-results',
    () => page.getByRole('searchbox').fill('exploratory testing'),
    () => expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5_000 })
  );

  console.log(`Interaction '${timing.name}': ${timing.duration.toFixed(1)}ms`);

  expect(
    timing.withinThreshold,
    `Interaction '${timing.name}' took ${timing.duration.toFixed(1)}ms — exceeds ${LATENCY_THRESHOLDS_MS[timing.name]}ms threshold`
  ).toBe(true);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `performance.mark()` timestamps are recorded in the browser's high-resolution time domain and include rendering pipeline overhead, but they do not include network round-trip time unless the action triggers a new navigation. For API-latency attribution, supplement this oracle with a `page.on('response')` handler that records response timing for the triggered request and cross-references it with the `performance.measure()` duration to distinguish "slow API" from "slow rendering" as root causes.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 383 — `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` Request-Spoofing Charter for A/B Test and Canary-Routing Exploration

Many applications route requests to experimental features via HTTP header flags (`X-Feature-Flag`, `X-AB-Test-Group`, `X-Canary-User`). These routing decisions happen at the edge (CDN, API gateway) and are invisible to feature-flag client libraries that operate in the browser. This charter uses `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` to inject custom routing headers and verifies that the correct variant is served, that the variant does not break the baseline UX, and that the header is not reflected back to the client in a way that exposes internal routing logic.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const VARIANTS = [
  { header: { 'X-AB-Test-Group': 'control' },   expectedTitle: /checkout v1/i },
  { header: { 'X-AB-Test-Group': 'treatment-a' }, expectedTitle: /checkout v2/i },
  { header: { 'X-AB-Test-Group': 'treatment-b' }, expectedTitle: /checkout v3/i },
] as const;

for (const { header, expectedTitle } of VARIANTS) {
  test(`checkout renders correct variant for ${JSON.stringify(header)}`, async ({ page }) => {
    // Inject routing header for all requests in this test
    await page.setExtraHTTPHeaders(header);

    await page.goto('/checkout');

    // Verify the correct variant is rendered
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveText(expectedTitle);

    // Verify internal routing header is NOT reflected in page content (info-leak check)
    const pageText = await page.textContent('body') ?? '';
    expect(pageText).not.toContain('X-AB-Test-Group');
    expect(pageText).not.toContain('treatment-a');

    // Verify checkout flow completes for this variant (smoke test each branch)
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay|continue/i })).toBeEnabled();
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` applies to all requests from the page, including third-party analytics, CDN asset fetches, and font loads — injecting custom headers to these requests may violate CDN caching policies or trigger CORS preflight rejections from origins that do not expect the custom header. Scope the header injection to application-origin requests only by combining it with a `page.route()` handler that removes the custom header from third-party requests before forwarding. Also note that headers set via `setExtraHTTPHeaders()` persist for the lifetime of the page object; always use a fresh page per variant to prevent header bleed between variant tests.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 384 — `page.coverage` JavaScript/CSS Coverage Charter for Dead-Code and Unused-Style Exploration

JavaScript and CSS coverage data reveals which lines of application code and which CSS rules are exercised during a user journey. Exploratory sessions that capture coverage can surface dead code paths (unreachable feature branches, orphaned error handlers), unused CSS rules that increase bundle size, and code paths that are only reachable through unusual interaction sequences. This charter uses Playwright's `page.coverage.startJSCoverage()` / `page.coverage.startCSSCoverage()` APIs to collect per-journey coverage and flags scripts or stylesheets where coverage drops below a meaningful threshold.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface CoverageReport {
  url: string;
  type: 'js' | 'css';
  totalBytes: number;
  usedBytes: number;
  usagePercent: number;
}

test('checkout user journey covers >60% of checkout bundle JS', async ({ page }) => {
  // Start coverage collection before navigation
  await page.coverage.startJSCoverage({ resetOnNavigation: false });
  await page.coverage.startCSSCoverage({ resetOnNavigation: false });

  // Execute representative checkout journey
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('tester@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/order-confirmed/, { timeout: 15_000 });

  // Stop and collect coverage
  const [jsCoverage, cssCoverage] = await Promise.all([
    page.coverage.stopJSCoverage(),
    page.coverage.stopCSSCoverage(),
  ]);

  const reports: CoverageReport[] = [];

  for (const entry of jsCoverage) {
    if (!entry.url.includes('checkout')) continue; // focus on checkout bundle
    const totalBytes = entry.text?.length ?? 0;
    const usedBytes = entry.ranges.reduce((sum, r) => sum + (r.end - r.start), 0);
    reports.push({
      url: entry.url,
      type: 'js',
      totalBytes,
      usedBytes,
      usagePercent: totalBytes > 0 ? (usedBytes / totalBytes) * 100 : 0,
    });
  }

  console.table(reports.map(r => ({
    url: r.url.split('/').pop(),
    type: r.type,
    usagePercent: r.usagePercent.toFixed(1) + '%',
    unusedKB: ((r.totalBytes - r.usedBytes) / 1024).toFixed(1),
  })));

  // Assert checkout bundle coverage threshold
  const checkoutReports = reports.filter(r => r.type === 'js');
  for (const r of checkoutReports) {
    expect(
      r.usagePercent,
      `Low JS coverage for ${r.url}: ${r.usagePercent.toFixed(1)}% — consider dead code removal`
    ).toBeGreaterThan(60);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.coverage` is Chromium-only — Firefox and WebKit do not expose the CDP coverage API, so this charter cannot run in cross-browser mode. Coverage percentages are also journey-specific: a checkout bundle may have 80% coverage in the happy path but 20% in the error-recovery path, so a single-journey coverage report overstates real-world coverage. Use this pattern as a discovery tool to identify candidate files for dead-code analysis, not as a hard gate. For production coverage analysis, supplement with Istanbul/nyc instrumentation in CI across all test suites to compute aggregate coverage.

**Tag:** [official]

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 53)

**G40. `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` does not clear headers set in a previous `page.goto()` call when the page navigates to a different origin via a server-side redirect — headers set before the initial navigation are re-sent on the redirect destination if it shares the same renderer process, causing the target origin to receive internal routing headers (e.g., `X-AB-Test-Group`, `X-Canary-User`) that were intended only for the originating origin, and in some configurations this triggers a CORS preflight rejection on the redirect destination.**
A team running A/B variant routing tests injected `X-AB-Test-Group: treatment-a` via `setExtraHTTPHeaders()` before navigating to a payment gateway redirect flow. The payment provider's `/callback` URL received the `X-AB-Test-Group` header and rejected the preflight request with `403 Forbidden` because their CORS policy did not allow custom headers from the application origin. The tests failed with an opaque network error that did not mention the extra header as the cause. The fix was to use `page.route('**/app-origin/**', async route => { ... })` to selectively inject the routing header only for application-origin requests, stripping it from all cross-origin requests before forwarding via `route.fulfill({ response, headers: stripped })`. WHY this matters: `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` is a blunt instrument that applies to every request in the page regardless of origin; for routing headers that are internal to your application, always use `page.route()` with origin-scoped patterns to prevent header leakage to third-party services that may reject or mis-process them.

**G41. `page.coverage.startJSCoverage()` silently produces empty ranges for scripts loaded via `<script type="module">` with dynamic `import()` calls when the test page uses a Vite or Rollup dev server in ESM mode — the coverage API tracks coverage at the script-URL level, but dynamically-imported module chunks have different URLs than the entry-point script, so the entry-point shows near-zero coverage while the actual executed code in the dynamic chunk is never reported, giving a false impression of very low test coverage.**
A team adopted `page.coverage` to measure checkout journey coverage and observed that their main `checkout.js` bundle showed only 3% coverage despite the entire checkout flow completing successfully. Investigation revealed that Vite had split the checkout bundle into 14 dynamic import chunks at URLs like `/assets/checkout-form-Cx2aK.js`, none of which appeared in the `jsCoverage` results because the test charter only filtered for entries matching `checkout`. The fix was to remove the URL filter and collect all coverage entries with `usedBytes > 0`, then group them by their originating feature based on file-path prefix. WHY this matters: modern ESM-based build tools produce many small dynamic chunks, and `page.coverage.startJSCoverage()` reports each chunk URL individually; always collect all coverage entries without a URL filter first, then apply grouping logic post-collection to avoid missing dynamically-imported code from your coverage analysis.

**G42. `context.waitForEvent('page')` for popup detection has a race condition when the action that opens the popup is a programmatic `window.open()` triggered inside a `setTimeout` or Promise microtask — if the `setTimeout` delay is shorter than the time for Playwright to register the `waitForEvent` listener, the popup `page` event fires before Playwright begins listening and is silently missed, causing the `Promise.all([context.waitForEvent('page'), action])` pattern to hang indefinitely rather than resolving.**
A team testing a "Share" button that opens a preview popup observed intermittent timeouts on `context.waitForEvent('page')` even though the popup was visually opening in slow-motion video captures. Code review revealed that the application's share handler called `window.open()` inside a `Promise.resolve().then()` microtask, which resolved before Playwright had finished setting up the event listener in the `Promise.all`. The fix was to register the `context.waitForEvent('page')` promise before calling any action (not inside `Promise.all`) and await the action separately, ensuring the listener was always registered before the popup was created. WHY this matters: `context.waitForEvent('page')` must be registered before the event-triggering action when the popup is opened asynchronously via microtasks or very short timeouts; the `Promise.all([listener, action])` pattern only reliably prevents race conditions when the popup is opened synchronously or via a macrotask (e.g., `setTimeout(..., 100)`).

**G43. `page.emulate({ locale: 'de-DE' })` in a BrowserContext sets `navigator.language` and the `Accept-Language` request header, but it does not automatically change the `Intl` collation rules used by JavaScript's `Array.prototype.sort()` when called with no comparator — application code that sorts arrays of strings using the default sort (which calls `String.prototype.localeCompare` only if explicitly coded to do so) will continue to sort in Unicode code-point order rather than locale-sensitive order, causing the emulated locale to appear correct in the browser header but not in sorted list data, producing false-positive test results for locale-sensitive sort features.**
A team testing a contact list page with locale emulation set to `sv-SE` (Swedish) observed that the contact names sorted in English alphabetical order with Å, Ä, Ö appearing before B, despite the real application showing them correctly at the end of the alphabet in production. Investigation revealed that the application used `contacts.sort((a, b) => a.name > b.name ? 1 : -1)` instead of `a.name.localeCompare(b.name, 'sv-SE')`, meaning the browser's locale emulation had no effect on the sort order. The test was asserting on DOM order, which reflected the incorrect sort, producing a false green. The fix was to add an explicit oracle that compared the DOM order against the expected locale-sensitive sort order computed in the test: `const expected = [...names].sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, locale))`. WHY this matters: Playwright locale emulation affects the browser's HTTP headers and `navigator.language` property, but it does not patch JavaScript's default sort comparator or automatically make string comparisons locale-sensitive; always write explicit locale-sort oracles that compute the expected order using `localeCompare` with the target locale and compare it against the DOM-rendered order.

**G44. `page.addInitScript()` scripts that call `Object.defineProperty(window, 'navigator', { ... })` to override browser properties (e.g., `navigator.language`, `navigator.userAgent`) will throw a `TypeError: Cannot redefine property: navigator` on Chromium 120+ because the `navigator` object is now non-configurable in the Chrome security model — the script fails silently in `addInitScript()` context (errors in init scripts are swallowed), meaning the override has no effect and the test proceeds using the real `navigator.language` value, producing results that appear locale-correct but are actually running under the host machine's locale.**
A team that pre-dated Playwright's built-in `locale` context option used `page.addInitScript()` with `Object.defineProperty(window, 'navigator', { value: { ...navigator, language: 'ja-JP' } })` to override the locale. After a Chrome update, the override silently stopped working — `navigator.language` returned the CI container's `en-US` locale, but no error was thrown and no test failure occurred because the assertions checked only that user-visible text was present, not that it was in Japanese. The fix was to migrate to `browser.newContext({ locale: 'ja-JP' })` which uses the Chromium CDP Emulation API instead of JavaScript property override. WHY this matters: `Object.defineProperty` overrides of non-configurable browser globals like `navigator` are silently swallowed by `addInitScript()` on modern Chromium — always use Playwright's first-class emulation options (`locale`, `userAgent`, `geolocation`) via `BrowserContext` configuration rather than attempting JavaScript property overrides, and add a post-navigation assertion that reads back `navigator.language` via `page.evaluate()` to verify the emulation actually took effect.

## Cycle 54 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 384: `page.route()` + `route.fulfill()` Static Offline Fallback Oracle** [official]
Intercept network requests and substitute canned responses to test how the application behaves when backend services are unavailable. This pattern verifies that every user-visible path has a graceful degradation state rather than a blank screen or unhandled exception. Charter focus: map each critical API endpoint to an expected fallback UI state, then confirm each state with a `toHaveText` or `toMatchAriaSnapshot` assertion.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard shows stale-data banner when /api/metrics is down', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept the metrics endpoint before navigation
  await page.route('**/api/metrics', async route => {
    await route.fulfill({ status: 503, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Service Unavailable' }) });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Verify graceful degradation: banner visible, chart skeleton shown
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /data unavailable/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('metrics-chart-skeleton')).toBeVisible();

  // Ensure no unhandled JS error surfaced
  const errors: string[] = [];
  page.on('pageerror', e => errors.push(e.message));
  await page.waitForTimeout(500);
  expect(errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.fulfill()` bypasses real network I/O so the test cannot detect latency-related regressions (e.g., a slow 503 that triggers a front-end timeout); pair with a `page.clock()` time-advance test to cover timeout-path degradation separately.

---

**Pattern 385: `page.route()` + `route.continue({ postData })` Request-Body Mutation Charter** [official]
Intercept POST/PUT requests mid-flight and replace the request body with boundary-value or malformed payloads before the server processes them. This lets exploratory sessions verify server-side validation without modifying the client under test, keeping the charter focused on server contract boundaries.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('server rejects order with negative quantity via mutation oracle', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/orders', async route => {
    if (route.request().method() === 'POST') {
      const original = JSON.parse(route.request().postData() ?? '{}');
      // Mutate: flip quantity to a negative value
      await route.continue({ postData: JSON.stringify({ ...original, quantity: -1 }) });
    } else {
      await route.continue();
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/shop/product/42');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();

  // Server should reject with a user-visible validation message
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/invalid quantity/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: The application's client-side validation may block the POST before the route intercept fires (especially for `required` field checks), making the mutation silently ineffective; always log `route.request().postData()` inside the handler to confirm the mutated payload was actually sent.

---

**Pattern 386: `context.route()` Scope-Elevated Network Oracle for Multi-Page Flows** [official]
Register routes at `BrowserContext` level rather than `page` level so the interception survives page navigations, new tabs, and popup windows opened during a session. This is the correct scope for charters that span more than one page object (e.g., payment redirects, OAuth popups, download manager windows).
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('analytics beacon is fired on checkout confirmation across redirect', async ({ context, page }) => {
  const beaconCalls: string[] = [];

  // Context-level route survives the /checkout → /order-confirmed redirect
  await context.route('**/analytics/event', async route => {
    beaconCalls.push(route.request().postData() ?? '');
    await route.continue();
  });

  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm order' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('**/order-confirmed');

  // Verify at least one purchase event was beaconed
  const purchaseEvent = beaconCalls.find(b => b.includes('"event":"purchase"'));
  expect(purchaseEvent).toBeTruthy();
  expect(JSON.parse(purchaseEvent!)).toMatchObject({ event: 'purchase', currency: 'USD' });
});
```
Tradeoff: Context-level routes accumulate across all pages in the context and can produce unexpected matches if a later test in the same worker reuses a warm context; always call `await context.unrouteAll()` in `afterEach` or use per-test contexts to keep interception state clean.

---

**Pattern 387: `page.on('response')` Streaming Chunk Oracle for Chunked-Transfer and SSE Endpoints** [official]
Attach a response listener before triggering an action that opens a streaming connection (e.g., an AI chat completion, a log tail, or a progress feed). Collect chunks via the response body stream to verify that the application renders intermediate states rather than buffering everything to a final render.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('AI chat renders tokens progressively, not in a single burst', async ({ page }) => {
  const renderTimestamps: number[] = [];

  // Monitor DOM mutations as a proxy for progressive render
  await page.exposeFunction('recordRender', (ts: number) => renderTimestamps.push(ts));
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    const observer = new MutationObserver(() => {
      (window as any).recordRender(Date.now());
    });
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => {
      const container = document.querySelector('[data-testid="chat-response"]');
      if (container) observer.observe(container, { childList: true, subtree: true, characterData: true });
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/chat');
  await page.getByPlaceholder('Ask a question').fill('Explain quantum entanglement');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click();

  // Wait for response to complete
  await expect(page.getByTestId('chat-response')).not.toBeEmpty({ timeout: 30_000 });

  // Progressive render oracle: at least 5 mutation events spread over >1 second
  expect(renderTimestamps.length).toBeGreaterThan(5);
  const span = renderTimestamps[renderTimestamps.length - 1] - renderTimestamps[0];
  expect(span).toBeGreaterThan(1000); // tokens arrived over >1 s
});
```
Tradeoff: `MutationObserver` fires for any DOM change inside the container including CSS class toggles and attribute updates — not only text content additions — so high-frequency style mutations can inflate `renderTimestamps.length`; scope the observer to `{ characterData: true, subtree: true }` with `{ childList: false }` if you want to count only text-content changes.

---

**Pattern 388: `page.emulate({ colorScheme: 'dark' })` Dark-Mode Visual Oracle** [official]
Verify that an application's dark-mode variant does not introduce readability failures (insufficient contrast, invisible text, broken icons) by emulating the system `prefers-color-scheme: dark` media query at the context level. Combine with `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` to assert that the ARIA semantic structure is unchanged between modes.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const CRITICAL_ROUTES = ['/', '/dashboard', '/settings', '/profile'];

for (const route of CRITICAL_ROUTES) {
  test(`dark mode: ${route} has no hidden text or broken layout`, async ({ browser }) => {
    const darkCtx = await browser.newContext({ colorScheme: 'dark' });
    const page = await darkCtx.newPage();
    await page.goto(route);

    // Visual oracle: screenshot diff against committed baseline
    await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(`dark-mode${route.replace(/\//g, '-')}.png`, {
      fullPage: true,
      maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.02,
    });

    // Structural oracle: ARIA tree unchanged vs light mode
    await expect(page.locator('main')).toMatchAriaSnapshot();

    // Contrast spot-check: primary CTA must remain visible
    const ctaVisible = await page.getByRole('button', { name: /get started|sign up|continue/i }).isVisible();
    expect(ctaVisible, 'primary CTA invisible in dark mode').toBe(true);

    await darkCtx.close();
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `toHaveScreenshot()` requires a committed baseline image; on the first run Playwright generates the baseline, which means CI will fail until the team commits the baseline images — use `--update-snapshots` on the initial run and lock the screenshots in a dedicated assets branch to prevent accidental baseline drift.

---

**Pattern 389: `context.grantPermissions(['geolocation'])` + `context.setGeolocation()` Geolocation Charter for Location-Sensitive Features** [official]
Test how an application behaves at geographic boundary conditions (country border transitions, coordinate extremes, geolocation denial) by manipulating the browser's geolocation API via Playwright context options. This is essential for features like currency selection, store-finder, shipping calculator, and map-based search that branch on latitude/longitude.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const GEO_SCENARIOS = [
  { name: 'EU user (Berlin)', lat: 52.52, lon: 13.405, expectedCurrency: 'EUR' },
  { name: 'US user (New York)', lat: 40.712, lon: -74.006, expectedCurrency: 'USD' },
  { name: 'Date-line edge (Fiji)', lat: -17.713, lon: 178.065, expectedCurrency: 'FJD' },
] as const;

for (const scenario of GEO_SCENARIOS) {
  test(`currency auto-detects correctly for ${scenario.name}`, async ({ browser }) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({
      permissions: ['geolocation'],
      geolocation: { latitude: scenario.lat, longitude: scenario.lon },
    });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await page.goto('/store');

    // Allow geo detection to complete
    await page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="currency-selector"]');
    const currency = await page.getByTestId('currency-selector').inputValue();
    expect(currency).toBe(scenario.expectedCurrency);
    await ctx.close();
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: Playwright geolocation spoofing only affects `navigator.geolocation` — it does not change the server's IP-based geo-detection; applications that use IP-geolocation middleware on the server will still see the CI runner's IP address, so server-side geo features require a separate test proxy or VPN tunnel to exercise end-to-end.

---

**Pattern 390: `page.emulate({ offline: true })` Offline-Mode Charter for PWA and Service-Worker Exploration** [official]
Verify that progressive web apps and service-worker-enabled applications serve cached content when the device loses connectivity. Toggle offline mode mid-session to simulate sudden connectivity loss after initial page load, then confirm the application presents an offline UI state rather than a broken blank page or uncaught network error.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('app serves cached home page when network drops after first load', async ({ context, page }) => {
  // First load: warm the service-worker cache
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Confirm service worker is active
  const swActive = await page.evaluate(() =>
    navigator.serviceWorker?.controller !== null
  );
  expect(swActive, 'Service worker must be active before offline test').toBe(true);

  // Simulate connectivity loss
  await context.setOffline(true);

  // Reload while offline — service worker should serve cache
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5_000 });

  // Verify offline banner or indicator
  const offlineBanner = page.getByRole('alert', { name: /offline|no connection/i });
  await expect(offlineBanner).toBeVisible();

  // Restore connectivity
  await context.setOffline(false);
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.setOffline(true)` blocks all new network requests but does not reset already-established WebSocket connections or in-flight fetch requests; if the application uses a persistent WebSocket, those connections will stay open and may mask the offline state — close WebSocket connections explicitly before the offline toggle or use `page.route('**', route => route.abort())` for a more complete offline simulation.

---

**Pattern 391: `page.emulate({ javaScriptEnabled: false })` No-JS Fallback Oracle for Progressive Enhancement** [official]
Disable JavaScript execution in the browser context to verify that the application's no-JS baseline is functional for critical content paths. This is especially relevant for marketing pages, e-commerce catalog pages, and authentication flows where SEO or accessibility compliance requires server-rendered fallbacks.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product catalog page renders critical content without JavaScript', async ({ browser }) => {
  const noJsContext = await browser.newContext({ javaScriptEnabled: false });
  const page = await noJsContext.newPage();

  await page.goto('/catalog');

  // Primary content oracle: product cards must be present in HTML
  const productCards = page.locator('[data-testid="product-card"]');
  await expect(productCards.first()).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });
  const count = await productCards.count();
  expect(count, 'At least 12 products must render without JS').toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(12);

  // Navigation oracle: main nav links must be reachable
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation').getByRole('link', { name: 'Home' })).toBeVisible();

  // Confirm no broken-layout indicators
  const errorMessages = page.getByText(/something went wrong|error loading/i);
  await expect(errorMessages).toHaveCount(0);

  await noJsContext.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright's `javaScriptEnabled: false` disables all JavaScript including Playwright's own injected helpers (e.g., `waitForSelector` polling), so some assertions may need wider timeouts or CSS-selector-only locators; also note that many modern SPAs will render a blank page without JS, so this oracle pattern is most valuable for applications that explicitly claim progressive enhancement support.

---

**Pattern 392: `page.route()` + `route.abort()` Selective Resource Blocking Charter for Core-Content Resilience** [official]
Block specific resource types (images, fonts, analytics scripts, third-party iframes) to verify that the application's core functionality remains intact when external resources are unavailable. This tests both performance resilience and dependency isolation — critical for applications that pull in third-party scripts that may be blocked by ad-blockers or corporate proxies.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const BLOCKED_RESOURCE_TYPES = ['image', 'font', 'media'] as const;
const BLOCKED_THIRD_PARTY_PATTERNS = ['**/gtm.js', '**/fbq.js', '**/analytics.js'];

test('checkout flow completes when all images and third-party scripts are blocked', async ({ page }) => {
  // Block images and fonts
  await page.route('**/*', async route => {
    if ((BLOCKED_RESOURCE_TYPES as readonly string[]).includes(route.request().resourceType())) {
      await route.abort();
    } else {
      await route.continue();
    }
  });

  // Block known third-party analytics scripts
  for (const pattern of BLOCKED_THIRD_PARTY_PATTERNS) {
    await page.route(pattern, route => route.abort());
  }

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('test@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/order-confirmed/, { timeout: 20_000 });
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.abort()` triggers `net::ERR_FAILED` events in the browser console which Playwright does not automatically propagate as test failures; if you want failed-resource errors to surface, combine this pattern with a `page.on('requestfailed', ...)` collector and assert that no first-party resource appears in the failed-request list.

---

**Pattern 393: `page.waitForRequest()` + `page.waitForResponse()` Paired Oracle for Request-Response Integrity** [official]
Use `waitForRequest` and `waitForResponse` in tandem to verify both the outgoing request shape (method, headers, body) and the incoming response shape (status, body structure) for a single interaction. This paired pattern is more reliable than listening to `page.on('request')` events when you need to assert on both sides of a single API call without race conditions.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('profile save sends PATCH with correct payload and receives 200', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/profile');
  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('Alice Tester');

  // Register both promises BEFORE the action that triggers the request
  const requestPromise = page.waitForRequest(req =>
    req.url().includes('/api/profile') && req.method() === 'PATCH'
  );
  const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(res =>
    res.url().includes('/api/profile') && res.status() === 200
  );

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save changes' }).click();

  const [request, response] = await Promise.all([requestPromise, responsePromise]);

  // Request oracle
  const body = JSON.parse(request.postData() ?? '{}');
  expect(body).toMatchObject({ displayName: 'Alice Tester' });

  // Response oracle
  const responseBody = await response.json();
  expect(responseBody).toMatchObject({ success: true, displayName: 'Alice Tester' });
});
```
Tradeoff: `waitForRequest` and `waitForResponse` use separate Promise chains — if the response arrives before the `waitForResponse` promise is registered (e.g., a very fast in-memory mock server), the response event is missed and the Promise hangs; always register both promises before triggering the action, never after.

---

**Pattern 394: `devices['...']` Device Registry Charter for Responsive Layout Exploration** [official]
Iterate over Playwright's built-in device registry to run layout and interaction charters across a representative device matrix without manually configuring viewport, user agent, and touch settings. Focus on breakpoint boundaries where layout shifts between single-column and multi-column, and between touch and hover interaction models.
```typescript
import { test, expect, devices } from '@playwright/test';

const DEVICE_MATRIX = [
  devices['iPhone 14'],
  devices['iPad Pro 11'],
  devices['Galaxy S9+'],
  devices['Desktop Chrome'],
] as const;

for (const device of DEVICE_MATRIX) {
  const deviceName = (device as any).defaultBrowserType ?? 'chromium';
  test(`navigation menu is accessible on ${device.userAgent.split(' ')[0]}`, async ({ browser }) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ ...device });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await page.goto('/');

    // On mobile, the hamburger menu should be the entry point
    const isMobile = device.isMobile ?? false;
    if (isMobile) {
      const hamburger = page.getByRole('button', { name: /menu/i });
      await expect(hamburger).toBeVisible();
      await hamburger.click();
    }

    // Primary nav links must be reachable regardless of device
    await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Products' })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Pricing' })).toBeVisible();
    await ctx.close();
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: Playwright's device registry reflects the user agent string and viewport at the time of library release — actual device characteristics can diverge from the registry entries as OS updates change the viewport-to-screen-pixel ratio; supplement the registry-based matrix with a manual check against real device screenshots using BrowserStack or Sauce Labs for final sign-off on high-stakes layout features.

---

**Pattern 395: `context.addCookies()` + `context.clearCookies()` Cookie-State Manipulation Charter for Session-Boundary Exploration** [official]
Programmatically inject, modify, and delete cookies before or during a session to explore authentication edge cases, expired-token handling, consent-banner re-appearance, and cross-domain cookie isolation. This pattern is faster than UI-driven login flows and allows precise control over cookie attributes (domain, path, sameSite, httpOnly, expires).
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session expiry mid-flow redirects to login with return-URL preservation', async ({ context, page }) => {
  // Inject a valid-looking but near-expired session cookie
  await context.addCookies([{
    name: 'session_token',
    value: 'expired-test-token-xyz',
    domain: 'localhost',
    path: '/',
    expires: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 1, // already expired
    httpOnly: true,
    sameSite: 'Lax',
  }]);

  await page.goto('/dashboard/reports');

  // Application should detect expired session and redirect to login
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/, { timeout: 10_000 });

  // Confirm return-URL is preserved in redirect
  const url = new URL(page.url());
  expect(url.searchParams.get('returnTo')).toContain('/dashboard/reports');
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.addCookies()` cannot set `httpOnly` cookies that are then readable by the application's JavaScript (by definition), but it can inject them so they are sent with requests — the limitation is that you cannot verify the cookie was set by reading `document.cookie` from the page; use `context.cookies()` (the Playwright context method) to assert cookie presence, not `page.evaluate(() => document.cookie)`.

---

**Pattern 396: `page.evaluate()` + `localStorage` / `sessionStorage` Manipulation Charter for Client-State Exploration** [official]
Read and write `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` entries directly via `page.evaluate()` to set up complex client-side state for exploration without going through the UI flow that normally produces that state. This is particularly valuable for features like onboarding wizard steps, feature-flag overrides stored client-side, and shopping cart state that would require many UI interactions to reproduce.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('onboarding resumes from step 3 when wizard state is pre-seeded in localStorage', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Pre-seed onboarding state directly — skipping steps 1 and 2
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    localStorage.setItem('onboarding_step', '3');
    localStorage.setItem('onboarding_profile', JSON.stringify({
      name: 'Alice',
      role: 'engineer',
      completedSteps: [1, 2],
    }));
  });

  await page.goto('/onboarding');

  // Application should resume at step 3
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toContainText(/step 3/i);
  await expect(page.getByText('Alice')).toBeVisible(); // name from prior step preserved

  // Verify steps 1 and 2 show as completed in the stepper UI
  await expect(page.getByTestId('step-1-indicator')).toHaveAttribute('data-status', 'complete');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('step-2-indicator')).toHaveAttribute('data-status', 'complete');
});
```
Tradeoff: `localStorage` set via `page.evaluate()` before navigation persists across navigations within the same origin but is wiped when `context.clearStorageState()` is called or when the browser context is recreated — if other tests in the same worker share the context, pre-seeded storage leaks between tests; always call `await page.evaluate(() => localStorage.clear())` in `afterEach` or use `storageState` snapshot/restore to avoid cross-test contamination.

---

**Pattern 397: `page.on('pageerror')` + `page.on('console')` Combined Error Oracle for Session Health Monitoring** [official]
Collect JavaScript exceptions and console error/warning messages throughout an exploratory session and score the session's health at the end. A session with zero `pageerror` events and fewer than three `console.error` events is a green health signal; anything above that threshold triggers an automatic branch in the charter to investigate the error source.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface SessionHealth {
  jsErrors: string[];
  consoleErrors: string[];
  consoleWarnings: string[];
}

test('dashboard session produces no JS errors across a full user journey', async ({ page }) => {
  const health: SessionHealth = { jsErrors: [], consoleErrors: [], consoleWarnings: [] };

  page.on('pageerror', err => health.jsErrors.push(err.message));
  page.on('console', msg => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') health.consoleErrors.push(msg.text());
    if (msg.type() === 'warning') health.consoleWarnings.push(msg.text());
  });

  // Execute representative session journey
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Reports' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Profile' }).click();

  // Health oracle
  expect(health.jsErrors, `Unexpected JS errors: ${health.jsErrors.join('; ')}`).toHaveLength(0);
  expect(
    health.consoleErrors.filter(e => !e.includes('favicon')), // ignore known benign favicon 404
    `Console errors during session: ${health.consoleErrors.join('; ')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.on('pageerror')` captures unhandled promise rejections and thrown exceptions, but it does not capture errors swallowed by `try/catch` blocks or errors in Web Workers; for comprehensive error coverage, supplement with `page.on('console')` filtering and add a `window.onerror` shim via `page.addInitScript()` that also reports caught exceptions via `page.evaluate()`.

---

**Pattern 398: `page.clock.freeze()` + `page.clock.fastForward()` Time-State Charter for Date-Sensitive Feature Exploration** [official]
Freeze the browser clock at a specific timestamp or fast-forward it to explore time-sensitive application states (trial expiry banners, subscription renewal prompts, session timeout warnings, scheduled content publish/unpublish, recurring billing previews) without waiting for real time to elapse.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('trial expiry banner appears 3 days before trial end', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install clock before navigation so Date.now() is frozen from the start
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-01T12:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('trial-expiry-banner')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Fast-forward to 3 days before trial end (trial started 2026-01-01, ends 2026-01-15)
  await page.clock.fastForward('12d'); // now at 2026-01-13

  // Reload to trigger server-side check with spoofed Date in API calls
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('trial-expiry-banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('trial-expiry-banner')).toContainText(/2 days/i);
});

test('session timeout warning appears after 14 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.clock.install();
  await page.goto('/app');

  // Fast-forward 14 minutes without any user interaction
  await page.clock.fastForward('14m');

  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /session timeout/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.fastForward()` manipulates the browser's `Date`, `setTimeout`, and `setInterval` but does not affect the test runner's Node.js clock or any server-side time checks that read from `Date.now()` on the server — server-side expiry logic will still use real wall-clock time; for full end-to-end time manipulation, the server must also accept a spoofed time header (e.g., `X-Test-Now`) or be configured with a test clock seam.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G45. `page.route()` handlers registered with glob patterns containing `{` and `}` curly-brace alternation syntax silently fall through to the network instead of matching — Playwright's simplified glob syntax supports `*`, `**`, `?`, and `{}` alternation, but the curly-brace pattern is matched case-sensitively against the full URL and the alternation group must not contain spaces; a pattern like `**/{api,API}/users` will not match `https://example.com/API/users` on a case-sensitive server even though both `api` and `API` are listed in the alternation group.**
A team attempted to intercept both `/api/users` and `/API/users` (a legacy endpoint still used in mobile) with the single pattern `**/{api,API}/users` expecting alternation matching. The pattern silently failed for all `/API/users` requests because the glob engine was performing a case-sensitive alternation match and the pattern group was `{api,API}` which correctly listed both cases, but the team had accidentally introduced a trailing space in the pattern string as `**/{api, API}/users` (note the space after the comma). Playwright's glob does not trim whitespace from alternation branches, so `' API'` (with a leading space) never matched `API`. The fix was to remove the space: `**/{api,API}/users` and verify the pattern in isolation using `micromatch.isMatch(url, pattern)`. WHY this matters: Playwright's glob pattern parser does not trim whitespace inside `{}` alternation groups, making a trailing or leading space an invisible source of silent route miss — always verify route patterns with a unit test using the `micromatch` package before relying on them in exploratory harnesses.

**G46. `page.waitForResponse()` with a URL-string predicate will never match if the application issues a redirect chain — Playwright resolves the response to the final redirect destination, but the `waitForResponse` URL-string match is applied to the original request URL, not the final redirected URL, causing the promise to time out even when the server ultimately responds successfully.**
A team waiting for a POST to `/api/submit` which redirected to `/api/submit/` (a trailing-slash redirect enforced by the framework router) found that `page.waitForResponse('**/api/submit')` timed out even though network logs showed a 200 response arriving. Investigation revealed that Playwright matched the URL against `**/api/submit` but the final response URL was `**/api/submit/` — the glob `**/api/submit` does not have a trailing wildcard so it did not match the slash-suffixed URL. The fix was to use a predicate function: `page.waitForResponse(res => res.url().includes('/api/submit') && res.status() === 200)` which matches regardless of trailing slash. WHY this matters: URL-string patterns in `waitForResponse` are matched exactly (with glob expansion) against the request URL, not the final redirect URL; for any endpoint that may have redirect chains (common with framework routers that normalise trailing slashes), always use a predicate function with `.includes()` or a RegExp rather than a bare glob string.

**G47. `context.clearCookies()` does not clear `HttpOnly` session cookies that were set by a `Set-Cookie` response header with the `Partitioned` attribute (CHIPS — Cookies Having Independent Partitioned State) introduced in Chrome 114+ — these partitioned cookies are stored in a separate partition keyed by the top-level site and are not enumerated by `context.cookies()` or cleared by `context.clearCookies()`, meaning tests that rely on `clearCookies()` to simulate a fully logged-out state may leave a partitioned session cookie in place and produce false-green authentication bypass results.**
A team testing a cross-site embedded widget (loaded in an iframe from `widget.example.com` in a host page at `app.example.com`) observed that after calling `context.clearCookies()` and reloading, the widget's session appeared to persist. DevTools inspection showed a `Partitioned` `Set-Cookie` response from `widget.example.com` that was stored in the CHIPS partition and was not visible in `context.cookies()`. The fix was to use `page.evaluate(() => document.cookie = 'session=; Max-Age=0; path=/')` inside the widget's frame context using `page.frame({ url: /widget.example.com/ })` to explicitly expire the cookie, and to file a Playwright feature request for CHIPS partition clearing. WHY this matters: Playwright's `context.clearCookies()` API predates the CHIPS partitioned cookie model and does not enumerate or clear partitioned cookies — teams testing cross-site embedded authentication flows must explicitly expire cookies via JavaScript inside the relevant frame context until Playwright adds first-class CHIPS support.

**G48. `page.emulate({ userAgent: '...' })` at the context level overrides the user agent for the initial navigation but does not update the `navigator.userAgent` property returned from `page.evaluate(() => navigator.userAgent)` until after the next full page navigation — reading `navigator.userAgent` immediately after `page.goto()` in the same test without a second navigation may still return the Playwright default user agent string, causing UA-sniffing assertions to produce false negatives.**
A team testing a mobile-redirect feature (which read `navigator.userAgent` on page load and redirected mobile browsers to `/m/`) found that their `page.emulate({ userAgent: MOBILE_UA })` context was not triggering the redirect even though the userAgent string appeared correct in `context.userAgentOverride()`. The root cause was that the UA override was being applied after the first `page.goto()` resolved, meaning the server had already responded before seeing the overridden UA in the `User-Agent` request header. The fix was to set the user agent via `browser.newContext({ userAgent: MOBILE_UA })` before calling `page.goto()`, not by calling `page.emulate()` after context creation. WHY this matters: Playwright's `page.emulate()` called post-context-creation cannot retroactively change the User-Agent on an already-completed navigation's server request; always set `userAgent` during context creation via `browser.newContext()` or `playwright.config.ts` `use.userAgent` to guarantee the overridden UA is sent in the initial HTTP request headers.

**G49. `page.on('console')` handlers registered after `page.goto()` do not capture `console.error()` calls triggered by synchronous code in the `<head>` `<script>` block or `DOMContentLoaded` handlers that run before Playwright finishes setting up the listener — this means that critical startup errors (e.g., a missing polyfill, a failed feature-detect, an initial fetch error) are silently lost even though they appear in browser DevTools.**
A team monitoring console errors via `page.on('console', ...)` registered the handler after `await page.goto('/')` and found their error oracle reported zero errors across a session that visually showed a broken layout. Chrome DevTools replaying the session showed four `console.error()` calls fired during `DOMContentLoaded` before Playwright's post-`goto()` listener was attached. The fix was to register the `page.on('console', ...)` handler before calling `page.goto()`, and additionally inject a `window.onerror` shim via `page.addInitScript()` to capture synchronous errors from early-boot scripts. WHY this matters: `page.on('console')` is a post-hoc listener — any `console.*` calls that complete before the listener is attached are silently dropped with no backlog; always register console and `pageerror` listeners before the first `page.goto()` call, and add `page.addInitScript()` shims to capture errors from synchronous boot-time code that runs before the document is interactive.

## Cycle 55 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 399: `page.addLocatorHandler()` Overlay-Dismissal Guard for Unpredictable Interstitial Exploration** [official]
Register a locator handler before starting an exploratory session so that unexpected overlays (cookie banners, promotional modals, soft-auth nudges, newsletter pop-ups) are dismissed automatically, allowing the charter mission to continue uninterrupted. This converts a session-killing blocker into a silent, logged dismissal event.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('explore checkout flow with overlay guard', async ({ page }) => {
  const dismissedOverlays: string[] = [];

  // Register handler for any generic modal dismiss button
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog').getByRole('button', { name: /close|dismiss|no thanks/i }),
    async (locator) => {
      const dialogText = await page.getByRole('dialog').innerText().catch(() => '(unknown)');
      dismissedOverlays.push(dialogText.slice(0, 80));
      await locator.click();
    }
  );

  // Also guard cookie consent banners
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all|accept cookies/i }),
    async (locator) => {
      dismissedOverlays.push('cookie-consent-banner');
      await locator.click();
    }
  );

  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Add to cart' }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /checkout/i })).toBeVisible();

  console.log('Overlays dismissed during session:', dismissedOverlays);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.addLocatorHandler()` runs before Playwright's built-in actionability checks and fires whenever the locator becomes visible — it incurs a brief actionability poll on every click or fill that could slow down dense sessions on slow machines; guard against handler loops by setting `{ noWaitAfter: true }` for handlers that trigger animations, and limit handler scope to contexts where interstitials are actually known to appear.

**Pattern 400: `page.consoleMessages()` + `page.pageErrors()` Post-Session Diagnostic Snapshot** [official]
After completing a charter's action sequence, drain the stored console message and page error buffers (up to 200 entries each, retained since Playwright v1.56) to produce a structured diagnostic snapshot — catching silent `console.error()` calls, unhandled rejections, and React/Vue hydration errors that were not visible in the UI.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface SessionDiagnostics {
  errors: string[];
  warnings: string[];
  networkErrors: string[];
  pageErrors: string[];
}

test('explore settings form and collect session diagnostics', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('invalid@');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Display Name').fill('A'.repeat(300)); // boundary test
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();

  // Drain diagnostic buffers after charter actions complete
  const messages = page.consoleMessages();
  const errors = page.pageErrors();

  const diagnostics: SessionDiagnostics = {
    errors: messages
      .filter(m => m.type() === 'error')
      .map(m => m.text()),
    warnings: messages
      .filter(m => m.type() === 'warning')
      .map(m => m.text()),
    networkErrors: messages
      .filter(m => m.text().includes('net::ERR') || m.text().includes('Failed to load'))
      .map(m => m.text()),
    pageErrors: errors.map(e => e.message),
  };

  console.log('Session diagnostics:', JSON.stringify(diagnostics, null, 2));
  // Assert no unhandled page errors
  expect(diagnostics.pageErrors, 'Unhandled JS errors during session').toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()` each cap at 200 entries — long exploratory sessions with chatty logging may roll the buffer and lose early errors; supplement with a streaming `page.on('console', ...)` listener registered before `page.goto()` that writes to an unbounded array when session length is unpredictable.
