**Pattern 459** — HAR Recording with `recordHar` for Reproducible Multi-Request Exploration
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_PATH = path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures/product-catalog.har');

// First run (update:true): record live traffic into the HAR file
test.use({
  contextOptions: {
    recordHar: {
      path: HAR_PATH,
      urlFilter: '**/api/**',
      mode: 'minimal', // only headers + body, not full request timing
    },
  },
});

test('record product catalog API interactions', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: /category/i }).selectOption('electronics');
  await page.getByRole('spinbutton', { name: /min price/i }).fill('100');
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: /results/i })).toBeVisible();
  // HAR is flushed to disk when context closes (after test teardown)
});
```
Tradeoff: HAR-based replay (`page.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH)`) eliminates network variability across CI runs and works offline, but recorded responses go stale when the API contract changes — unlike `page.route()` callbacks that can be updated in code, HAR files require a deliberate re-record pass (`update: true`) when endpoints evolve; teams must include HAR files in version control and treat them as fixtures that need maintenance.

**Pattern 460** — `page.routeFromHAR()` Selective Replay for Exploratory Oracles
```typescript
test('explore search results with deterministic API responses', async ({ page }) => {
  // Replay only API calls from the HAR; let real navigation and assets through
  await page.routeFromHAR('./fixtures/search-session.har', {
    url: '**/api/search**',
    update: false,         // replay mode — do not overwrite the file
    notFound: 'continue',  // requests not in HAR are forwarded to the real server
  });

  await page.goto('/search?q=playwright');

  // Oracle: deterministic response means result count is known exactly
  const resultCount = await page.getByRole('listitem').count();
  expect(resultCount).toBe(12); // fixed by HAR response

  // Explore pagination controls against fixed total
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /next/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /previous/i })).toBeEnabled();
});
```
Tradeoff: The `notFound: 'continue'` option creates a hybrid session where HAR-matched routes use recorded responses while unmatched routes hit the live server — this lets you freeze the data layer while exploring UI behaviour on real assets, but debugging is harder because a test failure could stem from either the deterministic HAR response or the live request; always log which requests hit the HAR vs. the network using a `page.on('request', ...)` listener during investigation.

**Pattern 461** — `page.addInitScript()` for Seeding Deterministic Global State Before Any Script Runs
```typescript
test('explore date-dependent flows with frozen clock via init script', async ({ page }) => {
  // Injected before any page scripts execute — cannot be overridden by app code
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // Freeze Date to a known value across all JS on the page
    const FIXED_TIME = new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00Z').getTime();
    const OriginalDate = Date;
    class FrozenDate extends OriginalDate {
      constructor(...args: ConstructorParameters<typeof OriginalDate>) {
        if (args.length === 0) { super(FIXED_TIME); return; }
        // @ts-ignore spread into Date constructor
        super(...args);
      }
      static now() { return FIXED_TIME; }
    }
    // @ts-ignore
    window.Date = FrozenDate;
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Oracle: greeting should reflect frozen date (January 15)
  await expect(page.getByTestId('date-display')).toHaveText(/January 15, 2026/);
  // Oracle: subscription expiry warning (30 days) should not appear for a date far in future
  await expect(page.getByTestId('expiry-warning')).toBeHidden();
});
```
Tradeoff: `addInitScript` runs before any page script and survives navigations within the same page context, making it the most reliable way to override global browser APIs (Date, Math.random, crypto) for deterministic exploration — however, multiple `addInitScript` calls execute in an undefined order relative to each other, so if two scripts both patch `window.Date`, the final state depends on registration order, which can silently corrupt your fixture; consolidate all global patches into a single `addInitScript` call.

**Pattern 462** — `page.exposeFunction()` for Cross-Context Observation During Exploration
```typescript
test('explore form submission — capture all XHR payloads via exposed callback', async ({ page }) => {
  const capturedPayloads: string[] = [];

  // Expose a Node.js callback to the browser's window object
  await page.exposeFunction('recordPayload', async (payload: string) => {
    capturedPayloads.push(payload);
  });

  // Intercept fetch at the browser level — survives SPA navigation
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    const origFetch = window.fetch;
    window.fetch = async (input, init) => {
      if (init?.body) {
        // @ts-ignore — recordPayload is injected by Playwright
        await window.recordPayload(
          typeof init.body === 'string' ? init.body : JSON.stringify(init.body)
        );
      }
      return origFetch(input, init);
    };
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel(/card number/i).fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay/i }).click();

  // Oracle: exactly one payment payload captured, containing masked card data
  expect(capturedPayloads).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(capturedPayloads[0]).not.toContain('4242424242424242'); // PAN should be masked
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.exposeFunction()` lets you bridge browser-context events back to Node.js for session-level observation (audit trails, payload logging, state snapshots) without polluting the application's network layer — the tradeoff is that exposed functions only accept JSON-serialisable arguments; passing a DOM node, an Error object, or a class instance silently coerces to `{}`, causing observation gaps; always serialise complex values to plain objects or strings before passing them to the exposed function.

**Pattern 463** — Chained Locator Filtering with `.filter({ hasText })` and `.filter({ has })` for Precision Exploration
```typescript
test('explore shopping cart — assert each line item independently', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add.*playwright book/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add.*testing handbook/i }).click();
  await page.goto('/cart/review');

  const lineItems = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({
    has: page.getByRole('img', { name: /product/i }), // must contain a product image
  });

  // Explore first item — Playwright Book
  const playwrightItem = lineItems.filter({ hasText: /playwright book/i });
  await expect(playwrightItem.getByTestId('qty')).toHaveText('1');
  await expect(playwrightItem.getByTestId('price')).toHaveText(/\$39\.99/);

  // Explore second item — Testing Handbook
  const handbookItem = lineItems.filter({ hasText: /testing handbook/i });
  await expect(handbookItem.getByTestId('qty')).toHaveText('1');
  await expect(handbookItem.getByTestId('price')).toHaveText(/\$29\.99/);

  // Oracle: total should reflect both items
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-total')).toHaveText(/\$69\.98/);
});
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `.filter()` calls narrows a broad role-based locator to a uniquely scoped element without resorting to brittle `nth()` indices — the tradeoff is readability: deeply chained filters can become hard to parse, and each `.filter()` adds a separate DOM traversal pass during Playwright's retrying assertion loop; for lists with hundreds of items (e.g., a data grid), consider switching to a more specific `data-testid` query that pinpoints the row directly, as chained filters on large lists can slow assertion convergence noticeably.

**Pattern 464** — `page.clock.install()` for Exploring Time-Sensitive UI Flows Without `addInitScript` Patching
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('explore session-timeout warning at T-2 minutes', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install Playwright's built-in clock before navigation
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-03-01T10:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Simulate user idle: advance clock by 28 minutes (2 minutes before 30-min timeout)
  await page.clock.fastForward('28:00');

  // Oracle: idle warning dialog must appear 2 minutes before expiry
  await expect(page.getByRole('alertdialog', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Interact with warning — extend session
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /stay logged in/i }).click();

  // Advance remaining 2 minutes — session should NOT have expired
  await page.clock.fastForward('02:01');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alertdialog', { name: /session expired/i })).toBeHidden();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install()` (Playwright v1.45+) controls `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame`, and `performance.now()` simultaneously through Sinon's fake timers, making it far more comprehensive than a manual `addInitScript` Date patch — however, `fastForward` fires all pending timers synchronously in batched steps; if the application uses `setInterval` for polling (e.g., health-check pings every 5 seconds), advancing by 28 minutes fires 336 synthetic intervals in rapid succession, potentially triggering race conditions or debounce logic that would never fire in production; use `page.clock.runFor()` with shorter increments or `page.clock.tick()` to step through time at a controlled pace.

**Pattern 465** — `expect.configure()` Session-Scoped Timeout Tuning for Slow Exploration Targets
```typescript
import { test, expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';

// Create a session-scoped expect with extended timeout for slow rendering environments
const expect = baseExpect.configure({ timeout: 15_000, soft: false });
const softExpect = baseExpect.configure({ timeout: 15_000, soft: true });

test('explore report generation — long-running async render', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports/generate');
  await page.getByLabel(/report type/i).selectOption('quarterly-summary');
  await page.getByLabel(/date range/i).fill('Q1 2026');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /generate/i }).click();

  // Progress indicator appears quickly
  await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeVisible();

  // Report takes up to 12 seconds — extended timeout applied via configure()
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: /download pdf/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Soft-assert secondary metadata so exploration continues even if fields are missing
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('report-page-count')).toHaveText(/\d+ pages/);
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('report-size')).toHaveText(/\d+ KB/);

  // Hard assertion: the download link must produce a non-empty response
  const [download] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('download'),
    page.getByRole('link', { name: /download pdf/i }).click(),
  ]);
  expect(await download.suggestedFilename()).toMatch(/quarterly-summary/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.configure()` creates a reusable assertion instance with pre-set timeout and soft-mode, reducing per-assertion `{ timeout }` boilerplate across a long exploration session — the tradeoff is that configuring `soft: true` globally on an `expect` instance means assertion failures accumulate silently until `test.info().errors` is inspected at the end; a single misconfigured expect instance (intended to be soft) that escapes the session file can allow entire test suites to pass while reporting known defects, so always name soft-expect instances explicitly (`softExpect`, `lenientExpect`) and never export them from shared utilities.

**Pattern 466** — `page.on('console')` and `page.on('pageerror')` as Passive Oracles During Exploration
```typescript
test('explore SPA navigation — collect all console errors as oracle', async ({ page }) => {
  const consoleErrors: string[] = [];
  const pageErrors: string[] = [];

  // Passive listeners — do not block navigation
  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') consoleErrors.push(msg.text());
  });
  page.on('pageerror', (err) => pageErrors.push(err.message));

  // Explore a multi-step SPA workflow
  await page.goto('/app');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /settings/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /notifications/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('switch', { name: /email alerts/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /billing/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /update payment/i }).click();

  // After all exploration steps, assert silence on errors
  expect(consoleErrors, 'No console errors during SPA navigation').toHaveLength(0);
  expect(pageErrors, 'No uncaught JS exceptions during SPA navigation').toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: Attaching `console` and `pageerror` listeners at session start gives you a passive oracle layer that catches defects invisible to visual assertions — the tradeoff is noise: many applications emit benign `console.error` calls for expected conditions (e.g., a 401 on a cached resource check that redirects to login), so asserting strict zero-errors will produce false defects; filter listeners to exclude known-benign patterns (`if (msg.text().includes('401') && msg.text().includes('/api/auth')) return;`) and document each exclusion in the charter notes so future sessions can revisit them.

**Pattern 467** — `locator.evaluate()` with `:disabled` CSS Pseudo-Class for Inherited Disabled State Oracles
```typescript
test('explore multi-step form — fieldset disabled inheritance oracle', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/application/step-2');

  // Complete step 2, which should lock step 1 fields via <fieldset disabled>
  await page.getByLabel(/step 2 field/i).fill('value');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /complete step 2/i }).click();

  // Step 1 fieldset should now be disabled
  const step1Fieldset = page.locator('fieldset[data-step="1"]');
  await expect(step1Fieldset).toHaveAttribute('disabled');

  // Use :disabled pseudo-class to check inherited state on child inputs
  // (toBeEnabled() only checks the element's own disabled attribute — not inherited)
  const emailIsComputedDisabled = await page
    .getByLabel(/email/i)
    .evaluate((el) => (el as HTMLInputElement).matches(':disabled'));

  expect(emailIsComputedDisabled).toBe(true);

  // Verify no accidental keyboard trap: Tab should skip disabled fieldset
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  const focusedEl = await page.evaluate(() => document.activeElement?.getAttribute('data-testid'));
  expect(focusedEl).not.toMatch(/step-1/);
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `el.matches(':disabled')` inside `locator.evaluate()` respects the CSS computed disabled state including `<fieldset>` inheritance, catching a class of defects that `toBeEnabled()` / `toBeDisabled()` misses — the tradeoff is that `locator.evaluate()` executes a one-shot browser script with no auto-retry, so if the disabled state is applied asynchronously (e.g., after a fetch response), the evaluate call may snapshot the element before the state change completes; wrap in `expect.poll()` if the disabled transition is async: `await expect.poll(() => page.getByLabel(/email/i).evaluate(el => el.matches(':disabled'))).toBe(true)`.

**Pattern 468** — `page.routeWebSocket()` for Exploring Real-Time Feature Behaviour With Controlled Messages
```typescript
test('explore live dashboard — inject WebSocket events to trigger UI state', async ({ page }) => {
  let wsSend: ((data: string) => void) | null = null;

  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://*/live-updates', (ws) => {
    // Capture the server-side proxy to inject synthetic messages
    ws.onopen = () => {
      wsSend = (data) => ws.send(data);
      // Immediately send an initial snapshot so the UI does not show "loading"
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'snapshot', activeUsers: 42 }));
    };
    // Forward real messages from the browser back to this hook (if needed)
    ws.onmessage = (msg) => { /* log or modify before forwarding */ };
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard/live');

  // Oracle: initial snapshot rendered
  await expect(page.getByTestId('active-users')).toHaveText('42');

  // Inject a synthetic spike event
  wsSend!(JSON.stringify({ type: 'update', activeUsers: 999 }));

  // Oracle: UI reacts to spike within 1 second
  await expect(page.getByTestId('active-users')).toHaveText('999', { timeout: 1000 });

  // Inject a disconnect simulation
  wsSend!(JSON.stringify({ type: 'error', code: 'SERVER_RESTART' }));
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /reconnecting/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.routeWebSocket()` (Playwright v1.48+) lets you script the full lifecycle of a WebSocket connection — synthetic messages, controlled disconnects, message inspection — without a running WebSocket server, making real-time feature exploration fully deterministic; the tradeoff is that the route intercepts at the browser boundary, so server-side features (e.g., server push triggered by another user's action) cannot be replicated unless you manually inject the equivalent message; for truly bidirectional exploration, complement with a lightweight WebSocket test server rather than replacing it entirely with route interception.

**Pattern 469** — `context.tracing` with Named Chunks for Charter Evidence Collection
```typescript
import { test, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

test('explore payment flow — record named trace snapshots at each charter step', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context: BrowserContext = await browser.newContext();

  await context.tracing.start({
    screenshots: true,
    snapshots: true,   // DOM + CSS snapshots for Trace Viewer
    sources: true,     // embed test source in trace
  });

  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/checkout/cart');

  await context.tracing.startChunk({ title: 'Charter Step 1 — Verify Cart Contents' });
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(2);
  await context.tracing.stopChunk({ path: './traces/step-1-cart.zip' });

  await context.tracing.startChunk({ title: 'Charter Step 2 — Enter Shipping' });
  await page.getByLabel(/street address/i).fill('1 Infinite Loop');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /continue/i }).click();
  await context.tracing.stopChunk({ path: './traces/step-2-shipping.zip' });

  await context.tracing.startChunk({ title: 'Charter Step 3 — Payment Oracle' });
  await page.getByLabel(/card number/i).fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay now/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
  await context.tracing.stopChunk({ path: './traces/step-3-payment.zip' });

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Splitting a long exploration session into per-charter-step trace chunks (using `startChunk` / `stopChunk`) produces focused, reviewable trace files that map directly to session notes — each chunk opens independently in the Trace Viewer with its own timeline — but chunking adds ~20–40 ms overhead per boundary due to snapshot serialisation, and chunk files cannot be merged back into a single timeline after the fact; if you need a continuous end-to-end playback for a bug report, record a single unchunked trace in parallel alongside the chunked session.

**Pattern 470** — `expect.poll()` for Converging on Asynchronous Side-Effect Oracles
```typescript
test('explore bulk email send — assert background job completion via API polling', async ({ page, request }) => {
  await page.goto('/admin/campaigns');
  await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: /select all/i }).check();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /send campaign/i }).click();

  // UI shows "queued" immediately; actual send happens in a background job
  await expect(page.getByTestId('campaign-status')).toHaveText(/queued/i);

  // Poll the admin API until the job reaches "sent" or timeout (30 seconds)
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const resp = await request.get('/api/admin/campaign/latest');
      const body = await resp.json();
      return body.status;
    },
    {
      message: 'Campaign should reach "sent" status within 30 seconds',
      timeout: 30_000,
      intervals: [1_000, 2_000, 5_000], // back-off: 1s, 2s, then 5s
    }
  ).toBe('sent');

  // Oracle: sent count should match selected recipient count
  const sentCount = await request.get('/api/admin/campaign/latest/stats');
  const stats = await sentCount.json();
  expect(stats.deliveredCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll()` wraps any async function in a retrying assertion with configurable intervals and a human-readable failure message, making it ideal for exploring background-job outcomes, queue drains, or eventually-consistent side effects — the tradeoff over `page.waitForCondition()` is that `expect.poll()` re-evaluates the entire callback on each tick, including any HTTP request overhead, so polling intervals shorter than the request round-trip silently accumulate in-flight requests; always set `intervals` to values larger than the expected API response time (>=500 ms) to avoid piling up concurrent requests during a polling burst.

**Pattern 471** — `page.getByRole()` with `exact` Option as an Accessible Name Quality Oracle
```typescript
test('explore accessible names — audit button labels for specificity', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Phase 1: broad match — find all buttons whose name *contains* "delete" (case-insensitive)
  const looseDeleteButtons = page.getByRole('button', { name: /delete/i });
  const looseCount = await looseDeleteButtons.count();

  // Phase 2: exact match — find buttons named exactly "Delete" (no trailing context)
  // Buttons like "Delete item" or "Delete account" should NOT match
  const exactDeleteButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete', exact: true });
  const exactCount = await exactDeleteButton.count();

  // Oracle: every delete button should have a descriptive name beyond bare "Delete"
  // (bare "Delete" buttons fail WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels and confuse screen readers)
  expect(exactCount, 'No button should be labelled bare "Delete" without context').toBe(0);

  // Phase 3: confirm all delete-related buttons have unique accessible names
  const names: string[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < looseCount; i++) {
    const name = await looseDeleteButtons.nth(i).getAttribute('aria-label')
      ?? await looseDeleteButtons.nth(i).textContent() ?? '';
    names.push(name.trim());
  }
  const uniqueNames = new Set(names);
  expect(uniqueNames.size, 'All delete buttons should have unique accessible names').toBe(looseCount);
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `getByRole('button', { name: /pattern/i })` for broad discovery followed by `{ name: 'exact', exact: true }` for precision creates a two-phase accessibility oracle that surfaces label-quality defects (generic labels, duplicate names) without brittle CSS selectors — the tradeoff is that `getByRole` resolves accessible names from `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, and visible text in that priority order, so a button with both a visible "Delete" text and an `aria-label="Delete row 3"` will NOT match `{ name: 'Delete', exact: true }` because the accessible name is the `aria-label` value; understand the accessible name computation algorithm before writing exact-match oracles.

**Pattern 472** — `test.step()` with `{ box: true }` for Collapsing Implementation Detail in Session Reports
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

async function loginAs(page: any, username: string) {
  await test.step(`Login as ${username}`, async () => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel(/username/i).fill(username);
    await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill('test-password');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /dashboard/i })).toBeVisible();
  }, { box: true }); // box: true collapses all child actions into a single step node
}

test('explore admin vs. regular user feature visibility', async ({ page }) => {
  await loginAs(page, 'admin@example.com');
  await test.step('Verify admin-only controls are visible', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: /user management/i })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /delete all/i })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await page.context().clearCookies();

  await loginAs(page, 'user@example.com');
  await test.step('Verify admin controls are hidden for regular user', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: /user management/i })).toBeHidden();
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /delete all/i })).toBeHidden();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step({ box: true })` (Playwright v1.39+) collapses the step and all its child actions into a single collapsible node in the HTML report, reducing report noise for infrastructure helpers (login, setup, navigation stubs) — the tradeoff is debuggability: a boxed step failure shows only the top-level step name in the report's error location, not the specific child action that failed; during active session exploration, omit `box: true` to get full action granularity, then re-enable it only in stabilised helper functions when the session transitions to a repeatable test suite.

### Community Gotchas

**G70: `page.addLocatorHandler()` handlers execute in an undefined order when multiple handlers match simultaneously — if two overlays become visible at the same time, only one handler fires per action cycle, leaving the second overlay in place and causing the next assertion to fail.**
Teams that registered separate handlers for a cookie banner and a "new feature tour" modal found that on first load both overlays appeared simultaneously; Playwright's internal scheduler fired only the cookie-banner handler before the next action's actionability check, leaving the tour modal visible. The test then failed at the next `click()` because the tour modal was still intercepting pointer events. The root cause is that Playwright processes one handler per action cycle — when the action retries after the first handler resolves, it re-checks and fires the second handler, but implementations that only have a single action after the handlers register never reach the second handler cycle.
Fix: Chain dismissal into a single handler that checks for all possible overlays, or ensure there is at least one asserting action after each expected overlay so that Playwright's retry loop has a chance to process subsequent handlers. Document in the charter which overlays are expected to co-appear and verify each is handled in the session setup.

---

**G71: `page.addInitScript()` does not re-execute on `page.reload()` by default when the script was registered after the initial `page.goto()` — scripts registered before any navigation execute on every navigation, but scripts registered after the page has already loaded only patched the current document and are lost on reload.**
A team exploring a feature that required refreshing the page mid-session (to test state persistence) found that their `addInitScript` Date patch was absent after `page.reload()`. The root cause is that `addInitScript` registers the script for future navigations — if called after `page.goto()` has already created the document, the current document receives the patch but the registration for future navigations still works correctly; however, if the script was called before `goto()` but the test subsequently called `page.goto()` a second time to a different URL, the script did execute again. The confusion arose because the team registered the script between two `goto()` calls, leading to inconsistent behaviour that appeared order-dependent.
Fix: Always call `page.addInitScript()` before the first `page.goto()` in the test. If the script must be added conditionally mid-session, use `page.evaluate()` for immediate one-shot injection and separately ensure the script is also registered via `addInitScript` at session start for navigation persistence.

---

**G72: `context.recordHar()` does not capture WebSocket frames — the HAR 1.2 specification does not include a standard format for WebSocket traffic, so Playwright's HAR files contain only HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 request-response pairs; WebSocket message streams are silently omitted.**
A team recording a session that relied heavily on WebSocket-driven updates found that their HAR file replayed all REST API calls correctly but the real-time data panel remained empty because the WebSocket events were never captured. The root cause is a limitation of the HAR format itself: the spec only models request/response pairs, not streaming protocols. The team initially assumed recording the context would capture all network activity, but `page.routeFromHAR()` replay also silently passes through WebSocket connections rather than replaying them, meaning the test appeared to run without error while missing the WS-driven DOM updates.
Fix: For WebSocket-dependent exploration, use `page.routeWebSocket()` to intercept and replay synthetic frames alongside HAR-based HTTP replay. Record WebSocket payloads separately using a `page.on('websocket', ...)` listener that writes frames to a JSON fixture, then inject them via `routeWebSocket` in replay mode. Do not assume HAR recording captures the full network surface of a modern SPA.

---

**G73: `expect.poll()` polling callbacks that throw an unhandled `Error` (as opposed to returning a non-matching value) terminate the poll immediately and fail the test — the retrying behaviour only applies to value mismatches, not to exceptions.**
Teams using `expect.poll()` to check an API endpoint found that when the API returned a 503 during a transient service restart, `request.get().json()` threw a JSON parse error (the 503 body was HTML, not JSON), which immediately failed the test rather than retrying after the configured interval. The team expected the poll to absorb transient errors the same way Playwright's web-first assertions absorb transient DOM states. The root cause is that `expect.poll()` wraps the callback in a try/catch that re-throws unhandled errors — only a return value that does not satisfy the matcher triggers a retry.
Fix: Wrap the callback body in a try/catch that returns a sentinel value on error: `async () => { try { const r = await request.get(url); return (await r.json()).status; } catch { return 'error'; } }`. This ensures transient HTTP or parse errors produce a non-matching return value that triggers a retry rather than an immediate test failure. Document the sentinel value in the poll's `message` option so failures clearly indicate whether the poll timed out waiting for the target state or never received a valid response.

---

**G74: `test.step({ box: true })` suppresses the inner error location in the HTML report — when a boxed step fails, the reported error points to the `test.step()` call site, not the specific assertion inside the step that failed, making it significantly harder to diagnose failures in CI without opening the full trace.**
Teams that aggressively boxed helper steps (login, navigation, data setup) in a large session suite found that CI failure emails showed only `Login as admin@example.com failed` with no indication of which of the eight actions inside the login step was the actual point of failure. The root cause is intentional: `{ box: true }` is designed for reporting clarity in stable tests, collapsing internal implementation details. However, during active exploratory refinement (when helpers are still changing), this hides the exact failure point and forces engineers to download and open the trace archive for every failure — a friction that slows triage cycles.
Fix: Use a feature flag or environment variable to control boxing: `{ box: process.env.CI === 'true' }` — this keeps reports clean in CI while retaining full action granularity in local exploration runs. Add a team convention: no step is boxed until it has been stable for at least five consecutive CI runs, documented by a comment in the step helper.

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 473** — Worker-Scoped Fixture for Shared Authentication State
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = { workerAuthToken: string };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  workerAuthToken: [async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
    // Authenticate once per worker, not per test — expensive SSO flows amortised
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill(`worker${workerInfo.workerIndex}@example.com`);
    await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill('session-password');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
    const token = await page.evaluate(() => localStorage.getItem('auth_token') ?? '');
    await context.close();
    await use(token);
    // teardown: nothing to clean up — token expires naturally
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

test('explore dashboard as pre-authenticated worker', async ({ page, workerAuthToken }) => {
  await page.addInitScript((token) => {
    localStorage.setItem('auth_token', token);
  }, workerAuthToken);
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /dashboard/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures run authentication exactly once per Playwright worker process and share the resulting token across every test in that worker, cutting overall session-setup time by 60–80% in large suites — the tradeoff is test isolation: if one test mutates or invalidates the token mid-session (e.g., by calling `/logout`), all subsequent tests in the same worker will silently receive a stale or missing token; guard against this by asserting the token is still valid in each test's `beforeEach` or by treating the worker fixture as strictly read-only and never navigating to `/logout` inside a worker-fixture-consuming test.

**Pattern 474** — Fixture Override to Pre-Navigate the `page` Fixture to `baseURL`
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  page: async ({ baseURL, page }, use) => {
    // Override the built-in page fixture to start every test at the app root.
    // Eliminates repetitive `await page.goto(baseURL)` in every exploratory test body.
    if (baseURL) {
      await page.goto(baseURL);
      await expect(page).toHaveURL(baseURL);
    }
    await use(page);
    // No teardown needed — base page fixture handles browser context cleanup.
  },
});

test('explore home page layout without explicit goto', async ({ page }) => {
  // page is already at baseURL — start exploring immediately
  await expect(page.getByRole('banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeVisible();
  const navLinks = page.getByRole('navigation').getByRole('link');
  await expect(navLinks).toHaveCount(await navLinks.count()); // charter: enumerate all nav entries
});
```
Tradeoff: Overriding the built-in `page` fixture to auto-navigate means every test in the suite unconditionally performs a `page.goto()` before the test body starts, which adds a measurable cold-start latency (~200–400 ms) to tests that themselves need to navigate to a different initial URL — if an exploratory session targets deep-link URLs or authentication flows that must start from a blank page, the auto-navigate override is a friction overhead; scope the override to a separate `export const appTest = test.extend(...)` so tests can opt in, rather than globally replacing the built-in `test`.

**Pattern 475** — `mergeTests()` to Compose Multi-Domain Fixture Sets for Cross-Cutting Exploration
```typescript
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as networkTest } from './fixtures/network-fixtures';
import { test as a11yTest } from './fixtures/a11y-fixtures';
import { test as perfTest } from './fixtures/perf-fixtures';

// Single composed test object exposes all fixture namespaces for cross-cutting sessions
export const test = mergeTests(networkTest, a11yTest, perfTest);

test('explore checkout flow: accessibility + performance + network in one session',
  async ({ page, routeInterceptor, axeScan, perfObserver }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    // Network dimension: intercept payment API and record request shape
    await routeInterceptor.captureRequests('/api/payment');
    // A11y dimension: scan the form before interaction
    const preFillResult = await axeScan.run(page);
    expect(preFillResult.violations).toHaveLength(0);
    // Perf dimension: measure LCP during user flow
    await perfObserver.startMark('checkout-fill');
    await page.getByLabel(/card number/i).fill('4242424242424242');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay now/i }).click();
    const metrics = await perfObserver.stopMark('checkout-fill');
    expect(metrics.lcp).toBeLessThan(2500);
    // Verify network capture
    const captured = await routeInterceptor.getRequests('/api/payment');
    expect(captured).toHaveLength(1);
  }
);
```
Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` lets a single exploratory session harvest coverage across network, accessibility, and performance dimensions simultaneously — the tradeoff is fixture-name collision: if `networkTest` and `a11yTest` both define a fixture named `page` override, `mergeTests` applies the last one registered, silently discarding the earlier override; audit merged fixture sets with `console.log(Object.keys(test.info().project.use))` and ensure each domain uses a namespaced fixture name (e.g., `routeInterceptor` not `helper`) to prevent silent merge shadowing.

---

**Pattern 476** — `route.fetch()` + `route.fulfill()` for Response Mutation During Exploration
```typescript
test('explore product page when inventory count is critically low', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/inventory/**', async (route) => {
    // Fetch the real response so the mutation is always based on live data shape
    const response = await route.fetch();
    const body = await response.json();
    // Mutate only the stock field; preserve all other real fields
    body.stockCount = 1;
    body.lowStockThreshold = 5;
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });
  });
  await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
  await expect(page.getByText(/only 1 left/i)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i })).toBeEnabled();
  // Charter: explore whether low-stock badge persists after cart add
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText(/only 0 left/i)).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `route.fetch()` before `route.fulfill()` fetches the real server response and lets you surgically mutate only the fields relevant to the exploratory charter, ensuring the rest of the payload stays realistic and boundary-condition bugs in unrelated fields remain detectable — the tradeoff is network dependency: `route.fetch()` makes an actual HTTP call to the server, so the test is not truly offline and will fail if the network or staging environment is unavailable; for fully offline exploration, fall back to a static fixture file and accept the risk that the fixture's shape drifts from the live API over time.

---

**Pattern 477** — `route.fallback()` for Layered Request-Transformation Middleware
```typescript
test('explore API behaviour when auth header is downgraded mid-session', async ({ page }) => {
  // Handler 1 (last registered, first executed): log every request URL to the session journal
  await page.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
    console.log(`[journal] ${route.request().method()} ${route.request().url()}`);
    await route.fallback(); // pass to next handler without modifying request
  });

  // Handler 2: downgrade the Authorization header to a read-only token
  await page.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
    await route.fallback({
      headers: {
        ...route.request().headers(),
        Authorization: 'Bearer readonly-token-for-exploration',
      },
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // Any write operation should now return 403 due to read-only token
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /delete report/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText(/you do not have permission/i)).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.fallback()` with header overrides allows stacking independent route concerns (logging, auth manipulation, latency injection) as separate handlers in registration order, mirroring a middleware pipeline — the tradeoff is execution order confusion: handlers execute in reverse registration order (last registered first), which is the opposite of most middleware mental models; always add a comment block at the top of a multi-handler route setup explicitly documenting the execution order, or use a single handler with clearly sequenced inline logic if the team finds the reverse-order semantics error-prone.

---

**Pattern 478** — `route.abort()` with Selective Error Code Injection for Resilience Exploration
```typescript
test('explore how UI handles simultaneous asset and API failures', async ({ page }) => {
  const failedRequests: string[] = [];

  // Abort image requests to simulate CDN outage
  await page.route('**/*.{png,jpg,jpeg,webp,svg}', async (route) => {
    failedRequests.push(route.request().url());
    await route.abort('failed'); // emulates network-level failure, not HTTP 404
  });

  // Abort a specific API endpoint to simulate backend degradation
  await page.route('**/api/recommendations', async (route) => {
    await route.abort('timedout');
  });

  await page.goto('/home');

  // Charter: verify the app degrades gracefully without crashing
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeVisible(); // no global error banner
  await expect(page.getByText(/recommendations/i)).not.toBeVisible(); // section removed
  // Verify image placeholders or alt text rendered instead of broken images
  const images = page.getByRole('img');
  const count = await images.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const img = images.nth(i);
    await expect(img).toHaveAttribute('alt');
  }
  console.log(`[session] ${failedRequests.length} asset requests aborted`);
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.abort('timedout')` versus `route.abort('failed')` produces meaningfully different browser behaviour — a `timedout` abort leaves the browser waiting until the network timeout elapses (up to 30 s per request) before the abort resolves, which makes the session feel realistic but dramatically extends test execution time; use `route.abort('failed')` for fast failure simulation during exploration and only switch to `timedout` when specifically chartering timeout-handling UI paths.

---

**Pattern 479** — Automatic Fixture (`{ auto: true }`) for Passive Console-Error Oracle
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ consoleErrors: string[] }>({
  consoleErrors: [async ({ page }, use) => {
    const errors: string[] = [];
    // Attach listener before test body — fires automatically without explicit fixture use
    page.on('console', (msg) => {
      if (msg.type() === 'error') errors.push(msg.text());
    });
    page.on('pageerror', (err) => errors.push(`[pageerror] ${err.message}`));
    await use(errors);
    // Post-test assertion: fail if any console errors were logged during the session
    if (errors.length > 0) {
      throw new Error(`Session produced ${errors.length} console error(s):\n${errors.join('\n')}`);
    }
  }, { auto: true }],  // auto: true means every test gets this oracle for free
});

test('explore multi-step wizard without explicitly requesting consoleErrors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/wizard/step-1');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /next/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /next/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText(/success/i)).toBeVisible();
  // consoleErrors fixture runs automatically — no explicit assertion needed here
});
```
Tradeoff: Marking the console-error oracle fixture as `{ auto: true }` means it passively monitors every test in the suite without any opt-in boilerplate, acting as a global regression guard for unhandled JS exceptions and network errors logged to the console — the tradeoff is signal-to-noise ratio: third-party scripts, browser extensions injected into the test context, and deliberately logged error messages (e.g., "No stored session found — prompting login") will all trigger false positives; maintain an explicit allowlist of known-benign error patterns using a regex filter inside the `page.on('console')` handler to prevent the oracle from becoming a source of flakiness.

---

**Pattern 480** — `test.extend()` with Dependency-Ordered Teardown for Multi-Resource Sessions
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type SessionFixtures = {
  dbSnapshot: string;
  sessionRecorder: { stop: () => Promise<void>; path: string };
};

export const test = base.extend<SessionFixtures>({
  dbSnapshot: async ({}, use) => {
    // Setup: create DB snapshot so the session can freely mutate data
    const snapshotId = await createDatabaseSnapshot();
    await use(snapshotId);
    // Teardown: restore snapshot — runs AFTER sessionRecorder teardown (reverse dep order)
    await restoreDatabaseSnapshot(snapshotId);
  },
  sessionRecorder: async ({ page, dbSnapshot }, use) => {
    // Depends on dbSnapshot — so it tears down BEFORE dbSnapshot restores DB
    const recorder = await startSessionRecording(page, { snapshotId: dbSnapshot });
    await use(recorder);
    // Teardown: stop recording and save artefact
    await recorder.stop();
    console.log(`[session] Recording saved to ${recorder.path}`);
  },
});

test('explore bulk data import with full session recording', async ({ page, sessionRecorder }) => {
  await page.goto('/import');
  await page.setInputFiles('input[type="file"]', 'fixtures/large-dataset.csv');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /import/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText(/import complete/i)).toBeVisible({ timeout: 30_000 });
  console.log(`[session] Artefact will be at: ${sessionRecorder.path}`);
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright's fixture teardown respects the dependency graph — fixtures with dependents tear down first, then their dependencies, guaranteeing that `sessionRecorder` stops before `dbSnapshot` restores the database (preventing the recording from capturing a partially restored state) — the tradeoff is cognitive overhead: the teardown order is implicit and determined by the dependency graph, not by the order of fixture declarations in the `test.extend()` call; teams that are unaware of this behaviour sometimes place assertions or cleanup logic in the wrong fixture and observe non-deterministic teardown races; document the intended teardown order explicitly in a comment block inside each fixture's `use()` call.

**Pattern 481** — `page.route()` with Predicate Function for Fine-Grained Charter-Driven Interception
```typescript
test('explore checkout flow — intercept only POST requests to payment API', async ({ page }) => {
  const capturedPaymentBodies: unknown[] = [];

  await page.route(
    // Predicate function: more precise than glob — matches method AND path AND content-type
    (url) => url.pathname.startsWith('/api/payment') && url.hostname === new URL(page.url()).hostname,
    async (route) => {
      const request = route.request();
      if (request.method() === 'POST') {
        // Capture the raw POST body for charter analysis before forwarding
        const postData = request.postDataJSON();
        capturedPaymentBodies.push(postData);
        // Forward the real request unmodified — we are observing, not mocking
        await route.continue();
      } else {
        // GET requests to /api/payment (status polling) pass through untouched
        await route.continue();
      }
    }
  );

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel(/card number/i).fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByLabel(/expiry/i).fill('12/26');
  await page.getByLabel(/cvv/i).fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText(/payment confirmed/i)).toBeVisible();

  expect(capturedPaymentBodies).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(capturedPaymentBodies[0]).toMatchObject({ currency: expect.any(String) });
});
```
Tradeoff: Using a URL predicate function instead of a glob string gives precise method-and-hostname filtering that prevents the route handler from accidentally intercepting requests from iframes, third-party analytics, or payment SDKs that share a URL path prefix — the tradeoff is that predicate functions are evaluated synchronously for every network request in the page, so a complex or slow predicate will add measurable latency to the overall request processing pipeline; keep predicates simple and rely on `url.pathname.startsWith()` rather than constructing new `URL` objects inside the predicate to minimise per-request overhead.

---

**Pattern 482** — `route.continue()` with Header Injection for Exploration Under Feature Flags
```typescript
test('explore beta checkout UI gated behind X-Feature-Flag header', async ({ page }) => {
  // Inject the feature-flag header into every request so the server enables the beta UI
  await page.route('**/*', async (route) => {
    await route.continue({
      headers: {
        ...route.request().headers(),
        'X-Feature-Flag': 'checkout-v2-beta',
        'X-Session-Charter': 'beta-checkout-exploration-2026-05-14',
      },
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Charter: verify beta UI elements are present and old UI elements are absent
  await expect(page.getByTestId('checkout-v2-header')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('checkout-v1-header')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Explore the full happy path under the beta flag
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /proceed to payment/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /payment details/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Injecting feature-flag headers via `route.continue()` allows exploratory sessions to activate server-side feature gates without modifying environment variables, browser cookies, or localStorage — the coverage is broad because the header is applied to every request including XHR and `fetch()` calls made by the app — the tradeoff is that `route.continue()` with `{ headers }` replaces the entire headers object with a merged copy, and if the app relies on cookie-derived headers that are normally added by the browser automatically (such as `Cookie` itself, which is a forbidden header for `route.continue()`), those headers may be inadvertently stripped; always spread `...route.request().headers()` as the base before adding custom headers.

**Pattern 483** — Fixture-Backed Session Charter with Structured Teardown Logging
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type CharterFixtures = {
  charter: {
    area: string;
    mission: string;
    risks: string[];
    log: (finding: string) => void;
    findings: string[];
  };
};

export const test = base.extend<CharterFixtures>({
  charter: async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    const findings: string[] = [];
    const charterMeta = {
      area: testInfo.title.split(':')[0]?.trim() ?? 'unspecified',
      mission: testInfo.title,
      risks: [] as string[],
      log: (finding: string) => findings.push(`[${new Date().toISOString()}] ${finding}`),
      findings,
    };
    await use(charterMeta);
    // Teardown: attach findings to the Playwright HTML report as a test attachment
    if (findings.length > 0) {
      await testInfo.attach('session-findings', {
        body: findings.join('\n'),
        contentType: 'text/plain',
      });
    }
  },
});

test('checkout: explore coupon code validation edge cases', async ({ page, charter }) => {
  charter.risks.push('coupon codes may accept expired codes if client-side only');
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByPlaceholder(/coupon code/i).fill('EXPIRED2023');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /apply/i }).click();
  const errorMsg = page.getByRole('alert');
  if (await errorMsg.isVisible()) {
    charter.log(`PASS: Expired coupon rejected — "${await errorMsg.textContent()}"`);
  } else {
    charter.log(`RISK: Expired coupon accepted — possible client-side bypass`);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: A fixture-backed charter object gives each exploratory test a structured way to record in-session findings that are automatically attached to the Playwright HTML report as named attachments, making session artefacts visible in CI without requiring a separate reporting tool — the tradeoff is attachment bloat: if every test in a large suite uses the charter fixture and logs verbose findings, the HTML report's attachment storage can grow significantly; apply the attachment only when `findings.length > 0` (already shown above) and enforce a maximum finding length of ~500 characters per entry via a helper to keep report sizes manageable.

---

**Pattern 484** — `page.route()` + `route.fulfill()` with Static Fixture for Offline Exploration
```typescript
import path from 'path';
import fs from 'fs/promises';

test('explore product listing offline using static JSON fixture', async ({ page }) => {
  const fixtureDir = path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures');

  // Serve static JSON fixture in place of the real API — enables offline/CI exploration
  await page.route('**/api/products*', async (route) => {
    const fixture = await fs.readFile(path.join(fixtureDir, 'products.json'), 'utf-8');
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: fixture,
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/products');
  // Charter: verify rendering with fixture's known edge cases (product with no image, zero price)
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card')).toHaveCount(25); // fixture has exactly 25 items
  const zeroPriceCard = page.getByTestId('product-card').filter({ hasText: '$0.00' });
  await expect(zeroPriceCard).toBeVisible();
  const noImageCard = page.getByTestId('product-card').filter({ hasText: 'No image available' });
  await expect(noImageCard).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Static fixture-backed `route.fulfill()` makes exploratory tests fully deterministic and runnable offline, with the fixture acting as a controlled boundary-condition generator that surfaces edge-case rendering bugs that live data rarely produces — the tradeoff is fixture drift: as the real API schema evolves, the static fixture silently diverges and the tests continue to pass against an unrealistic payload shape; integrate a nightly JSON schema validation job that fetches the live API and diffs it against each fixture's shape using `ajv` or `zod` to detect drift before it masks real regressions.

---

**Pattern 485** — `workerInfo.workerIndex` for Parallelism-Safe Unique Data Generation
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{}, { uniqueUser: { email: string; username: string } }>({
  uniqueUser: [async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
    // Each parallel worker gets a globally unique user identity — prevents test-data collisions
    const idx = workerInfo.workerIndex;
    const timestamp = Date.now();
    const user = {
      email: `explorer-w${idx}-${timestamp}@test.example.com`,
      username: `explorer_w${idx}_${timestamp}`,
    };
    await use(user);
    // Teardown: clean up the created user via API
    await fetch(`${process.env.BASE_URL}/api/test/cleanup-user`, {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({ email: user.email }),
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CLEANUP_TOKEN}` },
    });
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

test('explore user registration flow with unique per-worker identity', async ({ page, uniqueUser }) => {
  await page.goto('/register');
  await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill(uniqueUser.email);
  await page.getByLabel(/username/i).fill(uniqueUser.username);
  await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill('Expl0re!2026');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /create account/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText(/welcome/i)).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Combining `workerInfo.workerIndex` with a timestamp suffix guarantees each parallel worker operates on a unique user identity, eliminating the most common source of parallel-session data collision (duplicate email conflicts during registration) without requiring a central sequence generator or database lock — the tradeoff is that the cleanup `fetch()` in teardown runs outside any Playwright retry or error-handling context, so if it fails (e.g., due to a staging environment restart) the orphaned test users accumulate silently; supplement the per-test cleanup with a periodic full-sweep cleanup job that deletes all `explorer-w*@test.example.com` users older than 24 hours.

---

**Pattern 486** — `test.extend()` Automatic Fixture for Per-Session Performance Budget Assertion
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ perfBudget: void }>({
  perfBudget: [async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Inject a PerformanceObserver before navigation to capture Web Vitals passively
    await page.addInitScript(() => {
      window.__perfEntries = [];
      const observer = new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
        for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
          (window as { __perfEntries?: PerformanceEntry[] }).__perfEntries?.push(entry);
        }
      });
      observer.observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });
      observer.observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });
    });
    await use();
    // After each test: extract and assert Web Vitals budgets
    const entries = await page.evaluate(() => (window as { __perfEntries?: { entryType: string; startTime?: number; value?: number }[] }).__perfEntries ?? []);
    const lcpEntries = entries.filter(e => e.entryType === 'largest-contentful-paint');
    const clsEntries  = entries.filter(e => e.entryType === 'layout-shift');
    const lcp = lcpEntries.at(-1)?.startTime ?? 0;
    const cls = clsEntries.reduce((sum, e) => sum + (e.value ?? 0), 0);
    if (lcp > 2500) console.warn(`[perf] LCP ${lcp}ms exceeds 2500ms budget`);
    if (cls  > 0.1)  console.warn(`[perf] CLS ${cls.toFixed(3)} exceeds 0.1 budget`);
  }, { auto: true }],
});

test('explore product detail page Web Vitals during image-heavy load', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products/featured');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toBeVisible();
  // perfBudget fixture runs automatically — LCP and CLS emitted to console if exceeded
});
```
Tradeoff: An automatic performance-budget fixture that injects a `PerformanceObserver` via `addInitScript` gives every exploratory test passive Web Vitals monitoring without any per-test boilerplate, turning routine exploration sessions into a combined functional and performance audit — the tradeoff is environment noise: synthetic CI runners have lower CPU/memory resources than real user devices, so LCP values measured in CI can be 3–5× higher than real-user median values; treat the CI budget as an absolute ceiling (2500 ms) for obviously broken regressions rather than a precise UX proxy, and separately run Lighthouse or WebPageTest against staging for accurate real-user projections.

---

**Pattern 487** — `context.storageState()` Snapshot/Restore for Stateful Exploration Branching
```typescript
test.describe('explore checkout: branch from post-login state', () => {
  let postLoginState: string; // path to the storage state snapshot

  test.beforeAll(async ({ browser }) => {
    // Create a single logged-in state snapshot — all branch tests restore from this point
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill('explorer@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill('test-password');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /dashboard/i })).toBeVisible();
    postLoginState = `./tmp/storage-${Date.now()}.json`;
    await context.storageState({ path: postLoginState });
    await context.close();
  });

  test('branch A: explore checkout with saved card', async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: postLoginState });
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await expect(page.getByText(/use saved card/i)).toBeVisible();
    await context.close();
  });

  test('branch B: explore checkout with guest override after login', async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: postLoginState });
    const page = await context.newPage();
    // Start from same auth state but explore the "checkout as guest" flow
    await page.goto('/checkout?mode=guest');
    await expect(page.getByText(/checking out as guest/i)).toBeVisible();
    await context.close();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Capturing a `storageState` snapshot after login and restoring it in multiple parallel branch tests allows a session to explore multiple post-authentication paths without repeating the login flow, cutting total session setup time and enabling true branching exploration from a known-good state — the tradeoff is that `storageState` captures cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage at a single point in time; if the server issues a new CSRF token or short-lived JWT on each login, restoring a stale snapshot may cause 403 errors on the first authenticated API call; validate the snapshot's token expiry before restoring it, or use a short-lived snapshot with a `beforeEach` that refreshes the token via a lightweight API call rather than a full UI login.

### Community Gotchas

**G75: Worker-scoped fixtures that call `browser.newContext()` internally create a context that is outside Playwright's test-tracking scope — any failures or console errors from that context are not reported in the HTML test report and do not appear in the trace archive, creating a silent blind spot during session setup.**
Why this matters: Teams using worker-scoped fixtures for expensive authentication (spinning up a full browser context to log in and extract a token) found that when the login page intermittently showed a CAPTCHA or returned a 429 rate-limit response, the fixture threw an uncaught error that appeared only as a generic "Worker setup failed" message in the console, with no trace, no screenshot, and no HTML report entry showing which action failed. The root cause is that Playwright's tracing and reporting infrastructure is bound to test-scoped contexts created by the framework; contexts created manually inside `browser.newContext()` within a worker fixture are untracked. The fixture teardown also silently swallowed the inner context's `pageerror` events.
Fix: Inside worker-scoped fixture setup code that calls `browser.newContext()`, manually attach `page.on('console', ...)` and `page.on('pageerror', ...)` listeners that write to a log file (e.g., `fs.appendFileSync('worker-fixture-errors.log', ...)`). Wrap the setup in a try/catch that rethrows with a descriptive message including the URL and action that failed. In the project's `globalSetup` file, clean the log file before each run and check for entries in `globalTeardown` to surface worker fixture errors in the final CI summary.

---

**G76: `route.continue()` with a `headers` override does NOT merge with the browser's automatically computed headers — it replaces the entire user-provided headers object, meaning any header you specify in the override object fully replaces the headers that Playwright would have forwarded, potentially stripping app-specific defaults set by request interceptors.**
Why this matters: A team injecting a `X-Tenant-Id` header via `route.continue({ headers: { 'X-Tenant-Id': 'acme' } })` found that their app's outgoing `axios` interceptor, which normally added an `X-Request-Id` UUID to every request, stopped working. The root cause is that `route.continue({ headers })` requires the caller to supply the complete final headers map — if you omit any header that was in `route.request().headers()`, that header is dropped. The team only passed `{ 'X-Tenant-Id': 'acme' }` without spreading the existing headers, effectively stripping `X-Request-Id`, `Accept`, `Content-Type`, and all other app-set headers. The missing `Content-Type` caused a 415 Unsupported Media Type on POST requests, which was mistakenly attributed to a backend deployment issue.
Fix: Always use the spread pattern: `await route.continue({ headers: { ...route.request().headers(), 'X-Tenant-Id': 'acme' } })`. Write a lint rule or code review checklist item that flags any `route.continue({ headers: {` call that does not begin with a spread of `route.request().headers()`.

---

**G77: `test.extend()` with `{ auto: true }` fixtures that perform assertions in teardown (after `await use()`) do not count toward the test's pass/fail result in the HTML report — the test is marked as passed even if the auto-fixture teardown throws; the error appears only in the worker process stderr log, not in the per-test report row.**
Why this matters: Teams using automatic fixtures to enforce post-session invariants (e.g., asserting no console errors were logged, or that no test-data orphans were left in the database) were surprised to find that the HTML report showed "passed" for tests where the teardown assertion clearly failed with a thrown error. The root cause is a known Playwright behaviour: test result status is determined during the test body execution phase; teardown errors in `afterEach`-equivalent fixture teardown are reported as a separate "teardown" error category in the worker log but do not flip the test's primary status to "failed" in all reporter implementations. The Playwright HTML reporter does surface these errors, but CI integrations that parse the JUnit XML output may ignore teardown-phase failures.
Fix: Avoid placing hard assertions (`expect(...)`) in fixture teardown. Instead, set a flag in the fixture body and check it in an explicit `afterEach` hook, or attach findings as a named attachment and fail in the test body. If teardown assertions are unavoidable, add a `globalTeardown` script that parses the `test-results.json` for any result with `{ status: 'passed', errors: [...] }` (errors in the teardown of an otherwise-passing test) and exits non-zero to block CI merges.

---

**G78: `page.route()` handlers registered with a glob pattern are not automatically unregistered when a `test.step()` scope exits — if an exploratory test registers a route inside a `test.step()` and then navigates to a different URL outside the step, the handler continues to intercept matching requests for the rest of the test, potentially corrupting subsequent session branches that expect unmodified network behaviour.**
Why this matters: A team conducting multi-branch exploration (chartering both the happy path and the error path in the same test using `test.step()`) registered a `route.fulfill()` mock inside the error-path step and then attempted the happy path in the next step without explicitly unregistering the route. The happy path appeared to succeed visually, but the captured network log showed that the API was still being mocked, meaning the "happy path" was actually testing the mocked response rather than the real API. The root cause is that `page.route()` has page-level lifetime, not step-level lifetime — `test.step()` provides no automatic resource cleanup scope.
Fix: Always pair `page.route()` registration with an explicit `page.unroute()` call at the end of the step or branch: `await page.unroute('**/api/payment')`. For exploratory tests that deliberately branch between mocked and unmocked states, extract each branch into its own `test()` function with separate `page` fixture instances, or use `page.unrouteAll({ behavior: 'ignoreErrors' })` (Playwright v1.41+) at the start of each step to reset the route table to a clean slate.

---

**G79: `mergeTests()` silently drops fixture override chains when both merged test objects override the same built-in fixture — the last merged test's override wins, and earlier overrides are completely discarded without any warning, so combined fixture sets can behave differently from their individual components.**
Why this matters: A team created `networkTest` (which overrides `page` to inject a `X-Session-Id` header via `route.continue()`) and `a11yTest` (which overrides `page` to call `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` for accessibility audit headers). When they ran `mergeTests(networkTest, a11yTest)`, only the `a11yTest` page override took effect — the `X-Session-Id` header injection was silently dropped because both overrides targeted the same `page` fixture and `mergeTests` applies overrides in argument order, with later arguments winning. The root cause is that Playwright's `mergeTests` treats fixture overrides as a flat map keyed on fixture name; there is no override composition or stacking for the same fixture name.
Fix: Refactor conflicting `page` overrides into a single composed override that applies both modifications sequentially, or use distinctly named fixtures (`sessionPage` and `a11yPage`) that each extend `page` independently without overriding it. Before calling `mergeTests`, audit all fixture names in each merged set using `Object.keys(test.info)` patterns and document which set is authoritative for each overlapping name.
